“Alright.”

A few seconds passed. Then she asked,

“Are you feeling better?”

He looked out of the window. The sky above Munich had begun turning dark.

“Yes.”

“Really?”

“Really.”

“Good.”

Her voice softened.

“Then I did a good job.”

Declan smiled.

“An excellent job.”

She giggled. He was beginning to understand something about her.

CC wasn’t expressive with strangers. She didn’t seem to enjoy demanding attention, nor did she make a habit of telling people how she felt.

But when she became comfortable, she had this little tendency to seek reassurance. Not dramatically.

Just a quiet question here and there, as if she wanted to know that her presence was welcome. He wanted to give her that reassurance.

“CC.”

“Hm?”

“Thank you for calling.”

She went quiet. Then smiled.

“You’re welcome.”

He was back at the lake by six, in a better mood than the one he had left in.

His mother was in the dining room, speaking with the household staff about Saturday’s dinner arrangements. She looked up when he entered.

“You’re home early.”

“Some meetings were moved.”

“Good. You should have dinner with us.”

Declan removed his coat.

“Father?”

“In his study.”

“I’ll join you in a moment.”

His mother looked at him. Then smiled.

“You look better.”

Declan held her gaze.

“Better than what?”

“Better than this morning.”

He laughed.

“Was I that unpleasant?”

“Not unpleasant. Just rather quiet.”

He gave her a smile.

“Long day.”

She nodded.

“Well, don’t bring your work to the dinner table.”

“I’ll try.”

His mother returned to arranging the flowers. Then, almost casually, she said,

“Charlotte will be joining us on Saturday. I hope you’ve remembered.”

Declan loosened his cufflinks.

“You’ve mentioned it. Once or twice.”

“Good. She’s a lovely girl.”

“I’m sure.”

His mother glanced at him.

“You don’t sound very interested.”

“Mother, I haven’t met her.”

“That’s precisely why I’m arranging it.”

Declan laughed.

“Let’s have dinner first.”

His mother smiled, satisfied enough with that answer. He headed upstairs.

Upstairs, twenty minutes later, Declan had just finished changing when another message came in.

CC: Are you home?

Declan: Yes.

CC: Did you have dinner?

He smiled.

Declan: I’m about to.

CC: Good boy.

Declan stopped. Then laughed. He read the message again.

Declan: Good boy?

CC: Yes :)

Declan: Interesting.

CC: What?

Declan: Nothing. I rather like that.

CC sent a laughing sticker. He shook his head, smiling.

Declan: What are you doing?

CC: Watching a drama.

Declan: Which one?

She told him the title. Declan searched his memory.

He had heard of it, though he hadn’t watched it.

Declan: Is it good?

CC: Very! But I’m only on episode three.

Declan: Then I won’t disturb you.

CC: You can disturb me a little.

Declan smiled. He sat on the edge of his bed.

Declan: A little?

CC: Yes. I’m generous.

He laughed.

Declan: I see where you get it from.

CC: From you, obviously.

He shook his head. Then typed:

Declan: I have dinner with my family on Saturday.

CC: Oh! Is it a special occasion?

Declan: Not particularly. My mother is hosting.

CC: That’s nice. Do you see them often?

Declan: Whenever I’m in Munich.

CC: You must be close to them.

He considered the question.

Declan: Yes. We are.

CC: That’s good.

A moment later, she sent another message.

CC: I hope you have a nice dinner!

Declan studied the screen. He almost told her about Charlotte. About the introduction his mother was arranging.

About the fact that he would probably be spending part of Saturday evening having a polite conversation with a woman he had never met. But he decided against it.

There was no reason to involve CC in something that hadn’t even happened.

And, more importantly, he hadn’t quite figured out what he wanted to call whatever was developing between them. So he replied.

Declan: Thank you, sweetheart.

CC: Goodnight, Declan ♡

Declan: Goodnight, CC.

He placed his phone beside him. Then he laughed to himself.

He had been irritated by people, delayed by meetings, and thoroughly unimpressed by the competence of several senior executives.

Yet the only person who had managed to make him smile without even trying was a girl thousands of kilometres away, who thought sending him a photograph of strawberries was an appropriate solution to a bad day. It solved nothing. He found he didn’t mind.

He was usually a man who preferred fixing things himself.

But he was beginning to enjoy having someone who occasionally made him forget that something needed fixing in the first place.

chapters.title: A Picture Worth a Thousand Assumptions
chapters.desc: Dinner with the Weiss family ends with a handshake on the pavement and a photographer across the street. By Sunday, Bangkok is reading about Declan and Charlotte, and then about Declan and CC.
chapters.epigraph: “Don’t let strangers decide what you should think about me.”
chapters.content:
On Thursday, Declan Lincoln began the day the way he preferred to begin every day: by deciding how it would proceed before anyone else could.

“Move the Singapore call to eleven. I want the revised figures before then, not another presentation explaining why they aren’t ready.”

Alexander Weber made a note on his tablet. “Understood.”

“And tell New York I’ll review the acquisition proposal this afternoon. If they have another revision, they can send it before four.”

“Yes, sir.”

Declan glanced at his phone. A notification sat at the top of his screen.

CC: Good morning in Munich. Did you sleep properly?

The faintest change crossed his expression. Alexander, who had spent enough years working beside him to recognise the difference between a genuine improvement in mood and a merely less unpleasant one, politely looked down at his tablet. Declan picked up his phone.

Declan: Good morning, sweetheart.

Declan: I slept well. Did you?

The reply came a few minutes later.

CC: I did.

CC: But I woke up at eleven.

Declan: That isn’t late.

CC: My call was at ten. P’Nicha looked at me like I had personally ruined her morning.

He smiled.

Declan: Did you?

CC: No. I was very innocent.

Declan: I’m sure.

CC: You don’t believe me?

Declan: I believe you were very convincing.

A small pause.

CC: That’s different.

Declan: Is it?

CC: Yes.

Declan: I’ll remember that the next time you tell me something.

CC sent him a photograph before he could respond. It was breakfast at two in the afternoon, eaten in the back of a car: toast, scrambled eggs and sliced strawberries, with a coffee balanced on her knee. The bracelet was on her wrist, a thin bright line at the edge of the frame.

CC: See? I’m eating properly.

Declan studied the photograph.

Declan: Good.

Declan: Though I suspect someone reminded you.

CC: Maybe.

Declan: P’Nicha?

CC: Maybe.

Declan: Then I should thank her.

CC: Don’t. She’ll become even more annoying.

His smile deepened.

Declan: I’ll keep that in mind.

He set the phone down, but not before sending one more message.

Declan: Enjoy your breakfast at two in the afternoon, sweetheart. The bracelet suits it.

Across the office, Alexander waited until Declan returned his attention to the documents.

“Your mother called earlier,” he said.

Declan turned a page. “What does she want?”

“She asked whether you had confirmed Saturday evening.”

“I haven’t.”

“She asked me to remind you that dinner is at seven.”

Declan’s eyes remained on the document.

“Then remind her that I can read a calendar.”

Alexander gave a discreet nod. A moment later, Declan’s phone lit up again. He glanced at it.

CC: You too. Don’t skip lunch.

He reread the message for a second longer than necessary. Then he put the phone away.

“Alexander.”

“Yes, sir?”

“Have the car ready for the office at six.”

“Certainly.”

“And don’t schedule anything after that.”

Alexander looked at the calendar. “You have a call with the New York team at six-thirty.”

“Move it.”

“To when?”

“Monday.”

Alexander nodded, though he didn’t ask why. He had already learned that some things weren’t worth asking.

On Friday, the call from his mother came while Declan was reviewing a report in his private office. He answered without looking at the screen.

“Mother.”

“Declan, darling. Are you busy?”

“Yes.”

“Then I’ll be quick.”

He leaned back slightly. “That would be appreciated.”

His mother ignored the remark.

“I spoke with Charlotte’s mother this morning. They’re looking forward to tomorrow.”

“I see.”

“She’ll be arriving with her parents. Her father has been wanting to speak with you about the foundation’s new European initiative.”

“Then he can speak with me about it.”

“And Charlotte?”

Declan looked through the glass wall of his office. Beyond it, the executive floor moved with its usual quiet efficiency.

“What about her?”

His mother sighed.

“You really do make everything difficult.”

“I haven’t done anything yet.”

“Exactly. That’s the problem.”

He almost smiled.

His mother continued, “Charlotte is a lovely girl. Intelligent, well-mannered, and very accomplished. She has spent several years in London, and she understands the kind of life you lead.”

“I’m sure she does.”

“I would like you to make an effort.”

“I’ll be there.”

“Declan.”

“I said I’ll be there, Mother.”

There was a brief silence. Then her voice softened.

“I’m not asking you to marry her tomorrow. I only want you to meet someone properly. You’re thirty-one. You can’t spend your entire life working.”

“It’s a very efficient way to spend it.”

“Not funny.”

“I wasn’t trying to be.”

His mother sighed again, but this time there was affection beneath it.

“Seven o’clock. Don’t be late.”

“I won’t.”

“And please wear something other than your usual black suit.”

Declan glanced at the dark suit hanging on the stand near his wardrobe.

“I’ll consider it.”

“That’s what you said last time.”

“Then you already know what to expect.”

She made a small sound of exasperation before ending the call. Declan placed his phone on the desk. For several seconds, he returned to the report. Then he picked up his personal phone.

Declan: What are you doing, sweetheart?

CC answered almost immediately.

CC: Rehearsal.

CC: And you?

Declan: Working.

CC: Again?

Declan: It’s a habit.

CC: A bad one.

Declan: You’re becoming rather critical of me.

CC: You make it very easy.

He smiled to himself.

Declan: Are you free tomorrow evening?

There was a short pause before her reply appeared.

CC: I think so. Why?

He checked the message. He could have told her about the dinner. He could have explained that his mother had arranged an introduction, that Charlotte Weiss would be there, that he had no intention of allowing his family to make decisions on his behalf.

But he hadn’t yet decided how much importance to give the evening.

It was a family dinner. A meeting he had agreed to attend out of courtesy. Nothing more.

And he had no reason to make it sound like something it wasn’t.

Declan: Family dinner.

CC: Ah.

CC: Have fun.

Declan: That’s a rather unenthusiastic response.

CC: Should I say something else?

Declan: You could wish me a pleasant evening.

CC: I hope you have a very pleasant evening, Mr. Lincoln.

He laughed.

Declan: Much better.

CC: You’re welcome.

He considered asking whether she wanted to call later. Instead, he typed:

Declan: Are you working late?

CC: Not too late. Why?

Declan: I might call you.

CC: You can.

Declan: Even if you’re busy?

CC: I’ll tell you if I am.

Declan: Good girl.

The typing indicator appeared, disappeared, and appeared again.

CC: Don’t say that when I’m trying to concentrate.

His face changed, amusement settling into something warmer.

Declan: Then concentrate, sweetheart.

CC: I’m trying.

He put the phone away with a smile that remained for the rest of the afternoon.

On Saturday, dinner was at one of the private dining rooms his family had used for years, on a quiet street in Lehel.

It was discreet, elegant, and accustomed to hosting people who preferred their personal affairs kept out of the newspapers. Declan arrived a few minutes before seven.

He wore a charcoal suit with a white shirt, no tie. His hair was neatly styled, his watch understated despite its value. He looked precisely as he always did: composed, impeccably dressed, and entirely comfortable in the kind of room where everyone knew who he was. His mother was already waiting.

“You’re early,” she said, looking pleased.

“I’m on time.”

“That’s early for you.”

He kissed her cheek before greeting his father. Richard Lincoln stood near the window, speaking with Charlotte’s father. Both men turned when Declan approached.

“Declan. Good timing,” Richard said.

“Father.”

Introductions followed. Charlotte Weiss was standing beside her mother.

She was elegant in a pale champagne dress, her dark blonde hair arranged in soft waves. Her appearance was polished without seeming excessive. She had the easy confidence of someone accustomed to formal occasions and the social circles that came with them.

“Mr. Lincoln,” she said with a pleasant smile.

“Charlotte.”

“It’s lovely to finally meet you. I’ve heard quite a bit about you.”

“I hope none of it was too exaggerated.”

She laughed.

“Your mother was very complimentary.”

“Then I’m afraid she wasn’t being objective.”

His mother gave him a look. Charlotte smiled again. She seemed to understand his dry humour and didn’t appear offended by it. The conversation began easily enough.

Her father spoke about the European foundation initiative. Richard discussed a recent board decision. Charlotte mentioned her work in London, her time at Oxford, and the projects she had been involved in since returning to Germany. She was intelligent. Well-spoken. Pleasant company. There was nothing wrong with her.

That, Declan thought, was precisely the problem with these arrangements. Everyone seemed to believe that a list of admirable qualities was enough to establish compatibility.

His mother watched them from across the table with unmistakable satisfaction. At one point, Charlotte turned towards him.

“Do you spend much time in London?”

“Not as much as I used to.”

“That’s a shame. It’s a wonderful city.”

“It is.”

“I suppose your work keeps you between Munich and New York most of the time?”

“Primarily.”

“And Asia?”

“Occasionally. I was in Bangkok recently.”

“Bangkok? For business?” Charlotte asked.

“Yes.”

“What a coincidence. I have a friend who works in the entertainment industry there.”

Declan lifted his glass.

“It’s a large industry.”

“Of course.”

The conversation moved on. He didn’t volunteer anything more.

Dinner continued for another hour. His mother was pleased with the evening, his father appeared satisfied with the business discussion, and Charlotte remained gracious throughout.

When the meal ended, the families lingered over coffee.

Eventually, Charlotte’s father received a call and stepped away with Richard. Charlotte’s mother followed Declan’s mother towards the entrance to speak with the restaurant manager.

For a brief moment, Declan and Charlotte were left alone near the front of the private dining room.

“Your mother seems very happy,” Charlotte said.

Declan glanced towards the women.

“She tends to be when she has successfully arranged something.”

Charlotte smiled.

“I suppose we’re both aware of why tonight was arranged.”

He studied her. She wasn’t embarrassed. If anything, she seemed refreshingly direct.

“I imagine so.”

“I don’t mind meeting you. But I hope you don’t feel obligated to pretend this is something it isn’t,” she said.

A slight pause. Declan regarded her with renewed attention.

“That makes two of us.”

Charlotte laughed.

“Good. At least we agree on something.”

He gave her a small, polite smile.

“It’s a reasonable place to start.”

They walked towards the entrance together. Outside, the evening was cold. The restaurant’s entrance opened onto a quiet street, its warm lights spilling onto the pavement. A black car waited near the kerb. Declan’s driver stepped forward when he saw him.

“Sir.”

Declan nodded. Charlotte’s car was parked a little farther down the street. Her mother was still speaking with his mother near the entrance.

“Thank you for dinner,” Charlotte said.

“You’re welcome.”

“And thank you for the conversation.”

“Of course.”

She hesitated, then added, “I hope we can speak again sometime. Without our parents arranging the seating.”

Declan gave a faint smile.

“If there’s a reason to.”

“Fair enough.”

There was no awkwardness in the exchange. No promise, no suggestion of something neither of them intended. Charlotte extended her hand.

“Good night, Declan.”

“Good night, Charlotte.”

He shook her hand. And that was when the photograph was taken.

Across the street, the photographer had been waiting for almost an hour.

He wasn’t one of the usual paparazzi who crowded celebrities with cameras or called out names in the hope of getting a reaction. He had been positioned across the street, partly concealed behind the darkened window of a parked vehicle. He knew the restaurant. He knew the families.

And, more importantly, he knew exactly when to take the photograph.

The first image captured Declan and Charlotte standing close enough to speak comfortably beneath the restaurant lights. The second showed Charlotte smiling at him.

The third caught the moment he held her hand. It was a perfectly ordinary farewell.

But the photographer had no interest in ordinary explanations.

He sent the images to someone before leaving the street.

The person who received them already knew what to do.

Back at the lake, at three minutes past nine, Declan was halfway through removing his watch when Alexander called. He glanced at the screen.

“Alexander.”

“I’m sorry to disturb you, sir.”

“What’s happened?”

“There’s a situation involving the photographs from tonight.”

Declan stopped.

“What photographs?”

“Someone took pictures of you and Miss Weiss outside the restaurant. They’ve been sent to two entertainment outlets and one business publication.”

His face didn’t change.

“Who took them?”

“We’re looking into that. The photographer was unusually discreet. He appears to have known where to position himself.”

Declan placed his watch on the dresser.

“Have the photographs been published?”

“Not widely. One outlet posted a short item. We’ve already contacted them.”

“Get it taken down.”

“We’re working on it.”

“Don’t work on it. Have it done.”

A brief silence.

“Yes, sir.”

Declan walked towards the window.

“What does the article say?”

“It describes Miss Weiss as a potential partner and refers to tonight as a private dinner between two prominent families. The headline is more suggestive.”

Declan’s jaw tightened slightly.

“Suggestive how?”

Alexander read it out.

“‘Lincoln Heir Finally Steps Out With His Mystery Woman.’”

Declan said nothing.

Then, “Ridiculous.”

“I agree.”

“Contact the publication. Tell them the photograph was taken without consent and the implication is false. I want the article removed, not merely edited.”

“Understood.”

“And find out who supplied the information. The photographer didn’t happen to discover the dinner by accident.”

“Yes, sir.”

Declan ended the call. He stood still, looking at his phone. Then he opened CC’s conversation. There were no new messages.

He checked the time. It was past three in the morning in Bangkok. She was sometimes awake after schedules. He typed.

Declan: Are you still awake?

He waited. No reply. He called her once. It rang several times before going to voicemail. He didn’t call again. Instead, he contacted Alexander.

“Keep the photographs from spreading. I don’t want this turning into a story about something that doesn’t exist.”

“We’ll do what we can.”

“Not just the business outlets. Check the entertainment sites as well.”

“Of course.”

Declan ended the call and checked his phone again.

He had no particular concern about his own reputation. Nor did he care what people thought about his meeting with Charlotte. But he knew CC.

He knew how carefully she guarded her private life, how uncomfortable she could become when strangers made assumptions about her. She had spent years learning to live with public attention, but that didn’t mean she welcomed it.

And he had no intention of allowing an ordinary dinner to become something that disturbed her.

On Sunday morning, CC was sitting on the sofa in her apartment, her hair tied loosely behind her head.

She had spent the morning reviewing a recording schedule and was finally enjoying a quiet moment with a cup of tea. Her phone vibrated. A message from her friend, Pim, appeared.

Pim: CC.

Pim: Have you seen this?

CC glanced at the notification.

CC: Seen what?

A link arrived immediately. Then another message.

Pim: Don’t tell me you haven’t seen it.

CC frowned slightly. She tapped the link. The page took a moment to load. A photograph appeared.

Declan stood outside a restaurant, dressed in a charcoal suit. Beside him was a beautiful blonde woman in a champagne-coloured dress. They were facing each other. The woman’s hand was in his. The headline was printed above the image.

LINCOLN GROUP’S DECLAN LINCOLN SPOTTED WITH CHARLOTTE WEISS — A NEW POWER COUPLE? CC stared at the screen. For a few seconds, she didn’t move. She read the headline again. Then she took in the photograph.

It wasn’t intimate. They were standing outside a restaurant, probably saying goodbye. It could have been nothing. But the article didn’t present it that way.

It mentioned their families, their social standing, Charlotte’s education, and her family’s longstanding relationship with the Lincolns. It described the dinner as a private gathering that had reportedly been arranged by both families. CC scrolled. There were more photographs.

One showed Declan standing beside Charlotte near the entrance. Another showed them shaking hands.

A third caught him looking at her while she smiled. CC slowly lowered her phone. She remembered his message from Friday.

Family dinner.

She had wished him a pleasant evening. He had thanked her. That was all. Her phone vibrated again.

Pim: HELLO???

Pim: That’s Declan, isn’t it?

CC picked up her phone.

CC: Yes.

Pim: Wait. You know him?

CC read the message. She could have ignored it. Instead, she typed:

CC: We’ve met.

Pim responded almost immediately.

Pim: You’ve met???

Pim: CC, why are you saying it like that?

Pim: He’s not just some man. That’s Declan Lincoln.

CC pressed her lips together.

CC: I know.

Pim: Oh my god.

Pim: Are you two close?

CC didn’t answer. She returned to the article. The photograph was already circulating on several entertainment accounts. The original article had been reposted, translated, and shared across different platforms. The comments were multiplying. Some were congratulating the pair. Others were speculating about a possible engagement.

A few were discussing whether Charlotte had finally become the woman who could persuade Declan Lincoln to settle down.

CC read a little more than she intended to. Then she locked her phone. It was a strange feeling. Not quite sadness. Not quite jealousy.

Something uncomfortable had settled beneath her ribs, and she didn’t like it.

She reminded herself that Declan had never promised her anything. They weren’t in a relationship.

He was free to meet whoever he wanted, and she had no right to question him.

On Friday he had said he might call. She had said he could. He hadn’t.

There was a missed call from him just after three this morning, and a message asking whether she was awake. She had seen both when she woke up and wondered what he had wanted to say at three in the morning. Now she thought she knew.

She put her tea down and tried to return to the schedule on her tablet. Her phone vibrated again.

Pim: CC, are you okay?

CC looked at it.

CC: I’m fine.

Pim: You sound very not fine.

CC: I’m just surprised.

Pim: That’s understandable. The whole internet is talking about them.

CC didn’t reply. She didn’t want to discuss it.

But Pim, who had known her long enough to recognise when she was avoiding a subject, sent another message.

Pim: You know, if you want to tell me something, you can.

CC stared at the screen. Then, after a moment, she typed:

CC: There’s nothing to tell.

She set the phone down. She didn’t know that, in Munich, Declan had already made several calls to have the photographs removed.

And she didn’t know that the original article had been published through a contact connected to Charlotte’s family’s circle.

At a quarter to one, the message that changed everything didn’t come from Declan. It came from Pim.

CC was in the middle of getting ready for an afternoon schedule when her friend sent her a screenshot.

Pim: CC. I’m sorry, but look at this.

The screenshot showed a post from a popular entertainment account. The headline read:

THAI IDOL CC AND LINCOLN GROUP CHAIRMAN DECLAN LINCOLN — MORE THAN A BUSINESS CONNECTION? CC froze. She opened the post.

The account had collected photographs from the Lincoln Foundation gala in Geneva, a blurred fan photo from last Monday of a black Maybach outside AVEN’s building, and a still from the regional business news of Declan arriving at the brand meeting.

It had also found a fan’s photograph of CC arriving at a fitting on Thursday, the bracelet on her wrist, and set it beside a post from a Geneva jewellery house showing the same piece.

The caption suggested that the two had been seen together privately and questioned whether their connection had been romantic from the beginning. It wasn’t accurate. But it was convincing enough to attract attention. The comments were moving quickly. Some fans were excited. Some were confused.

Others were asking whether CC had been secretly dating a wealthy European businessman.

A few were already comparing her to Charlotte Weiss. CC’s phone vibrated repeatedly. Pim called. She answered.

“CC?”

“Mm?”

“Have you seen the post?”

“Yes.”

“Are you okay?”

CC looked down at the photograph of the bracelet. Her thumb brushed the edge of the phone.

“I’m okay.”

“Are you sure? It’s getting big. People are sharing it everywhere.”

CC said nothing. Pim lowered her voice.

“Listen, I know you don’t like talking about these things, but you should be careful. People are already making up stories.”

“I know.”

“Do you want me to come over?”

“No, it’s okay.”

“CC—”

“Really. I’m fine.”

Pim hesitated.

“Okay. But call me if you need anything.”

“I will.”

After ending the call, CC sat on the edge of her bed. She opened the post again. The number of shares had increased. Then another account reposted it. Then another.

Within minutes, the topic began appearing on trending lists. CC DECLAN LINCOLN Her name and his were side by side. CC stared at the screen.

She had spent years learning how to live with strangers discussing her appearance, her work, and her personal choices. But this was different.

Because this time, the person being discussed with her was someone she had begun to look forward to hearing from.

Someone who called her sweetheart. Someone who remembered her favourite dessert.

Someone who had once asked whether she had eaten and then made sure she did. Her phone lit up again. Declan calling… CC checked the screen. She watched it ring. Once. Twice. Then the call ended. A message appeared.

Declan: Sweetheart, call me when you can.

She held the phone in her hand. Outside her apartment, Bangkok carried on as usual.

Inside, the first wave of speculation was only beginning.

And somewhere in Munich, Declan Lincoln was looking at the same trending topic, already understanding that removing a few photographs would no longer be enough.

In Munich, a little after eleven, Alexander stood in front of Declan’s desk.

“It’s still circulating.”

Declan had been awake for some time. He had already spoken to the legal team, the communications department, and the editor of the publication that had first released the photographs. Two articles had been removed. One had been corrected.

A third had replaced its original headline with a more cautious description. But the photographs had already spread.

“Who gave them the information?” Declan asked.

“We’re narrowing it down. The photographer seems to have been working with someone who knew about the dinner.”

“Someone from the restaurant?”

“Possibly. But the initial distribution appears to have come from a private contact connected to the Weiss family.”

Declan’s eyes lifted.

“Connected how?”

“We don’t have confirmation yet.”

He leaned back.

“Find out.”

Alexander nodded.

“And the Thai post?” Declan asked.

Alexander hesitated. “Still trending in Bangkok. Two of the larger accounts have taken it down. It has been reposted more than forty times.”

Declan took the tablet and read through the posts himself: the gala, the car outside her building, her wrist beside a jeweller’s photograph. None of it proved anything. All of it was about her.

“Get the rest down.”

Alexander nodded. Declan returned the tablet.

“And don’t allow anyone to contact her on behalf of the company.”

“Understood.”

He picked up his phone. CC’s conversation remained open. His last message was still unanswered. He typed.

Declan: Sweetheart, have you seen the articles?

He waited. No reply. He tried calling again. This time, the call connected.

“Hello?”

Her voice was soft. But it wasn’t the familiar softness he had grown accustomed to. It sounded measured, as if she had been preparing herself to speak to him.

“Hello,” he said.

“Hello.”

“Are you busy?”

“Not really.”

He paused.

“Have you seen the photographs?”

A small silence followed.

“Yes.”

Declan looked out of the window.

“I was going to tell you about the dinner.”

“You don’t have to.”

“CC.”

“It’s okay, Declan.”

He recognised the carefulness in her voice. He had heard it before, when she was being polite to someone she didn’t know well. It wasn’t how she usually spoke to him.

“The dinner was arranged by my mother. Charlotte is a family acquaintance. Her parents were there, as were mine,” he said.

“I understand.”

“There was nothing between us.”

CC was quiet.

Then she said, “You don’t need to explain.”

“I know I don’t need to. I want to.”

She didn’t answer. Declan’s fingers rested against the edge of his desk.

“Those photographs were taken without our knowledge. Someone seems to have arranged for them to be circulated.”

“Why would someone do that?”

“I intend to find out.”

Another pause.

Then CC said, “It looks like a very nice dinner.”

His gaze lowered.

“It was dinner.”

“I know.”

“Sweetheart.”

“I’m not upset.”

He didn’t immediately respond. He could hear faint background noise on her end, perhaps the television or someone moving around in her apartment.

“I was just surprised to see it,” she said gently.

“I understand.”

“I hope your family had a nice evening.”

“They did.”

“Good.”

He wanted to ask whether she was truly fine. Whether she had been reading the comments. Whether she had spoken to anyone about the photographs.

But he knew that pressing her would only make her retreat further.

So he said, “I’ll call you later.”

“Okay.”

“And CC?”

“Yes?”

“Don’t let strangers decide what you should think about me.”

There was a small silence.

Then she answered, “I won’t.”

He believed that she meant it. He was less certain that she hadn’t already been hurt.

chapters.title: The Intention Behind His Return
chapters.desc: He flies back overnight to explain the dinner in person, and asks to court her properly, exclusively, meaning to make her his girlfriend. She says yes, on one condition.
chapters.epigraph: “I want to court you, CC. Properly.”
chapters.content:
Declan Lincoln changed his plans an hour after that call.

It wasn’t an impulsive decision. He had been awake since three, reading what strangers had decided about his life, and by the time she said I won’t in that careful, polite voice, his mind was already made up. He was going back to Bangkok.

The photographs could be handled from anywhere, and he had no interest in explaining himself to the public. The reason was simpler: there was a woman in Bangkok who mattered to him, and he had left her too much room to doubt it.

He had enjoyed their conversations. He enjoyed the way she sent him photographs of her meals, the way she occasionally became stubborn when he teased her, and the way her voice softened when she was tired. He liked making her happy. He liked being the person she called when she had a little free time.

But he had never given what they were a name.

At first, he had considered it sensible. They had only recently met. He didn’t want to rush her, nor did he want to turn something pleasant into an obligation. Now, however, he understood something.

He had been comfortable allowing things to develop naturally because he knew his own intentions.

CC didn’t have the benefit of knowing what was in his head.

She had seen photographs of him with another woman. She had watched strangers speculate about his personal life. And she had been left to interpret a situation he could have explained much earlier.

He didn’t want her wondering whether she was someone he enjoyed spending time with until another arrangement came along.

He had no intention of treating her that way.

“Sir?”

Alexander stood by the desk with the revised itinerary.

“The jet can leave at ten tonight. You’ll land at Don Mueang a little after two tomorrow afternoon, Bangkok time. I’ve arranged for the Munich meetings to be handled by Mr. Keller and moved your New York call to Wednesday.”

“Good.”

“There is one more thing.”

Declan looked up.

“Your mother called.”

“What did she say?”

“She asked whether you were still planning to attend the foundation board dinner next week.”

“I haven’t decided.”

“She also asked whether something happened after Saturday’s dinner.”

Declan’s expression remained neutral.

“What did you tell her?”

“That you had an unexpected change in schedule.”

“Good.”

Alexander hesitated.

“Would you like me to inform the Weiss family that you won’t be available for further meetings?”

Declan closed the folder in front of him.

“Yes. Politely.”

“Of course.”

“And Alexander?”

“Yes, sir?”

“Find out exactly who arranged the photographs. I want the information, not speculation.”

“I’ll have an update by tomorrow.”

Declan nodded. Alexander turned to leave, but Declan spoke again.

“Have the car at the house by eight.”

“Yes, sir.”

Once the door closed, he picked up his phone, looked at her name, and put it down again. It was evening in Bangkok, and she had sounded tired. He would tell her when she woke.

He told her from the air. At a quarter to nine the next morning, Bangkok time, somewhere over Pakistan, he opened their conversation and typed.

Declan: Good morning, sweetheart.

He waited a moment before sending another.

Declan: I’m coming to Bangkok today.

He reread the message, then added:

Declan: I’d like to see you.

He didn’t know whether she would be pleased. But he wanted her to hear what he had to say from him, not through an article or a photograph.

On Monday morning, CC was sitting in the back of her manager’s car when the messages arrived.

She had been looking through her schedule, but the moment Declan’s name appeared on her screen, her attention shifted. She read his first message. Then the second. Then the third. Her thumb hovered above the keyboard. He was coming back? He had only left Bangkok six days ago.

CC: Good morning.

She paused.

CC: You’re coming to Bangkok?

Declan: I’m somewhere over Pakistan, so yes.

CC: For business?

A few seconds passed.

Declan: Partly.

CC looked at the reply. She wasn’t sure what to say. P’Nicha, sitting beside her, noticed her expression.

“Who is it?”

“No one.”

Nicha turned her head.

“That’s a very suspicious answer.”

CC locked her phone.

“It’s just a message.”

“From the same person who has been making you smile at your phone all week?”

CC looked at her.

“P’Nicha.”

“What?”

“Please.”

Nicha grinned and returned to her own phone. CC waited until she was no longer looking before reopening the conversation.

CC: When do you arrive?

Declan: This afternoon.

CC: That’s soon.

Declan: I thought so.

CC: You just left.

Declan: I noticed.

She almost smiled. Then another message appeared.

Declan: Can I take you to dinner tonight?

CC stared at it. Part of her wanted to say yes immediately.

Another part remembered the photographs, the headlines, and the strange feeling she had experienced the previous day.

She didn’t want to behave as if nothing had happened.

But she also didn’t want to make a problem out of something she had no right to question.

CC: I have a recording session until six.

Declan: I’ll work around your schedule.

CC: You don’t have to.

Declan: I know.

She looked at those three words. They were familiar.

He had said something similar when he bought her the bracelet, when he arranged lunch, and when he insisted on sending a car for her.

He never seemed to do these things because he expected anything in return. Still, she typed:

CC: Let me finish my schedule first. I’ll tell you.

Declan: Of course, sweetheart.

She put her phone down. Nicha glanced at her.

“So?”

CC pretended to read her schedule.

“So what?”

“He’s coming back.”

CC turned towards the window.

“Yes.”

Nicha raised her eyebrows.

“And?”

“And what?”

“Nothing. I just think someone is suddenly very interested in the traffic outside.”

CC pressed her lips together, trying not to smile.

“P’Nicha.”

“I’m quiet.”

“You’re not.”

“Fine. I’ll wait.”

CC shook her head and returned to her schedule.

But the rest of the drive, she kept checking the time more often than necessary.

The jet landed at Don Mueang a little after two, and by twenty-five to four Declan was walking out of the private terminal with Alexander a step behind. His luggage had already been collected by the staff, and the driver was waiting.

“Your hotel has been prepared. The meeting tomorrow has been moved to ten. The regional director will be expecting you,” Alexander said.

“Good.”

“Would you like to go directly to the hotel?”

Declan checked his phone. There was a message from CC.

CC: My recording session finished earlier than expected.

A second message followed.

CC: I’m free tonight.

He replied immediately.

Declan: Then I’ll see you tonight.

CC: Okay.

He slipped his phone into his pocket.

“Hotel first,” he told Alexander.

“Understood.”

Alexander opened the car door. As Declan settled into the back seat, he glanced once more at his phone. He wanted to see her.

But more than that, he wanted to make sure she understood that the previous evening hadn’t changed anything about his intentions. If anything, it had made him more certain.

That evening, CC arrived at the restaurant ten minutes before the reservation.

It was a quiet establishment tucked away from the busiest part of the city, with a private dining room that overlooked a small garden. Declan had chosen it after asking his assistant to find somewhere discreet and comfortable.

Her car was waved through a side gate into a covered driveway, where nobody on the street could see who stepped out. A member of staff was waiting at the door and took her straight upstairs, past no one. Someone had thought about cameras before she had.

She wore a simple cream dress with a light cardigan. Her hair fell loosely over her shoulders, and she had kept her makeup minimal after the recording session. The hostess led her to the private room. Declan was already there. He stood when she entered.

“Hello, sweetheart.”

CC smiled.

“Hello.”

He approached her and greeted her with a light touch at her elbow.

“You look lovely.”

“Thank you.”

His eyes moved over her face.

“You look a little tired.”

“I was recording.”

“So I hear.”

He pulled out her chair.

“Sit down.”

CC settled into it, placing her handbag beside her.

Declan took the seat opposite her, though he moved it slightly closer than the arrangement required. They looked at each other.

Then CC said, “You really came back.”

“I did.”

“Wasn’t your schedule busy?”

“It was.”

She tilted her head.

“Then why?”

Declan regarded her calmly.

“I wanted to see you.”

Her face softened, but she lowered her gaze to the menu.

“Oh.”

He watched her.

“Is that all?”

She looked up.

“What?”

“An ‘oh’?”

A faint blush appeared on her cheeks.

“What am I supposed to say?”

“I’m sure you can think of something.”

She gave him a small, helpless smile.

“You’re teasing me already.”

“It’s been several days. I have some catching up to do.”

CC laughed. The waiter came to take their orders. Declan let her choose first, then ordered for himself. They began with familiar conversation: her recording session, his flight, the weather, and the inconvenience of crossing several time zones. He asked whether she had eaten properly. She told him she had. He asked what she had eaten. She gave him a look.

“Why do you need details?”

“I’m checking.”

“I’m not one of your employees.”

“No. My employees don’t usually send me photographs of strawberries.”

CC laughed.

“You remember that?”

“I remember quite a lot.”

She looked down at her glass, smiling. The food arrived, and for a while they ate comfortably.

But the conversation wasn’t quite as effortless as it had been before.

Declan noticed the way she occasionally glanced at him, then looked away. He noticed that she was choosing her words more carefully.

He decided not to let the evening pass without addressing it.

“CC.”

She looked up.

“Hmm?”

“About Saturday.”

Her fingers paused around her glass. He continued in an even voice.

“I want to explain what happened.”

She met his eyes.

“Okay.”

“The dinner was arranged by my mother. Charlotte’s family is acquainted with mine. Her father wanted to discuss a foundation project with my father, and my mother thought it would be a good opportunity for us to meet.”

CC nodded.

“I see.”

“Charlotte and I had never met before that evening.”

“Really?”

“Yes.”

He watched her expression.

“We had dinner with our parents. We spoke. Then we left.”

CC nodded again.

“It’s okay, Declan. You don’t have to tell me every detail.”

“I know.”

He paused.

“But I want you to understand that there was no romantic arrangement between Charlotte and me.”

She looked down.

“Your mother wanted you to meet her, though.”

“Yes.”

“Because she wants you to get married?”

A faint smile touched his mouth.

“You’re very perceptive.”

CC gave a small laugh.

“It’s not difficult to guess.”

“My mother believes that if she introduces me to enough suitable women, eventually one of them will convince me to stop working.”

“Maybe she’s right.”

“Are you volunteering to help her?”

CC’s eyes widened slightly.

“No!”

He smiled.

“That was fast.”

She covered her smile with her hand.

“Don’t.”

Declan let her recover before continuing.

“My mother arranged the dinner. She did not arrange my future.”

CC’s expression became thoughtful.

“Did she know about the photographs?”

“I don’t believe she arranged them. But I am looking into who did.”

“Why would someone do that?”

“Publicity. Influence. Perhaps someone thought there was something to gain from making the evening look more significant than it was.”

He drank some water.

“Whatever the reason, I don’t appreciate people using my private life as a means of creating a story.”

CC nodded slowly.

“Me neither.”

“I know. That’s partly why I came.”

He looked at her.

“And I’m sorry that it reached you.”

She shook her head.

“You didn’t take the photographs.”

“No. But I should have told you about the dinner before it happened.”

CC was quiet.

He said, “I didn’t think it was important enough to mention. That was my mistake.”

She turned to him.

“You didn’t think I would care?”

“I didn’t know whether you would.”

Her lips parted slightly, but she didn’t answer. Declan leaned back, giving her room to think.

“I wasn’t hiding anything from you. But I can understand why it might have looked that way,” he said.

CC looked at her hands. She seemed to be considering how honest she wanted to be.

Then she said, “I wasn’t angry.”

“I didn’t think you were.”

“I just didn’t know what to think.”

He nodded.

“That makes sense.”

“I mean… We never really talked about what we are.” She paused, searching for the right words.

Declan remained still. She continued, her voice softer.

“So when I saw the photographs, I thought maybe I had misunderstood something.”

His eyes went to her face.

“Misunderstood what?”

CC gave a small shrug.

“Us.”

The word settled between them. Declan’s expression changed, though only slightly.

He had been waiting for her to say it. He took no pleasure in her uncertainty. It only confirmed what he had been thinking since Munich.

He had been allowing their relationship to develop without defining it.

And she had been trying to understand where she stood.

“CC,” he said.

She looked up.

“I don’t want you to misunderstand us.”

Her eyes stayed on his.

“I don’t want you to feel that I’m simply keeping you company when it’s convenient, or that I’m free to entertain other arrangements while expecting you to remain available to me.”

She didn’t move. Declan’s voice remained calm, but there was no teasing in it now.

“I’ve been enjoying getting to know you. More than I initially expected. I look forward to speaking with you. I think about you when you’re not around. And I came back to Bangkok because I wanted to see you, not because I needed to attend another business meeting.”

CC’s fingers curled lightly around her napkin. He continued.

“I should have been clearer about my intentions.”

She looked at him, her cheeks beginning to warm.

“What are your intentions?”

A faint smile appeared.

“That’s a very direct question.”

“You said you wanted to explain.”

“I did.”

“So explain.”

He laughed.

“Of course.”

He placed his glass down.

“I want to court you, CC. Properly. I want to date you with the intention of building something serious. I don’t want to leave you guessing whether I’m interested in someone else or whether you’re simply one of several possibilities.”

Her eyes widened a little.

“Declan…”

“I know we’ve only known each other for a short time. I’m not asking you to make promises about the future. I don’t expect you to decide everything tonight.”

He paused.

“But I would like to make my intentions clear. I want you to be the woman I’m pursuing. Exclusively.”

CC stared at him. For a few seconds, she couldn’t find an answer. She had expected an explanation. Perhaps reassurance. Perhaps an apology.

She hadn’t expected him to speak so directly about wanting a serious relationship with her. Declan watched her carefully.

“Would you be comfortable with that?”

She blinked.

“Are you asking me to be your girlfriend?”

His mouth curved slightly.

“I am asking whether you’ll allow me to court you with the intention of making you my girlfriend.”

She looked at him, then down at the table.

“That’s a very long way to ask.”

“I thought you deserved a proper question.”

Her smile appeared before she could stop it.

“You’re very formal.”

“I can be more concise if you prefer.”

She shook her head.

“No.”

“Then?”

She looked up again. Her cheeks were pink.

“I like you too.”

His face softened.

“I know.”

CC’s eyes widened.

“You know?”

“I had a suspicion.”

She gave him a small pout.

“That’s not fair.”

“Would you like me to pretend I didn’t notice?”

“No.”

He smiled. She looked down again, smiling despite herself.

“I like spending time with you. And I like talking to you. Even when you’re busy,” she said.

“When I’m busy?”

“Not especially.”

“That’s disappointing.”

She laughed. Then her face grew a little more serious.

“But I don’t want to be something complicated in your life.”

Declan’s gaze remained on her.

“You aren’t.”

“Your family is important. Your work is important. And I know your life is very different from mine.”

“I’m aware of the differences.”

“I don’t want to be introduced to people as someone who is just… There because you happen to like having me around.”

He understood what she meant. He leaned forward slightly.

“Then I won’t introduce you that way.”

CC looked at him.

“If we decide to do this, I won’t treat you as a secret or an inconvenience. I won’t make promises I cannot keep, but I will be honest with you about my life. And I expect the same from you.”

She listened.

“I also don’t want you to feel that you have to change anything about yourself to fit into my world.”

Her eyes softened.

“You say that very easily.”

“Because it’s simple.”

“It’s not always simple.”

“I know. But it is my responsibility to make sure you don’t feel that you have to earn a place beside me.”

CC’s expression shifted. Something about the way he said it made her chest feel unexpectedly warm.

She hadn’t realised how much she needed to hear that until he said it.

He reached across the table, his palm resting open beside her hand.

“May I?”

She looked at his hand, then placed hers in it. His fingers closed gently around hers.

“I’m serious about you, sweetheart.”

She smiled.

“I think I understand.”

“Good.”

“But I have one condition.”

His eyebrows lifted slightly.

“Already?”

She nodded.

“You have to let me spoil you back.”

He considered her.

“Explain.”

“You always arrange things. The restaurant, the car, the gifts… If we’re going to do this, I want to give you things too. Small ones. And you have to take them.” She glanced at him.

A smile slowly appeared on his face.

“Small ones?”

“Yes.”

“Very well.”

“And sometimes I pay for dinner.”

He looked amused.

“Sometimes?”

“Yes.”

“I’ll consider it.”

“Declan.”

“Sweetheart.”

She narrowed her eyes at him. He laughed.

“Fine. We’ll negotiate.”

She seemed satisfied with that answer. Then she looked down at their joined hands.

“Okay.”

His thumb moved lightly across her knuckles.

“Okay?”

She nodded.

“I’d like that.”

Declan’s expression lost its restrained amusement entirely. He looked genuinely pleased.

“Good.”

CC held his gaze.

“That’s all?”

“What else would you like?”

“Nothing.”

“Then I’ll try not to ruin the moment.”

She laughed, and he lifted her hand to his lips, pressing a brief kiss against her knuckles. It was a small gesture.

But it made her face turn pink all over again.

Dinner lasted longer than either of them had planned. They talked about ordinary things afterwards.

CC told him about a song she had been listening to repeatedly. Declan asked to hear it, and she played a short section from her phone. He listened without interrupting. When it ended, she looked at him expectantly.

“What do you think?”

“I like it.”

“That’s all?”

“Would you prefer a technical review?”

She laughed.

“No.”

“Then I like it.”

She smiled and put her phone away. Later, when the waiter brought dessert, CC read the menu and pointed to the mango sticky rice. Declan glanced at her.

“Of course.”

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“You’re judging me.”

“Not at all.”

“You’re smiling.”

“I’m pleased that you’re predictable.”

She gave him an offended look.

“I have many interests.”

“Name three.”

“And I’m not predictable.”

“Of course not, sweetheart.”

She took a bite of dessert and ignored him. Declan watched her, amused. He liked this version of her.

The one who could become stubborn over a harmless comment, who smiled into her spoon when she was pleased, and who sometimes forgot to be reserved around him. He had wanted to make her feel secure.

Now, watching her sit comfortably across from him, he realised he wanted something more than the satisfaction of having clarified their relationship. He wanted to keep getting to know her.

He wanted to discover the parts of her that hadn’t yet appeared in their conversations.

And he wanted to be the person she could come to without wondering whether she was asking for too much.

When dinner ended, he walked her to the car. Her driver was waiting outside. CC turned towards him.

“Thank you for dinner.”

“You’re welcome.”

“And for explaining.”

He glanced at her.

“You don’t need to thank me for that.”

“I know. But I wanted to.”

He smiled. She hesitated before speaking again.

“So… good night?”

“That’s all?”

She tilted her head.

“What else?”

He stepped a little closer, lowering his voice.

“I’ve just asked to court you properly. I thought I might at least receive a slightly warmer good night.”

Her cheeks turned pink.

“Good night, Declan.”

“Better.”

She laughed. He reached up and gently tucked a loose strand of hair behind her ear.

“Get home safely. Message me when you’re there.”

“I will.”

“And eat something if you’re hungry later.”

She looked at him.

“We just had dinner.”

“I’m aware.”

“Then why?”

“Because I know you.”

She shook her head, smiling.

“Good night, sweetheart,” he said.

CC paused.

Then, “Good night.”

She got into the car. Declan remained by the pavement until the vehicle pulled away.

Only when it disappeared into traffic did he return to his own car.

At home, CC had barely finished washing her face when her phone vibrated.

Declan: Home?

CC: Yes.

Declan: Good.

Declan: Did you enjoy dinner?

CC: I did.

Declan: And the company?

She smiled at the screen.

CC: The company was okay.

Declan: Only okay?

CC: Maybe a little better than okay.

Declan: I’ll accept that.

A moment later:

Declan: I enjoyed having you across the table tonight.

CC sat on the edge of her bed. She read the message twice. Then she typed:

CC: I enjoyed it too.

Declan: Good night, sweetheart.

She hesitated, then replied.

CC: Good night, Declan.

She was about to put her phone down when another message appeared.

Declan: One more thing.

CC: What?

Declan: I meant what I said tonight.

Declan: I want to pursue you seriously. Don’t let the photographs make you doubt that.

CC’s smile softened.

CC: I won’t.

CC: And don’t work too late.

Declan: I’ll try.

CC: Not try. Do it.

He smiled at the screen.

Declan: Yes, sweetheart.

CC placed the phone beside her pillow. The knot that had sat under her ribs since Sunday began, slowly, to loosen.

She didn’t know what the future would look like.

She didn’t know how his family would react, or how the public would respond if they eventually learned about them. But she knew what he had asked. And she had said yes.

Declan stood by the window of his hotel suite, looking over the city. His phone rang. Alexander. He answered.

“Go ahead.”

“We’ve identified the person who coordinated the photographs.”

Declan’s expression became attentive.

“Who?”

“It was arranged through an associate of the Weiss family. We believe the intention was to generate attention around the possibility of a relationship between you and Miss Weiss.”

Declan’s face became unreadable.

“Does Charlotte know?”

“We haven’t established that.”

“Then don’t assume she does.”

“Understood.”

“Has the family been informed that I won’t be pursuing the arrangement?”

“Not yet.”

“Send the message tomorrow. Make it clear that Saturday was a courtesy dinner, nothing more.”

“Yes, sir.”

Declan looked down at the city.

“And Alexander?”

“Yes?”

“Keep CC’s name out of any response. I don’t want her dragged into a public dispute.”

“Of course.”

The call ended. Declan placed his phone on the table.

He had spent the evening making one thing clear to CC.

Now he intended to make sure his actions matched his words.

He had no interest in leaving her uncertain again.

The next step in his personal life had begun to matter more than the next item on his calendar.

chapters.title: The Difference Between Welcome and Wanted
chapters.desc: Alexander’s report names who arranged the photographs. Eleanor Lincoln deals with the Weiss family herself, then asks her son whether there is someone else. This time he says yes.
chapters.epigraph: “They have mistaken my patience for agreement.”
chapters.content:
On Tuesday, Declan Lincoln was halfway through his morning meeting when Alexander placed a thin black folder on the table in front of him. The meeting continued for another three minutes.

Declan listened to the regional director’s explanation, asked two questions about the revised figures, and gave his approval for the next stage of the project. Only after the other executives had left did he open the folder.

“Is this the result of yesterday’s investigation?” he asked.

“Yes, sir.”

Alexander remained standing. Declan read the first page. Then the second.

His face didn’t change, but the slight movement of his jaw suggested that he was less than impressed.

“Mr. Weiss?”

“Not directly, sir. The arrangements were coordinated by his wife, but the instructions came through their daughter.”

Declan turned another page. Charlotte Weiss. The name appeared in the report several times, accompanied by a timeline of messages, a payment record, and the photographer’s statement. He read everything without interruption.

The photographer hadn’t been waiting outside the restaurant. He had been contacted two days before the dinner and given the exact time and location. He had been instructed to capture Declan and Charlotte together, preferably during a moment that could be interpreted as intimate. The photographs had then been sent to a small public relations agency with connections to several entertainment and business publications. The intention was clear.

Create the impression that Declan Lincoln and Charlotte Weiss were being introduced as a potential couple. Allow the story to circulate. Encourage public speculation. Make the two families appear to be moving towards an alliance.

And, perhaps most importantly, make the arrangement difficult for Declan to dismiss without appearing unreasonable. Alexander continued.

“The agency was also instructed to emphasise the Weiss family’s relationship with the Lincolns. They wanted the coverage to appear as though the relationship had already received the families’ approval.”

Declan closed the folder.

“Did they expect me to cooperate?”

“Possibly. The assumption seems to have been that you would remain silent rather than publicly embarrass the family.”

A faint, humourless smile appeared.

“They have mistaken my patience for agreement.”

Alexander said nothing. Declan stood and walked towards the windows.

“Was Charlotte aware of the plan?”

“According to the information we have, she knew photographs would be taken. We haven’t found evidence that she personally contacted the agency, but she was aware of the intended publicity.”

Declan looked at him.

“And her parents?”

“Her mother was directly involved. Her father appears to have been informed afterwards.”

The office was silent. Declan returned to his desk.

“Send the complete report to our legal team. I want the agency’s contract, the payment records, and the original correspondence preserved.”

“Yes, sir.”

“Have our communications department issue a statement if necessary. No speculation, no emotional language. Simply state that Saturday’s dinner was a private family gathering and that no romantic arrangement exists.”

“Understood.”

“And contact the Weiss family.”

Alexander hesitated.

“Would you like to speak with Mr. Weiss personally?”

“Yes.”

“Certainly.”

Declan picked up his phone.

Before Alexander could leave, he said, “One more thing.”

“Yes, sir?”

“Make sure CC’s name isn’t included in any of this.”

Alexander nodded.

“I’ll ensure that.”

Declan looked down at the folder once more. He wasn’t concerned about the photographs anymore. They could be removed, corrected, or contradicted.

What bothered him was the deliberate attempt to manipulate his personal life and attach his family name to a narrative that had never existed.

His mother had arranged the dinner out of genuine affection, even if her methods were occasionally intrusive.

Someone had taken that goodwill and used it as an opportunity. And that was something he wouldn’t overlook.

At ten to five that afternoon in Bangkok, Declan called his mother. In Munich it wasn’t yet eleven, and Eleanor Lincoln was arranging flowers in the sitting room. She answered with a smile.

“Declan. How are you, darling?”

“I’m well, Mother.”

“You sound busy.”

“I have something to discuss with you.”

Her hands paused over the flowers.

“Is everything all right?”

“Yes. It’s about Saturday’s dinner.”

Eleanor placed the scissors down.

“Charlotte? Did something happen?”

“I’ve received information about the photographs taken outside the restaurant.”

Her face changed.

“What photographs?”

Declan explained. He told her about the photographer, the public relations agency, and the deliberate arrangement to create a romantic narrative between him and Charlotte. He didn’t exaggerate or speculate. He presented the facts that had been established. Eleanor listened without interrupting.

By the time he finished, the pleasant expression she had worn at the beginning of the call had disappeared.

“Are you telling me Charlotte knew?”

“She knew photographs would be taken.”

“And her mother?”

“Was involved in arranging it.”

Eleanor was quiet. For several seconds, she seemed unable to decide which part of the information offended her more.

“I invited that girl into our home,” she said finally.

“I know.”

“I welcomed her. I treated her like a guest.”

“I know, Mother.”

“And her mother thought she could use our family dinner to manufacture a relationship?”

Declan didn’t answer immediately.

“That’s what the evidence suggests.”

Eleanor leaned back in her chair. She had genuinely liked Charlotte.

She had admired her education, her manners, and the way she seemed comfortable in their social circle. She had thought Charlotte would make a suitable acquaintance for her son. Perhaps, if things went well, something more.

But she had never intended for anyone to force the matter.

“I don’t understand. If they wanted you to consider their daughter, why couldn’t they simply allow you to meet her?” Eleanor said, her voice tightening.

“Because they wanted to influence the outcome.”

“How presumptuous.”

Declan remained silent. Eleanor looked towards the window.

“I may have wanted you to meet Charlotte, but I never gave her family permission to arrange your life for you.”

“I know.”

“And I certainly never gave them permission to use our name.”

Her voice was no longer merely disappointed. It was cold.

“Mother,” Declan said calmly, “I wanted you to know before I dealt with them.”

“You did the right thing.”

He heard her take a breath.

“I’m going to speak to her mother.”

“There’s no need to make a scene.”

“I have no intention of making a scene, Declan.”

He could almost picture her expression.

“I intend to make it very clear that the Lincoln family does not appreciate being manipulated.”

A faint smile touched his mouth.

“That would be sufficient.”

“No, darling. It wouldn’t.”

He raised an eyebrow, though she couldn’t see him. Eleanor continued.

“I can accept that you don’t want to marry Charlotte. I can accept that you may have no interest in her at all. What I cannot accept is someone attempting to turn our family into a tool for their own ambitions.”

Declan’s expression softened slightly.

“Thank you.”

“Don’t thank me. I’m your mother.”

A brief pause followed.

Then Eleanor asked, “Is there someone else?”

Declan looked out at the city beyond his office.

The question she had been circling for weeks had finally landed. He could have avoided it.

He could have given her the same answer he had given before. But he had made a decision.

“Yes.”

Eleanor went completely still.

“Someone else?”

“Yes.”

“Oh.”

Her voice changed immediately.

“Who?”

Declan smiled.

“Her name is Cela Chanya. She goes by CC.”

Eleanor repeated the name.

“CC.”

“She works in the entertainment industry. She’s Thai-Chinese, born in Canada. She’s twenty-four.”

“Twenty-four?”

“Yes.”

A small pause.

“And how long have you known her?”

“Since the foundation gala in Geneva.”

Eleanor was silent.

Then she asked, “Is she the reason you weren’t interested in meeting Charlotte?”

“Partly.”

“Partly?”

Declan smiled.

“I wasn’t particularly interested in the arrangement to begin with.”

“Declan.”

He laughed.

“Mother.”

She sighed, but there was a different quality to it now. Curiosity had begun to replace her irritation.

“Do you like her?”

He didn’t hesitate.

“Yes.”

The answer was simple. It was also the first time he had said it so directly to his mother. Eleanor’s expression softened.

“Oh.”

Declan leaned back.

“We’re getting to know each other. I’ve told her that I want to pursue her seriously.”

“And she agreed?”

“She did.”

His mother was quiet. Then she smiled.

“Well.”

Declan could hear the change in her voice.

“That’s rather important news to tell your mother over the telephone.”

“I thought it would be better than letting you discover it through another photograph.”

Eleanor laughed despite herself.

“You’re unbelievable.”

“I get it from you.”

“Is she kind?”

“Yes.”

“Does she treat you well?”

“Very well.”

“Do you treat her well?”

Declan’s smile deepened.

“I try to.”

“Try?”

“I believe she’d say I spoil her too much.”

Eleanor laughed again.

“That sounds promising.”

Declan looked down at his desk. He hadn’t intended to reveal so much during this call, but the conversation had become unexpectedly pleasant.

“Mother.”

“Yes, darling?”

“Please don’t contact her yet.”

Eleanor immediately understood.

“She doesn’t know you’ve told me.”

“Not yet.”

“Very well. I won’t.”

“And don’t arrange anything.”

There was a small silence.

“Declan.”

“Yes?”

“I am capable of meeting someone without arranging a marriage.”

He smiled.

“I’ll keep that in mind.”

Eleanor didn’t wait long before making her own call. At a quarter past one, Charlotte’s mother answered on the second ring.

“Eleanor, how lovely to hear from you.”

“Good afternoon, Marianne.”

“Are you calling about Saturday? Charlotte was telling me how pleasant the evening was.”

“Was she?”

There was something in Eleanor’s tone that made Marianne pause.

“Yes. She enjoyed speaking with Declan.”

“I see.”

Eleanor sat down on the sofa.

“I’ve recently received some information about the photographs taken outside the restaurant.”

A brief silence. Marianne recovered quickly.

“Oh, those. I hope they haven’t caused too much inconvenience. You know how these photographers are.”

“I do.”

Eleanor’s voice remained polite.

“However, I understand that this particular photographer was invited.”

Another silence.

“I beg your pardon?”

“The photographer was given the time and location of our private dinner. He was also instructed to capture photographs that would suggest a romantic relationship between our children.”

Marianne gave a small, uncertain laugh.

“I think there may have been a misunderstanding.”

“I don’t believe there was.”

“Eleanor, surely you don’t think we would deliberately—”

“I have seen the correspondence, Marianne.”

The other woman stopped speaking. Eleanor continued.

“I understand that you wanted Declan and Charlotte to become acquainted. I arranged the dinner myself. There was no need to manufacture anything.”

“We only thought—”

“You thought what?”

Her voice was still quiet. But the warmth had disappeared.

“You thought that if the photographs were convincing enough, Declan would be forced to accept an arrangement he had never agreed to?”

“That is not how it was intended.”

“Then perhaps you should explain what was intended.”

Marianne didn’t answer. Eleanor looked down at her hands.

“I like Charlotte. I have said that before, and I mean it. She is a lovely young woman. But I will not allow anyone to use my family name to create a public relationship that does not exist.”

“Eleanor, please. We have known each other for years.”

“Which is why I find this particularly disappointing.”

Marianne tried again.

“We only wanted to help them. Declan is difficult to approach. You know that better than anyone. We thought a little publicity might encourage him to take the matter seriously.”

Eleanor’s expression hardened.

“Then you have misunderstood my son rather badly.”

“I’m sure we can resolve this privately.”

“We will resolve it privately. But I want to be very clear. There will be no further arrangement between our families regarding Declan and Charlotte.”

Marianne inhaled sharply.

“Eleanor—”

“I wish Charlotte well. I genuinely do. But this has gone beyond an awkward misunderstanding.”

Eleanor paused.

“And please tell your husband that the Lincoln family does not appreciate being used to improve anyone’s social standing.”

She ended the call. For several moments, she remained seated. Then she picked up her phone again. She had one more person to call. Forty minutes later, Charlotte answered from her apartment.

“Mrs. Lincoln?”

“Hello, Charlotte.”

“Good afternoon. How are you?”

“I’m well, thank you. And you?”

“Very well.”

Eleanor was quiet.

“I’ve spoken with your mother.”

Charlotte’s expression changed.

“Oh.”

“I wanted to speak with you directly as well.”

“Yes, of course.”

“I understand you knew that photographs would be taken outside the restaurant.”

Charlotte didn’t respond immediately.

Then she said, “Yes.”

Eleanor closed her eyes.

“May I ask why?”

Charlotte’s voice became more cautious.

“My mother thought it would be helpful.”

“Helpful to whom?”

“To both families.”

“Charlotte, I arranged that dinner because I wanted you and Declan to meet. I did not ask anyone to create a story about the two of you.”

“I know.”

“Then why did you agree?”

Charlotte hesitated.

“I thought it might give us an opportunity.”

Eleanor’s expression softened slightly, though her disappointment remained.

“An opportunity to do what?”

“To see whether something could develop.”

Eleanor sighed.

“Something cannot develop if one person has not agreed to it.”

Charlotte said nothing.

“I don’t dislike you, dear. I want you to understand that. I have always thought well of you.”

“Thank you.”

“But my son is not a prize to be secured through publicity. And I will not have our family treated as though our approval can be manufactured.”

“I understand.”

“I hope you do.”

Charlotte’s voice was quieter when she replied.

“I’m sorry.”

Eleanor accepted the apology, but she didn’t soften her position.

“I wish you well, Charlotte. But I think it would be best if we left this matter here.”

The call ended. Charlotte remained seated with her phone in her hand.

Only now did she seem to understand that the photographs hadn’t brought her closer to Declan. They had done the opposite.

In Bangkok it was half past eight in the evening, and Declan was finishing a call with New York when his mother rang again. He answered.

“Mother.”

“I spoke with Marianne.”

“And?”

“She was not particularly convincing.”

He smiled.

“I expected as much.”

“I also spoke with Charlotte.”

Declan looked at the documents in front of him.

“Was that necessary?”

“Yes.”

“Mother.”

“Don’t ‘Mother’ me. I wanted her to hear directly from me that I had no intention of allowing this to continue.”

He leaned back.

“Thank you.”

Eleanor paused.

“Declan, I want you to understand something.”

He waited.

“I may have wanted you to meet Charlotte. I may have thought she was a suitable young woman. But I would never want you to be with someone because I thought it was convenient.”

His face softened.

“I know.”

“And I certainly wouldn’t want a woman who believes she has to create a public relationship to secure your attention.”

He let out a quiet breath.

“Neither would I.”

“Good.”

A pause followed.

Then Eleanor asked, almost casually, “You said this girl is in Bangkok?”

“Yes.”

“CC?”

“Yes.”

“Is she an actress?”

“She’s an idol. She sings and performs.”

“Oh. Does she have a large following?”

“Quite a large one.”

Eleanor hummed thoughtfully.

“Then the photographs must have been uncomfortable for her.”

“They were.”

“Have you spoken to her?”

“Yes. I returned to Bangkok yesterday and explained everything.”

“And?”

“She understands.”

“Does she?”

Declan looked down at his phone.

“I believe she does.”

Eleanor smiled.

“You sound very fond of her.”

He didn’t deny it.

“I am.”

His mother was quiet.

Then she said, “I’d like to meet her one day.”

Declan smiled.

“One day.”

“Not tomorrow. I’m not going to frighten the poor girl.”

He laughed.

“That’s considerate.”

“Don’t be sarcastic.”

“I’m not.”

Eleanor laughed. Then her voice became gentler.

“I’m happy for you, darling.”

He looked out of the window.

“Thank you, Mother.”

“And Declan?”

“Yes?”

“Don’t let your work make you careless with her feelings.”

His smile faded into something more thoughtful.

“I won’t.”

“I mean it. You have a habit of deciding what is best and expecting everyone to understand afterwards.”

He considered that. It wasn’t an unfair observation.

“I know.”

“Then be patient with her. Let her have her own opinions. Don’t overwhelm her simply because you’re used to getting things done quickly.”

Declan smiled again.

“I think she already has enough opinions for both of us.”

Eleanor laughed.

“Good. Then perhaps she’ll be able to manage you.”

Across the city, a little after nine, CC was sitting on the floor of her living room, sorting through a few things she had bought after work.

Her phone was propped against a cushion, playing a drama in the background. A message arrived.

Declan: What are you doing?

She glanced at the screen.

CC: Nothing important.

Declan: That sounds suspicious.

CC: I’m organising my things.

Declan: Should I be concerned?

CC: Why?

Declan: You said nothing important. I assumed you were doing something important.

She laughed.

CC: You’re confusing me.

Declan: I know.

She sent him a photograph of the small collection of skincare and stationery she had spread across the floor.

CC: Look.

Declan: That’s quite an operation.

CC: It is.

Declan: Do you need assistance?

CC: No.

Declan: Disappointing. I was prepared to offer executive-level support.

CC: Can you organise my drawers?

Declan: I can hire someone.

CC: That’s not the same.

He smiled at the message.

Declan: Then I’ll have to learn.

She laughed. A few minutes later, his name appeared on her screen. She answered.

“Hello.”

“Hello, sweetheart.”

CC smiled.

“Are you finished working?”

“For now.”

“That’s good.”

He heard the television in the background.

“Watching something?”

“Mm-hmm.”

“What?”

She told him the title. He listened as she explained the story, occasionally interrupting to ask about a character or point out a plot inconsistency.

“You haven’t watched it,” she accused.

“No.”

“Then how do you know?”

“Because you’ve told me enough to identify the problem.”

She laughed.

“It’s not a problem.”

“Then why are you defending it?”

“Because I like it.”

“Very well. I won’t interfere with your entertainment.”

“Thank you.”

He let the silence settle. Then he said, “I spoke to my mother today.”

CC turned slightly.

“Oh?”

“Yes.”

“About the photographs?”

“Among other things.”

She lowered the volume of the television.

“What did she say?”

“She was rather displeased.”

CC blinked.

“Why?”

“Because she believes someone attempted to use our family name to create an arrangement that neither of us had agreed to.”

She considered that.

“Your mother was upset?”

“Very.”

“Was she angry with Charlotte?”

“More with her family.”

CC nodded slowly. Declan continued.

“She likes Charlotte. That hasn’t changed. But she dislikes what her family did.”

“That’s understandable.”

“Yes.”

He paused.

“There’s something else.”

CC waited.

“I told her about you.”

Her eyes widened.

“Me?”

“Yes.”

“What did you tell her?”

“That your name is Cela Chanya, that you go by CC, and that you’re twenty-four.”

She stared at the phone.

“You told her all that?”

“I did.”

CC looked down at the cushion beside her.

“What did she say?”

“She asked whether you were kind.”

CC’s expression softened.

“What did you say?”

“That you were.”

A small smile appeared.

“And?”

“That you treated me well.”

She laughed.

“Did she ask anything else?”

“She wanted to know whether I liked you.”

CC became still.

“What did you say?”

“That I did.”

Her cheeks warmed. Declan’s voice was calm, almost casual.

“I didn’t think there was any reason to hide it.”

CC looked at the television, though she was no longer paying attention to it.

“Is she going to meet me?”

“Not unless you want her to.”

She smiled.

“Maybe one day.”

“One day. She also asked me not to overwhelm you,” he agreed.

CC laughed.

“That’s very thoughtful of her.”

“I thought so.”

“Do you listen to her?”

“Occasionally.”

“Declan.”

He smiled.

“I’ll make an effort.”

She shook her head. She was quiet. Then she said, “I’m glad you told her.”

He looked out at the Bangkok skyline.

“I’m glad too.”

“Does she know we’re…?”

“Getting to know each other seriously?”

CC smiled.

“Yes.”

“She does.”

There was a comfortable silence. Then she spoke again.

“Your mother sounds nice.”

“She can be.”

“Only sometimes?”

“She has a tendency to interfere.”

CC laughed.

“Then I think we might get along.”

Declan smiled.

“I suspect you will.”

In Munich, a little after four that afternoon, Eleanor stood in the doorway of Richard’s study. Her husband looked up from his papers.

“Have you spoken to Declan?”

“I have.”

“And?”

“He’s seeing someone.”

Richard removed his glasses.

“Someone?”

“A young woman named CC. She is Thai-Chinese, born in Canada, and works in entertainment.”

Richard regarded his wife.

“Is this serious?”

Eleanor smiled.

“Apparently.”

“Apparently?”

“He told me he wants to pursue her properly.”

Richard leaned back.

“That sounds like Declan.”

“Yes. Though I suspect this girl has already managed to make him considerably less predictable.”

Richard gave a small laugh.

“Then she may be good for him.”

Eleanor walked farther into the room.

“I hope so.”

She sat opposite him and folded her hands.

“Richard, I want to make one thing clear. I don’t care how suitable Charlotte might have been on paper. What her family did was unacceptable.”

Richard nodded.

“I agree.”

“They tried to create a public impression that our son had chosen their daughter. They thought the family name would make it difficult for him to object.”

“Then they don’t know him very well.”

“No. They don’t.”

Eleanor’s expression became thoughtful.

“I wanted Declan to meet someone. I wanted him to have a life outside the company. But I don’t want a daughter-in-law who comes into our family through manipulation.”

Richard smiled.

“Then perhaps you should let him choose.”

“I intend to.”

She paused.

“Though I would still like to meet this CC.”

Richard laughed.

“I thought you said you weren’t going to interfere.”

“I said I wasn’t going to frighten her.”

“That’s not quite the same thing.”

Eleanor gave him a look. Richard returned to his papers, still smiling.

At twenty-five to eleven, Declan had just finished reading the day’s last report when a message appeared.

CC: Are you still awake?

He replied immediately.

Declan: Yes, sweetheart.

CC: I wanted to say good night.

A faint smile appeared.

Declan: You could have called.

CC: I thought you were busy.

Declan: I’m not too busy for you.

She sent a small heart. He looked at it. Then:

Declan: Good night, CC.

CC: Good night.

Declan: Sleep well.

CC: You too. And don’t work too late.

Declan: I’ll behave.

CC: I hope so.

He laughed. Then he set his phone down. The matter with the Weiss family would be dealt with. The photographs would eventually disappear from the headlines, and the speculation would move on to something else.

But the evening had left him with a different kind of certainty. He had told his mother about CC. He had told CC what he wanted.

And he had no intention of allowing someone else’s ambitions to interfere with something he was beginning to value.

His mother was no longer asking him to consider a suitable woman.

She was waiting to meet the woman he had chosen to pursue.
