And that, Declan thought, was a much better place to begin.

chapters.title: The Girl on His Screen
chapters.desc: CC sends Declan her festival stage and a teaser nobody outside her company has seen. His mother finds her poster, watches her sing, and asks him not to make her perform for their approval.
chapters.epigraph: “Am I important?”
chapters.content:
Declan Lincoln had watched CC perform before.

He had seen her at the Lincoln Foundation gala in Geneva, where she had stood beneath the ballroom lights with the kind of quiet confidence that made it difficult to look elsewhere. He had watched several of her older performances afterwards, partly out of curiosity and partly because he had wanted to understand the work behind the woman who had unexpectedly occupied so much of his attention.

He had seen her dance, sing, and interact with thousands of fans. He had watched interviews, concert clips, and a few behind-the-scenes videos that her fans had uploaded. But tonight was different.

Tonight, he was watching her as the man who had asked to court her. The distinction was surprisingly significant.

He was no longer curious about an accomplished performer. He was looking forward to seeing someone he liked, someone whose messages he had been checking between meetings, someone who had begun to occupy a familiar place in his daily routine.

And, perhaps most importantly, someone who had agreed to let him pursue her.

On Wednesday afternoon, his laptop was open on the coffee table in his apartment in Lehel. He had flown back from Bangkok that morning, landed in Munich at half past two, and sent Alexander on to the office without him. Declan had intended to review a report.

Instead, he was looking at a notification from CC.

CC: Are you still working?

He picked up his phone.

Declan: No. Why?

CC: Nothing.

Declan: That’s usually not how conversations begin.

CC: I just wanted to ask something.

Declan: Go ahead, sweetheart.

A few seconds passed.

CC: Are you free right now?

He glanced at the clock.

Declan: I am now.

CC: Really?

Declan: Would you like me to prove it?

CC: No need.

Then she sent him a link.

CC: Our performance from tonight was uploaded.

Declan opened it.

Declan: Should I watch it?

CC: If you want to.

He smiled.

Declan: I wouldn’t have asked if I didn’t.

CC: Okay.

Another message arrived.

CC: Don’t laugh at me.

His eyebrows lifted.

Declan: Why would I laugh at you?

CC: Just don’t.

He looked at the link again.

Declan: I’ll be a very serious audience.

CC: Good.

A moment later, she sent a small smiling sticker.

Declan put his phone down and opened the video.

It was BLUE HOUR’s set from a year-end music festival at Impact Arena, filmed two hours earlier. The performance began with a dark stage.

A low electronic beat filled the arena, followed by a gradual rise in the instrumental. Lights swept across the audience, revealing thousands of light sticks moving in unison. Then CC appeared.

She was positioned at the centre of the stage, wearing a fitted black performance outfit with silver detailing. Her hair was styled in loose waves, and the stage makeup made her eyes appear more defined. The camera moved closer as the music began. Declan leaned back against the sofa.

He had seen her in elegant dresses, casual clothes, and the occasional photograph where she looked as if she had just woken up. He was familiar with the soft, reserved woman who sometimes apologised for making a noise during their calls. This woman was different.

She moved with precision, her expressions changing naturally with the music. There was confidence in the way she held the stage, a quiet command that didn’t require exaggerated gestures.

When she sang, her voice was clear and controlled. When she danced, every movement seemed deliberate.

And when the camera focused on her during the chorus, she smiled directly into the lens. Declan watched more closely. He had known she was good.

He hadn’t quite understood how much of herself she gave to performing until he watched the entire stage without interruption.

The performance ended with a final formation. CC stood at the centre, breathing lightly, smiling as the audience erupted into cheers.

The camera caught her laughing at something one of the other members said. Declan’s mouth curved. He replayed the last thirty seconds. Then he watched the ending again. His phone vibrated.

CC: Did you watch?

He typed.

Declan: I did.

CC: And?

Declan: You were wonderful.

A pause.

CC: You’re just saying that.

Declan glanced at the screen.

Declan: I watched the entire performance, sweetheart. I think I’m qualified to give an opinion.

CC: Maybe you’re biased.

Declan: Undoubtedly.

She sent a laughing sticker.

Declan: But I can still recognise a good performance.

CC: Thank you.

He returned to the video.

Declan: The second chorus was particularly good.

CC: You noticed?

Declan: I was paying attention.

CC: What about the ending?

Declan: You looked happy.

There was a longer pause this time.

CC: I was.

Declan: It showed.

CC checked the message on her side, sitting in the dressing room with a towel around her shoulders.

She had expected him to say something nice. She hadn’t expected him to notice that particular detail. She typed:

CC: I really enjoyed tonight.

Declan: I could tell.

CC: The audience was very loud.

Declan: I noticed that too.

CC: Were you jealous?

Declan raised an eyebrow. He read the message again, then smiled.

Declan: Of the audience?

CC: Maybe.

Declan: Should I be?

CC: No.

Declan: Then I’m perfectly comfortable with them cheering for you.

He paused before adding:

Declan: Though I wouldn’t mind having you perform for me privately sometime.

On the other side of the world, CC stared at the message. Her cheeks warmed.

CC: What does that mean?

Declan: Exactly what it sounds like.

CC: You’re teasing me.

Declan: A little.

She sent him a small pout. He smiled at it.

Declan had just closed the performance video when another notification appeared. It was from CC.

CC: Wait.

CC: There’s something else.

She sent him a second link. This one went to the company’s private review page, with a password underneath.

This time, the thumbnail was a close-up of her face.

The background was dark, with a narrow beam of light falling across one side of her cheek. Her hair was pulled back, and she wore a simple white outfit with delicate silver accessories. Her expression was calm, almost distant. Across the thumbnail were the words: CELA — THE FIRST LIGHT Declan opened it. A short teaser began.

The screen was black for the first two seconds. Then a piano note sounded.

CC appeared in a quiet room filled with morning light. She stood near a large window, her back turned to the camera. The scene shifted to a close-up of her fingers touching the surface of a piano, then to her face as she slowly turned towards the lens. A voice-over began in Mandarin.

“Yǒuxiē guāng, bú shì wèile zhàoliàng shìjiè.”

Some light wasn’t meant to illuminate the world. The scene changed.

She walked through a corridor with sunlight falling across the floor. Another shot showed her sitting alone in a field, looking towards the horizon. The music grew slightly louder.

A few seconds of the solo track played, revealing a soft, delicate melody with a gentle beat underneath. Then the screen faded to black. CELA — THE FIRST LIGHT SOLO MUSIC VIDEO — COMING SOON Declan watched it twice. He understood why she had sent it.

The performance had been a group stage, something she shared with the other members of her team. This teaser was hers alone. He picked up his phone.

Declan: Is this your solo project?

CC: Yes.

Declan: The first one?

CC: My first solo music video.

Declan: When is it released?

CC: The teaser on Monday. The full video on the Wednesday after.

CC: Nobody outside the company has seen this yet.

Declan: Except me.

CC: Except you. Don’t screenshot it.

He looked at the teaser again.

Declan: Congratulations.

CC: Thank you.

Declan: I like the concept.

CC: Really?

Declan: Yes. It’s different from your usual performances.

CC: That’s what I wanted.

He paused the video on the frame where she stood beside the window.

Declan: The title is beautiful.

CC: You understand it?

Declan: I understand the words.

CC: But what do you think it means?

He considered the question.

Declan: That not everything meaningful needs to be seen by everyone.

There was no immediate reply. Declan watched the typing indicator appear and disappear. Finally:

CC: That’s actually quite close.

Declan: Then I must be improving.

CC: Maybe.

He smiled.

Declan: It’s in Mandarin.

CC: The whole song is.

Declan: The language you don’t have to think in.

The typing indicator appeared and stopped twice.

CC: You remembered that.

Declan: You told me over mango sticky rice. Tell me about it.

And she did. In Bangkok, CC was still in the dressing room at Impact Arena.

Most of the other members had already left, while the staff were packing equipment and collecting personal belongings.

She sat in front of the mirror, her performance makeup partially removed, holding her phone with both hands.

Declan had asked her about the music video, and she ended up explaining more than she usually did.

She told him that the solo project had been in development for months. The company wanted to give each member opportunities to explore individual artistic identities, and she had been interested in something quieter than her usual stage performances.

The concept was inspired by the idea of light that didn’t need to be loud to be noticed. She wanted the music video to feel intimate. Less like a performance.

More like someone opening a small window into a private part of herself.

Declan: Did you have much involvement in the concept?

CC: Quite a lot.

CC: I discussed the visual direction with the creative team and suggested some changes to the arrangement.

Declan: I thought you might.

CC: Why?

Declan: You seem like someone who has opinions about things she cares about.

She smiled.

CC: I do.

Declan: I noticed.

CC: Is that a bad thing?

Declan: Not at all. I prefer people who know what they want.

She read the message. Then she sent him a photograph of the teaser poster.

It showed her standing beneath a pale sky, with the title placed in small lettering near the bottom.

CC: This is the official poster.

Declan enlarged the image. He studied it carefully.

“Beautiful,” he murmured.

Then he typed:

Declan: I like this one even more.

CC: Why?

Declan: You look peaceful.

CC: That’s the feeling I wanted.

Declan: Then it worked.

She smiled at the screen. A staff member approached to remind her that the car was ready. CC nodded and began putting her things away. Before leaving, she sent him one more message.

CC: I hope you’ll watch the full video when it comes out.

Declan replied almost immediately.

Declan: I’ll be waiting for it.

CC: Even with your meetings?

Declan: I can make time.

CC: You say that now.

Declan: Sweetheart, I have already rearranged an entire evening to watch you sing. I think you can trust me on this.

She laughed.

CC: Okay.

Declan: Get home safely.

CC: I will.

Declan: And remove your makeup before you fall asleep.

CC stared at the screen.

CC: How do you know I’m going to be sleepy?

Declan: Because you always become quiet when you’re tired.

She smiled.

CC: You’re observant.

Declan: Only when it concerns you.

She put her phone down, but the smile remained.

On Thursday, CC arrived at the company earlier than usual.

The building was already busy. Staff members were moving between the offices, the creative department was preparing materials for the solo release, and a few members of the marketing team were reviewing the promotional schedule.

AVEN ENT had been investing heavily in its artists’ individual identities while expanding its regional music distribution. BLUE HOUR was its most successful act, and the solo project was meant to introduce a different side of her. P’Nicha was waiting outside the meeting room.

“You look happy.”

CC glanced at her.

“Nice to see you as well.”

“Good morning. Now answer my question.”

“What question?”

“Why are you smiling?”

“I’m not.”

Nicha looked at her face.

“CC.”

“What?”

“Your mouth is literally doing it.”

CC pressed her lips together. Nicha laughed.

“Was it him?”

CC picked up the folder in her hands.

“Can we go inside?”

“That’s a yes.”

“P’Nicha.”

“Fine, fine.”

They entered the meeting room. The creative director was already there, along with two members of the marketing team. A large screen displayed the teaser poster and the release timeline.

The team discussed the promotional plan, the short-form video content, and the media schedule. CC listened carefully, occasionally offering suggestions.

When the discussion moved to the teaser’s social media caption, she raised a small concern about how the concept was being described.

“I think we should avoid making it sound too dramatic. The song is quite gentle. I’d prefer the caption to feel simple,” she said.

The creative director nodded.

“That’s reasonable. What would you suggest?”

CC considered it.

“Maybe something about finding a little light in ordinary moments. Not something too grand.”

The marketing executive typed it down.

“That’s good. We’ll develop a few options around that.”

Nicha watched her with a smile. CC was always polite, but when it came to creative work, she became more certain. She knew what she wanted to express and was willing to explain why. The meeting continued.

When it ended, Nicha walked beside her towards the elevator.

“By the way,” she said casually, “the poster is getting good reactions.” The company had put it up at eight that morning, CELA — THE FIRST LIGHT and a date, nothing else.

CC nodded.

“That’s nice.”

“Your solo project is attracting attention.”

“It’s only a poster.”

“Still.”

Nicha glanced at her.

“And I hear someone in Munich has already seen the teaser. Before our own board did.”

CC looked straight ahead.

“He said he liked it.”

Nicha smiled.

“Very professional.”

CC turned towards her.

“P’Nicha.”

“What? I’m happy for you.”

CC shook her head, but she was smiling again.

In Munich, at a quarter to three, Declan was reviewing a proposal when Alexander came in.

“Sir, the marketing team has sent the final version of the regional campaign proposal.”

“Leave it there.”

Alexander placed the folder on the desk. He then noticed the laptop screen.

The paused video showed a young woman standing in a sunlit room. He recognised her.

“Miss Chanya’s teaser?”

Declan glanced up.

“Yes.”

Alexander nodded politely.

“The poster went up this morning. It’s doing well.”

“It’s well done.”

Alexander allowed himself a smile.

“Would you like me to bring the AVEN partnership review forward, sir? It could be done in person.”

Declan looked at him.

“Why?”

“For thoroughness, sir.”

“It’s scheduled for January.”

“Yes, sir.”

Declan returned to the document. Alexander waited.

Then, with the discretion of someone who knew precisely when to stop speaking, he said, “I understand.”

Declan looked up again.

“Understand what?”

“Nothing, sir.”

A faint smile appeared.

“Good.”

Alexander left. Declan returned to the video. He had watched it several times since the previous evening.

There was something appealing about seeing her work outside the context of their conversations. He was beginning to understand the difference between the woman who sent him photographs of her breakfast and the performer who stood before an audience of thousands. They weren’t different people. They were different parts of the same woman. And he liked both. His phone vibrated.

CC: What are you doing?

Declan: Working.

CC: Did you watch the teaser again?

He reread the message. Then at the paused screen.

Declan: Why?

CC: I just wanted to know.

He smiled.

Declan: I did.

CC: How many times?

Declan considered lying. Then decided against it.

Declan: Several.

CC sent a laughing sticker.

CC: You’re exaggerating.

Declan: Would you like me to send you the viewing history?

CC: No!

He laughed.

Declan: Then don’t accuse me of exaggerating.

CC: You’re very competitive.

Declan: Only when necessary.

CC: Watching my teaser isn’t a competition.

Declan: It is if you’re trying to prove I haven’t watched it enough.

She sent another sticker. He looked at it, smiling. Then typed:

Declan: I like seeing you do something you’re proud of.

Her reply came more slowly.

CC: I’m proud of this one.

Declan: You should be.

CC: Thank you.

He put the phone down, but a moment later picked it up again.

Declan: Eight o’clock on Wednesday, Bangkok time?

CC: Yes. Why?

He checked his calendar. Wednesday. He would be in New York by then.

The time difference meant the release would happen early in the morning for him. He typed:

Declan: I’ll watch it.

CC: You don’t have to wake up early.

Declan: I wasn’t planning to sleep through it.

CC: Declan.

Declan: CC.

She laughed at the screen.

CC: Fine. But don’t complain if you become sleepy.

Declan: I’ll take responsibility.

At ten to four, a message arrived from his mother.

Eleanor: I saw the photograph you sent me.

He frowned slightly. He hadn’t sent her anything. A second message arrived.

Eleanor: The young woman. CC.

He looked at the conversation. Then he understood. His mother had evidently found the official poster through the company’s social media account.

Declan: You found her already?

Eleanor: I didn’t go looking for her.

Eleanor: Your father showed me the company’s announcement.

Declan smiled.

Declan: Of course.

Eleanor: She’s very pretty.

He glanced at the poster again.

Declan: She is.

Eleanor: And the project looks lovely. Is she the one singing?

Declan: Yes.

Eleanor: I also found a clip of her singing. From last night, I think.

Declan raised an eyebrow.

Declan: You watched it?

Eleanor: I wanted to hear her voice.

A moment later:

Eleanor: She has a beautiful voice.

Declan leaned back. He liked that his mother had taken the time to look.

Declan: I’ll tell her you said that.

Eleanor: Don’t embarrass me.

Declan: I wouldn’t dream of it.

Eleanor: Declan.

Declan: Yes, Mother?

Eleanor: Please don’t let her think she has to impress us.

His face softened.

Declan: I won’t.

Eleanor: Good. I want to meet the girl you’re fond of, not someone who feels she has to perform for our approval.

He checked the message. Then he replied.

Declan: I think you’ll like her.

Eleanor: I hope so.

Declan called CC as soon as his last meeting ended, at twenty past five. In Bangkok it was nearly half past eleven. She answered on the fourth ring.

“Hello?”

“Hello, sweetheart.”

“Are you finished?”

“For tonight.”

“Good.”

He heard a little rustling on her end.

“What are you doing?”

“Getting ready for bed.”

“Already?”

“It’s late.”

He smiled.

“Very responsible.”

“Unlike someone.”

“I’m improving.”

She laughed. He settled into the sofa.

“My mother has seen your poster. And a clip of last night’s stage.”

CC went quiet.

“Your mother?”

“Yes.”

“What did she say?”

“She liked it.”

CC blinked.

“Really?”

“She said you have a beautiful voice.”

A small smile appeared on her face.

“That’s very kind of her.”

“I thought you’d like to know.”

“Thank you for telling me.”

He could hear her smiling.

Then she went quiet. “Which part of the stage?”

“She didn’t say. Someone had posted a clip.”

“Your mother watched me dance.”

“I suspect she’ll watch the rest.”

CC laughed.

“Your mother is curious.”

“She is.”

“Does she always ask you about everything?”

“Only the things she considers important.”

CC became quiet.

Then, in a softer voice, “Am I important?”

Declan’s expression changed. He hadn’t expected the question. He leaned back, looking towards the ceiling before answering.

“Yes, sweetheart.”

There was no teasing in his voice.

“You are.”

CC was quiet on the other end. He continued.

“I wouldn’t be telling my mother about you if you weren’t.”

She smiled to herself.

“Okay.”

“Okay?”

“Mm-hmm.”

He laughed.

“That’s all?”

“What else do you want me to say?”

“Perhaps that you’re pleased.”

She laughed.

“I’m pleased.”

“Good.”

A pause followed.

Then she said, “I wish you could watch the full music video with me.”

Declan glanced at the clock.

“I’ll be in New York by then. I fly tonight.”

“I know.”

“But I can watch it when it’s released.”

“It’s early there.”

“I’ll manage.”

She hesitated.

“You’ll be tired in all your meetings.”

“Then they’ll be shorter. Everyone wins.”

She was quiet. Then she said, “Okay. I’ll send you the link when it’s out.”

“I’ll be waiting.”

“Don’t fall asleep.”

“I’ll do my best.”

She laughed. He listened to her for a few seconds, enjoying the sound.

Then he said, “May I send something to your apartment? It isn’t flowers.”

“What is it?”

“Executive-level support.”

She started laughing. “The drawers.”

“Assembly not required.”

“Declan.”

“Is that a yes?”

“Fine. Yes.”

“Good night, sweetheart.”

“Good night, Declan.”

“And CC?”

“Yes?”

“I’m looking forward to seeing the full version.”

Her voice softened.

“I hope you like it.”

“I already know I will.”

She smiled. After they ended the call, Declan remained on the sofa for a while. He opened the teaser again.

The screen returned to the first shot: CC standing beside the window, her face turned slightly away from the camera.

He watched it once more. He had seen her perform before they became acquainted. He had admired her talent before he knew what she liked to eat, how she sounded when she was sleepy, or how she smiled when he called her sweetheart.

But now, watching her on the screen, he noticed things that had nothing to do with the choreography or the camera work. He noticed the confidence in her eyes. The restraint in her expressions.

The quiet sincerity that seemed to remain even when she was performing for thousands of people.

And he smiled at the thought that, after all those lights and cameras, she would eventually return home, wash her face, put on comfortable clothes, and perhaps send him a photograph of whatever she had for dinner. His phone lit up once more.

CC: I forgot to tell you something.

He replied.

Declan: What is it?

CC: Thank you for watching.

He read the message. Then typed:

Declan: Thank you for letting me see it.

A few seconds later, she sent a small heart. Declan put his phone down. He had watched CC perform before.

But this was the first time he had watched her knowing that, somewhere behind the stage lights, the woman he was courting was waiting to hear what he thought.

He wanted to be there for all of it: the performances, the beautiful moments she shared with the world, and the quiet ones she didn’t.

chapters.title: The Things He Sent Her
chapters.desc: Two days before her teaser, flowers fill AVEN’s reception, followed by a cardigan, pearl earrings and a basket with mangoes in it. On Sunday morning she sees him at home, in a sweater.
chapters.epigraph: “Wear them because you like them. Not because I sent them.”
chapters.content:
By Friday morning, Cela Chanya had begun to suspect that her calendar was personally offended by the concept of free time.

Her solo project was no longer just a music video waiting to be released. It had become a full promotional campaign, carefully planned by AVEN ENT to introduce CELA as an artist in her own right, not only as one quarter of BLUE HOUR. The schedule was ambitious.

A recorded entertainment show on Monday. A radio interview on Tuesday. A filmed conversation with a music producer on Wednesday. Two magazine interviews, one digital cover shoot, a podcast appearance, and a guest invitation for a variety programme that wanted her to participate in a cooking segment.

There was also a discussion about a possible reality show appearance. CC had read the proposal twice. Then she looked at Nicha.

“Cooking?”

Her manager, seated across the conference table, nodded.

“They think it would be interesting.”

“I don’t think they know what they’re asking for.”

Nicha smiled. “You can cook.”

“I can cook when nobody is watching.”

“That’s precisely why they want to watch.”

CC lowered her eyes to the schedule again. She was dressed in a cream cardigan and dark trousers, her hair tied loosely behind her head. A pen rested between her fingers as she studied the arrangements.

“Will the podcast be recorded in the studio?”

“Yes. It’s a music and lifestyle podcast. They want to talk about your solo project, your creative process, and your life outside the group.”

“That’s fine.”

“And the reality show is only a guest appearance. One episode. They’re still discussing the concept.”

CC nodded, making a small note beside the programme.

She wasn’t nervous about the interviews. She had been performing in front of cameras for years, and she knew how to handle questions. But this campaign would be different. There would be more conversations about herself, her own music, her thoughts, and the things she usually kept private. It was a little frightening. Not unpleasantly so. Just unfamiliar. Nicha watched her.

“You’re thinking about something.”

“I’m thinking about whether I should prepare answers for the question about why I chose the title.”

“You’ve already answered that question in three interviews.”

“They might ask differently.”

“Then answer differently.”

CC looked up.

Nicha leaned back in her chair, smiling. “You don’t have to make every answer perfect, you know.”

“I know.”

“You say that, but your face says otherwise.”

CC gave her a small, unconvincing smile. Her phone vibrated beside the schedule.

Declan: Good morning, sweetheart.

She glanced at the screen, and the corners of her mouth softened almost immediately.

CC: Good morning.

Declan: Have you started working?

CC: Meeting about promotion.

Declan: How is it going?

She looked at the crowded schedule.

CC: I think they are trying to make me live at the company.

His response came almost immediately.

Declan: An ambitious proposal. Have they at least offered you a comfortable room?

She laughed.

CC: No. Just more cameras.

Declan: Then I shall have to object.

CC: You can’t object to my company’s schedule.

Declan: I can object to anything I dislike. Whether people listen is another matter.

CC shook her head, smiling at the screen. Nicha, who had been pretending not to watch, finally spoke.

“Mr. Lincoln?”

CC’s fingers stopped.

“How did you know?”

“Because you only look at your phone like that when it’s him.”

“Like what?”

“Like someone just gave you a present.”

CC put her phone away. Nicha laughed.

“I’m not teasing you. I’m happy you’re happy.”

CC looked back at the schedule, though her expression had become noticeably lighter. A moment later, her phone vibrated again.

Declan: What time will you finish today?

CC: I’m not sure. Probably late afternoon.

Declan: Eat lunch.

CC: I will.

Declan: That was suspiciously quick.

CC: I promise.

Declan: Very well. I’ll believe you for now.

She put the phone away, unaware that a few thousand kilometres away, Declan was already considering how to make her upcoming week a little more enjoyable.

In New York, at twenty to eleven that morning, Declan Lincoln was in the middle of a discussion about the group’s European expansion when his phone lit up. He had landed from Munich the evening before.

He didn’t usually look at personal messages during meetings.

Alexander Weber, seated to his right, had learned that there were only a handful of exceptions. CC was one of them.

Declan glanced down. Home. I ate lunch. AND dinner. Report complete. He returned the phone to the table.

“Mr. Lincoln?”

The director across from him had paused. Declan looked up.

“Continue.”

The meeting resumed. His attention remained entirely on the presentation, but there was a faint difference in his expression. Alexander noticed it, as he had begun noticing many things lately.

The chairman had always been efficient. He had also always been difficult to read.

Now, every so often, there was a private amusement in his eyes that hadn’t been there before.

When the meeting ended, Alexander followed him into the adjoining office.

“Your afternoon appointments have been confirmed,” he said, handing over the revised schedule.

Declan glanced through it.

“Good.”

Alexander waited.

Declan looked up. “Something else?”

“I received the information regarding Ms. Chanya’s solo promotion schedule.”

Declan’s eyes returned to him.

“From whom?”

“Your request to have the public campaign schedule monitored. Her company released the promotional outline this morning.”

Declan nodded once.

“Send flowers to her company tomorrow. She has the final review there before the teaser.”

Alexander had anticipated something of the sort.

“What arrangement would you prefer?”

“Something substantial, but not ridiculous.”

Alexander’s expression remained professional.

“May I ask what you consider ridiculous?”

Declan looked at him. Alexander lowered his eyes to the tablet.

“I’ll arrange something tasteful.”

“Good. Have it delivered to her company. Include a note.”

“Of course.”

Declan returned to the document in his hand, then added, almost casually, “And find out whether she has everything she needs for the promotional week.”

Alexander looked up.

“Everything?”

“Wardrobe, travel arrangements, meals between recordings. Whatever is appropriate. Don’t interfere with her company’s work. I don’t want to make things difficult for her.”

“Understood.”

“And don’t send anything to her home without asking.”

“Certainly.”

Declan turned a page.

“She’s going to be busy.”

Alexander nodded. There was a brief silence.

“I would prefer that she enjoy it,” said Declan.

Alexander allowed himself the smallest pause.

“I’ll see to it, sir.”

On Saturday, two days before the teaser release, CC was at the company for a final promotional review.

The teaser itself had already been completed. The digital team was preparing the official posts, the press materials, and the scheduled release across multiple platforms.

The campaign’s visual identity remained consistent with the music video: soft light, muted colours, and a quiet atmosphere.

CC sat beside the creative director, watching the final cut on a large screen. The opening piano note played.

The camera moved through the sunlit room. Her fingers rested on the piano keys. A corridor appeared, washed in pale afternoon light. Then the field. Then her voice.

Yǒuxiē guāng, bú shì wèile zhàoliàng shìjiè.

Some light wasn’t meant to illuminate the world. The screen faded into the title. CELA — THE FIRST LIGHT CC watched until the screen went dark.

“Good,” she said.

The creative director smiled. “You’re happy with it?”

“I am.”

“Any changes?”

She considered it before shaking her head.

“No. I think it’s ready.”

Nicha, seated behind them, checked her phone.

“Speaking of ready…”

CC turned.

“What?”

“Someone has sent something for you.”

“Who?”

Nicha looked at her with an expression that immediately made CC suspicious.

“Your very generous gentleman.”

CC blinked.

“My what?”

Nicha stood up. “Come and see.”

She followed her manager out of the review room and into the reception area.

There, near the front desk, stood an arrangement of flowers so large that several employees had gathered around it.

It was composed of white garden roses, pale pink peonies, soft cream ranunculus, and delicate greenery. The arrangement was elegant rather than overly colourful, placed in a wide ivory vase with a small card attached. CC stopped walking. She looked at it.

“That’s…”

“Yours,” Nicha said.

CC approached slowly, reading the card.

For your first light.

May the world see what I’ve already had the pleasure of discovering.

I’m proud of you, sweetheart.

— Declan

Her cheeks warmed. Nicha watched her read it.

“Well?”

CC looked at her.

“It’s very beautiful.”

“That’s all?”

“What else should I say?”

“That your admirer has apparently decided ordinary bouquets are beneath him.”

CC looked back at the flowers.

“They’re really lovely.”

She reached out and touched one of the pale pink petals with her fingertip.

It was such a simple gesture that Nicha almost felt bad for teasing her. Almost.

“Do you want to take a picture?”

CC hesitated.

“Maybe.”

“Then stand beside it.”

“P’Nicha…”

“I’m only helping.”

CC gave her a helpless look, but eventually stood beside the arrangement while one of the staff members took a photograph. She didn’t send it to social media. She sent it to Declan.

CC: It arrived.

A few moments later, his reply appeared.

Declan: Do you like it?

CC: Very much. It’s beautiful.

Declan: Good.

CC: It’s also very big.

Declan: I was informed.

CC: I think the reception area has become a flower shop.

Declan: Then I hope the other flowers are not jealous.

She laughed.

CC: Thank you. Really.

Declan: You’re welcome, sweetheart.

CC: You didn’t have to do this.

Declan: Your reception desk would disagree. I’m told they’ve taken photographs.

She typed, deleted, and typed again.

CC: You’re spoiling me.

Declan: That was rather the idea.

CC: P’Nicha says you’ve decided ordinary bouquets are beneath you.

Declan: P’Nicha is very perceptive. Tell her I said so.

CC laughed again, and Nicha, standing a little distance away, looked entirely too pleased.

The flowers were only the beginning. A little after four, another delivery arrived at AVEN. It was a collection of carefully wrapped boxes.

There was a small leather case in a warm ivory shade, a delicate pair of pearl earrings, and a soft cashmere cardigan in the pale grey she wore in half her airport photographs.

There were also several boxes of sweets from a well-known patisserie, along with fresh fruit arranged in a neat basket. CC stared at the collection. Nicha looked at the delivery staff.

“Are we expecting more?”

The staff member checked his tablet.

“No, ma’am. These are all the items listed for Ms. Chanya.”

CC turned to Nicha.

“P’Nicha.”

“Yes?”

“Why is there so much?”

Nicha’s smile grew.

“I think you should ask the person who sent them.”

CC picked up the card.

For the long days ahead. Something comfortable, something pretty, and something sweet.

You don’t have to use any of it. I thought you might like them.

Declan.

She looked at the cardigan first. It was beautiful. The fabric looked impossibly soft, and the colour was exactly the sort of shade she tended to choose.

The earrings were delicate, too. Not the sort of jewellery that demanded attention, but something she could wear with almost anything. She touched the leather case.

“It’s too much,” she murmured.

Nicha leaned against the counter.

“Did he ask you to wear all of them at once?”

CC looked up.

“No.”

“Then perhaps you can enjoy them one at a time.”

CC bit back a smile. She picked up her phone.

CC: Declan.

Declan: That sounds serious.

CC: I received another delivery.

Declan: I hope everything arrived safely.

CC: There are so many things.

Declan: There are only a few.

CC: A few?

Declan: I exercised restraint.

CC laughed, looking down at the boxes.

CC: You have a very unusual understanding of restraint.

Declan: You should see what I didn’t send.

CC: The cardigan is beautiful.

Declan: I thought you might like it.

CC: And the earrings. And the sweets. And the fruit.

Declan: I wasn’t certain what you would feel like eating, so I arranged a few things.

She looked at the basket again. There were mangoes. Of course there were mangoes. Her face softened.

CC: You remembered.

Declan: You ordered it twice in one week. I notice patterns.

She stared at the message. It wasn’t elaborate. He hadn’t written anything poetic or dramatic. But somehow, that made it more effective.

CC: Thank you. I really like everything.

Declan: That’s all I wanted.

She hesitated, then sent another message.

CC: I wish you were here.

In New York it wasn’t yet five in the morning.

His reply came two hours later, the first thing he did when he woke.

Declan: So do I, sweetheart.

CC held the phone close to her chest for a brief moment before putting it down. Nicha had noticed. She said nothing. For once.

On Sunday evening, the night before the teaser release, CC was at home, sitting on the sofa with her legs tucked beneath her.

The cardigan Declan had sent was draped over her shoulders.

She had spent most of the day preparing for the week ahead. Her interview notes were organised, her wardrobe fittings confirmed, and her manager had sent her the final schedule. It was going to be a demanding week. She was looking forward to it. Her phone rang. Declan. She answered immediately.

“Hello?”

“Good evening, sweetheart.”

“It’s morning there.”

“It’s evening where you are. I’m being polite.”

She laughed and looked properly at the screen.

It was twenty to eight on a Sunday morning in New York, and Declan was sitting at a kitchen counter she had never seen, in a grey sweater, his hair still damp and not combed into anything. A cup of coffee stood at his elbow. She had seen him in a tuxedo, in a charcoal suit, in a navy travel suit with no tie. She had never seen him look like someone’s Sunday.

“You’re not wearing a suit.”

“It’s Sunday.”

“I didn’t know you owned other clothes.”

“I own a great many things you don’t know about.”

She studied him. “You look different.”

“Better or worse?”

“Younger.”

“I’ll take that.”

She glanced down at the cardigan.

“I’m wearing it.”

“I can see that.”

“Did you sleep?”

“Seven hours. Someone in Bangkok keeps telling me it’s important.”

“Because you never do it.”

“Because you worry.”

CC looked away, a little embarrassed by how easily he had said it. Declan watched her.

“Is the cardigan comfortable?”

“Very.”

“Good.”

She ran her fingers over the soft sleeve.

“It’s really nice. I think I’ll wear it a lot.”

“I’d be pleased if you did.”

“You’re going to make me feel guilty if I don’t wear everything.”

“Then don’t.”

She looked back at him.

“Don’t?”

“Wear them because you like them. Not because I sent them.”

His tone was calm, without the slightest hint of expectation. CC smiled.

“I know.”

“Good.”

She was quiet before asking, “Are you going to watch the teaser tomorrow?”

“Of course.”

“It’s only a short teaser.”

“I know.”

“You’ve already watched it several times.”

“I have.”

She laughed.

“Then you know what happens.”

“I know what happens in the video. I haven’t seen the world react to it yet.”

“That’s different?”

“Very.”

He leaned back slightly.

“Tomorrow is important to you. I want to see it when it happens.”

CC looked at him, her expression becoming gentler.

“It’s not the full music video yet.”

“I know, sweetheart.”

“The full one is next Wednesday.”

“And I haven’t forgotten.”

“You’ll be in New York.”

“I’ll make time.”

She tilted her head.

“You have meetings.”

“I also have a phone.”

She laughed.

“That’s not what I meant.”

“I know what you meant.”

He watched her smile, then added, “I’ll be there in whatever way I can.”

She didn’t answer immediately. There was something reassuring about the way he said it. He made no promise to rearrange the world around her, only that he intended to show up.

“Thank you,” she said.

Declan’s expression softened.

“You don’t need to thank me for being interested in something that matters to you.”

CC looked down at the sleeve of the cardigan.

“Still.”

He let the silence settle between them. Then his eyes moved over her face.

“You look lovely tonight.”

She blinked.

“I’m wearing a cardigan.”

“I noticed.”

“And no makeup.”

“I noticed that, too.”

“Then?”

“Then you’re lovely.”

Her lips curved before she could stop them.

“Declan.”

“Yes, sweetheart?”

“You’re very good at this.”

“At what?”

“Making me smile.”

His smile was slow and unhurried.

“I’m glad.”

She tucked her hair back.

“I should sleep early. Tomorrow will be busy.”

“Then I won’t keep you.”

“Are you going to work all day?”

“Only some of it.”

“Promise?”

He raised an eyebrow.

“Are you making me promise again?”

“Yes.”

“Very well. I promise.”

She smiled with satisfaction.

“Good night, Declan.”

“Good night, sweetheart.”

He waited until she had ended the call before setting his phone down. It rang again almost at once. Alexander didn’t believe in Sundays.

“The deliveries were all signed for, sir.”

“I know. She wore the cardigan.”

There was a pause on the line. “May I say something, sir?”

“Go ahead.”

“You’ve been rather generous this week.”

“Have I?”

Alexander had worked for him long enough to recognise that particular tone. “Yes, sir.”

“Then I suppose I should be careful. Have the flowers at her company refreshed on Wednesday. Something smaller. And no more deliveries unless she asks for something.” Declan looked at the dark screen of his phone.

“Understood.”

Alexander rang off sounding amused. On Monday, at eight in the evening, the teaser went live.

CC stood in a small viewing room with Nicha, the creative director, and several members of the digital team. The official countdown reached zero. Then the video appeared. The first piano note played. The room became quiet.

CC watched the screen, her hands loosely clasped in front of her. Even though she had seen the teaser countless times during editing, the moment it was finally released to the public felt different.

It no longer belonged only to her and the people who had worked on it. It belonged to everyone who chose to watch. The final title appeared. CELA — THE FIRST LIGHT Then the screen faded. Nobody spoke. Then Nicha turned to her.

“Congratulations.”

CC smiled.

“Thank you.”

The digital team began checking the release across platforms. The first comments appeared almost immediately. Fans praised the cinematography, the music, and the softer image of CELA. Some expressed surprise at how different the solo concept felt from her group performances.

CC read a few comments, her expression gradually brightening. Then her phone vibrated.

Declan: I watched it.

She smiled.

CC: Already?

Declan: I was waiting.

CC: What did you think?

His reply came after a short pause.

Declan: I liked it the first time you showed me. I like it even more now that I know it’s yours.

She read it twice. Another message appeared.

Declan: You should be proud of yourself, sweetheart.

CC studied the screen, then at the teaser playing silently on the monitor behind her.

CC: I am.

Declan: Good.

CC: Thank you for watching.

Declan: I wouldn’t have missed it.

A moment later, another message arrived.

Declan: And I hope the flowers weren’t too much.

She laughed.

CC: Declan.

Declan: Yes?

CC: The flowers were beautiful. The gifts were beautiful. Everything was beautiful.

Declan: Then I seem to have made the right decisions.

CC: You did.

Declan: I’m pleased.

She looked at the growing number of notifications on the company’s screen. The teaser was beginning to circulate beyond her usual fan community. Several entertainment accounts had already shared it.

She felt a small, unfamiliar mixture of excitement and nervousness.

Then she glanced at the cardigan folded over the back of her chair, the earrings resting safely in their box inside her bag, and the photograph of the enormous bouquet that Nicha had taken earlier. Declan had been thousands of kilometres away.

Yet somehow, he had found a way to make the day feel as if someone had been standing beside her celebrating. Her phone vibrated once more.

Declan: One more thing.

CC: What?

Declan: When the full music video is released on Wednesday, I expect to be informed immediately.

She smiled.

CC: You already know the date and time.

Declan: I do. I’m merely making sure you haven’t forgotten to tell me.

CC: I won’t forget.

Declan: I’ll hold you to it, sweetheart. In person, eventually.

Her cheeks warmed. She looked around the room to make sure nobody was watching her screen. Unfortunately, Nicha was watching her face.

“Is he congratulating you?”

CC locked her phone.

“Yes.”

“And?”

“He liked the teaser.”

Nicha smiled.

“Of course he did.”

CC tried to return her attention to the team, but the small smile remained.

For Declan, it had been a simple thing: flowers, a few thoughtful gifts, and a promise to watch.

For CC, it was the accumulation of all those little gestures. The fact that he remembered what she liked. That he had paid attention to the schedule. That he wanted her to be comfortable during a demanding week. That he celebrated something important to her without making it about himself.

She was beginning to understand that being spoiled by Declan Lincoln didn’t always mean receiving expensive things.

Sometimes it meant being remembered in the middle of his busiest day.

And sometimes, it meant looking at a phone screen in a crowded company office and smiling because a man on the other side of the world had somehow made her feel less alone.

Across the world, in New York, Declan opened the teaser once more.

He watched the final shot of her sitting in the field, sunlight falling gently across her face.

Then he closed the video and returned to his work. His phone remained beside his hand. He had a meeting in twelve minutes. But for the moment, he was perfectly content.

His sweetheart’s first light had finally reached the world.

And he had every intention of being there to see what came after.

chapters.title: When the Light Finally Appeared
chapters.desc: THE FIRST LIGHT comes out at eight o’clock in Bangkok. In New York, Declan watches it at eight in the morning, then watches her live, and tells her the song suits her.
chapters.epigraph: “I think you made something very honest.”
chapters.content:
On Wednesday, by seven thirty-five in the evening, CC had checked her phone four times. She wasn’t uncertain about the release.

The music video had been finalised weeks ago. The audio had been mastered, the colour grading approved, the subtitles checked, and every promotional detail arranged. There was nothing left for her to change. Still, tonight felt different.

She was sitting in a small private room at AVEN ENT, wearing a soft ivory blouse and a pale grey skirt. Her hair fell loosely over her shoulders, and her makeup was understated. A stylist had finished touching up her appearance earlier, but CC had asked to keep everything natural.

On the table in front of her sat a bottle of water, her phone, and a small plate of cut mango and strawberries that had arrived at six with no card. At AVEN, lately, no card meant only one person.

Nicha was reviewing the livestream setup with the digital team.

“Your live starts at eight-thirty. Thirty minutes after the music video goes public,” she reminded CC.

“I know.”

“Keep it relaxed. Talk about the filming, the song, the meaning behind it. Read some comments, but don’t feel like you have to answer everything.”

CC nodded.

“And after the live, we’ll record the short promotional videos. One about the meaning of the title, one about the lyrics, one behind-the-scenes clip, and a short message for the fans.”

“Right.”

Nicha glanced at her.

“Are you nervous?”

CC considered the question.

“A little.”

“That’s normal.”

“I think I’m more nervous about people misunderstanding the song.”

Nicha pulled a chair closer.

“Why would they?”

“Because it’s quite personal. I don’t want people to think it’s about one particular person or one particular experience.”

“Then explain what it means to you. You don’t have to explain every detail.”

CC nodded slowly. That was the part she had been thinking about.

The song wasn’t written about a romantic relationship. It wasn’t about losing someone, either. Its emotions came from something less specific and, perhaps, more difficult to explain: the feeling of being surrounded by people while struggling to understand oneself.

There were days when she felt tired without knowing how to describe it. Days when she wanted to be understood but didn’t know what she would say if someone asked what was wrong.

She had wanted the song to hold those feelings without making them sound hopeless. Her phone lit up.

Declan: Are you ready, sweetheart?

She smiled.

CC: I think so.

Declan: That’s a very convincing answer.

CC: I’m a little nervous.

Declan: You don’t need to be perfect tonight.

She reread the message.

CC: I know.

Declan: Let them hear what you wanted to say. That’s enough.

A moment later, another message arrived.

Declan: And remember to drink water before your live.

CC laughed.

CC: You sound like P’Nicha.

Declan: I shall take that as a compliment.

She put her phone down, feeling a little more settled. Across the room, Nicha noticed her expression.

“Mr. Lincoln?”

CC looked up.

“Maybe.”

Nicha smiled knowingly.

“Good. Keep him around. He seems useful.”

“P’Nicha.”

“What? He remembers your water.”

CC shook her head, smiling despite herself. At exactly eight o’clock in Bangkok, the music video went live.

In New York, it was eight o’clock in the morning.

Declan Lincoln was seated in his office, a cup of black coffee beside his laptop. His first meeting had been moved by fifteen minutes after he had made it clear that the adjustment was necessary. Alexander hadn’t asked why. He knew. Declan opened the official link. The screen turned dark. A piano note sounded. And then CC appeared.

Not the performer he had watched on a concert stage, surrounded by lights and dancers. Not the young woman who laughed at his teasing during their video calls. This was something quieter.

The camera showed her sitting near a window, sunlight resting across the floor. She looked out of the frame, almost as if she were listening to something nobody else could hear. The first verse began.

Wǒ bǎ chénmò cáng jìn le yè lǐ
bǎ méi shuō de huà liú gěi zìjǐ

I tucked my silence into the night,
and kept the words I couldn’t say.

Declan’s expression changed almost imperceptibly. He listened. The melody was gentle, but there was a sadness beneath it. Her voice didn’t reach for dramatic notes or force emotion into the words. It remained soft, almost conversational. The scene shifted.

CC walked down a long corridor. Light entered through the windows, falling across her face as she passed. The next lines appeared.

Rúguǒ wǒ yě céng hàipà tiānmíng
shìfǒu hái néng děngdào nà shù guāng láilín

If I was once afraid of morning,
could I still wait for the light to find me?

Declan leaned back slightly. He understood now why she had wanted the song to feel intimate. It wasn’t about sadness. It was about the exhaustion of carrying it.

The chorus began, and the arrangement opened with a gentle lift in the melody.

Qǐng ràng wǒ mànmàn xuéhuì hūxī
zài méiyǒu dá’àn de rìzi lǐ

Let me learn to breathe again,
even on the days without answers.

The camera moved through the field. CC sat among the grass, her face turned towards the sunlight. She wasn’t smiling, exactly, but she no longer looked. The final chorus came.

Yuánlái wēiguāng yě kěyǐ jiāndìng
búbì zhàoliàng zhěnggè shìjiè

Even a little light can remain steady,
it doesn’t have to illuminate the whole world.

The music faded. The screen remained on her face. Then the final title appeared. CELA — THE FIRST LIGHT Declan didn’t move immediately.

He watched the screen after the video ended, his eyes resting on the still image. Then he replayed the final minute.

He had understood it the first time. He wanted to hear it again.

Seventeen minutes later, Alexander came in with a folder.

“Mr. Lincoln, the ten o’clock meeting has been moved to the conference room.”

Declan nodded without looking away from his screen. Alexander glanced at the video.

“Has it been released?”

“Yes.”

“And?”

Declan paused the video.

“It’s very good.”

Alexander’s gaze shifted to him. It was a simple statement, but he knew his employer well enough to recognise when something had genuinely impressed him.

“I’m glad.”

Declan opened the official social media page. The comments were already multiplying.

Fans were praising the cinematography, the restrained arrangement, and the way the song allowed CC’s voice to carry the emotional weight without overwhelming the visuals.

Some were surprised by how different it sounded from her group’s music. Others were drawn to the lyrics. A few comments stood out.

Her voice sounds like someone telling you a secret.

The lyrics are so painfully gentle. I didn’t expect this kind of song from CELA.

The line about learning to breathe on days without answers... I wasn’t ready.

This feels like a song for people who are tired but don’t know how to explain why.

The music video is beautiful, but the lyrics are what stayed with me.

Declan read the last comment twice. He understood why it had stayed with people. The song didn’t ask anyone to be happy. It allowed them to be tired. His phone vibrated.

CC: It’s out.

He smiled.

Declan: I’ve watched it.

CC: What did you think?

He looked at the paused image of her in the field.

Declan: I think you made something very honest.

A few seconds passed.

Declan: The lyrics are beautiful, sweetheart. Especially the part about learning to breathe without having all the answers.

Her reply came quickly.

CC: That part is one of my favourites too.

Declan: I can see why.

CC: Does it feel too sad?

Declan considered his answer.

Declan: No. It feels sad, but it doesn’t leave me feeling hopeless.

He continued.

Declan: I think that’s what makes it beautiful. It doesn’t pretend the difficult days disappear. It simply suggests that they aren’t the only days waiting for you.

CC stared at the message. She hadn’t expected him to understand it quite that way.

CC: That’s exactly what I wanted.

Declan: Then you succeeded.

She smiled at the screen.

CC: Thank you for watching so quickly.

Declan: I told you I would.

Then another message appeared.

Declan: Now go and enjoy your evening. I believe you have a live appearance in thirteen minutes.

CC laughed.

CC: You’re keeping track?

Declan: It’s in my calendar. Between a board call and a budget review.

At half past eight in Bangkok, the livestream began.

CC sat in front of a simple backdrop featuring the key art for THE FIRST LIGHT. A small bouquet of pale flowers rested on a side table, and the lighting was warm and soft. She greeted the viewers with a smile.

“Hello, everyone. It’s been a while since I’ve done a live by myself.”

Comments flooded the screen.

CC!!!

Congratulations!

I just watched the MV!

Your voice is so beautiful.

The lyrics made me cry.

CC laughed.

“Thank you. I was a little nervous about releasing this song, so seeing everyone here makes me happy.”

She glanced at the comments.

“Did you enjoy the music video?”

More comments appeared.

YES.

The cinematography is so pretty.

The lyrics!!!

I love this version of you.

She smiled.

“I wanted the video to feel quiet. I didn’t want too many things happening at once. I wanted people to have time to listen to the music and look at the details.”

One comment caught her attention.

Is the song about heartbreak?

CC read it aloud.

“Is it about heartbreak?”

She thought.

“Not exactly. I think heartbreak can be part of it, but I didn’t write it about one specific relationship.”

She folded her hands in her lap.

“For me, it’s more about those moments when you feel a little lost. Sometimes you don’t know what you’re feeling, and you don’t necessarily have the words to explain it. You just continue doing what you need to do.”

She paused, considering how to phrase the next part.

“I wanted the song to remind people that it’s okay to take your time. You don’t always need to have an answer immediately.”

The comments moved quickly.

This is exactly how I’ve been feeling.

Thank you for making this.

I think I needed to hear that.

CC’s expression softened.

“I’m glad if it makes you feel understood, even just a little.”

Another comment appeared.

Why THE FIRST LIGHT?

She smiled.

“I think light is usually described as something big. Something that makes everything brighter. But I wanted to talk about a smaller kind of light.”

She looked towards the camera.

“Something that doesn’t have to change the whole world. Maybe it just helps you see where you’re standing.”

She laughed gently.

“That sounds a little philosophical, doesn’t it?”

The comment section filled with hearts. She continued answering questions about the recording process, the piano arrangement, and the field location. She explained that she had been involved in the creative direction and had worked closely with the music team to make sure the arrangement didn’t become too heavy.

When someone asked whether she had cried while recording, she smiled.

“Not while recording. But I did feel emotional when we listened to the final version together for the first time.”

Then she read another comment.

Your voice sounds different here.

CC nodded.

“I think I used a different approach. I didn’t want to sing too strongly. The song is quite personal, so I wanted it to feel as though I was talking to someone.”

She smiled again.

“Or maybe talking to myself.”

At that exact moment, in New York, Declan was watching the livestream on his laptop.

His meeting had been delayed by another five minutes.

He had informed Alexander that he would join remotely.

Alexander, who had learned not to question these things, arranged it.

Declan watched CC answer questions, occasionally smiling when she became amused by a comment. She looked comfortable. A little shy when people praised her. And increasingly animated when she explained the music.

He noticed that she touched the sleeve of her blouse whenever she was thinking. He had seen her do that during their conversations, too. A comment appeared on the screen.

CC, are you happy with the result?

She read it and nodded.

“I am. I think this is something I wanted to make for a long time.”

She paused.

“I’m very grateful that I had the chance to do it.”

Declan looked over. Then he sent a message.

Declan: You’re doing wonderfully.

CC’s phone was positioned just below the camera. She saw the notification while the digital staff were preparing the next question. She didn’t open it. But her smile changed. Just slightly. The livestream ended after approximately thirty-five minutes.

CC thanked everyone, waved at the camera, and watched as the digital team closed the session.

“Good job,” Nicha said.

CC exhaled.

“That was longer than I expected.”

“You did well.”

“Did I talk too much?”

“No.”

“Was I too serious?”

Nicha laughed.

“CC, you released a song about quiet emotional exhaustion. I think you were allowed to be serious.”

CC laughed, finally relaxing against the back of her chair.

The next part of the schedule began almost immediately. The team moved her to a different setup for a series of recorded promotional videos. The first was a short behind-the-scenes feature.

She sat in front of a monitor showing still photographs from the music video.

“During the filming, I wanted to make sure that the scenes felt natural. I didn’t want to act as though I was sad. I wanted to let the emotions come through in a quieter way,” she explained.

The second video focused on the lyrics. The producer asked her to choose a few lines and explain why they were important. CC looked at the lyric sheet.

“There’s one part I really like.”

She read it aloud:

Bǎ méi shuō de huà liú gěi zìjǐ.
I kept the words I couldn’t say.

She smiled.

“I think sometimes we don’t say things because we don’t know how. It’s not always because we don’t trust someone. Sometimes we just haven’t understood our own feelings yet.”

The producer nodded.

“And the line about learning to breathe?”

CC looked at the next line.

“That’s about giving yourself permission to be imperfect. You don’t have to understand everything immediately. You can still continue, even if you’re not completely okay.”

The third video was lighter. She was asked to share three things fans might not know about the filming process.

She mentioned that the field scene had been filmed early in the morning, that the piano in the music video wasn’t the instrument used for the final recording, and that she had almost laughed during one of the supposedly serious shots because a member of the production team had stumbled behind the camera. The crew laughed. CC covered her mouth.

“Please don’t use that part.”

The producer grinned.

“We’ll consider it.”

“That’s not reassuring.”

By the time the recorded content was finished, it was approaching ten o’clock.

There were still several short promotional messages to film, including a thank-you video for international fans and a clip introducing the next stage of her solo campaign. CC was tired, but her mood was good. She had expected the release to feel overwhelming. Instead, it felt strangely warm.

A little after ten, CC finally checked her messages properly while Nicha arranged for her car. There were several from Declan.

Declan: The live was lovely.

Declan: You explained the song very well.

Declan: I particularly liked your answer about not needing to understand everything immediately.

Then:

Declan: Are you finished?

CC smiled.

CC: Almost. We just finished the recorded videos.

Declan: Long evening.

CC: A little.

Declan: Did anyone make you sit down at any point?

She laughed under her breath.

CC: Twice. Once was for makeup.

Declan: I’ll take it.

CC: Did you really watch the whole live?

Declan: Every minute.

CC: You had work.

Declan: I still have work.

She shook her head.

CC: You shouldn’t let me distract you.

Declan: I don’t consider watching you work a distraction.

CC checked the message, then typed.

CC: You’re biased.

Declan: Entirely.

She laughed. Another message arrived.

Declan: I also saw the comments.

CC: There were so many.

Declan: People seem to have understood what you wanted to say.

CC: I’m happy about that.

Declan: You should be.

She paused.

CC: I was worried it might be too sad.

Declan: I told you. It isn’t hopeless.

Then:

Declan: And for what it’s worth, I think the song suits you.

She read the sentence again.

CC: Why?

Declan was quiet before replying.

Declan: Because there’s a gentleness to it, but it isn’t fragile. It doesn’t demand attention. It simply stays with you.

CC’s expression softened.

Declan: Rather like the person who made it.

She lowered her phone, smiling to herself. Nicha approached with her handbag.

“Car is ready.”

CC nodded, putting the phone away.

“Thank you.”

As she walked towards the exit, she glanced at the screen once more.

Declan: Get home safely, sweetheart. You’ve done enough for today.

She sent him one final message.

CC: Good night. Thank you for being there.

His reply arrived before she reached the car.

Declan: Always happy to be there for you.

In New York it was still Wednesday, a quarter to eight in the evening, and Declan was still at his desk.

The release hadn’t disrupted his day, though he had watched the music video twice more between meetings. Alexander entered with the day’s briefing.

“Mr. Lincoln, the marketing team has prepared the updated report for the Bangkok regional partnership.”

Declan nodded, taking the document. Alexander placed another folder on the desk.

“And congratulations to Ms. Chanya. The release appears to be receiving a very positive response.”

Declan glanced at him.

“You’ve seen it?”

“Only briefly.”

“Watch it properly when you have time.”

Alexander gave a small nod.

“I will.”

Declan opened the report, but his phone vibrated before he could begin reading. A photograph from CC.

It was a picture of her breakfast, taken at home. A small bowl of congee, a cup of tea, and a neatly folded napkin.

CC: I’m having breakfast before I leave for the company.

Declan smiled.

Declan: Excellent. A very promising development.

CC: Why does that sound like you’re reviewing my performance?

Declan: Because I am pleased with the results.

CC: Should I expect a quarterly report?

Declan: Only if breakfast keeps performing.

She sent him a laughing emoji. Then another message.

CC: I read some more comments this morning. People really liked the lyrics.

Declan: I’m not surprised.

CC: Some people said they listened to it when they couldn’t sleep.

Declan checked the screen.

Declan: Then I hope it gives them a little company.

CC replied with a small heart. He set the phone down, his expression still amused.

The song had been released to the world. People would interpret it in their own ways, attach their own memories to its lyrics, and perhaps find something familiar in its quiet sadness. That was what music did.

It allowed a person to say something personal without having to explain every part of it. Declan understood that now.

He had watched her sing about words left unsaid, about days without answers, about a light that didn’t need to illuminate the whole world.

And perhaps that was why the song had stayed with him.

Because, for all her public confidence, he was beginning to understand that CC had a private world she rarely invited people into. She had opened a small window.

And he was grateful she had allowed him to look through it.

He glanced once more at the paused music video on his screen. Then, with a smile, he returned to work.

There was still another recording, another interview, and an entire promotional week ahead of her.

Next week she would sing it again, live, with strings. He intended to hear it from wherever he was. Every small light she chose to share, he wanted to see.

chapters.title: The Distance Between Two Busy People
chapters.desc: The offers pour in and CC enjoys every one of them. What she misses is him in the room, and at midnight she finally says so. He finds four days.
chapters.epigraph: “I think I miss having you around.”
chapters.content:
By Thursday morning, fourteen hours after its release, THE FIRST LIGHT had brought more attention than CC had anticipated.

The music video had passed a number Nicha kept refreshing just to see it change. The song was being shared across different platforms, and several music reviewers had praised its understated production, emotional lyrics, and the contrast between CC’s familiar stage persona and the quieter identity she presented as a solo artist.

The response had also opened doors. Some of them had started opening on Monday, with the teaser.

A luxury skincare brand had approached AURELIA ENTERTAINMENT about a campaign. A jewellery house wanted to discuss a possible ambassadorship. Two fashion labels had requested meetings, while a premium lifestyle brand was interested in having her appear in a digital campaign.

There were also invitations to appear on a popular YouTube interview channel, a live studio performance programme, and a music podcast that featured artists discussing their creative process.

One YouTuber, known for inviting musicians to spend an afternoon talking about their lives and playing casual games, had specifically requested CC. Nicha placed another proposal on the table.

“And this one wants you to perform a live acoustic version of THE FIRST LIGHT.”

CC looked up.

“Really?”

“Yes. They’ve been watching the response to the music video. They think an intimate studio performance would suit you.”

CC read through the details. The studio was known for its excellent acoustics and minimalist visual style. The performance would be recorded in one take, with only a piano and a small string arrangement.

“I’d like to do this.”

“I thought you would.”

CC smiled.

“What about the YouTube interview?”

“Confirmed, if you’re happy with the date. They want to film next week.”

She nodded.

“And the skincare brand?”

“Their team wants to meet you tomorrow. They like your image and the response to your solo project.”

CC continued reading. It was a lot. But it was the kind of busy she enjoyed.

She liked talking about music. She liked visiting studios and discovering how other people worked. She enjoyed the slightly unpredictable nature of interviews, especially when the hosts were genuinely curious rather than asking the same promotional questions.

She also liked the possibility of working with brands whose creative direction she appreciated.

“Let’s consider the jewellery campaign carefully. I don’t want to accept something just because it’s a good offer,” she said.

Nicha smiled.

“That’s why I brought the proposals to you.”

CC placed the documents into separate piles.

“I’m excited.”

“I can tell.”

She looked at the schedule again.

“It’s going to be a busy month.”

“Very.”

CC nodded, still smiling. Her phone vibrated.

Declan: How is my hardworking girl today?

Her face softened immediately.

CC: Very busy.

Declan: I suspected as much.

CC: More offers came in.

Declan: Good ones, I hope.

CC: A lot of them. A skincare campaign, jewellery, fashion, YouTube interviews, a live studio performance.

Declan: Sounds like people are beginning to recognise what I’ve been telling you.

She smiled.

CC: That you’re biased?

Declan: That you’re talented.

CC laughed.

CC: I really want to do the studio performance.

Declan: Then you should.

CC: It’s a live acoustic version of The First Light.

Declan: I would very much like to hear that.

CC: I’ll send you the recording when it’s ready.

Declan: I would prefer to be there while you record it.

She paused.

CC: You can come?

His reply took a little longer.

Declan: Let me see what I can arrange.

She smiled at the screen, feeling a small flicker of hope.

Then Nicha called her attention back to the schedule.

“CC, we need to discuss tomorrow’s meeting.”

She put her phone down.

“Right.”

On Friday afternoon, the skincare brand meeting went well.

CC arrived at the company’s office with Nicha and two members of AURELIA’s management team. The brand representatives were welcoming, and their creative director explained that they were interested in a campaign centred around natural confidence and personal expression.

They had seen the music video and liked the way CC presented herself.

“We think your image has a very distinctive quality. It’s elegant, but not distant. The campaign is about feeling comfortable in your own skin,” the creative director explained.

CC listened attentively, asking questions about the campaign’s message, visual direction, and the products involved. She didn’t immediately agree to anything.

Instead, she asked for the full proposal and said the company would review it. After the meeting, Nicha looked pleased.

“You handled that very well.”

“They were nice.”

“They clearly want you.”

CC smiled.

“Let’s see the full contract first.”

“Of course.”

They had lunch before returning to the company. On the way, CC received another invitation.

A YouTube channel wanted her to appear on a programme called A Little More About You. The format was relaxed: an afternoon conversation, a few games, and a short musical segment. She read the invitation and laughed.

“What?”

Nicha glanced over.

“They want me to guess songs from only three seconds.”

“That sounds dangerous.”

“I might embarrass myself.”

“You’ll be fine.”

CC shook her head, smiling. She was enjoying all of it.

The meetings, the new opportunities, the conversations about her music. It was exciting to see something she had worked on privately begin to create opportunities of its own.

But when the car stopped outside the company, she checked her phone again. No new message from Declan.

She wasn’t expecting one. He had mentioned that he would be occupied with meetings in New York.

Still, she opened their conversation and looked at the last few messages.

His time zone was different. His days were full.

Sometimes their conversations overlapped perfectly. Other times, she would send him something in the morning and receive his reply while she was already preparing to sleep. It wasn’t a problem. She understood his work. She missed him.

In New York, late on Saturday morning, Declan was reviewing a proposal when Alexander came into his office.

“Mr. Lincoln, the Munich team has sent the revised figures.”

“Leave them here.”

Alexander placed the folder on the desk.

“There is also a message from Bangkok. Ms. Chanya’s management confirmed the proposed schedule for her upcoming promotional appearances.”

Declan looked up.

“Have they confirmed the studio performance?”

“Not yet. They’re still coordinating the date.”

Declan nodded.

“Keep me informed.”

Alexander hesitated.

“Would you like me to check your travel schedule for Bangkok?”

Declan glanced at his calendar. The coming two weeks were crowded with board meetings, an investor dinner, and a scheduled visit to the Munich headquarters. There was also a major negotiation involving the American division.

“Not yet,” he said.

“Understood.”

Alexander started to leave.

“Alexander.”

He stopped.

“Find me a suitable window. Even if it’s only a few days.”

“Certainly, sir.”

Declan returned to the document. His phone vibrated. A photograph from CC.

She was sitting in a studio, wearing headphones, with a microphone positioned in front of her. Her expression was focused, and a music producer was visible in the background.

CC: Today’s meeting was about the live studio performance.

He smiled.

Declan: You look very serious.

CC: I was listening to the arrangement.

Declan: I can see that.

CC: They want to record it next Thursday.

He glanced at his calendar. Thursday was difficult.

Declan: That’s wonderful.

CC: I wish you could hear it in person.

He read the message again. There was no complaint in it. No expectation that he should rearrange his schedule. But he knew what she meant.

Declan: I wish I could be there too.

CC: It’s okay. I’ll send it to you.

Declan: I know you will.

A moment passed.

CC: What are you doing right now?

Declan: Reading about tariffs.

CC: On a Saturday.

Declan: Tariffs don’t observe weekends.

CC: That’s the saddest thing you’ve ever told me.

He was about to put his phone down when another message arrived.

CC: I miss you a little.

Declan’s expression softened. He sat back, looking at the screen.

Declan: Only a little?

CC: Maybe more than a little.

He smiled.

Declan: That’s unfortunate.

CC: Why?

Declan: Because I miss you considerably more.

She sent a small heart. Declan looked at it for another moment before returning to his work.

The document in front of him hadn’t become any less complicated. But he was thinking about Bangkok.

On Monday, the YouTube interview was more entertaining than CC had expected.

The host, a young woman named Mew, was energetic and naturally funny. The studio had a relaxed atmosphere, with a sofa, a small table covered in snacks, and a wall decorated with photographs of previous guests.

CC sat comfortably, dressed in a light blue blouse and jeans.

“First of all,” Mew began, “congratulations on THE FIRST LIGHT. I think a lot of people were surprised by the direction.”

“Thank you.”

“Was this the kind of music you always wanted to make?”

CC considered the question.

“I think I’ve always liked this kind of music. But I didn’t know when I would have the opportunity to make something like it.”

“It’s very different from your group performances.”

“Yes. My group music is often energetic, and I enjoy that. But I also wanted to show another side of myself.”

Mew nodded.

“I noticed that the lyrics are quite emotional. Are you secretly a very sad person?”

CC laughed.

“I’m not sure.”

“That’s a suspicious answer.”

“I think everyone has days when they’re a little sad.”

“That’s true.”

Mew leaned forward.

“But you seem very calm. I wonder what makes you lose your composure.”

CC smiled.

“Maybe when someone eats my food without asking.”

The crew burst into laughter.

“That’s very specific!”

“I like cooking, but I don’t like people taking things from the kitchen before I’m finished.”

Mew laughed.

“Okay, so we have a protective side.”

CC nodded solemnly.

“Very protective.”

The conversation moved into a game segment. CC had to identify songs from short instrumental clips, answer questions about her childhood, and choose between several hypothetical situations. She was surprisingly competitive during the game.

When she lost a round, she stared at the scoreboard.

“That was unfair.”

Mew laughed.

“You agreed to the rules!”

“I didn’t realise you were going to make them difficult.”

The production team laughed again. By the end of the recording, CC was smiling broadly.

She thanked the host, took a few photographs with the crew, and left the studio feeling lighter. It had been a good afternoon.

In the car, she opened her phone and sent Declan a message.

CC: I just finished a YouTube interview.

Declan: How was it?

CC: Fun. We played games.

Declan: Did you win?

CC: No.

Declan: I see.

CC: Don’t laugh.

Declan: I wouldn’t dare.

She sent him a photograph from the studio. He replied with a compliment and asked her to send the link when the episode was released. She smiled. Then she looked out of the window.

The city was moving around her, the evening traffic thickening as the car approached the company. She had enjoyed the day.

But she wished she could have told him about it over dinner, rather than through a few messages between meetings.

She wanted to see his expression when she described the game she had lost. She wanted to hear him tease her about being competitive. She wanted to sit across from him. It was a simple wish. And lately, it had been appearing more often.

At five to midnight on Tuesday, CC was still awake.

Her schedule for the next day had been sent to her earlier. There was a magazine interview in the morning, a fitting in the afternoon, and a short recorded promotional video in the evening.

She had already washed her face and changed into comfortable clothes. Her phone was on the bed beside her. She opened Declan’s conversation.

The last message was from him, sent two hours earlier.

Sleep early, sweetheart. You have a long day tomorrow.

She had replied with a goodnight message, but she wasn’t sleepy yet. She opened the music video instead. The familiar piano note played.

She watched a little of the opening, then stopped it.

For some reason, she was thinking about the recording studio again.

She imagined Declan sitting in the control room, his attention fixed on her while she sang. She imagined finishing the last take and looking through the glass to find him waiting. It was a pleasant thought. Perhaps too pleasant. She turned off the video. Then she called him.

It was late in Bangkok, but in New York it was nearly noon. He answered after the second ring.

“Hello, sweetheart.”

His voice was calm, and she could hear the faint sound of a keyboard in the background.

“Are you working?”

“I was reviewing something.”

“Sorry.”

“You don’t have to apologise.”

She smiled a little.

“Did I disturb you?”

“No.”

There was a pause.

“Why are you awake?”

CC pulled the blanket over her legs.

“I don’t know. I wasn’t sleepy.”

“Long day?”

“Not especially. Just a lot of things.”

“Good things?”

“Yes. The YouTube interview was fun. And the brand meeting went well.”

“I heard.”

She smiled.

“Nicha told you?”

“No. You told me.”

“Oh.”

“You sent me the photograph.”

“Right.”

He laughed. She listened to the sound.

Then she said, “Declan?”

“Yes?”

“I think I’m getting tired.”

“Then you should rest.”

“Not that kind of tired.”

He became quiet. CC looked down at her fingers.

“I like everything I’m doing. I really do. I like the interviews, the recordings, meeting people, and talking about the song. It’s exciting.”

“I know.”

“But…”

She hesitated.

“I think I miss having you around.”

The words came out more than she intended. There was no dramatic pause on the other end, but Declan’s attention shifted entirely.

“Sweetheart.”

She looked towards the window.

“I know you’re busy. And I’m busy too. I don’t want you to think I’m complaining.”

“I don’t.”
