“It’s just that when something happens, I want to tell you about it. And sometimes I think it would be nice if you were there.”

Declan rested his pen on the desk. He understood the distinction.

She wanted nothing from him except to say it: she missed him in the room. Nobody had said that to him in a long time without wanting something else attached. And he missed her too.

“I’ve been thinking about that too,” he said.

“Really?”

“Yes.”

He glanced at the calendar on his desk.

“I’ve been looking for a window in my schedule.”

CC sat a little straighter.

“Are you coming to Bangkok?”

“I’m trying to arrange it.”

Her face brightened, but she didn’t want to assume.

“When?”

“I don’t have a confirmed date yet. I should know within a day or two.”

She nodded, even though he couldn’t see her clearly.

“Okay.”

“I don’t want to promise you something before I’m certain.”

“I understand.”

He paused.

“Would you like me to come for a few days?”

Her answer was immediate.

“Yes.”

Then she seemed to realise how quickly she had answered. She smiled shyly.

“I mean… if you can.”

Declan’s mouth curved.

“I heard you the first time.”

She laughed, hiding her face against the pillow.

“Don’t tease me.”

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

“Perhaps a little.”

She smiled. Neither spoke.

Then Declan said, “I would like to be there too. Not just for the important things. I’d like to have dinner with you when you finish work. Pick you up when you’re tired. Hear you complain about losing a game on a YouTube programme.”

CC laughed.

“I didn’t complain.”

“You said it was unfair.”

“It was!”

“I see.”

She shook her head, smiling.

“I wish you could have seen it.”

“I wish I had.”

He studied the photograph she had sent earlier.

“You looked happy.”

“I was.”

“Then I’m glad.”

CC was quiet.

“Do you think it’s silly that I miss you even though we haven’t been apart for that long?”

“No.”

His answer was immediate.

“It’s not silly.”

She pulled the blanket closer.

“I just didn’t expect to miss you this much.”

Declan’s expression softened.

“Neither did I.”

He let that settle between them. “But I would rather you tell me than pretend you’re perfectly content with the distance,” he said.

CC smiled.

“Okay.”

“Good.”

“Are you going to finish working?”

“Soon.”

“You should sleep too.”

“I will.”

She narrowed her eyes.

“Promise?”

He smiled.

“Promise.”

She checked the time.

“I should go to sleep.”

“Yes.”

“Good night, Declan.”

“Good night, sweetheart.”

She was about to end the call when he spoke again.

“CC?”

“Hmm?”

“I’m looking forward to seeing you.”

Her smile became softer.

“Me too.”

She ended the call a little later than she had intended. And then, at last, she felt sleepy.

On Wednesday, Declan arrived at the office earlier than usual. Alexander was already waiting with the revised schedule.

“Good morning, sir.”

“Good morning.”

“I’ve found a possible window for Bangkok.”

Declan looked at him. Alexander placed the calendar on his desk.

“If the Munich visit moves to the week after, you can fly out tomorrow morning, land in Bangkok on Friday afternoon, and stay until Monday evening. The investor dinner can be handled remotely, and the remaining appointments can move to the following week.”

Declan studied the schedule.

“Would that affect the acquisition meeting?”

“No. The finance team can proceed with the preparation, and you can attend the final review from Bangkok.”

He considered it.

“Arrange it.”

Alexander nodded.

“Certainly.”

“And have the Bangkok office prepare the necessary arrangements. Keep it discreet. I don’t want to disrupt her schedule.”

“Understood.”

Declan signed the first document. Then he looked at the calendar once more. Friday to Monday. Not nearly enough time.

But enough to have dinner with her, see her in person, and perhaps spend one quiet morning together before the city woke up. His phone vibrated.

CC: Good morning.

He smiled.

Declan: Good morning, sweetheart.

CC: I have a magazine interview today.

Declan: I hope it goes well.

CC: Thank you. What are you doing?

Declan: Arranging something.

CC: What something?

Declan: Something I believe you’ll like.

She sent a question mark. Declan smiled and put the phone down. He wasn’t going to tell her yet. Not until everything was confirmed.

That night in Bangkok, CC had just finished her last recorded promotional video.

She was sitting in the car, her head resting lightly against the seat. Her day had been long, but productive. Her phone lit up.

Declan: Are you home?

CC: Almost.

Declan: Good.

CC: Why?

Declan: I have something to tell you.

She sat up.

CC: What is it?

Declan: I’ll be in Bangkok on Friday.

She stared at the screen. She didn’t type anything. Then:

CC: Really?

Declan: Yes.

CC: For how long?

Declan: Until Monday evening, at least.

Her smile appeared so quickly that the driver glanced at her through the rear-view mirror.

CC: You’re really coming?

Declan: I believe that’s what I just said.

She laughed.

CC: I miss you.

Declan read the message, his expression becoming noticeably warmer.

Declan: I know, sweetheart.

Then another message arrived.

Declan: And I miss you too.

CC looked out of the window. The city lights passed by, but she barely noticed them.

She had a full schedule waiting for her. There would be more interviews, more recordings, more meetings, and more opportunities to come. She was grateful for every one of them.

But now she had something else to look forward to. A few days. A dinner together.

His hand resting on the small of her back as he guided her through a crowded entrance. His familiar voice beside her. The quiet comfort of being able to tell him something without having to type it first. She smiled down at her phone.

CC: I’m going to save Friday evening.

Declan: You don’t need to rearrange your schedule for me if you’re busy.

CC: I want to.

Declan read the message. Then he replied:

Declan: Then Friday evening is mine.

She laughed.

CC: Just Friday evening?

Declan: I was trying to be considerate.

CC: You can have Saturday too.

His smile widened.

Declan: Very generous of you, sweetheart.

She sent him a heart. For the rest of the drive, she kept looking at the date on her calendar. Friday was two days away. And the distance didn’t feel quite so exhausting.

Because the next time she finished a long day, she wouldn’t have to wonder whether he was awake on the other side of the world.

She would be able to call him from the car.

And he would be there to answer beside her.

chapters.title: The First Time He Kissed Her
chapters.desc: He lands on Friday and she cooks for the man who once volunteered not to comment. She plays him the song on her own piano. He asks before he kisses her.
chapters.epigraph: “Now I know you kiss me back.”
chapters.content:
Declan Lincoln arrived in Bangkok on Friday evening. His jet had landed at Don Mueang twenty minutes ahead of schedule, and by the time he reached the city, the sky had begun to turn a soft shade of blue-grey. Alexander had arranged the necessary transportation and confirmed the following day’s appointments with the regional office.

Declan, however, had only one personal plan for the evening. Cela Chanya.

His phone vibrated as the car approached her neighbourhood.

CC: Are you here yet?

He smiled.

Declan: Almost.

CC: How almost?

Declan: Five minutes.

CC: Okay.

A moment later:

CC: I’m waiting.

He could almost picture her looking at her phone, perhaps checking the time again despite having already asked him twice.

Declan: Should I bring anything?

CC: An appetite.

Declan: That’s all?

CC: You volunteered. At the St. Regis. You said you don’t comment on cooking.

Declan: I remember. I stand by it.

CC: We’ll see.

He realised he was smiling at a phone in the back of a car again, and didn’t bother to stop.

When the car stopped outside her apartment building, Declan put his phone away and stepped out.

He had brought a small arrangement of flowers with him, not nearly as extravagant as the previous deliveries. Pale pink roses and white tulips, wrapped in cream paper.

He had considered sending them earlier, but decided he would give them to her himself.

The building’s security staff greeted him. CC had already informed them that he was expected.

A few minutes later, the lift opened onto her floor. She was standing near her apartment door.

She wore a soft, pale yellow dress that fell just below her knees, with her hair loosely styled over her shoulders. Her makeup was minimal, and she had a pair of small earrings in her ears. Neither moved. Then her face brightened.

“Declan.”

He smiled.

“Hello, sweetheart.”

She walked towards him, stopping just in front of him.

It was almost instinctive to look up at his face.

“You’re here.”

“I am.”

She smiled, a little more shyly than she had intended. He held out the flowers.

“For you.”

CC looked down.

“They’re beautiful.”

“I thought you’d like them.”

She accepted the bouquet carefully, bringing it closer to smell the flowers.

“Thank you.”

“You’re welcome.”

There was a brief pause. Then Declan opened his arms.

“Come here.”

CC stepped into them. For the first few seconds, she rested her cheek against his chest, her arms around his waist. Declan held her gently, one hand settling between her shoulder blades.

He hadn’t realised how much he had missed the simple experience of having her close until she was actually there.

“You’re finally here,” she murmured.

His hand moved lightly over her back.

“I am, sweetheart.”

She stayed there a little longer. Declan lowered his head slightly.

“Have you missed me?”

She lifted her face.

“Didn’t I tell you?”

“I’d like to hear it again.”

CC gave him a small, suspicious look.

“You’re enjoying this.”

“Very much.”

She tried to look unimpressed, but the smile betrayed her.

“Yes, I’ve missed you,” she admitted.

Declan watched her.

“Good.”

She laughed.

“Good?”

“It’s reassuring to know I wasn’t the only one.”

Dinner at her apartment had been his idea, in a way. At the St. Regis, nearly four weeks ago, he had volunteered to be the one audience who didn’t comment on her cooking. Tonight she was collecting.

She also wanted to spend time with him somewhere quiet.

Their previous meetings had mostly taken place in restaurants, hotels, or professional settings. Even their video calls had usually happened between work appointments.

She wanted him to see the place where she lived. Not the public version of her life. Just her home.

“Come in.”

Declan stepped inside, taking a moment to look around.

Her apartment was warm and tastefully arranged, with neutral colours, soft lighting, and a few personal touches. There were books on a shelf, framed photographs, and a small collection of decorative objects. A piano stood near the window, beside a comfortable chair. It was clearly lived in, but tidy.

“You have a lovely apartment,” he said.

“Thank you.”

She looked around for a vase, remembered she didn’t own one, and put the flowers in the tall glass water jug from the kitchen instead. Declan watched her do it and said nothing.

“Would you like something to drink?”

“Water would be fine.”

“Okay.”

He removed his jacket and draped it over the back of a chair.

As she walked into the kitchen, he followed at a comfortable distance.

“Can I help?”

CC looked over her shoulder.

“You’re a guest.”

“I can still help.”

“You can sit down.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“Is that an instruction?”

“Yes.”

A faint smile appeared on his face.

“Very well.”

He returned to the living room. CC filled two glasses of water and brought them over. When she sat down opposite him, she looked a little more relaxed.

“Was your flight comfortable?”

“Yes.”

“Did you sleep?”

“A little.”

She gave him a look.

“You always say that.”

“And you always ask.”

“Because I care.”

The words came out naturally. Then he smiled.

“I know.”

CC reached for his water aware that she had said it directly. She looked around the room.

“Have you been to Bangkok before this trip?”

“Several times.”

“But not to my apartment.”

“No.”

She smiled.

“Now you have.”

“I’m honoured.”

She laughed. He looked around again, noticing a small framed photograph on the shelf. CC stood between two women, all three laughing at something outside the frame.

“Your family?”

“That’s my mother and my aunt. My father refuses to be in photographs. He says his butter tarts are photogenic enough for the family.”

“You look very happy.”

“We were on holiday.”

She stood and walked over to the shelf.

“My mother likes taking photographs. She takes pictures even when nobody is ready.”

Declan looked at the photograph.

“That’s a useful quality.”

“Why?”

“Because otherwise, you might never have photographs of yourself when you’re not posing.”

CC smiled.

“That’s true.”

She returned to the sofa.

“Would you like to eat something?”

“Have you prepared dinner?”

“A little.”

He tilted his head.

“You didn’t need to.”

“You volunteered. I’m holding you to it.”

She stood.

“I made congee. And some vegetables. It’s simple.”

Declan rose as well.

“Then I’ll be happy to try it.”

The dinner was simple, exactly as CC had promised.

She had prepared a pot of congee with chicken, ginger, and spring onions, along with a small plate of stir-fried vegetables. There was also a light soup.

Declan sat at the dining table while she placed the dishes in front of him. He looked at the food.

“You made all of this?”

“It’s not difficult.”

“Still.”

She handed him a spoon.

“Try it before you compliment me.”

He smiled.

“Yes, chef.”

CC laughed. He tasted the congee. It was warm, delicate, and well seasoned. The ginger was subtle, and the texture was smooth.

“It’s very good.”

She watched his expression.

“Not just because I made it?”

“I promised not to comment. Praise doesn’t count.”

“That’s a loophole.”

“I’m a businessman.”

She laughed. “Then keep praising it.”

CC smiled, satisfied. They ate while talking about the past few days.

She told him about the skincare brand meeting and the YouTube interview, and about yesterday: recording THE FIRST LIGHT live in one take, with a piano and four strings. Halfway through the afternoon, a flask of honey and ginger tea had arrived at the studio for her, with a box of pastries for the musicians and no card.

“No card,” she said, looking at him.

“How mysterious,” said Declan, and asked about the arrangement.

When she described losing the song-guessing game, he gave her an amused look.

“You seem to have been very affected by that.”

“It was unfair.”

“You keep saying that.”

“Because it was.”

He smiled.

“What song was it?”

She told him. Declan considered it.

“I would have recognised it.”

CC stared at him.

“You don’t even know the game.”

“I know the song.”

“That’s different.”

“Perhaps.”

She narrowed her eyes.

“You’re very confident.”

“Usually for good reason.”

She laughed and shook her head. After dinner, Declan insisted on helping her clear the table. She protested once. He ignored her.

“You can wash the dishes,” she eventually offered.

“Very generous.”

“I’m letting you help.”

He glanced at her.

“I’m honoured again.”

She laughed. They stood side by side at the sink, CC washing while Declan dried the dishes. It was an unexpectedly domestic scene.

At one point, she handed him a plate without looking. He took it. Their fingers brushed. Neither said anything.

But CC became aware of how close he was standing.

She could smell his cologne, familiar and understated. She could see the neat line of his shirt cuff and the watch on his wrist. She found the plate in her hand interesting. Declan noticed. He didn’t tease her. He continued drying the dishes. After dinner, CC made tea.

They sat on the sofa, with the city lights visible through the large windows.

Declan had loosened his tie and rolled his sleeves back slightly. CC sat beside him, holding her cup with both hands.

“It’s nice here,” he said.

She studied his face.

“Really?”

“Yes.”

“I like being at home.”

“I can see why.”

She looked towards the window.

“Sometimes I get tired of going everywhere. Hotels, studios, company, events. It’s nice to come back to somewhere quiet.”

Declan nodded.

“I imagine.”

“Do you have a favourite place at home?”

“In Munich?”

She nodded.

“Probably the library.”

“Your family library?”

“Yes. It’s quiet, and nobody expects me to answer a phone call while I’m there.”

She laughed.

“That’s important.”

“Very.”

She took another sip of tea.

Then, after a little hesitation, she said, “I wanted you to come here.”

Declan turned towards her.

“I gathered that.”

Her eyes went to his.

“Not just because I wanted to cook.”

“I hoped so.”

She smiled, then looked down.

“I wanted you to see my home. And I wanted to spend time with you without having to leave again after two hours.”

His face softened.

“I’m glad you invited me.”

“Are you comfortable?”

“Very.”

She nodded. For a while, they talked about ordinary things.

His upcoming schedule. Her recording. The possibility of him returning to Bangkok again. Her mother’s habit of sending her photographs of food. His mother’s increasing curiosity about the woman her son had finally decided to pursue seriously.

When CC heard that last part, she looked up.

“Your mother?”

“Yes.”

“What did she say?”

“She asked when she might meet you.”

CC blinked.

“Really?”

“Yes.”

“What did you tell her?”

“That I would ask you first.”

Her face softened.

“That’s considerate.”

“I promised you I wouldn’t arrange anything without your agreement.”

She smiled.

“I remember.”

He looked at her.

“Would you like to meet her one day?”

CC considered the question.

“Yes. I think I would.”

“Good.”

“I’m a little nervous, though.”

Declan’s mouth curved.

“You don’t need to be.”

“What if she doesn’t like me?”

“She will.”

“How do you know?”

“Because I do.”

CC lifted her eyes to his. The answer was so direct that she forgot what she had been about to say. Declan watched her expression change. Then he smiled.

“Was that convincing enough?”

She lowered her gaze, smiling.

“Maybe.”

Declan glanced at the piano by the window.

“I believe I once asked for a private performance.”

CC followed his gaze. “You asked in a message. Two weeks ago.”

“I’m a patient man. I’m asking again.”

She hesitated for exactly as long as it took her to realise she wanted to. Then she went to the piano, sat down, and played the opening of THE FIRST LIGHT the way she had played it at the studio yesterday, without the strings, a little slower.

She sang the first verse in Mandarin, the way you sing in a room where one person is listening and the neighbours might be too.

Declan didn’t move until she stopped, after the chorus, with her hands still on the keys.

“That’s all you get,” she said, without turning round.

“I’d like to renegotiate.”

She laughed and came back to the sofa, and sat closer to him than she had before. After that, the conversation became quieter.

CC had moved closer to him without quite realising it. Her tea was finished, and the empty cup rested on the coffee table.

Declan was telling her about a meeting in Munich when she began to notice the small details of his face.

The way his eyes narrowed slightly when he was considering something. The faint movement of his mouth when he was about to smile.

The calmness he carried even when discussing complicated matters. She had seen him in many settings now. In a tailored suit at a gala. Across a restaurant table. On her phone screen, thousands of kilometres away. But this was different.

He was sitting beside her, close enough that she could reach out and touch his hand. And she wanted to.

She looked down at his hand resting on the sofa.

Declan stopped speaking. He had noticed where she was looking. He turned his hand over on the cushion between them, palm up, and waited. Slowly, she put her hand in his.

She felt a little shy, because he was looking at her.

“What?” she asked.

“Nothing.”

“You stopped talking.”

“I noticed.”

She smiled. His fingers slipped between hers. The gesture was simple.

But it made her heart beat a little faster. Declan met her eyes.

“Are you comfortable?”

She nodded.

“Yes.”

He studied her expression.

“Good.”

A small silence settled between them. CC could feel the warmth of his hand around hers.

Then she said, almost, “I’ve wanted to do this for a while.”

His eyes remained on her.

“Do what?”

She glanced at their joined hands. Then back at him.

“Be close to you.”

His face softened.

“You can.”

She looked at him for another moment. He noticed her hesitation.

“Sweetheart?”

“Hmm?”

“You look as though you’re thinking very hard.”

She laughed nervously.

“I’m not.”

“Are you sure?”

She nodded, then shook her head. He smiled.

“Which is it?”

CC looked down, smiling at herself.

“Can I ask you something?” he said.

“Of course.”

“May I kiss you?”

CC went still. He had said it the way he said everything, without hurry, as if there were no wrong answer.

Her cheeks warmed. “Have you wanted to?”

“Yes.”

“Since when?”

He considered her.

“Would you like the honest answer?”

She nodded.

“Since Geneva.”

CC blinked.

“Really?”

“I remember thinking that I would like to kiss you when you smiled at me after I gave you the shawl.”

She looked away.

“That’s a long time ago.”

“Not particularly long.”

“It feels like a long time.”

He smiled.

“Then perhaps we should stop discussing it.”

She looked back at him. Declan’s thumb moved gently over her knuckles.

“You haven’t answered me.”

CC understood what he was asking. He wasn’t going to assume.

Even now, after all their conversations, their dinners, the gifts, and the way they had begun to rely on each other’s presence, he was giving her the choice. She looked at him.

“Yes.”

His face softened further. He lifted their joined hands and placed a gentle kiss against her knuckles. Then he leaned closer.

Slowly enough that she had time to change her mind. CC didn’t move away. Instead, she tilted her face towards him.

Their first kiss was barely a kiss at all, at first: the lightest brush of his mouth against hers, a question asked a second time. Then she breathed in, and he felt it, and his hand came up to cradle her cheek.

The city outside went away. So did the work waiting for her in the morning, and every one of the days she had spent missing him. There was only the warmth of his palm, the faint taste of ginger tea, and the slow, dizzy certainty that he had wanted to do this for a long time. When he drew back, he didn’t move far. He looked at her face.

“Are you all right?”

CC nodded.

“Yes.”

Her voice was softer than usual. Declan brushed his thumb lightly along her cheek.

“Good.”

She looked at him, her cheeks still warm. Then she smiled. He returned the smile.

“What?” he asked.

“Nothing.”

“That’s twice tonight you’ve said that.”

She laughed.

“I don’t know what to say.”

“You don’t have to say anything.”

She looked at his lips for a brief second, then quickly back at his eyes. Declan noticed. His smile became slightly more amused.

“Something on your mind, sweetheart?”

She shook her head.

“No.”

“Are you certain?”

“Liar,” he said gently, and kissed her again.

This time his hand settled at the side of her neck, his thumb resting just under her jaw where her pulse was racing, and she leaned into it. The kiss went slower and deeper, and when her fingers found the front of his shirt and held on, he made a low sound she felt more than heard.

When they separated, CC lowered her face, trying to hide her smile. Declan turned to her.

“Now you’re shy?”

She pressed her lips together.

“Maybe.”

He laughed.

“That’s rather sweet.”

She considered him.

“Don’t tease me.”

“I wouldn’t dare.”

“You’re smiling.”

“I am.”

“Why?”

He looked at her.

“Because I’ve wanted to do that for quite some time.”

Her face softened. She rested her forehead lightly against his shoulder.

Declan wrapped an arm around her, holding her close. Neither felt the need to speak immediately. They remained on the sofa for some time.

CC was sitting close against him now, her head resting on his shoulder. His arm was around her, and her fingers were playing absentmindedly with his hand. Every so often, she looked up at him. Declan eventually noticed.

“Something wrong?”

She shook her head.

“No.”

“Then why do you keep looking at me?”

She smiled.

“I’m looking at you.”

“I can see that.”

“Is it not allowed?”

“It’s very much allowed.”

She laughed. Then she looked down at their hands.

“Declan?”

“Yes?”

“Does this mean we’re…”

She stopped. He waited. She tried again.

“Are we still courting?”

Declan’s expression became thoughtful.

“We are.”

She nodded slowly.

He said, “I’m still courting you. And I still intend to ask you to be my girlfriend when I believe the time is right.”

CC glanced up at him.

“Do you think the kiss changes anything?”

“It changes something.”

Her eyes widened slightly.

“What?”

His mouth curved.

“Now I know you kiss me back.”

She stared at him. Then she burst into laughter.

“Declan!”

He smiled, entirely pleased with himself.

“Was that not what you meant?”

She lightly hit his arm.

“You did not just say that.”

He caught her hand before she could pull it away and brought it to his lips.

“Perhaps.”

She was still smiling. Then he became more serious.

“But I don’t want you to feel that one kiss means you have to move faster than you’re comfortable with. I want us to enjoy this properly.”

CC looked up.

“I know.”

“Good.”

She rested her head against his shoulder again. She murmured, “I liked it.”

Declan looked down at her.

“The kiss?”

She nodded. He smiled.

“So did I.”

She lifted her head slightly.

“Very much?”

His face became amused.

“Would you like me to quantify it?”

She laughed.

“No.”

“Then I’ll simply say very much.”

CC smiled and settled against him again. It was getting late when Declan finally stood to leave. CC walked him to the door.

She had been enjoying the evening so much that she had almost forgotten he had an early appointment the following morning.

“You should rest,” she said.

“So should you.”

“I will.”

He put on his jacket. Then he turned towards her.

“Thank you for inviting me.”

She smiled.

“Thank you for coming.”

He reached for her hand.

“I’m glad I came.”

She looked at him, then at their joined hands. There was a small pause.

“One more. For the road,” Declan said.

CC laughed, embarrassed. “You’re very bold tonight.”

“I’ve been patient for four weeks.”

He stepped closer and held out his hand. She did.

He kissed her once more, gently, before resting his forehead against hers.

“Good night,” he murmured.

“Good night.”

He stepped back. Then, just before opening the door, he looked at her again.

“Lock the door after me.”

She smiled.

“Yes.”

“And message me when you’re settled.”

“I will.”

“Good girl.”

Her cheeks warmed again. He noticed, of course. But this time he only smiled and left.

CC closed the door, locked it, and leaned against it. Her fingers rose to her lips. She smiled to herself.

Then she went to the living room, where the flowers he had brought stood in a water jug on the dining table. She took a photograph of them. And sent it to him.

CC: They’re pretty.

Declan: I’m glad you like them.

CC: I like the person who brought them too.

His reply came almost immediately.

Declan: That’s very reassuring.

She laughed.

CC: Good night, Declan.

Declan: Good night, sweetheart. Sleep well.

She put her phone down. For once, the apartment didn’t feel quite as quiet as it usually did.

And across Bangkok, in the back of his car, Declan looked at her last message for a little longer than necessary.

He had arrived intending to spend a few days with her.

He hadn’t expected the evening to feel quite so significant.

But as he watched the city lights pass beyond the window, he smiled. He had kissed her. And she had kissed him back.

For a man who was accustomed to planning every important decision with precision, it was pleasant to discover that some of the best things in life happened without needing to be scheduled.

chapters.title: Even Between Her Appointments
chapters.desc: He brings breakfast and a vase, feeds her whole recording team, sends flats to her fitting, and ends the day with butter tarts on the river. She warns him she’s going to start spoiling him back.
chapters.epigraph: “But you might have to let me spoil you sometimes too.”
chapters.content:
On Saturday morning, CC woke to the sound of her phone vibrating against the bedside table.

She reached for it without opening her eyes, expecting a message from Nicha about the day’s schedule. Instead, she found Declan’s name.

Declan: Good morning, sweetheart.

Declan: Are you awake?

She glanced at the time.

CC: I am now.

Declan: An unfortunate way to begin your morning. I’ll make it up to you.

A small smile appeared on her face.

CC: How?

Declan: Open your door.

CC blinked. She sat up, pushed her hair away from her face, and looked towards the bedroom door as if he might somehow be standing there.

CC: What?

Declan: Your front door, CC.

She hurried out of bed, pulled a cardigan over her sleepwear, and walked towards the entrance. Through the peephole, she saw a familiar figure standing outside, dressed in a dark navy shirt and tailored trousers, holding a paper bag in one hand and, under his other arm, a plain glass vase. She opened the door.

Her hair was slightly messy, her face still soft with sleep, and she was wearing a cardigan that was clearly too large for her. His expression warmed.

“Good morning.”

“Good morning. What are you doing here?” She looked at the bag.

“Bringing breakfast.”

“You came all the way here just to bring breakfast?”

“I was under the impression that was a rather straightforward activity.”

She gave him a look. He smiled, then lifted the bag slightly.

“May I come in?”

She stepped aside, still looking at him with mild disbelief.

Declan came in, placed the bag on the dining table, and set the vase down beside the water jug full of roses.

“You noticed the jug,” she said.

“I noticed the jug.”

He took a moment to look around the apartment. He had been there only the night before, but the familiarity of the place felt different in the morning. Sunlight filtered through the curtains. Her piano stood by the window, and a half-finished book lay beside the sofa.

“What time do you need to leave?” he asked.

“Ten.”

“Let me guess. Coffee, and a promise to eat later.”

She hesitated. Declan held her gaze.

“CC.”

“I was going to.”

“That wasn’t a denial.”

She smiled sheepishly. “I was going to have something after showering.”

“Then I’m just in time.”

He opened the bag. Inside were two breakfast boxes from a well-regarded bakery, a selection of fresh fruit, warm pastries, and two drinks. CC leaned closer.

“You bought so much.”

“I wasn’t certain what you’d want.”

“You could have asked.”

“I could have. But then I would have missed the opportunity to surprise you.”

She picked up a small box and examined its contents.

“You remembered I like this.”

“Of course.”

It was a small pastry filled with custard, something she had mentioned liking during one of their earlier conversations. She watched him.

“Thank you.”

Declan reached over and gently smoothed a strand of hair off her cheek.

“Eat first. You can thank me properly after.”

Her cheeks warmed.

“That’s a very demanding breakfast arrangement.”

“I’m a demanding man.”

“Only about breakfast?”

“Not exclusively.”

She laughed, and he looked satisfied with himself. For the next twenty minutes, he sat across from her while she ate. He had already taken a few calls that morning, but he put his phone aside when she began telling him about the day’s schedule.

She had a recording session at eleven, a short interview at one, a brand fitting in the afternoon, and a meeting with the creative team for an upcoming promotional campaign.

“That’s quite a full day,” he observed.

“It’s manageable.”

“I’m sure it is.”

She took another sip of her drink.

“You’re looking at me like you don’t believe me.”

“I believe you can manage it. I’m less certain you should have to manage it without eating properly.”

“Declan.”

“CC.”

She narrowed her eyes at him. He smiled.

“Finish your fruit.”

At ten to ten, Declan walked her down to the car.

Her manager, P’Nicha, was already waiting inside. The moment she noticed Declan, her face changed into something far too knowing.

“Good morning, Khun Declan.”

“Good morning, Nicha.”

CC opened the rear door, but Declan reached it first and held it for her.

“Have a good day, sweetheart.”

She looked up at him.

“You too.”

“Message me when you arrive.”

“I will.”

“And eat lunch.”

She gave him an amused look. “You already fed me breakfast.”

“I’m aware. Lunch is a separate matter.”

Nicha made a small sound that was suspiciously close to a laugh.

CC climbed into the car, trying not to smile too much.

Declan closed the door gently. Before stepping away, he looked through the window and gave her a small nod. The car pulled out.

Nicha waited until they were a reasonable distance away before speaking.

“Breakfast delivery?”

CC turned towards her.

“Don’t start.”

“I haven’t said anything.”

“You’re smiling.”

“Am I not allowed to be happy that someone is taking such good care of my artist?”

CC looked out the window. Nicha laughed.

“Very cute.”

“P’Nicha.”

“Fine, fine.”

But CC’s smile remained for the rest of the drive.

At the AVEN studio, the recording session was going well. Today it was the Thai version of THE FIRST LIGHT, for the local release.

CC stood inside the booth with headphones over her ears, listening to the producer explain a small adjustment to the second verse. She was focused, attentive, and precise, asking for one additional take to test a softer delivery.

Outside, Nicha reviewed the day’s schedule with a staff member. Her phone vibrated. A message from Declan.

Declan: How is the recording going?

She glanced towards the booth. CC was listening to the playback, one hand resting against the headphones.

Nicha: Going well. She’s recording now.

A few seconds later, another message arrived.

Declan: Please don’t let her skip lunch.

Nicha stared at the screen. Then she laughed.

Nicha: You’re very concerned about her meals, Khun Declan.

Declan: I have noticed that she’s very good at forgetting them when she’s working.

Nicha: That’s unfortunately true.

Declan: I’ve arranged lunch for the team. It should arrive around twelve thirty. Nothing elaborate, just a selection of dishes. Please make sure she gets something she likes.

Nicha reread the message again. He hadn’t asked her to interrupt the recording. He hadn’t asked CC to leave work or change her schedule. He had arranged for lunch to come to them. She glanced at the studio door.

“Ah, this man,” she murmured.

Around half past twelve, the delivery arrived. It wasn’t an extravagant spread, but it was generous: individual meal boxes, fresh salads, warm soup, fruit, and desserts from a restaurant CC had once mentioned enjoying.

There was a separate small box with her name written on it. Inside was mango sticky rice. And a note.

For the person who is making something beautiful today. Please remember to take care of the person making it, too.

— D.

CC read it twice. Then she looked at Nicha.

“Did he arrange all of this?”

Nicha nodded.

“He did.”

“For everyone?”

“Everyone.”

CC opened the box again, looking at the dessert.

“He didn’t have to.”

“No. He didn’t,” Nicha agreed.

CC’s expression softened. She took out her phone.

CC: Lunch arrived.

Declan: Good.

CC: You ordered for everyone?

Declan: I thought it would be rude to feed only you.

CC: That’s very thoughtful.

Declan: I’m pleased you think so.

CC: Thank you. I like the mango sticky rice.

Declan: I suspected you might.

CC: You remembered the restaurant too.

Declan: You told me their khao soi got you through your trainee years. It seemed relevant.

She stared at the message. Then, despite the people around her, she smiled.

CC: You’re making it difficult for me to concentrate.

Declan: Then I’ll stop messaging until you’re finished.

A moment later:

Declan: But I expect a report on the mango sticky rice.

She shook her head, smiling to herself. At twenty to two, in the interview lounge, everything was running slightly behind schedule.

CC sat on a cream sofa beneath soft studio lighting, answering questions about her solo debut. She spoke about the meaning of The First Light, the creative process, and how it felt to release a song that was more personal than anything she had done before. The interviewer asked whether she had been nervous.

“A little. I think whenever you share something personal, there’s a part of you that wonders whether people will understand it. But I was very happy with the response,” CC admitted.

“And what has been the most memorable reaction so far?”

CC thought.

“There were people who told me that the song made them feel less alone. I think that’s probably the most meaningful thing an artist can hear.”

The interview continued. Declan, meanwhile, was in the back seat of his car on the way to a business lunch.

He had a meeting with the regional investment team at two thirty, followed by a conference call with Munich. His schedule was no less demanding than hers.

But he had received a short video from Nicha that morning, showing a few seconds of her recording session. He had watched it three times.

There was nothing extraordinary about the clip. It was her, standing behind the microphone, eyes closed as she sang. He liked seeing her doing something she loved. His phone lit up.

CC: Interview finished.

Declan: How did it go?

CC: Good. They asked about the song again.

Declan: And you gave them a good answer, I’m sure.

CC: I think so.

Declan: I have no doubt.

She sent him a photograph of herself in the interview lounge, holding a small bouquet of flowers given to her by the production team.

CC: They gave me these.

Declan studied the photograph.

Declan: Pretty.

CC: The flowers?

Declan: The woman holding them.

She checked the message for several seconds before typing.

CC: You’re very smooth today.

Declan: Only today?

She laughed.

CC: I have to go to my fitting now.

Declan: Then I’ll let you go. Have a good afternoon, sweetheart.

CC: You too. Don’t work too hard.

Declan: I’ll try to behave.

CC: That’s not what I meant.

Declan: I know.

She put her phone away, still smiling. At the fashion house that afternoon, the fitting took longer than expected.

CC had three outfits to try on for an upcoming campaign, each requiring adjustments. She was patient throughout, though by the third outfit, her feet were beginning to hurt.

She sat in front of the mirror while the stylist adjusted the hem of a pale blue dress.

“Is it comfortable?” the stylist asked.

“Yes, thank you.”

Nicha, who was standing nearby, glanced at her.

“Your shoes?”

CC looked down.

“They’re fine.”

Nicha gave her a look.

“They’re not fine. You’ve been rubbing your ankle for ten minutes.”

CC stopped immediately.

“It’s okay.”

“Don’t say that just because we’re working.”

Before CC could reply, her phone vibrated.

Declan: How is the fitting?

CC: Almost done.

Declan: Are you comfortable?

She glanced at her shoes. A small smile appeared.

CC: Mostly.

Declan: That sounds suspiciously like a qualification.

CC: My shoes are a little uncomfortable.

Declan: Take them off while you’re waiting.

CC: I’m in the middle of a fitting.

Declan: Then ask them. Your feet are more important than the shoes.

She read the message, then at Nicha. Nicha raised an eyebrow.

“Declan?”

CC nodded.

“What did he say?”

“He told me to take my shoes off.”

Nicha smiled.

“Good advice.”

CC shook her head, but slipped off the shoes anyway.

A few minutes later, a staff member approached Nicha with a delivery.

It was a small box from a luxury department store, accompanied by a discreet note.

Nicha opened it and found a pair of elegant soft leather flats in a warm beige shade. They were simple, comfortable, and exactly the sort of thing CC would wear between appointments. There was a card inside.

For the hours between beautiful shoes. I thought you might appreciate something more comfortable.

— Declan

Nicha looked at CC. CC looked back. Neither spoke. Then CC covered her face with one hand.

“He didn’t.”

“He did.”

“He can’t keep doing this.”

Nicha examined the shoes.

“Apparently, he can.”

CC took the card, her cheeks pink.

“He’s going to spoil me.”

Nicha gave her a knowing smile.

“I think that is precisely what he’s trying to do.”

CC looked down at the shoes again. They were lovely. More importantly, he had noticed something she hadn’t even thought to mention properly. She typed a message.

CC: The shoes arrived.

Declan: Good.

CC: You can’t keep doing this.

Declan: Technically, I can.

CC: Declan.

Declan: Wear them to dinner and I’ll consider stopping.

CC: Will you?

Declan: No.

She bit her lower lip to stop herself from smiling.

CC: What dinner?

Declan: You’ll see.

By the time CC finished her last appointment, the sky had turned a soft shade of violet.

She was tired, but in a good way. The brand fitting had gone smoothly, the creative team was pleased, and she had received confirmation that the campaign would move forward.

She was changing out of her outfit when Nicha appeared at the dressing room entrance.

“Your car is ready.”

CC nodded, collecting her handbag.

“Thank you.”

“And there’s something else.”

“What?”

Nicha gave her a smile.

“Your evening is free.”

CC frowned.

“My evening?”

“I checked with the team. Everything is finished for today.”

“Okay…”

“Someone has made dinner arrangements.”

CC stared at her.

“Nicha.”

“What?”

“Did you know?”

“I know nothing.”

“You’re smiling.”

“I am simply pleased that you have a nice evening ahead of you.”

CC shook her head, but her heart had already begun to beat a little faster. Her phone vibrated.

Declan: Are you finished?

CC: Yes.

Declan: Good. I have a car waiting for you.

CC: Where are you?

Declan: Somewhere you can have dinner without discussing work.

CC: That’s very mysterious.

Declan: I thought I’d give you something to look forward to.

She reread the message, then at Nicha.

“I’m leaving.”

“Enjoy your evening, CC.”

CC gave her manager a small, embarrassed smile.

“I will.”

Declan was waiting when she arrived, a little after seven.

He had chosen a quiet riverside restaurant with an intimate private dining area. The table was set beside a large window overlooking the Chao Phraya River, where the evening lights shimmered across the water. He stood as she approached.

She wore a simple cream dress, her hair falling over her shoulders. The beige flats he had sent were on her feet. His gaze lowered.

“You wore them.”

She looked down, then back at him.

“They’re comfortable.”

“I’m glad.”

“Thank you.”

He offered her his hand. She took it.

“Long day?”

“A little.”

“Then tonight, no schedules.”

She smiled.

“Are you sure? I have a very important appointment.”

“With whom?”

She met his eyes.

“You.”

His face softened.

“Then I hope I won’t disappoint.”

He pulled out her chair and waited until she was seated before taking his own.

Dinner was relaxed. They spoke about her day, his meetings, and a few amusing things that had happened in the office. Declan told her about a regional director who had attempted to explain a delay using a presentation with forty-seven slides.

“Forty-seven?” CC repeated.

“Forty-seven.”

“Was it a very complicated problem?”

“No. It could have been explained in three sentences.”

She laughed.

“What did you do?”

“I asked him to summarise it.”

“And?”

“He did. In two sentences.”

CC laughed again, and Declan watched her with quiet satisfaction.

He liked this part of being with her. Not the restaurant, the arrangements, or the beautiful view. He liked that she could relax enough to laugh without thinking about the next thing she needed to do. When dessert arrived, it wasn’t mango sticky rice.

It was a plate of small tarts, golden and slightly uneven, the filling just set, a crust of sugar at the edges. CC stared at them.

“Those are butter tarts.”

“The pastry chef here spent two years in Toronto. I rang him on Thursday.”

She picked one up, bit into it, and closed her eyes.

“They’re not my dad’s,” she said finally.

“No. I imagine I’d have to meet him for those.”

She looked at him across the table and, didn’t answer.

“I only said it once. At the St. Regis,” she said.

“I remember the things that matter.”

Her face changed slightly. She lowered her eyes, smiling.

“That’s a very unfair answer.”

“Why?”

“Because I can’t argue with it.”

He reached across the table and gently touched her fingers.

“Then don’t.”

Neither said anything. CC turned her hand slightly, letting her fingers rest more comfortably against his.

“Today was nice,” she said.

“Even with the schedule?”

“Because of the schedule most of all.”

He studied her.

She said, “You didn’t ask me to cancel anything. You didn’t make me feel like I had to choose between seeing you and doing my work. You just… You found ways to be there.” She paused, searching for the right words.

Declan’s thumb moved lightly over the back of her hand.

“I know how important your work is to you.”

“It is.”

“I wouldn’t want you to give that up for me.”

She looked at him.

“And I wouldn’t want you to think that because I’m busy, I don’t want you around.”

His face softened.

“I don’t.”

“Good.”

He smiled.

“Although I admit, I rather enjoy having excuses to send you things.”

She laughed.

“I noticed.”

“Is that a complaint?”

“No.”

“Good.”

She tilted her head.

“But you might have to let me spoil you sometimes too.”

Declan looked at her with mild amusement.

“I look forward to seeing what you come up with.”

“You sound unconvinced.”

“Not at all. I’m simply curious.”

She narrowed her eyes.

“I can be very thoughtful.”

“I know.”

“And generous.”

“I’ve never doubted it.”

“And I can buy you things.”

His smile deepened.

“I’m sure you can, sweetheart.”

She gave him a small, satisfied nod. After dinner, they walked along the riverside for a little while. Declan held her hand, matching her pace without making her feel hurried. The evening was warm, the river breeze gentle. CC leaned a little closer to him.

“Are you going to be busy tomorrow?”

“Somewhat. I have a call with Munich in the morning and a few things to review.”

She nodded.

“Then I can see you after?”

“If you’d like.”

She turned to him.

“I would.”

“Then I’ll arrange it.”

“Don’t arrange too much.”

He glanced down at her.

“What would you prefer?”

“Something simple.”

“Dinner at your apartment?”

She considered it.

“Maybe. I could cook.”

His expression was thoughtful.

“Would you enjoy that?”

“Yes.”

“Then I’d be delighted.”

She smiled.

“But you have to help.”

“I can manage.”

“You don’t know if I can cook properly.”

“I’ve eaten your cooking.”

“That was only once.”

“And I survived.”

She laughed, lightly nudging his arm.

“Declan.”

He looked down at her, smiling.

“I’m looking forward to it.”

They reached the car a little later. He opened the door for her, but before she got in, she turned towards him.

“Thank you for today.”

His eyes went to her face.

“You’re welcome.”

“For breakfast. Lunch. The shoes. Dinner.”

“I enjoyed all of it.”

“You didn’t even get to spend much time with me.”

“I saw you several times.”

“Through messages and photographs.”

“And I liked those too.”

She smiled, then hesitated. Declan noticed.

“What is it?”

“Nothing.”

He waited. She glanced towards the car, then back at him, and he understood before she could decide whether to ask.

“You can ask,” he said.

He leaned down, giving her time to meet him halfway.

Their lips touched gently. It was a brief kiss, warm and familiar, though still new enough to make her cheeks turn pink when they parted. Declan brushed his thumb along her cheek.

“Goodnight, sweetheart.”

“Goodnight.”

She got into the car, but before he closed the door, she caught his hand.

“One more thing.”

“Yes?”

“Tomorrow, you don’t have to bring anything.”

He looked at her.

“Not even myself?”

She laughed.

“You can bring yourself.”

“Then I think I can manage that.”

He closed the door gently. As the car pulled away, CC looked back through the window.

Declan was still standing there, watching until the car turned out of sight.

Her phone vibrated before she had even reached the main road.

Declan: You forgot something.

She frowned.

CC: What?

Declan: Your goodnight kiss was rather brief.

She laughed, covering her mouth.

CC: You asked for a goodnight, not a long one.

Declan: A reasonable distinction. I’ll remember to specify tomorrow.

She shook her head, smiling at the screen.

CC: Goodnight, Declan.

Declan: Goodnight, my sweet girl.

She read the last message again. Then she placed her phone against her chest, looking out at the passing city lights.

She had spent the entire day moving from one appointment to another, surrounded by people, cameras, schedules, and conversations.

And somehow, in the middle of all of it, Declan had made her feel.

He hadn’t asked her to stop working. He hadn’t asked her to make room for him at the expense of anything else.

He had found a way to make himself part of her day. And perhaps that was what she liked most.

In his hotel suite, a little after ten, Declan had just finished reviewing the documents Alexander had sent over when his phone lit up. A photograph.

CC was sitting on her sofa, wearing a loose cardigan, her hair tied back. Beside her was the little box of mango sticky rice from lunch, now empty.

CC: I ate everything.

He smiled.

Declan: I’m very proud of you.

CC: Don’t sound so pleased.

Declan: I have reason to be.

CC: Goodnight. Really this time.

Declan: Sleep well, sweetheart.

He put the phone down, but his attention lingered on the photograph.

Alexander had once remarked that Declan seemed to be in a better mood whenever he was in Bangkok.

At the time, Declan had merely acknowledged the observation. Now he understood it well.

He had spent the day in meetings, calls, and traffic, but none of it had felt burdensome. He had managed his work, seen her between appointments, made sure she ate, and ended the evening with her hand in his.

None of it had been grand. He wanted to be there for her ordinary days, too.

And if that meant breakfast at her door, lunch delivered to a recording studio, comfortable shoes between fittings, and dinner after a long day, he saw no reason to stop. Declan picked up his phone once more.

Declan: One more thing.

A minute passed.

CC: What?

Declan: Tomorrow, I’ll bring myself.

CC: That’s all I need.

He checked the message. Then he smiled. For a man who had spent most of his adult life acquiring things, building things, and making arrangements, it was unexpectedly satisfying to discover that the thing he most wanted to give her was his time.

chapters.title: Help in the Kitchen
chapters.desc: Sunday dinner at her apartment was his idea, and so was helping. He can run a company on three continents but not cut vegetables, and she finally tells him how she knows he likes ginger.
chapters.epigraph: “You sent ginger tea to a photo studio at seven in the morning.”
chapters.content:
On Sunday afternoon, Declan Lincoln was standing in front of her kitchen island, examining a chopping board as if it contained a complicated business proposal.

CC watched him from the other side of the counter.

“Why are you looking at it like that?”

“I’m deciding where to begin.”

“You can begin by washing the vegetables.”

He glanced at the bowl beside him.

“Those?”

“Yes.”

“Understood.”

She returned to preparing the ingredients, trying not to smile.

It had been his idea, by the river last night: dinner at her apartment, and he would help. She had agreed, mostly to see what “help” would look like.

He had arrived at four thirty carrying a small paper bag from a bakery and a bottle of sparkling water. No flowers this time, no elaborate surprise. Just himself, as promised.

He had also changed into a pale blue shirt with the sleeves still buttoned at the wrists.

CC had looked at him for approximately three seconds before pointing towards the sink.

“You’re going to have to roll those up.”

Declan looked down at his cuffs.

“Of course.”

He began undoing the buttons. CC turned away before he could notice her watching.

It was a small, ordinary thing, but she liked seeing him in her apartment like this. Not in a suit, not surrounded by assistants or people waiting for his decisions. Just a man standing in her kitchen, looking mildly uncertain about what to do with a bowl of vegetables. He rolled his sleeves neatly to his forearms.

“Where would you like me?”

She held his gaze.

“Excuse me?”

“In the kitchen.”

“Oh. You can start with the vegetables.” She laughed.

He nodded with the seriousness of someone accepting an important assignment.

“Very well.”

For the first few minutes, things went reasonably well.

He washed the vegetables, dried them, and arranged them on the chopping board. CC explained which ingredients she needed first, and he listened carefully. Then she handed him a knife.

“Can you cut these?”

He looked at the vegetables.

“How small?”

“Not too small.”

“That’s rather subjective.”

She stared at him.

“Declan.”

He smiled.

“All right. Show me.”

She stepped beside him, took one of the vegetables, and demonstrated.

“Like this.”

He watched her hands.

“Understood.”

She returned to the stove. A moment later, she heard a series of uneven chopping sounds. She looked over.

Declan had produced three pieces of noticeably different sizes. CC pressed her lips together. He noticed.

“Something wrong?”

“No.”

“Your expression suggests otherwise.”

“It’s fine.”

He looked down at his work.

“I’m beginning to suspect you disagree.”

She walked over and examined the chopping board.

“Why is this one so big?”

“It seemed appropriate.”

“And this one?”

“An adjustment.”

She laughed. He looked at her, perfectly composed.

“I’m doing my best.”

“I can see that.”

“Are you laughing at my best?”

“A little.”

He gave a quiet chuckle and stepped aside to let her take over.

She finished the vegetables in a few quick movements. Declan watched her.

“You’re very efficient.”

“I cook quite often.”

“So I see.”

“You don’t have to say it like that.”

“Like what?”

“Like you’re impressed.”

“I am impressed.”

She tilted her head. He was smiling.

“You’re very good at this,” he said.

“It’s just cutting vegetables.”

“Not everyone can do it well.”

She shook her head, returning to the stove.

“Go sit down.”

“Am I dismissed?”

“For now.”

He looked at the chopping board.

“I was hoping to contribute more.”

“You can help me with the soup later.”

“An opportunity to redeem myself.”

“Exactly.”

He laughed and leaned against the counter, watching her cook.

The apartment gradually filled with the smell of ginger, garlic, and warm broth.

CC moved comfortably around the kitchen, occasionally tasting the soup and adjusting the seasoning. Declan remained nearby, asking questions whenever she reached for something.

He was, she had to admit, an attentive assistant. A slightly inconvenient one.

“Can you pass me that bowl?”

He handed her the wrong one.

“The smaller one.”

He exchanged it.

“The other smaller one.”

He looked at the two bowls.

“Are you certain these are different sizes?”

She laughed.

“Yes.”

He finally found the right one and placed it beside her.

“Anything else?”

“Could you stir this?”

He took the spoon.

“Of course.”

She turned to prepare the next ingredient. For a little while, there was only the soft sound of cooking and their quiet conversation.

Then Declan asked, “How much longer?”

“Maybe fifteen minutes.”

“Good.”

She glanced at him.

“Are you hungry?”

“A little.”

“You should have eaten before coming.”

“I wanted to have dinner with you.”

She looked back at the stove, smiling.

“You could have had a snack.”

“I could have.”

“Why didn’t you?”

“Because I was looking forward to this.”

She lowered her eyes. It was becoming increasingly difficult to pretend that his simple remarks didn’t affect her.

“Don’t stir too quickly,” she murmured.

He slowed down.

“Like this?”

“Yes.”

“I’m learning.”

“You are.”

He watched her before saying, “I must admit, I enjoy seeing you here.”

She studied his face.

“Here?”

“In your own space. Doing something you enjoy.”

She turned the heat down.

“I like having people over when I have time. But I don’t cook for many people.”

“Why not?”

“I don’t like being watched while I cook.”

He considered that.

“Then I should be grateful you allowed me into the kitchen.”

“You’re not watching. You’re working.”

“An important distinction.”

She smiled.

“And you’re not very good at it, so I don’t feel pressured.”

He laughed.

“That’s reassuring.”

She took the spoon from him and tasted the soup.

“It’s good.”

“I’m pleased.”

“You stirred it.”

“I contributed.”

“You did.”

He looked satisfied with that small acknowledgment. Then she reached for the cupboard above the counter.

Before she could stretch, Declan stepped forward and retrieved the bowl she needed.

“Here.”

“Thank you.”

He placed it in her hands, then glanced around the kitchen.

“Is there anything else I can do?”

She looked at the counter.

“You can set the table.”

“Finally, a task I can complete without supervision.”

“Don’t be too confident.”

He smiled. She watched him walk towards the dining area, carrying the plates. There was something unexpectedly intimate about the sight.

His sleeves were still rolled up. His watch caught the light as he arranged the cutlery. He moved with the same calm precision she had seen in business settings, except now he was deciding where to place her water glass. CC looked down at the soup. She was smiling again. Dinner was simple.

CC had prepared ginger chicken, steamed vegetables, a light soup, and rice. There was also a small plate of fruit on the side. Declan tasted everything without rushing. CC watched him carefully.

“Is it okay?”

He looked up.

“It’s very good.”

She smiled.

“Which one do you like best?”

He considered the dishes.

“The chicken.”

“I thought you might.”

“Why?”

“Because you like ginger.”

He paused. “I don’t believe I’ve ever told you that.”

“You sent ginger tea to a photo studio at seven in the morning. And to the recording studio. People send what they like.”

He looked at her, then smiled.

“That’s very good detective work.”

He looked at her, his expression becoming softer.

“Thank you for making dinner.”

“You helped.”

“I stirred the soup and arranged the plates.”

“And cut the vegetables.”

“Rather badly.”

She laughed.

“Not that badly.”

“I appreciate your generosity.”

She took another bite, then looked at him.

“Do you cook at home?”

“Not particularly.”

“Not even when you’re in Munich?”

“I have people who prepare meals at the house.”

“Your family house?”

“Yes. My mother has a cook she has worked with for years.”

CC nodded.

“Do you eat with your parents often?”

“When I’m there, usually.”

“That’s nice.”

“It is. Although my mother has a habit of deciding that every meal is an opportunity to discuss my personal life.”

CC looked amused.

“Does she?”

“She’s been trying to persuade me to settle down for some time.”

She lowered her eyes, smiling.

“Has she stopped?”

“Not entirely.”

“Because of me?”

Declan considered her.

“Partly.”

He continued calmly, “I told her there is someone I’m serious about. That I’m taking my time because I want to do things properly.”

CC’s expression softened.

“What did she say?”

“She was pleased.”

“Really?”

“She asked whether you were happy.”

CC blinked.

“She asked that?”

“Yes.”

“And what did you tell her?”

“That I hoped you were.”

She looked down at her plate, a little shy. Declan watched her.

“Would you like to know something else?”

“What?”

“She asked whether I would be spending Christmas in Munich.”

CC nodded.

“Will you?”

“Yes. My parents will be there. We usually spend Christmas at the family residence.”

“What is it like?”

“Quiet, compared to the rest of the year. My father prefers a small gathering. My mother disagrees.”

CC laughed.

“How many people does she invite?”

“Enough to make my father’s definition of small rather irrelevant.”

She smiled.

“Does your mother decorate the house?”

Declan’s expression shifted into something amused.

“Very enthusiastically.”

“Really?”

“She has a large Christmas tree in the main hall. She insists on decorating it herself, although she usually ends up directing everyone else.”

CC laughed.

“I can imagine.”

“She has boxes of ornaments. Some are quite old. There are glass decorations my grandmother bought years ago, and a collection of little wooden figures she adds to every year.”

“That sounds beautiful.”

“It is.”

He drank some water.

“My mother likes the house to feel warm during Christmas. She says the rest of the year is too busy for people to remember to enjoy it.”

CC smiled at that.

“She’s right.”

“I suspect you’ll like her.”

The words were delivered casually, but CC looked up.

“Do you think so?”

“I do.”

She hesitated.

“I’m a little nervous about meeting her.”

“You don’t need to be.”

“What if she doesn’t like me?”

Declan put his glass down.

“CC.”

She looked at him.

“My mother may ask too many questions. She may offer you more food than you can possibly eat. She may try to show you every Christmas decoration she owns.”

CC smiled.

“But she won’t expect you to be anyone other than yourself.”

He reached across the table and touched her hand.

“And I wouldn’t bring you into my family if I didn’t want you there.”

She looked at their hands. She didn’t say anything.

Then she turned her palm slightly, letting her fingers rest against his.

“I’d like to meet her someday.”

“She’ll be insufferable about it.”

“Maybe not immediately.”

“Whenever you’re comfortable.”

She smiled.

“Thank you.”

He gave her hand a gentle squeeze before letting her return to her meal. After dinner, CC began collecting the plates. Declan stood immediately.

“I’ll help.”

“You can wash them.”

He looked towards the sink.

“Certainly.”

She raised an eyebrow.

“Are you sure?”

“I believe I can manage washing dishes.”

“That’s what you said about the vegetables.”

He smiled.

“I’m prepared to defend my reputation.”

She handed him a plate.

“Then we’ll see.”

They stood side by side at the sink. CC rinsed the dishes while Declan washed them, and for the first few minutes, the arrangement worked surprisingly well.

He was careful, perhaps overly so, but he followed her instructions.

“Not too much soap,” she reminded him.

He glanced at the bottle.

“How much is too much?”

She laughed.

“Just a little.”

He adjusted the amount.

“Like this?”

“Yes.”

“Good.”

A moment later, he handed her a clean plate. She dried it with a towel.

“See? You’re doing well.”

“I appreciate the encouragement.”

“Don’t get used to it.”

He smiled. She placed the plate in the cupboard, then turned back towards him.

There was a small streak of soap near his wrist.

“Wait.”

He glanced at her.

“What is it?”

She reached for his arm, gently wiping the soap away with the towel. Her fingers rested against his skin. Declan looked down at her hand. Then at her face. She noticed his expression.

“You’re smiling.”

He leaned slightly closer.

“I was just thinking that this is a rather pleasant way to spend a Sunday.”

She looked at him, her expression softening.

“It is.”

He reached for the towel in her hand and placed it on the counter. Then he touched her waist lightly. He held out his hand. She stepped closer. He lowered his head and kissed her forehead.

It was such a simple gesture that she almost smiled before he had even pulled away.

“Thank you for dinner, sweetheart.”

“You’re welcome.”

“And for allowing me to demonstrate my culinary abilities.”

She laughed against his chest.

“I wouldn’t call them abilities.”

“That’s rather harsh.”

“You’re better at eating.”

“I’ll accept that.”

Her eyes went to his.

“Maybe next time I’ll teach you.”

“Next time?”

She nodded.

“If you want to cook again.”

His smile was quiet.

“I’d like that.”

They moved to the sofa after the kitchen was clean.

CC sat with her legs tucked beneath her, holding a glass of water. Declan had removed his watch and placed it on the coffee table. His sleeves remained rolled up, and the top button of his shirt was undone. He looked comfortable. Perhaps a little too comfortable. She glanced at him, then at his wrist. Something caught her attention.

His watch was elegant, understated, and expensive. His clothes were similarly restrained: navy, charcoal, black, white, and the occasional pale blue.

She thought about the photographs she had seen of him at business events. Dark suits. White shirts. Navy ties. Almost always navy ties. She looked at him again.

“Declan?”

“Yes?”

“Do you like colourful things?”

He looked over.

“Some.”

“Like what?”

“Art, architecture, certain pieces of furniture.”

She smiled.

“I mean clothes.”

He considered the question.

“I prefer simple colours.”

“Navy?”

“Among others.”

“Grey?”

“Yes.”

“Black?”

“Occasionally.”

She tilted her head.

“Do you own any ties that aren’t navy?”

He looked amused.

“Of course.”

She waited.

He said, “A few.”

“How many?”

“I’m not certain.”

“More than five?”

“Probably.”

“More than ten?”

He watched her.

“Is this an interrogation?”

She laughed.

“I’m just curious.”

“I have several colours. Navy happens to be practical.”

She nodded thoughtfully.

“Practical.”

“Precisely.”

She looked at him for another moment. Then she asked, “Do you ever wear burgundy?”

“Not often.”

“Green?”

“Rarely.”

“Light blue?”

“Occasionally.”

She hummed, as if storing the information away. Declan watched her.

“Why?”

“No reason.”

“CC.”

She looked at him innocently.

“What?”

“You’re asking an unusual number of questions about my ties.”

“Am I not allowed to?”

“You are.”

She smiled and reached for his water. He let the matter go, although the expression on her face suggested there was more to it.

A few minutes later, she leaned against his shoulder.

“Do you miss Munich when you’re away?”

“Sometimes.”

“What do you miss?”

“My parents, occasionally. The house. The quiet.”

She listened.

“Christmas, too. It’s one of the few times of the year when everyone slows down,” he said.

“Do you like Christmas?”

“I do.”

He said, “My father usually complains about the tree being too large, but he is the one who insists on putting the star on top.”

“That sounds very sweet.”

“It is.”

CC rested her cheek against his shoulder.

“Do you think you’ll enjoy Christmas this year?”

Declan looked down at her.

“I think so.”

“Because of your family?”

“Because I have something to look forward to.”

She lifted her head slightly.

“What?”

He looked at her.

“Someone.”

Her face softened. She didn’t ask him to explain.

Instead, she reached for his hand and threaded her fingers through his.

The evening passed more quickly than either of them expected.

Declan had a breakfast meeting with the regional office the following morning, and CC had a rehearsal before her afternoon commitments. He had no intention of keeping her up late.

At the entrance, she stood in front of him, holding the small paper bag he had brought earlier.

“You forgot this,” she said.

He glanced at it.

“Those are the pastries.”

“That’s why I’m giving them back.”

“Keep them.”

“There’s too much.”

“Then share them with Nicha.”

She smiled.

“I’ll do that.”

He adjusted the collar of her cardigan, his fingers brushing her neck.

“I’ll see you tomorrow before I leave.”

She nodded.

“What time?”

“My flight is in the evening. I can spend the afternoon with you.”

Her smile faded just a little.

“Right. Monday.”

He noticed the change.

“Yes.”

She looked down.

“I know.”

Declan touched her chin gently, inviting her to look at him.

“It’s only a few weeks.”

“I know.”

“And we’ll speak.”

“I know.”

He smiled.

“You’ve said that three times.”

“Because I know.”

He laughed, then leaned down and kissed her. This time, she reached up to hold his arm, keeping him close longer. When they parted, she looked at him.

“I’ll miss you.”

His face softened.

“I’ll miss you too, sweetheart.”

She gave him a smile.

“Even though I’m sure you’ll be very busy.”

“Being busy doesn’t make me miss you less.”

She looked away, smiling. He kissed her temple once more.

“Goodnight, CC.”

“Goodnight.”

He stepped into the corridor, but she called his name before he could turn away.

“Declan?”

He looked back.

“Yes?”

“Next time, I’ll cook something different.”

“I’ll look forward to it.”

“And you can help again.”

His smile deepened.

“I’ll prepare myself.”

She laughed.

“Good. You need practice.”

He gave her a small nod. Then he left.

CC remained by the door until she heard the lift arrive. Only then did she close it.

She returned to the living room, where the sofa still held the faint warmth of where he had been sitting.

On the coffee table, his watch had left a small circular impression in the soft fabric of the coaster. She picked it up and moved it aside. Then she glanced at her phone. There was already a message.

Declan: Thank you for tonight.

CC: Thank you for coming.

Declan: I enjoyed every minute.

CC: Even the vegetables?

Declan: Especially the vegetables.

She laughed.

CC: You’re lying.

Declan: I wouldn’t dare.

She smiled at the screen. Then, after a moment, she opened her browser and searched for men’s silk ties. She wasn’t planning to buy anything immediately. She only wanted to look.

A few minutes later, she was comparing shades of burgundy, deep forest green, and muted champagne.

She thought about Declan standing in her kitchen, sleeves rolled up, concentrating far too seriously on cutting vegetables. She imagined him wearing something that wasn’t navy. Something he would never choose for himself. Her smile grew.

Perhaps it was time she returned a little of his attention. Not with anything extravagant.

Just something that would remind him of her when he was far away. She saved a few options.

Then she closed the browser and sent him one last message.

CC: Sleep well. Don’t forget to rest.

Declan: I will.

CC: And thank you for being my assistant today.

Declan: It was an honour.

CC: Goodnight, my very inexperienced chef.

Declan read the message in the back of his car. He laughed. Then he replied.

Declan: Goodnight, sweetheart. I look forward to my next lesson.

He was already looking forward to something that had nothing to do with business.

He was already certain he would be terrible at it.

But if she was the one teaching him, he was perfectly willing to try again.

chapters.title: The Part Where He Looks Back
chapters.desc: His last day in Bangkok: a silver bookmark for the book by her sofa, lunch above Sukhumvit, and a goodbye through the glass at Don Mueang, where he turns round at the foot of the jet stairs.
chapters.epigraph: “I’ve been on board for forty seconds and I already miss you.”
chapters.content:
On Monday morning, CC was trying hard not to look at the clock. It was becoming increasingly difficult.

Declan’s jet was due to leave Don Mueang at seven in the evening. He had a few business matters to attend to before leaving, but he had promised to spend the afternoon with her. By any reasonable measure, they still had plenty of time.

Yet she had already checked the clock four times in the last twenty minutes.

She stood in front of her wardrobe, considering whether to change her outfit.

She had initially chosen a white blouse and a soft grey skirt. Then she had decided it looked too much like something she would wear to an interview. She changed into a pale blue dress, only to wonder whether it was too formal for an afternoon together.

In the end, she returned to the white blouse. It was comfortable.

And Declan had once told her he liked seeing her in white.

She was fastening her watch when her phone vibrated.

Declan: I’m downstairs.

She read the message.

CC: Coming.

A moment later, she picked up her handbag and headed for the door.

Downstairs, Declan was standing beside the car, speaking with Alexander.

He wore a charcoal suit today, a white shirt, and a dark navy tie. His jacket was unbuttoned, and one hand rested in his trouser pocket as he listened to his assistant.

When he saw CC approaching, his attention shifted immediately. Alexander followed his gaze.

“Good morning, Miss Chanya.”

“Good morning, Alexander.”

“Good morning, sweetheart.”

Declan leaned forward and kissed her cheek. She smiled.

“You’re early.”

“I finished sooner than expected.”

“That’s good.”

He studied her face.

“Did you sleep well?”

“Yes.”

“Breakfast?”

She gave him a look. “I finished the pastries you left. All of them.”

“Nicha was meant to have half.”

“Nicha doesn’t need to know.”

Alexander, who had been waiting beside the car, glanced down at his tablet.

“I’ll give you both a moment. The luggage is already loaded, sir.”

Declan nodded.

“Thank you, Alexander.”

The assistant stepped away. CC looked at the car.

“Are we going somewhere?”

“Lunch first. Then I thought we could spend the afternoon together.”

She nodded.

“Okay.”

He opened the rear door for her. As she settled inside, she noticed a small paper bag on the seat.

“What’s that?”

“Something for you.”

She lifted her eyes to his.

“Another surprise?”

“A small one.”

She picked it up but didn’t open it immediately.

“Can I look now?”

“Of course.”

Inside was a slim ivory leather case, small enough to fit in her handbag. She opened it carefully. A delicate silver bookmark lay inside.

It was beautifully made, with a tiny engraved crescent at one end and a fine chain attached to it. On the back, there were two small words.

Until soon.

CC ran her thumb over the engraving. She didn’t say anything. Declan watched her.

He said, “I thought you might like something you could keep with you. There was a book beside your sofa last night, with a receipt keeping your place.”

She looked up.

“You remembered that?”

“I noticed the receipt.”

She examined the bookmark again.

“It’s beautiful.”

“I’m glad.”

She looked at him, her expression softening.

“Thank you.”

He reached over and gently brushed his fingers against hers.

“It’s only a little thing.”

“It’s not.”

He held her gaze. She closed the case carefully and placed it inside her handbag.

“I’ll use it.”

“I hope you do.”

Then the car pulled away. Lunch, in a private room above Sukhumvit, was quieter than their previous meals.

They hadn’t run out of things to talk about. There were plenty of things to discuss: her upcoming recording schedule, his work in Munich, the Christmas preparations at his parents’ house. But there was an awareness between them now. Every hour was bringing his departure closer. CC tried not to let it show.

She asked him about the meeting he had attended that morning, listened to his explanation about a regional investment proposal, and told him about a new song she had been considering recording. Declan listened as attentively as he always did.

At one point, she reached for her glass and noticed him watching her.

“You’re looking at me.”

“I’m allowed to.”

She smiled.

“That’s true.”

He reached across the table and moved a small piece of fruit towards her plate.

“Eat.”

She gave him an amused look.

“You left me enough pastries for breakfast.”

“And now I’m feeding you lunch.”

“I’m beginning to think you enjoy this too much.”

“I do.”

She laughed.

Then, after a moment, she asked, “When will you be back?”

Declan put down his glass.

“I haven’t fixed the exact date yet. I’ll have to see how the schedule develops after Christmas.”

She nodded.

“Before New Year?”

“I’ll try.”

She looked down at her plate.

“Okay.”

He noticed the change in her expression.

“CC.”

She looked up.

“I don’t want to promise you a date and then disappoint you.”

“I understand.”

“I’ll make the arrangements as soon as I can.”

She nodded again. “Okay.”

He reached across the table and took her hand.

“I’ll be in touch every day.”

She smiled a little. “You’re going to be very busy.”

“I’ll be busy and in touch. I can do both.”

She considered him. Her fingers curled gently around his.

“Then I’ll look forward to it.”

They returned to her apartment after lunch. Declan had intended to spend the afternoon with her without any particular plan. They settled on the sofa, and CC put on a quiet playlist while he reviewed a few messages on his phone. For a while, she read.

The bookmark he had given her was already inside her book. Declan noticed it when she shifted the pages.

“You’ve used it.”

She looked down.

“Of course.”

“Already?”

“I wanted to.”

He smiled and returned to his phone. A few minutes later, CC closed her book.

“Are you still working?”

“Just reviewing something.”

“Is it important?”

“Not particularly.”

She looked at him.

“Then put it away.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“Am I being dismissed from work?”

“Yes.”

He considered her expression, then locked his phone and placed it on the table.

“Very well.”

She looked pleased.

“Thank you.”

He leaned back against the sofa.

“Now what?”

“Nothing.”

“Nothing?”

“We can just sit.”

He tilted his head. Then he opened his arm.

She moved closer without hesitation, resting her head against his chest. Declan settled his arm around her shoulders. The music continued in the background.

Outside, Bangkok carried on with its usual afternoon rhythm. Cars moved along the road below, the occasional motorcycle passed, and somewhere in the building, a door closed.

Inside, there was only the quiet sound of the music and the steady rhythm of his breathing.

CC traced a small line along the seam of his shirt.

“Will you be cold in Munich?”

“It’s winter. Probably.”

“Do you have enough warm clothes?”

“Yes.”

“Properly warm ones?”

He looked down at her.

“I’m thirty-one, sweetheart. I know how to dress for winter.”

She smiled.

“I know. I’m just asking.”

He brushed his fingers through her hair.

“I’ll be fine.”

She was quiet. Then she asked, “Will you send me a picture of your mother’s Christmas tree?”

He smiled.

“Of course.”

“And the house?”

“If you’d like.”

“I would.”

“I’ll show you everything.”

She looked up. She laughed. Then her face became thoughtful.

“Do you think she’ll decorate it before you arrive?”

“Almost certainly. She usually begins in early December.”

“Does she have a favourite ornament?”

He considered the question.

“There is a small glass star that belonged to my grandmother. My father puts it on the top every year, and my mother tells him it’s crooked.”

CC smiled.

“That’s lovely.”

“It is.”

She glanced up at him.

“I’d like to see it.”

“You will.”

He said it, without turning it into a grand promise. And somehow, that made her feel better. At twenty past three, Declan’s phone rang. Alexander.

He answered, speaking in English, his voice returning to its usual businesslike calm.

CC moved away slightly to give him privacy, though he caught her hand before she could stand.

“You don’t have to leave.”

She looked at him. He gave her a small nod towards the sofa. She settled back while he took the call.

The conversation concerned a document that required his approval before departure. Declan listened, asked two precise questions, and gave instructions about the revised version. It lasted less than ten minutes. When he finished, he placed the phone down.

“Sorry.”

She shook her head.

“It’s okay.”

“Everything is arranged.”

“Good.”

He glanced at the clock.

“We should leave in about forty minutes.”
