They had arranged a private instructor for CC’s first proper lesson. Declan had offered to teach her himself, but she had declined.

“I don’t want you to spend the entire morning worrying about me falling.”

He had looked amused.

“I wouldn’t mind.”

“I would.”

So they had agreed on an instructor. For the first hour, CC concentrated on learning how to stand, move, and stop. She was careful, a little tense, and occasionally frustrated when her skis seemed to have a mind of their own. Declan watched from a short distance away. He didn’t interfere.

When she finally managed to make it down a gentle slope without falling, he applauded. CC looked towards him, smiling broadly.

“Did you see?”

“I did.”

“I didn’t fall!”

“An excellent achievement.”

She laughed.

“Don’t sound so surprised.”

“I’m not surprised, sweetheart. I’m impressed.”

She smiled and continued towards him. Then, as she reached the bottom, one ski slipped slightly. Declan stepped forward instinctively. She caught herself, but her face changed. He was beside her immediately.

“Are you all right?”

She nodded.

“Yes.”

“Sure?”

“Yes. Just surprised.”

He checked her balance before letting her move again.

“Take your time.”

She turned to him.

“I’m trying.”

“You’re doing well.”

His voice was calm, without a trace of impatience. She smiled.

“Will you stay with me?”

“Of course.”

And he did. For the rest of the morning, he stayed nearby, occasionally offering encouragement, never making her feel slow or inexperienced. By lunchtime, CC had improved.

She was still cautious, but she had begun to enjoy herself.

They stopped at a mountain restaurant overlooking the slopes. CC sat down with a satisfied sigh.

“My legs are tired.”

Declan removed his gloves.

“Understandable.”

She held his gaze.

“Are you tired?”

“Not particularly.”

“Of course not.”

He smiled.

“Would you like something warm?”

“Hot chocolate.”

“Anything to eat?”

She read the menu.

“Maybe soup.”

He ordered for both of them, making sure they had a table near the window.

When their drinks arrived, CC wrapped both hands around her cup. She took a sip. Then she looked at him.

“This is a very good holiday.”

He smiled.

“I’m glad.”

“I like the farm.”

“I noticed.”

“And the skiing.”

“Even after this morning?”

She laughed.

“Yes. Especially after I managed not to fall.”

He raised his cup.

“To your successful morning.”

She clinked hers gently against his.

“To not falling.”

By the time they returned to the farmhouse, CC was exhausted.

She had changed into soft clothes and was sitting on the rug in front of the fireplace, her legs stretched out beneath a blanket. Declan came downstairs with two cups of tea.

He placed one on the low table beside her.

“Here.”

She looked up.

“Thank you.”

He sat on the sofa behind her.

“How are your legs?”

“Still attached.”

He laughed.

“That’s reassuring.”

She leaned back against the sofa, resting her head near his knee.

“I’m tired.”

“I can see that.”

“Will you massage my legs?”

He looked down at her.

“Of course.”

She smiled and shifted slightly so he could sit more comfortably.

He moved closer and gently began massaging her calves through the soft fabric of her trousers. CC closed her eyes.

For several minutes, the room was quiet except for the crackling fireplace.

Then she said, “I think I want to do this again tomorrow.”

“Skiing?”

She nodded.

“Maybe I’ll be better.”

“I suspect you will.”

She opened one eye.

“Will you ski with me?”

“Of course.”

“Not go ahead?”

He looked amused.

“I’ll stay with you.”

She smiled and closed her eyes again. After a while, she reached for his hand. He stopped and let her take it.

She turned his palm upward and traced the lines lightly with her finger.

“Thank you for bringing me here.”

He looked down at her.

“You don’t have to thank me.”

“I want to.”

He brushed her hair away from her cheek.

“I wanted to spend time with you somewhere we could both forget about work for a little while.”

She smiled.

“I think we have.”

He kissed her temple.

“Good.”

She looked up at him.

“Do you like it?”

“The farm?”

“The holiday.”

He considered the question.

“I like waking up with you. I like having breakfast with you. I like watching you make friends with animals that seem determined to steal your clothes.”

She laughed.

“And?”

“I like that you ask me to ski with you even though I’m not very good at being patient on beginner slopes.”

She gave him a look.

“You’ve been very patient.”

“Then I’m improving.”

She smiled. He dipped his head and kissed her gently. When he drew back, she was still smiling.

“I’m glad it’s you,” she whispered.

His face softened.

“So am I, Cela.”

On the fourth morning, CC had decided she wanted to help Anna prepare breakfast.

Declan discovered this when he came downstairs and found her standing in the kitchen wearing an apron. He stopped at the doorway.

“What are you doing?”

She turned.

“Helping.”

He looked at the apron.

“Are you?”

“Yes.”

Anna laughed from beside the counter.

“She is. She’s been helping me with the bread.”

Declan approached.

“Should I be concerned?”

CC tilted her head.

“Why?”

“I’ve never seen you look so serious about flour.”

She gave him her best wounded look.

“I’m concentrating.”

He smiled and kissed her cheek.

“Then I won’t disturb you.”

But he stayed. He watched her knead the dough, occasionally brushing flour from the counter. When she asked him to hold a bowl, he did. When Anna asked him to fetch something from the pantry, he went without complaint.

At one point, CC noticed a little flour on his sleeve. She reached over and brushed it away.

“There.”

He looked over.

“Thank you.”

“You’re helping.”

“I’m doing my best.”

She smiled. “It shows.”

Anna watched them with a fond expression.

“You make a good team.”

Declan glanced at CC.

“I think so.”

CC lowered her eyes, smiling. Later, when they sat down to breakfast, Anna placed two small loaves in front of them.

“One each. You’re going to different cities, Declan tells me.”

CC looked delighted.

“Really?”

“Of course.”

“Thank you so much.”

Declan looked at the loaf.

“We’ll have to make room in the luggage.”

She smiled. “Mine is coming home with me.”

“Then we’ll make room.”

Their final morning arrived too quickly. CC stood on the balcony in a thick sweater, looking out over the fields.

The sky was pale, and the mountains were quiet beneath their covering of snow. Declan came out carrying two cups of coffee. He handed one to her.

“Good morning.”

She accepted it.

“Good morning.”

He stood beside her.

“Enjoying the view?”

She nodded.

“I don’t want to leave.”

He smiled.

“We can come back.”

“Promise?”

“Of course.”

She turned towards him.

“Next time, I want to spend more time with the animals.”

“Not more skiing?”

“Both.”

“Then we’ll arrange it.”

She smiled and leaned against his shoulder. They stood there, drinking their coffee.

After a while, she said, “I think I understand why you wanted somewhere like this.”

He looked down at her.

“Why?”

“Because nobody expects anything from us here.”

He listened.

“We can wake up, eat breakfast, walk around, do silly things. Nobody is waiting for me to perform or for you to attend a meeting.”

He smiled.

“Exactly.”

She looked towards the fields.

“I like being ordinary with you.”

Declan turned slightly towards her.

“Sweetheart.”

She looked up.

“I don’t think there’s anything ordinary about having you here.”

She laughed.

“You know what I mean.”

“I do.”

He took her free hand.

“And I like it too.”

She leaned into his shoulder.

“Can we have more holidays like this?”

“As many as you’d like.”

She smiled.

“Don’t promise too much.”

He kissed the top of her head.

“I’m quite comfortable with that promise.”

That afternoon, they were back at Zurich Airport. Her flight to Bangkok left first, and his to Munich an hour after it.

They stood together near the departure area. Zurich wasn’t Bangkok; no one here was looking for her.

CC had her coat over one arm and her handbag on her shoulder.

Declan held the small bag with her loaf from the farmhouse. She looked at it.

“You’re carrying the bread.”

“Yes.”

“It’s not fragile.”

“It’s yours. That makes it fragile.”

She laughed. He reached for her hand.

“Did you enjoy your first holiday with me?”

She nodded.

“Very much.”

“Good.”

“I liked the farm. I liked skiing. I liked breakfast.”

She smiled. He laughed.

“I’ll remember that.”

She looked at him.

“Thank you for making it so lovely.”

He brushed his thumb over her hand.

“You made it lovely.”

She smiled. Then he bent and kissed her. It was a familiar goodbye, but somehow a little different now. They were no longer wondering what they meant to each other. They had a place in each other’s lives, and this holiday had given them something that belonged entirely to them. When they drew apart, CC looked at him.

“Next time, somewhere with a beach?”

He smiled.

“Certainly.”

“And no goats.”

“I can’t guarantee that.”

She laughed.

“Declan!”

He kissed her hair.

“Go on, sweetheart. You’ll be late.”

She stepped away, then turned back.

“Call me when you land.”

“I will.”

“And send me the goat photos. All of them.”

He smiled.

“Yes, Cela.”

She grinned. Then she took her bread from him and walked towards security.

Declan watched her until she disappeared into the crowd. A few minutes later, his phone vibrated.

Cela: I already miss the farm.

He smiled.

Declan: We haven’t even left Switzerland.

Cela: I’m at the gate. That counts.

Declan: I’ll take you back.

Cela: Promise?

Declan: Promise.

A photograph followed. It was the picture he had taken on the first morning at the farm: CC standing beside the cow, laughing, her hair slightly windswept and her cheeks pink from the cold.

Declan: I think she misses you too.

CC replied almost immediately.

Cela: Tell her I’ll come back.

He took in the photograph again, smiling to himself. Then he typed:

Declan: I’ll tell her, sweetheart.

He put his phone away and picked up his own loaf of bread.

Their first holiday was over, and he already knew which photograph he would keep. Not the mountains or the farmhouse. CC laughing beside a cow, her cheeks pink from the cold. Nothing about it was extraordinary, and it was the best thing on his phone.

chapters.title: The Most Entertaining Thing on His Screen
chapters.desc: Her variety show comes out, and Declan watches a thirty-one-second dance more times than he will admit. Frankfurt waits half an hour.
chapters.epigraph: “A very strange potato, sweetheart.”
chapters.content:
On Thursday afternoon, the day after they left Switzerland, Declan had a video conference scheduled for three.

He had finished reviewing the documents Alexander had sent him, answered two messages from his father, and was now sitting in his office with a glass of water beside his laptop. In Bangkok, it was half past eight in the evening. His phone lit up.

Cela: Are you working?

He glanced at the message and smiled.

Declan: I was. I’m taking a break.

Cela: Good.

Declan: How was your day, sweetheart?

Cela: Busy. I landed this morning and went straight to filming.

Declan: Straight from the plane?

Cela: I slept on the plane. In the bed you booked.

Declan: Everything went well?

Cela: Yes! I think it was fun.

Declan: What did you film?

Cela: A variety show. I’ll send you the link when it’s released.

Declan: I’ll look forward to it.

Cela: Don’t expect too much. I was just talking most of the time.

Declan smiled at that.

Declan: I can’t imagine that being a problem.

Cela: Declan.

Declan: What?

Cela: You’re biased.

Declan: Undoubtedly.

She sent him a laughing emoji. He put the phone down and returned to his work.

He didn’t think much more about the programme until the following Wednesday afternoon, when CC sent him a message with a link.

Cela: It’s out!

A second message followed.

Cela: Please don’t laugh at me.

Declan checked the screen. Then he smiled.

Declan: Now I’m particularly interested.

Cela: That’s not reassuring.

Declan: I’ll be kind.

Cela: You’d better.

It was twenty to four. Frankfurt was at a quarter past. He opened the link. The programme began with a lively introduction.

It was a popular Korean-style entertainment format adapted for Thai television, with a panel of hosts, rotating celebrity guests, games, conversations, and a few unexpected challenges. CC appeared a little after the opening segment.

She was wearing a soft blue outfit, her hair falling neatly over her shoulders. Her makeup was light, and she smiled politely as the hosts welcomed her. Declan leaned back.

He had seen her in countless photographs. He had attended events where she was surrounded by cameras, watched her perform under stage lights, and seen the polished version of her that the public knew.

But he still caught himself looking at her as if he hadn’t seen her in a while. She was beautiful. He knew that already. It wasn’t a new discovery.

Yet sometimes, when he saw her unexpectedly, the thought arrived with such force that he had to pause.

Her face was delicate without looking fragile. Her expressions were lovely because she never seemed to realise how much they changed. When she listened, her eyes were attentive. When she was amused, her smile appeared gradually, almost as if she were trying to contain it. And when she laughed— Declan’s mouth curved.

He had always thought her laughter was one of his favourite things.

On screen, one of the hosts asked her about her hobbies. CC answered politely.

“I like reading, listening to music, and sometimes cooking.”

The host asked what she liked to cook.

“Usually simple things. Soup, noodles, congee.”

“Can you cook well?”

CC considered the question.

“I think I can cook enough to feed myself.”

The hosts laughed.

She smiled, then added, “I’m not sure whether that’s the same as cooking well.”

Declan laughed. He paused the video, looking at her frozen expression. Then he shook his head, smiling to himself.

“Sweetheart.”

He resumed. The host asked whether she ever cooked for other people.

“Sometimes.”

“Do people enjoy it?”

“I think so. Nobody has complained.”

The panel laughed again. One of the hosts leaned forward.

“Maybe they’re afraid of you.”

CC’s eyes widened.

“Why would they be afraid?”

“Because you’re beautiful. Maybe they’re too nervous to tell you the truth.”

She looked genuinely puzzled. Then she said, seriously, “But if the food is bad, I should know. Otherwise, I’ll keep making it.”

Declan laughed. Not a polite laugh. A proper one.

He leaned back, his eyes still on the screen.

She hadn’t done anything extraordinary. She wasn’t trying to be funny. She wasn’t performing a rehearsed joke or deliberately creating a moment for the camera. She was answering questions. And somehow, that was enough. The programme moved into a game segment.

The guests were asked to identify objects from close-up photographs. CC was given a picture of something that looked like a complicated kitchen utensil. She stared at it for several seconds.

“Is it a potato?”

The host blinked.

“A potato?”

“Maybe a very strange potato.”

The panel burst into laughter. The photograph was revealed to be a kitchen scrubber. CC looked at it.

“Oh.”

She nodded, accepting the result.

“I was close.”

The host laughed.

“How was that close?”

“They’re both in the kitchen.”

Declan covered his mouth. He glanced at the screen, then at the time. He had a meeting in less than twenty minutes. He should stop watching. Instead, he adjusted his position and continued.

The next segment involved the guests answering questions about their habits.

One host asked CC what she usually did when she was nervous. She thought about it.

“I become quiet.”

“Really? You don’t look nervous.”

“I think that’s because I become even quieter.”

The host laughed.

“Then how do we know you’re nervous?”

CC smiled.

“You probably don’t.”

Declan’s expression softened. He liked that answer.

It was so distinctly her: honest, unembellished, and funny without trying to be.

He watched her listen to the other guests, nodding when they spoke, occasionally adding a small comment that made the hosts laugh. She was comfortable.

Not overly talkative, not trying to dominate the conversation, but attentive and naturally responsive.

He enjoyed the programme far more than he had anticipated.

At one point, she laughed at something another guest said and leaned forward, covering her mouth. Declan paused the video. He stared at the screen. Her eyes were almost closed from laughing. He smiled.

Then, he said, “You’re ridiculous.”

He resumed the programme. The show moved into a short challenge.

The hosts announced that each guest would have to demonstrate a popular TikTok dance. CC looked immediately uncomfortable. Declan straightened. The host turned towards her.

“CC, do you know this dance?”

She studied the screen they were showing her.

“I’m not sure.”

The host laughed.

“You’re an idol. Surely you know TikTok dances.”

CC gave a small, helpless smile.

“I’m an idol, but I’m not necessarily good at TikTok dances.”

Declan’s eyebrows lifted. He was already smiling. The hosts explained the choreography.

It was a short dance, cheerful and slightly playful, with a sequence of hand movements, a small shoulder movement, and a final pose. CC watched carefully. Then she tried it once. She missed one of the movements. The hosts laughed. She stopped and looked at them.

“Wait. I need to see it again.”

The host replayed the demonstration. CC nodded with concentration.

“Okay. I understand.”

She tried again. This time, she got most of it right, but her timing was slightly off. She looked towards the host.

“Was that correct?”

“Almost!”

She smiled.

“Almost is good.”

Declan laughed. Then the music started again. CC stood in front of the camera. And did the dance.

She wasn’t trying to make it look cute. She followed the choreography, her expression focused at first, then gradually turning into a smile when she reached the final movement.

At the end, she tilted her head slightly and made the final pose. The hosts applauded.

One of them exclaimed, “That’s so cute!”

CC laughed, looking a little embarrassed.

“Thank you.”

Declan didn’t move. He stared at the screen. The programme continued, but he was still thinking about the dance. He rewound. Watched it again. Then once more. He sat back, smiling in disbelief.

“Oh, sweetheart.”

He replayed it. The little movement of her shoulders. The way she had looked so concentrated at the beginning. The smile that appeared when she realised she had managed to get through it. The final pose. He watched it again. Then he laughed, shaking his head. It was absurd.

He had seen her perform complicated choreography on enormous stages. He had watched her dance in music videos with professional lighting, elaborate costumes, and perfectly coordinated movements.

But somehow, this thirty-second segment was proving more difficult to stop watching. He replayed it again. His phone rang. Alexander. Declan glanced at the time.

“Alexander.”

“Mr. Lincoln, I wanted to confirm whether we’re proceeding with Frankfurt at a quarter past four.”

Declan looked at the laptop. The programme was paused on CC’s final pose.

“Yes. Give me five minutes.”

“Certainly.”

Alexander hesitated.

“Everything all right?”

Declan glanced at the screen again.

“Quite.”

“Very good. I’ll have everyone ready.”

The call ended. Declan looked at the video. Then he pressed play again. Five minutes later, Alexander received another message.

Declan: Move Frankfurt to a quarter to five, please.

Alexander reread the message. He glanced at the calendar. Then he replied.

Alexander: Certainly, Mr. Lincoln.

He didn’t ask why. He had worked for Declan long enough to recognise when a matter wasn’t urgent enough to interrupt his employer’s attention.

And lately, there seemed to be a specific person capable of doing that. Declan finally reached for his phone.

Declan: I’ve watched your programme.

CC replied a few seconds later.

Cela: Already?

Declan: Yes.

Cela: Was it okay?

He smiled.

Declan: Very entertaining.

Cela: Really?

Declan: You were very good.

Cela: I didn’t do much.

Declan: That was precisely the point.

She sent a confused emoji.

Cela: What does that mean?

Declan: You made an entire programme enjoyable simply by being yourself.

There was a pause. Then:

Cela: You’re being biased again.

Declan: I warned you I was.

She sent a laughing emoji. Then another message.

Cela: Did you see the dance?

Declan checked the screen. He smiled.

Declan: I did.

Cela: I was so embarrassed.

Declan: Why?

Cela: Because I didn’t know the dance properly.

Declan: You did perfectly well.

Cela: I almost missed the last part.

Declan: I noticed.

She sent a horrified emoji.

Cela: You noticed?!

He laughed.

Declan: I noticed everything.

Cela: That’s embarrassing.

Declan: I thought it was adorable.

A moment passed. Then she replied.

Cela: Please don’t replay it.

Declan glanced at the screen. He glanced at the video still open on his laptop. Then he typed.

Declan: I wasn’t planning to.

He paused. Then added:

Declan: Although I may have watched it a few times.

CC’s reply came almost immediately.

Cela: DECLAN.

He laughed.

Declan: What?

Cela: How many times?

He considered lying. Then decided against it.

Declan: Enough to know the choreography.

She sent a series of embarrassed emojis. He smiled so broadly that he had to put his phone down.

At twenty-four minutes past four, CC called him. In Bangkok, it was nearly half past ten. He answered almost immediately.

Her face appeared on the screen. She was sitting on her sofa, wearing a soft white top, her hair loosely tied back. She looked at him with narrowed eyes.

“Why did you watch it so many times?”

He settled back.

“Because I liked it.”

“It’s only a short dance.”

“Thirty-one seconds.”

“You’ve seen me dance properly.”

“I have.”

“Then why?”

He smiled.

“Would you like an honest answer?”

She nodded.

“Because you looked very cute.”

Her face changed.

“Declan.”

He laughed.

“What?”

“You’re making it sound like I was doing something ridiculous.”

“You weren’t.”

“Then why are you laughing?”

“Because I find you very endearing.”

She looked away, smiling despite herself. He watched her.

There was something about her expression that made him want to reach through the screen and pull her into his arms. It wasn’t that he found her beautiful. He did, very much.

But there were moments when her beauty seemed to make him almost helplessly fond of her.

The way she blinked when she was confused. The way she tried to hide her smile.

The way she became slightly defensive when she was embarrassed, even though she was clearly pleased.

He had a strange urge to kiss her forehead, pinch her cheeks gently, and tell her she was too lovely for her own good.

It was an almost overwhelming tenderness, bordering on ridiculous.

He had once heard someone call it cuteness aggression. He understood the phrase better now.

“What’s that expression?” CC asked.

He watched her.

“What expression?”

“You’re smiling.”

“Am I not allowed to?”

“You’re smiling like you know something.”

He gave a quiet laugh.

“I do know something.”

“What?”

“That I miss you.”

Her face softened.

“Oh.”

“And that I would very much like to kiss you right now.”

She smiled.

“You could have said that earlier.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“Would you have allowed it?”

She nodded.

“Maybe.”

“Maybe?”

She gave him a small, playful look.

“You’ll have to come and find out.”

He laughed.

“That’s a rather tempting invitation.”

She smiled, then rested her chin on her hand.

“Did you really watch the whole programme?”

“From beginning to end.”

“Even the game?”

“Yes.”

She looked offended.

“Why?”

“Because you looked so certain that a kitchen scrubber was a potato.”

She burst out laughing.

“It looked like one!”

He laughed with her.

“A very strange potato, sweetheart.”

She covered her face.

“I can’t believe you watched that.”

“I enjoyed every minute.”

She lowered her hands. He tilted his head. She groaned.

“Please.”

He smiled.

“I’m afraid that part may become a favourite.”

She gave him a look.

“Don’t you dare show anyone.”

“I wouldn’t.”

His answer was immediate and sincere. He wouldn’t share something because he found it adorable. The moment belonged to her, and he liked being the person who could enjoy it privately. CC seemed to understand. She smiled.

“Good.”

The conversation continued for another twenty minutes, while Frankfurt waited without knowing it.

CC told him about the filming day, the hosts, and how one of them had insisted she try the dance again after the first attempt. Declan listened, occasionally asking questions. Then she remembered something.

“Oh, I forgot.”

“What?”

“The producer said the clip might be posted separately.”

He looked interested.

“Will it?”

“I think so.”

“Then I’ll look forward to it.”

She smiled.

“You’ve already seen it.”

“I can watch it again.”

She laughed.

“Of course you can.”

He glanced at the time.

“Shouldn’t you be getting ready for bed?”

“Are you telling me to sleep?”

“I’m suggesting it.”

“Because you have work?”

“Because I want you to rest.”

She smiled.

“Okay.”

He looked at her.

“Goodnight, Cela.”

Her face softened at the name.

“Goodnight, Declan.”

“Sleep well, sweetheart.”

“You too.”

They ended the call. Declan returned to the programme.

He watched the final segment, then closed the page. His meeting with Frankfurt began shortly afterwards. The meeting ended a little before six.

Alexander sent him the revised documents for the following morning, and Declan reviewed the first few pages before closing his laptop. His phone lit up with a notification. CC had sent him a short video.

It was the TikTok dance clip, edited into a vertical format.

Cela: They posted it.

He opened it. Watched once. Then again. The third time, he caught himself smiling at the same moment she had smiled during the final pose. He shook his head.

There was no reasonable explanation for how much he enjoyed such a small thing. He typed:

Declan: I’ve seen it.

Cela: And?

Declan: Still adorable.

Cela: You need a hobby.

Declan: I appear to have found one.

Cela: Unfortunately.

He laughed.

Declan: Very unfortunate.

She sent him a heart. Declan saved the video.

Not to a public folder, not to anything shared with his assistants. Just to his own phone. He gave it a private name.

Cela — TikTok.

That night, at home, he placed the phone on his bedside table and turned off the light.

A few minutes later, he picked it up again. He watched the video one last time.

Or at least, he told himself it would be the last time.

On Thursday morning, Alexander entered Declan’s office with a folder.

“Good morning, Mr. Lincoln.”

“Good morning.”

Alexander placed the folder on his desk.

“The Frankfurt team has confirmed the revised figures. I’ve also moved your afternoon call to accommodate the New York office.”

“Thank you.”

Alexander noticed the phone beside the folder. The screen was illuminated. A familiar young woman was frozen mid-dance. He looked at it for half a second. Then looked away. Declan followed his gaze. A faint smile appeared.

“Something to add, Alexander?”

“No, sir.”

“Good.”

Alexander opened his notebook.

“Your first meeting is at nine.”

“I’m aware.”

There was a brief pause.

Then Alexander, with the careful neutrality of a man who valued his employment, said, “I hope you enjoyed the programme.”

Declan looked up. He said nothing. Then he smiled.

“Very much.”

Alexander nodded.

“I’m glad to hear it.”

He turned to leave.

“Alexander.”

“Yes, sir?”

“Send me the link to the full episode. I’d like to keep it.”

Alexander paused.

“Of course.”

When he left, Declan picked up his phone. He opened the saved clip again.

His girlfriend appeared on screen, smiling at the camera, looking slightly embarrassed and entirely unaware of how much affection she was about to inspire. Declan watched her move through the little choreography. Then he smiled to himself.

He had spent years surrounded by people who were impressive.

People who could command a room, negotiate a deal, deliver a performance, or hold the attention of thousands. CC could do all of those things.

But what he loved most was that she didn’t need to do any of them to make him happy.

Sometimes she only had to answer a question about a potato.

He watched the dance once more before his first meeting.

chapters.title: The View from the Other Side
chapters.desc: He tells her he’s tied up with meetings that weekend, then watches BLUE HOUR from a suite at Impact Arena. Backstage, Nicha has emptied a room.
chapters.epigraph: “You hold the microphone with both hands for the first song.”
chapters.content:
Declan had attended concerts before.

He had sat through private performances at charity galas, listened to orchestras in halls with ceilings painted by artists long dead, and watched internationally acclaimed musicians perform from seats that cost more than most people’s annual salaries. He understood the mechanics of a large production. The lighting, the sound engineering, the choreography, the logistics of moving hundreds of people through a venue without anyone noticing the machinery behind it.

He had never enjoyed the noise. Tonight, at Impact Arena on the first Saturday of February, he was beginning to suspect that he had misunderstood something.

“Mr. Lincoln, the performance will begin in approximately fifteen minutes.”

Declan glanced at his watch.

“Thank you, Alexander.”

His assistant stood beside him in the private viewing suite, holding a tablet. Through the glass, the enormous concert hall was gradually filling. Thousands of people were finding their seats, waving light sticks, taking photographs of the stage, and calling out the names of the performers.

BLUE HOUR filled the screens: four girls who had debuted together at nineteen and had been filling arenas ever since. On the banners in the crowd, one name appeared more than any other.

CC. Declan looked at it. Then his phone vibrated.

Cela: Are you still working?

He smiled.

Declan: For the moment.

Cela: Don’t work too late.

Declan: I’ll try to behave.

A few seconds passed.

Cela: That doesn’t sound convincing.

He leaned back in his seat.

Declan: I’m capable of behaving when properly motivated.

Cela: You sound very confident.

Declan: I have a good incentive.

He could almost picture her expression. She was probably sitting in front of a mirror while someone adjusted her hair, reading his message with that small, reluctant smile she tried not to show when other people were around. He put the phone away. Alexander looked at him.

“Would you like me to have the refreshments brought in?”

“No, thank you.”

“Of course.”

Alexander hesitated before adding, “P’Nicha will bring you through the staff corridor after the performance. Miss Chanya has not been told, as you asked.”

“Good.”

“The suite is booked under Lincoln Group, as a brand partner. No one will think twice.”

“Thank you, Alexander.”

Alexander’s expression remained perfectly professional. Declan looked back towards the stage.

He had told CC that he might be occupied with business this weekend. Technically, he hadn’t lied. He had meetings in Bangkok, two dinners with regional partners, and a Monday morning departure. He had neglected to mention that he had arranged his schedule around her concert. He wanted to see her perform.

Not through a screen, not through a carefully edited recording, and not through the occasional video she sent him from rehearsals. He wanted to see her from the audience.

To understand, even, what it felt like to be one of the thousands of people who looked towards the stage and waited for her to appear. The lights went down. The crowd erupted.

And Declan finally understood that he had underestimated the volume of affection a person could receive from strangers.

The opening performance began with a burst of light. The group appeared onstage in coordinated outfits, moving through the first sequence with the precision of people who had rehearsed the same eight counts until their bodies could remember them without thought. The audience screamed. Declan watched. He recognised CC immediately.

Her hair was styled differently from how she usually wore it, and the stage makeup sharpened her features. Under the lights, she looked almost unfamiliar. Then she smiled.

Brighter than the polite smile she gave interviewers, or the smaller one she saved for his teasing: confident, and entirely at ease.

She moved with the music, her expressions changing naturally as the performance unfolded. She knew where the cameras were. She knew when to turn, when to hold a pose, when to let the audience see her. She was good. He had known she was good.

But watching her from this distance made him appreciate something different: how much of herself she gave to the people in front of her. When her part came, the audience sang along. Declan watched the people rather than the stage.

A young girl in the front section was holding a banner with CC’s name written in silver letters. Two friends beside her were jumping excitedly. Further back, a group of fans held up photographs from different eras of the group. They were happy. Because of her. He returned his attention to the stage. A small smile appeared on his face.

The first unexpected moment happened halfway through the concert. The group had just finished a song when the lighting changed for the next segment. A brief technical delay followed.

The members stood together near the centre of the stage while the crew worked behind the screens.

One of the other members leaned towards CC and whispered something. CC looked at her, then at the audience. She laughed. The crowd immediately reacted. A microphone was brought to her.

“Sorry. They’re making us wait a little,” she said in Thai, smiling.

The audience cheered. She glanced towards the side of the stage, where the crew were still working, then turned back.

“Should we talk while they fix it?”

The crowd screamed louder. She listened to someone calling her name.

“CC!”

“Yes?”

“Are you hungry?”

She blinked. Then she laughed, genuinely caught off guard.

“That’s a very important question.”

The audience laughed with her.

“Have you eaten?” another person shouted.

CC looked towards the audience, her expression turning thoughtful.

“I had something before coming here.”

A pause.

“But I’m thinking about what to eat after.”

The crowd erupted again. Declan’s smile deepened. One of the members leaned into her microphone.

“She has been thinking about food all day.”

CC turned towards her with an expression of mild betrayal.

“That’s not true.”

The member nodded solemnly.

“She asked what we were having after rehearsal.”

“That was a reasonable question.”

The audience laughed. CC shook her head, looking down before lifting her microphone again.

“I’m just making sure everyone eats properly.”

She wasn’t trying to be funny. She was responding as herself, with a quiet sincerity that made even the smallest remark entertaining.

Declan looked down, smiling to himself, and sent Nicha one message: What does she eat after a show? The lights came back on. The members cheered, and the audience followed.

CC turned towards the stage crew and gave them a small thumbs-up. The concert continued.

By the time the final song began, Declan had stopped checking his phone entirely.

He had missed two messages from Alexander and one from a business partner. He didn’t care.

The stage was now bathed in warm golden light. The group stood in a line, their voices blending with the music as the final chorus approached. CC stood slightly to the left.

Her face softened as she looked out over the crowd.

There was a moment when she seemed to recognise someone holding a particular banner. She pointed towards them, smiled, and waved. The fan nearly collapsed. Declan watched the exchange.

He understood, watching it, that the person he knew privately belonged to a much larger world.

There were people who had followed her for years, people who had found comfort in her music, people who knew the smallest details of her career and had travelled across cities to see her tonight. He wasn’t threatened by it.

Nor did he feel any need to claim a part of her that belonged to someone else. He felt proud.

When the final notes ended, the audience rose to their feet. CC bowed with the others.

“Thank you for coming tonight. Please get home safely. And don’t forget to eat something,” she said in Thai.

The audience laughed. She smiled.

“Thank you for staying with us,” she said.

Declan applauded. He didn’t shout her name. He didn’t need to.

For a few seconds, he watched her standing beneath the lights, surrounded by the people who loved her work. Then the members disappeared backstage. The concert was over. And he was about to see his girlfriend.

Backstage, CC was halfway through removing her earrings when P’Nicha appeared at the dressing-room door.

“You’re not leaving yet.”

CC looked up.

“Why?”

“Someone is here.”

“Who?”

P’Nicha gave her a suspiciously innocent expression. CC narrowed her eyes.

“P’Nicha.”

“What?”

“Who?”

“Go and see.”

CC stared at her manager for another moment before setting the earring down.

“Is something wrong?”

“No.”

“Did the company need me?”

“No.”

“Then—”

“CC. Just go.” Nicha smiled.

CC stood, pulling her cardigan over her stage outfit.

She stepped into the corridor, still holding her phone.

A few staff members passed by, congratulating her on the performance. She thanked them, bowing slightly, before turning into the small waiting room at the end of the corridor, which Nicha had emptied. Then she saw him. Declan stood near the window, speaking with Alexander.

He had changed into a charcoal suit, his jacket unbuttoned, his tie slightly loosened. One hand rested in his trouser pocket.

He looked entirely at home among the folding chairs and garment rails. CC stopped. Declan turned. His face changed immediately.

Not dramatically. Just a subtle easing around his eyes, followed by the familiar smile that seemed to belong exclusively to her.

“Hello, sweetheart.”

CC blinked. Then she looked towards Alexander. Alexander offered a polite nod.

“Good evening, Miss Chanya.”

Then he stepped out and closed the door behind him. She looked back at Declan.

“You’re here?”

“I am.”

“In Bangkok?”

“That’s generally where this building is.”

She gave him a look. His smile widened slightly.

“I thought you had meetings.”

“I did.”

“And dinner?”

“I had dinner.”

“And you didn’t tell me?”

“I wanted to surprise you.”

CC looked at him for another second before walking closer.

“You came to the concert?”

“I did.”

Her face softened.

“You watched?”

“Every minute.”

She looked almost embarrassed.

“Why?”

“You were entertaining.”

She fought a smile and lost. Then she reached him.

Declan opened his arms, and she stepped into them without hesitation.

He held her carefully, mindful of the stage outfit. One hand settled between her shoulder blades while the other rested lightly against the back of her head.

She smelled of perfume, hairspray, and the warm, familiar scent of her skin. He lowered his head.

“You were wonderful.”

CC’s cheek rested against his chest.

“Thank you.”

“I mean it.”

“I can tell.”

He kissed her hair. For a few seconds, neither spoke. Then she tilted her face upwards.

“Did you enjoy it?”

“Very much.”

“Really?”

“Cela.”

His voice was low, amused.

“I rearranged my weekend to be here. I would hope you believe I enjoyed it.”

She laughed.

“You could have told me.”

“And lost the opportunity to see your face when you found me?”

She looked away.

“I wasn’t that surprised.”

“You stopped walking.”

“I was thinking.”

“About what?”

“Whether you were real.”

He looked down at her.

Then, with a faint smile, he said, “I can assure you I am.”

She laughed again, and he brushed his thumb lightly along her cheek.

He had seen her smiling on a screen earlier that week. He had replayed a little dance more times than he intended to admit. But this was better. Much better.

They were given a private room to rest before CC left.

Her stylist came in to help remove the remaining accessories, while Nicha reviewed the departure arrangements with Alexander.

Declan sat on the sofa, watching CC take off her stage earrings. She caught his gaze in the mirror.

“You’re looking at me.”

“I am.”

She turned slightly.

“Why?”

“Because you’re there.”

Her face changed. It was such a simple answer that she didn’t immediately know what to say.

She looked back at the mirror, hiding a smile.

After the stylist left, she walked over to him.

“Do I look strange?”

He looked up. She was still wearing her stage outfit, though the elaborate accessories had been removed. Her makeup was intact, but her hair had begun to loosen around her face.

“No.”

“Are you sure?”

“Very.”

She studied his expression.

“You’re biased.”

“Extremely.”

She laughed and sat beside him. He adjusted the cardigan around her shoulders.

“Are you tired?”

“A little.”

“Hungry?”

She turned towards him. He raised an eyebrow.

“That’s a yes.”

“Maybe.”

“I’ve arranged for dinner.”

Her eyes brightened.

“What did you get?”

“Mango sticky rice.”

She looked delighted.

“And?”

“Several other things. I asked Nicha what you might want.”

CC turned towards the door, where her manager was standing with Alexander.

“P’Nicha!”

Nicha looked over.

“What?”

“You told him?”

“I didn’t tell him anything. I merely prevented him from ordering food you wouldn’t eat.”

Declan looked mildly amused.

“I appreciate the assistance.”

Nicha gave him a knowing smile.

“She forgets after shows. I’ve been feeding her for five years.”

CC looked between them.

“I eat.”

“Yes, when someone reminds you,” Nicha replied.

Declan’s expression remained composed, but the amusement in his eyes was unmistakable. CC turned back to him.

“Don’t listen to her.”

“Of course not.”

“You’re smiling.”

“I wouldn’t dream of taking sides.”

She made a face at him. He leaned closer.

“Although I did notice you told the audience not to forget to eat.”

Her eyes widened.

“You heard that?”

“I did.”

“It’s a normal thing to say.”

“Certainly.”

“And the question about what I was eating was not—”

“An indication that you were hungry?”

She studied his face. He looked back, entirely serious. Then she laughed and lightly pushed his arm.

“You’re teasing me.”

“Only a little.”

He caught her hand before she could withdraw it and brought her knuckles to his lips.

“Come on, sweetheart. Let’s get you home.”

They left the arena ten minutes apart, CC in the company van and Declan in his own car, and the covered side entrance of her building did the rest.

The apartment was quiet when they arrived. CC had changed in the van into a soft cream-coloured lounge set. Her hair was now loose, and she had removed the remaining makeup with the help of a cleansing wipe.

Declan had taken off his jacket and rolled his sleeves to his forearms. The food was arranged on the dining table. CC stood in front of it, looking pleased.

“You ordered too much.”

“I was advised that you might be hungry.”

“P’Nicha.”

“She was quite persuasive.”

CC sat down and lifted the lid of the mango sticky rice container. Declan watched her take the first bite. Her eyes closed. He smiled.

“Good?”

She nodded.

“Very.”

He sat opposite her, helping himself to the other dishes.

For a while, they ate and talked about the concert. CC told him about a small mistake during rehearsal, the member who had nearly forgotten a costume change, and how the technical delay had happened because one of the stage screens needed to be reset. Declan listened.

He asked questions, not because he needed to know the technical details, but because he liked hearing her talk about her work. Eventually, CC put down her spoon.

“Can I ask you something?”

“Anything.”

“Which part did you like most?”

He considered the question.

“The final song.”

“Why?”

“You looked happy.”

She lowered her eyes to the table.

“That was a nice part.”

“I also liked the technical delay.”

She looked up.

“Why?”

“You were talking to the audience.”

She smiled.

“I didn’t know what else to do.”

“You didn’t seem particularly worried.”

“The crew were working. There wasn’t much I could do.”

“You made them laugh.”

She tilted her head.

“They were being nice.”

“They were responding to you.”

She looked at him, then reached for her water.

“Did you think I was different?”

“Different from what?”

“From how I am normally.”

Declan leaned back slightly. He understood what she was asking.

“Onstage?”

She nodded. He considered her carefully.

“Yes.”

Her face became a little uncertain.

“Different how?”

“More expansive, perhaps. You’re quieter when we’re alone. Onstage, you give people a version of yourself that is still genuine, but much larger.”

“And you seem very comfortable there. Not because you’re never nervous, but because you know what you’re doing,” he said.

CC looked down at her hands.

“I used to be more nervous.”

“I imagine.”

“Sometimes I still am.”

“I know.”

She looked up.

“How?”

“You hold the microphone with both hands for the first song. After that, one.”

She stared at him. Nobody had ever told her that. He covered her hand.

He said, “But I don’t think you need to be the same person in every room. You can be the woman who stands in front of thousands of people and performs beautifully. You can also be the woman who asks me whether we’ve ordered enough dinner.”

CC laughed.

“Those are both important roles.”

“I’m aware.”

She moved her hand beneath his, letting their fingers settle together.

“I was happy when I saw you.”

“I noticed.”

“You did?”

“You looked towards the side entrance twice.”

Her mouth fell open.

“You saw that?”

“I was watching you.”

She gave him an embarrassed smile.

“I didn’t know you were there.”

“That was the idea.”

“I think I was looking because I thought P’Nicha was supposed to tell me something.”

“Then I’m grateful she didn’t.”

CC laughed. Declan lifted her hand and kissed her fingers.

“I liked seeing you from there,” he said.

“From where?”

“The audience.”

Her eyes went to his.

“Why?”

“Because I know you as my girlfriend. I see you when you’re tired, when you’re happy, when you’re deciding what to eat, when you’re trying to convince me that you don’t need another dessert.”

“I don’t do that.”

“You do.”

She smiled.

“But tonight I saw the part of your life that existed before I came into it. The people who have supported you, the work you’ve done, the happiness you give them.”

His thumb moved gently over her knuckles.

“It was nice to see.”

Then she said, “I’m glad you came.”

“So am I.”

“Next time, tell me.”

“Next time?”

She nodded.

“I want to know you’re there. Then I can look for you.”

Something in his face softened. He brought her hand to his lips once more.

“Then next time, I’ll make sure you know.”

She smiled.

“Good.”

Later, after they had put the food away, CC returned from the bedroom carrying her phone.

Declan was sitting on the sofa, reading a message from Alexander. She stopped in front of him.

“Can I see something?”

He looked up.

“Of course.”

She sat beside him and opened the concert recording someone from the company had already sent her.

She moved through the video until she found the moment when the technical delay had happened. Then she turned the screen towards him.

“Look.”

He watched. On the screen, she stood under the lights, smiling into the audience.

“Should we talk while they fix it?”

The crowd screamed. Declan looked at her.

“You’re showing me my favourite part?”

She smiled.

“You said you liked it.”

“I did.”

She moved closer, resting her head against his shoulder.

“Then you can watch it again.”

He looked down at her.

“Is this permission?”

“Yes.”

“Very generous.”

She laughed. He took the phone from her and set it on the table.

Then he turned towards her, drawing her gently into his arms.

“Thank you for tonight, Cela.”

She looked up.

“For what?”

“For letting me see you.”

Her smile became smaller, warmer.

“You moved your whole weekend, sat through three hours of screaming, and you’re thanking me?”

He brushed a loose strand of hair away from her cheek.

“Every minute of it.”

She reached up and touched his jaw.

“I’m happy you’re here.”

He bent and kissed her. It was a quiet kiss, without hurry. When he drew back, she remained close, her hand still resting against his cheek. His gaze held hers.

“It’s late, and you’ve had a long night. May I stay?”

She nodded.

“I’d like that.”

He kissed her cheek.

“Then I’ll stay.”

CC settled against him, her cheek resting over his chest. Declan wrapped an arm around her, his hand resting comfortably at her waist.

Outside, Bangkok continued its usual restless movement. Cars passed below the apartment, distant voices rose and faded, and somewhere in the city, thousands of people were probably still talking about the concert. Inside, CC was already growing sleepy. Declan looked down at her.

“Cela?”

“Mm?”

“Next time, I want a seat closer to the stage.”

She lifted her head.

“Why?”

“So I can see your expressions properly.”

She smiled.

“You could come backstage.”

“I could.”

“Then you wouldn’t need a ticket.”

He considered that.

“A reasonable proposal.”

She settled back against him. A moment passed. Then she murmured, “But I like knowing you’re watching from the audience.”

Declan looked down at her, his expression quiet.

“Then that’s where I’ll be.”

She smiled against his shirt. And he held her a little closer, thinking that he had spent much of his life being the person people watched when he entered a room.

Tonight, for once, he had been perfectly content to sit in the dark and watch someone else shine.

chapters.title: The Morning After
chapters.desc: The morning after Impact Arena, he loses a fight with her coffee machine and wins every other one. A blurry photo of his car gets a paper trail by lunch, and by Monday there is a new machine with one button.
chapters.epigraph: “I don’t believe we need to discuss that.”
chapters.content:
Declan Lincoln ran a company on three continents. CC’s coffee machine had three buttons, and a little after seven on Sunday morning it had beaten him.

He stood in her kitchen in yesterday’s white shirt, sleeves rolled up, and studied it. One button was probably espresso. One had a cup on it. The third had something to do with milk, and he had pressed it first.

The machine made a noise that suggested it was disappointed in him, and produced something black and bitter.

He tasted it. “Interesting.”

Behind him, the apartment was quiet. The living room curtains were half open, and early light lay across the wooden floor. A cream blanket had slipped off the sofa. Two glasses of water stood on the coffee table, one still half full, and CC’s phone was charging beside the vase he had brought her in December. In the bedroom, his girlfriend was asleep.

Last night, at the end of four hours at Impact Arena, he had asked whether he could stay. She had said yes before he finished the question. This morning, for the first time, he had woken up in her home with nowhere he had to be.

He looked at the coffee again and decided she didn’t need to know about it.

CC woke slowly, to sunlight and warmth, and reached across the bed. The other side was empty.

From the kitchen came a cupboard closing, then a mechanical whine she didn’t recognise from her own machine. She smiled. Declan was awake, and losing.

She pulled the blanket closer and tried to call him.

“Declan?”

It came out as a rasp. Her throat felt like sandpaper. Four hours of singing would do that.

He appeared in the doorway with a glass of water.

“Good morning, sweetheart.”

He set the glass on her bedside table. “Don’t try to talk yet.”

He sat on the edge of the bed and touched the back of his fingers to her forehead.

“You’re warm, but not feverish.”

She raised her eyebrows at him.

“Your voice,” he explained. “How does your throat feel?”

She tilted her hand from side to side.

“I see.”

He held out the glass. “Drink a little.”

She sat up and took a few careful sips.

“Better?”

She nodded.

“Good.”

She looked at the clock. “You’re up early,” she whispered.

“I’ve been awake for a while.”

“Why?”

“Coffee.”

He paused. Then he said, “I attempted to make some.”

Her eyes brightened.

“Did you?”

“Yes.”

She was already smiling. He met her eyes with great dignity.

“I don’t believe we need to discuss that.”

She laughed, and winced. He raised one eyebrow.

“Careful.”

He brushed her hair off her face. “There’s something in the kitchen for you. I had it delivered at seven.”

“What?”

“Honey, fresh ginger, throat lozenges and a small steam inhaler. The pharmacist recommended all four.”

“You ordered a pharmacy?”

“Part of one.”

She reached for his hand.

“Thank you.”

He brought her hand to his lips.

“You’re welcome, Cela.”

In the kitchen, he took the honey from her before she could start opening everything herself. “Sit down.”

“I can help.”

“I know.”

“Then—”

“Today, you can supervise.”

She narrowed her eyes.

“That’s not very fair.”

“I’m prepared to accept the criticism.”

She sat at the island in a pale pink cardigan and watched him slice the ginger. He was better with a knife than he had been with her vegetables in December. Not much, but better. He caught her watching.

“You’re looking at me.”

She rested her chin on her hand.

“I’m allowed.”

“Certainly.”

He put the ginger on to simmer, and her gaze travelled past him to the coffee machine.

“What happened to your coffee?”

“An unfortunate misunderstanding.”

She started laughing, silently, because laughing hurt.

“Don’t.”

She pressed her lips together, but her shoulders were shaking.

“Cela.”

She lifted one hand in surrender. He held out a moment longer, then smiled. “I’m glad you’re enjoying yourself.”

When the drink was ready, he let it cool, stirred in some honey and set the cup in front of her. “Try this.”

She took a sip and closed her eyes.

“Good?”

She nodded, then typed on her phone and turned the screen to him: You’re good at this.

“I’ve been informed that I’m not good at making coffee.”

She gave him a look of pure mischief. He leaned one hand against the counter.

“Apparently, my other abilities remain under evaluation.”

Her eyes widened. Then she lowered her gaze, smiling into her cup.

At nine, P’Nicha video-called. CC was curled up on the sofa under the blanket, and Declan sat at the other end with a document on his tablet.

“P’Nicha?” CC rasped.

Nicha frowned through the screen. “CC. What happened to your voice?”

CC pointed at her throat.

“I know. Don’t speak too much.”

CC nodded.

“Did you sleep enough?”

Another nod.

“Good. And is someone looking after you?”

CC’s eyes slid sideways. Declan looked up from his tablet, and Nicha saw it.

“Oh.”

CC gave her a warning look, which Nicha ignored.

“Good morning, Khun Declan.”

“Good morning, Nicha.”

Then Nicha’s voice changed. “There’s something you should know before anyone asks you about it.”

CC sat up.

“Someone posted a photograph last night. It’s blurry. A black car at the arena’s side entrance, and a caption about a mysterious visitor. A few people have started guessing that someone important came to see you.”

Declan set the tablet down.

“That’s all?” CC whispered.

“That’s all anyone can see. No faces, no plate. It isn’t a problem yet. I just don’t want you surprised.”

“May I?” Declan asked.

CC passed him the phone.

“That was my car,” he said. “Lincoln Group booked the suite as a brand partner. Were partner vehicles on the arena’s transport list?”

“Yes. Partners and guests all used that entrance.”

“Then the booking exists on paper. Would you send me the event’s transport schedule? I’ll have Alexander match my car to the partner list.”

Nicha looked surprised. “Of course.”

He said, “There’s no reason to make this more interesting than it is. If anyone asks, a partner’s car used the partner entrance. We should have that in writing.”

He turned to CC. “Only if you’re comfortable with that.”

Nicha looked relieved. “I’ll send everything shortly. CC, rest today.”

“And don’t let him make you talk too much.”

“I’ll do my best,” Declan said.

Nicha’s smile turned knowing.

“I’m sure you will.”

Alexander had the transport schedule within the hour, along with the partner list, the car’s registration and the arena’s written request for the side entrance. It was entirely ordinary, which was why Declan wanted it on file. He read it himself before sending it on.

Declan: The booking is confirmed and matches the partner list. Please keep the original with the event records. If anyone asks, it was a partner vehicle at the partner entrance.

Nicha: Received. Thank you, Khun Declan. It’s on file.

He put the phone down and found CC watching him from the other end of the sofa. He raised his eyebrows.

“What?”

She typed and held up the screen: You have a serious face when you’re doing business.

“It’s a business matter.”

She typed again: You look like you’re buying a company.

“I might be.”

She stared at him. He smiled.

“Not this morning.”

She laughed without a sound, then moved closer, taking the blanket with her, and tucked herself against his shoulder.

“Work. An acquisition proposal. Nothing urgent,” he said.

She looked at the tablet, then up at him.

“You’d like me to put it away?”

He closed it without hesitating. “Done.”

She settled against him, and he rested his hand over hers.

The photograph wasn’t a problem yet. But people were curious about her, and more and more curious about him beside her, and privacy wasn’t something two people could keep on good intentions alone. He meant to be careful for her, and never secretive with her.

At lunch CC insisted on helping, and was allowed to wash the vegetables after a look that told him he was becoming unreasonable. He made a simple soup. She sat on a stool beside the counter and supervised.

She typed and held up the phone: You’re taking over my kitchen.

“I’m following instructions.”

“The pharmacist’s. And yours, from December. Onions first,” he said.

A little later she touched his forearm and pointed at the pot.

He tasted it, added a little salt, and raised his eyebrows at her. She gave him a thumbs-up.

He bent and pressed a kiss into her hair. “High praise.”

They ate at the dining table. She finished most of her soup and some rice and sat back, content.

She typed: I like this.

He read it. “This?”

She waved a hand at the room and whispered, “The kitchen. Lunch. You.”

He reached across the table and laced his fingers through hers. “Then we’ll do it again.”

The afternoon passed without much happening, which was what she needed. She read and showed him passages she liked. He answered a few emails and closed the laptop when she started drifting towards him. At some point she fell asleep against his shoulder, and he didn’t move.

When his phone buzzed for the third time, he eased her head onto a cushion and took the call on the balcony.

“Alexander.”

“Good afternoon, sir. The revised documents are in your inbox. And tomorrow is confirmed: wheels up at seven from Don Mueang, and the car will be downstairs at four thirty.”

“Thank you.”

“Shall I book you into the hotel tonight? It’s closer to the airport.”

Declan looked through the glass doors at the sofa. “No.”

He stayed on the balcony a minute longer. He had known Monday was coming. It felt different from here.

When he came back in, CC was sitting up, rubbing one eye.

“Did I wake you?”

He sat beside her.

She shook her head and typed: What time tomorrow?

“The car comes at four thirty.”

She made a face at the screen.

“I’d like to stay tonight as well. If you’ll have me,” he said.

She typed: Then you can have breakfast before you go.

“I’d like that.”

He cupped her jaw and kissed her, slowly, as if he had the whole afternoon and meant to use it. Her phone slid off her lap. When he finally drew back, she had forgotten what she was going to type, and he looked far too pleased about it. “Rest your voice.”

She typed: You keep saying that.

“Because you keep forgetting.”

By dinner she had some of her voice back, hoarse and low. Declan discouraged her from using it, which she found mildly irritating, and told him so on her phone.

You’re strict today.

“I’m being considerate,” he said, clearing the plates.

It feels like being managed.

He met her eyes.

“Would you prefer to manage yourself?”

She nodded. He smiled.

“Very well. I’ll simply observe.”

She laughed, shaking her head. Later, she checked his things for the morning, although Alexander had already sent everything he needed to the airport: passport, wallet, phone charger.

She looked at the small overnight bag. “Anything else?”

“No.”

“Are you sure?”

“Quite sure.”

She took his watch from the bedside table and laid it beside his phone, where he would see it at four.

He caught her hand before she could turn away. “Cela. I’ve enjoyed today.”

Her face softened.

“Me too.”

“It was nice to have a day without an agenda.”

She smiled.

“You had an agenda.”

“I did?”

She pointed towards the kitchen.

“The coffee.”

He laughed.

“An ambitious project.”

She leaned her head against his chest, and he wrapped his arms around her.

“I’m glad you stayed,” she whispered.

“So am I.”

She tipped her face up. “Will you come back soon?”

“As soon as I know my schedule. And when you’re ready, I’d like you to come to Munich.” He brushed his thumb over her cheek.

Her eyes brightened.

“Really?”

“Very much.”

She smiled.

“I want to see the tree.”

“It’s February.”

“I know.”

He laughed. “Then we’ll find something else to show you.”

She thought about it. “Your office?”

“If you’d like.”

“And your home?”

“My home too.”

She smiled.

“Then I want to see all of it.”

He kissed her. “Then it’s a date.”

At twenty past four the next morning, the apartment was still dark. CC stood by the door in a soft cardigan, holding a small paper bag. Declan had his coat on and his overnight bag at his feet.

“You should be asleep,” he said.

She shook her head and handed him the bag. Inside were a breakfast sandwich, a box of cut fruit and a bottle of water.

“You made this?”

She nodded.

“Thank you.”

He packed it into his carry-on.

“I’ll call when I land. And again after the morning meetings.”

He drew back to see her face. “Rest your voice. Drink water. Eat breakfast.”

She gave him a look. He smiled.

“I’m aware of the irony.”

He kissed her temple, then her mouth. “Goodbye, Cela.”

He opened the door, and stopped.

“I’ll miss waking up here.”

“Then come back.”

He smiled.

“I intend to.”

Then he was gone, and the door closed behind him. CC went back to the bedroom. Her phone buzzed before she reached it.

Declan: I haven’t reached the lift yet, and I already miss you.

CC: You haven’t even left the building.

Declan: An unfortunate detail.

Declan: Thank you for breakfast. And for letting me stay.

CC: Thank you for making my coffee terribly.

Declan: I believe we agreed not to discuss that.

She laughed, careful of her throat, and lay down on his side of the bed. The pillow still smelt of him. She was asleep again before his car reached the expressway.

At ten, the concierge rang up about a delivery. Two men carried in a coffee machine the size of a small suitcase, with exactly one button, and a card in handwriting she knew.

Fewer buttons. A barista is booked for Thursday to teach me how it works. D.

She stared at it. Then she laughed until her throat hurt, and made herself a perfect cup on the first try.

chapters.title: Her First Love
chapters.desc: A photograph of a little girl with a pink cake, and the man whose hand rests on her chair. CC calls him her first love. Declan is calm about it for almost four minutes.
chapters.epigraph: “I’m not trying to replace anything he gave you, Cela. I only want to add to it.”
chapters.content:
It began with a photograph.

Nothing remarkable to anyone else. CC had sent it that afternoon, when Munich was still at work and Bangkok was winding down: a girl of seven or so at a restaurant table, with a little pink cake in front of her. Two small ponytails, a white dress with a ribbon at the collar, round cheeks, a wide smile, one hand wrapped around a glass of juice.

Declan had looked at it several times from his office before he noticed the man beside her.

Only half of him was in the frame: a shoulder, a hand resting on the back of the little girl’s chair, the edge of a watch.

Declan: Who took you to that restaurant?

Her reply came a minute later.

CC: My first love.

He was halfway through a contract. He stopped, read the message again, and calmly put his phone away. A few seconds passed. He picked it up.

Declan: I see.

Cela: You see what?

Declan: Nothing, sweetheart.

Cela: That sounds suspicious.

He enlarged the photograph. He didn’t appreciate the way that hand rested behind her chair.

He wasn’t an unreasonable man. CC had a life before him: school, friends, travel, a great many things that had nothing to do with him. He had no intention of being jealous of her past. But first love was a different phrase. He called her.

She answered on video, smiling, in her apartment in Bangkok, in a cream cardigan with her hair loosely tied back.

“Hello.”

“Hello, sweetheart.”

“You sound very serious.”

He leaned back. “I was looking at your photograph.”

“Which one?”

“The one with the pink cake.”

“Oh. That one’s very old.” She smiled.

“I noticed.”

He let a moment pass. Then he asked, with deliberate casualness, “You mentioned your first love.”

CC blinked, and then a smile appeared.

“Oh.”

He narrowed his eyes.

“What’s that expression?”

“Nothing.”

“You’re enjoying something.”

“Maybe.”

He waited. She tucked a strand of hair behind her ear.

“My first love was very handsome.”

His face stayed composed.

“Was he?”

“Very.”

“Older?”

“Much older.”

“How much older?”

She bit back a laugh.

“Declan.”

“Yes?”

“You’re jealous.”

“I’m curious.”

“You’re jealous.”

“I asked a perfectly reasonable question.”

She laughed at first, then brightly enough that he smiled despite himself.

“He’s very kind. He always gave me whatever I wanted. He bought me pretty things, took me to nice restaurants, carried me when I was tired, and never let me walk too far if my shoes hurt,” she said.

Declan listened. His face stayed pleasant. His eyes didn’t.

“An extravagant man.”

“Very.”

“Did he have a habit of buying you jewellery?”

“Sometimes.”

“Flowers?”

“Of course.”

He was silent.

“And where is this gentleman now?”

CC finally burst out laughing.

“He’s at home in Markham.”

Declan blinked.

“Markham?”

“Yes.”

“Your first love lives in Markham?”

“With my mother.”

He met her eyes. She was practically glowing.

“Declan,” she said, still laughing, “it’s my father.”

There was a brief silence. Then Declan closed his eyes and breathed out through his nose, and a helpless smile reached the corner of his mouth.

“Your father.”

“My first love.”

“Are you relieved?”

He looked back at her.

“Immensely.”

She laughed again.

“Poor you.”

“I believe I’ve just experienced an entirely unnecessary emotional disturbance.”

“You asked!”

He glanced at the photograph again, at the hand behind the little girl’s chair.

“Tell me about him,” he said, and meant it.

Her face softened.

“My father?”

“Your first love.”

She gave him a fond look, and then, as if the photograph had opened a door she hadn’t been through in a while, she told him.

When she was little, her father had one weakness, and it was her.

He was a sensible man. He was up at four for the bakery six days a week, kept his promises, and believed children should learn the value of things and not expect the world to arrange itself around them. Then his daughter came into the room, and most of those principles became negotiable.

When she was five, she fell in love with a pair of pink shoes in a shop window: a small bow on the front, a little strap across the ankle. Her mother said she already had enough shoes. Her father looked at the little girl. She looked back at him, and pointed. He bought them.

His wife stared at him when he came home with the bag.

“She has three other pairs.”

“These are different.”

“They’re pink.”

“Exactly.”

His daughter was already on the floor with the box in her lap, and when he opened it she said, “Daddy!” as if he had brought her the moon.

He fastened the tiny straps himself. She walked across the living room, one step, two steps, and turned round.

“Pretty?”

“Very pretty.”

Her mother watched from the kitchen. “She’ll expect you to buy her everything now.”

He looked at his daughter, who was carefully examining her shoes. “Not everything. Just the things she really likes.”

He learned which fruit she preferred, which playground, which noodle shop she would eat at without complaint. She was allowed one pastry from his own glass case after school, and she chose. He knew she pretended she wasn’t tired until she went quiet, and that when she was upset she didn’t always cry; sometimes she just sat beside him and leaned against his arm. He knew that if she fell asleep in the car, she woke up frightened if someone moved her too fast.

So he carried her, even when she was getting too big for it.

One winter afternoon when she was seven, it was snowing, and they were on their way home from the shops when she stopped in front of a bakery that wasn’t his. His own bakery didn’t make strawberry cakes, which she considered a serious flaw.

He looked at the little cakes in the window, then at her.

“Would you like one?”

She nodded.

“Which one?”

She considered them with great seriousness, and pointed to the smallest. He bought it, and two extra pastries. She looked at the bag.

“Why two?”

“One for you. One for Mummy.”

She thought about that.

“What about you?”

“I’ll have yours if you don’t finish.”

That seemed fair. They sat at a little table by the window, and he took off her mittens and opened the box, and she ate slowly, collecting the cream with her fork. Some of it landed on the tip of her nose. He reached over with a napkin.

“Hold still.”

She held still while he wiped it away, then looked up at him.

“Daddy? Why doesn’t your bakery make this one?”

He smiled.

“Because then you’d never come shopping with me.”

“Will you learn it?”

He gave it proper thought.

“For your birthday.”

She grinned.

“With extra strawberries?”

“Definitely.”

Satisfied, she went back to her cake. It was a small, ordinary afternoon, and he remembered it, as he remembered most of them. Children grew up, and the things they once asked for so earnestly became things they could buy for themselves. He knew, even then, that he would miss being the person she looked for whenever she wanted something.

He never let her birthday be an ordinary day, however busy the bakery was. On her eighth, he closed the shop at noon.

That morning there was a small box beside her bed, and inside it a necklace with a tiny star pendant. She ran downstairs with it and found him at the stove. He turned round.

“Happy birthday, princess.”

She hugged him around the waist. He put the spatula down and hugged her properly.

Her mother came in with a cup of tea, took one look at them, and said, “You’ve spoiled her again.”

He kissed the top of his daughter’s head.

“She’s allowed.”

That afternoon he took her to the restaurant in the photograph. She wore a white dress and the necklace and kept asking whether the pendant was straight, and he straightened it every time. She chose a dessert much too large for one person, and he ordered it anyway, and she pushed the first spoonful towards him and ate the rest herself.

At the end of the meal he gave her a card. She couldn’t read joined-up writing quickly yet, so he read it to her: that he loved watching her grow, that he was proud of her, and that however old she was, she would always have a home with him.

She folded it and held it against her chest.

“Daddy? When I’m big, can I still come with you?”

“Whenever you want.”

Declan didn’t interrupt once. By the time she finished, the jealousy had gone entirely, and something quieter had taken its place.

“Your father sounds like a remarkable man.”

“He is.”

He looked at the photograph again. “Who took it?”

“My mum. That’s his hand on the chair.”

Declan nodded slowly. “Then I owe him a great deal of respect.”

“Why?”

“Because he established an exceptionally high standard.”

She laughed. “Declan.”

“I’m serious.”

“You don’t have to compete with my father.”

“I wasn’t aware I was competing.”

“You were jealous five minutes ago.”

“I was operating with incomplete information.”

“Very serious incomplete information.”

“Your father has had a considerable head start.”

She shook her head, amused.

“He was my father. You can’t compete with that.”

“I know. And I wouldn’t want to. He was there when you were little. He knew you before the world did, and he gave you all of it without expecting anything back. That’s a different kind of love, and I think it’s wonderful that you had it,” he said, warmly.

She touched the edge of her cardigan.

“He still calls me his little girl.”

“I imagine he will continue to do so.”

She leaned closer to the camera.

“Do you know what he does when I visit?”

“What?”

“He still opens the passenger door for me. Even when I’m perfectly capable of doing it myself.”

Declan considered that.

“Good.”

“And he carries my bags.”

“Also good.”

“And if I say I’m cold, he gives me his coat.”

Declan’s eyes lit with amusement.

“I see.”

“Now you understand why I said he was my first love.”

“I do.”

“Although I should warn you that I may be learning from him.”

CC blinked.

“What does that mean?”

“That I intend to keep opening doors, carrying your bags and making sure you have a coat.”

She laughed. “You already do those things.”

She glanced up at him.

“I think Dad would like you.”

“I hope so.”

“He might be a little intimidating.”

“I’ve negotiated with more difficult men.”

She grew thoughtful. “Actually, I think he’d like that you listen. People think spoiling someone means buying things. But Dad remembers things. What I like, what I don’t, when I’m tired. He doesn’t say much, but he notices.”

“I understand.”

“You do that too.”

It pleased him more than he could have said, hearing it from her.

“I try.”

“I know.”

Neither of them spoke.

Then Declan said, “I’d like to meet him properly.”

“You will.”

“When you think the time is right.”

“Maybe on my birthday. That’s always when I wish I was home.”

“That would be lovely.”

She brightened. “He might bring you butter tarts.”

“I remember hearing about those.”

“Dad makes very good ones.”

“Then I look forward to trying them.”

She gave him a little mischief.

“Don’t eat too many. He’ll think you like them more than me.”

His smile widened.

“I suspect that would be difficult.”

“Why?”

“Because I’ve already decided I like his daughter a great deal.”

Her cheeks went pink.

“You’re flirting.”

“With my girlfriend. Yes.”

She reached for her phone, plainly about to message her father at once, and he stopped her.

“Tomorrow, sweetheart.”

“Why?”

“Because it’s late there, and I’d like a little more time with you before you start discussing me with your father.”

“You’re nervous?”

He considered it, and his smile turned self-deprecating.

“I may be.”

She looked delighted.

“Really?”

“Your father has been spoiling you for twenty-four years. I have some catching up to do.”

“You don’t have to catch up.”

His voice softened.

“I’m not trying to replace anything he gave you, Cela. I only want to add to it.”

Her smile went small and tender.

“That’s why I like you.”

“Only one of the reasons?”

“One of many.”

“Good. I would hate to have been reduced to my gift-giving.”

She laughed.

“Goodnight, Cela.”

Her message came the next morning, before his first meeting.

Cela: I told Dad you asked about my first love.

He smiled at his desk.

Declan: And what did he say?

Cela: He says he hopes you know I was very expensive to raise.

Declan laughed out loud, alone in his office.

Declan: I believe him.

Cela: He also said thank you for taking care of me.

He read that one twice before he answered.

Declan: Please tell him that it’s my pleasure. And that I hope I can do it well.

A moment later:

Cela: He says you sound like a good man.

Cela: But he’s still the first love.

Declan: I wouldn’t dream of challenging his position.

Cela: Good. Because he would win.

Declan: I have no intention of disputing the result.

She sent a laughing face. He opened the photograph once more: the white dress, the pink cake, the hand behind the chair. He had thought, for one unreasonable minute, that he had a rival. He had found instead the man who taught her what it felt like to be cherished, long before anyone else had the chance.

He saved the photograph to his phone and went in to his meeting.

chapters.title: Red Envelopes
chapters.desc: Lunar New Year, twelve hours from home. He asks if he may say hello to her parents, her father makes him wait for the butter tarts, and a red envelope arrives with two seats to Markham inside.
chapters.epigraph: “Would you like me to say hello to them?”
chapters.content:
The first thing CC noticed on Saturday morning was the quiet.

Not the ordinary quiet of her apartment, which the traffic below and the kettle usually broke. It was Lunar New Year, and nobody was in her kitchen but her.

At home, her mother would already have been cooking for two days. Her father would be pretending not to be involved while somehow making half the food. There would be relatives on the phone, photographs of dishes, and the familiar chaos of people asking whether everyone had arrived yet.

Markham was twelve hours behind Bangkok. It was still Friday evening there, New Year’s Eve, and the reunion dinner would just have been cleared.

CC sat at the dining table in a red cardigan with the small arrangement she had made that morning: a bowl of mandarins, a few flowers, and two red envelopes from the shop downstairs.

She had spent New Year away before. Schedules, performances and travel had made it hard to be home every year. But some days, being independent felt a lot like being far away. Her phone lit up.

Mum: Have you eaten?

CC smiled.

CC: Yes. Have you?

Mum: Your father is making butter tarts.

CC stared at the message.

CC: For Lunar New Year?

Mum: He said he wanted to make something.

A second message appeared.

Mum: I think he just wanted an excuse to eat the filling.

CC laughed. She sent a photograph of the mandarins and flowers.

CC: Happy New Year. I miss you.

Mum: We miss you too, Cela.

CC read it twice before she put the phone down.

In Munich, it was half past three in the morning, and Declan was awake for no particular reason.

He had already sent her a message, and she had answered with a photograph of her mandarins and her flowers and her two red envelopes.

It looked like someone trying to fit a piece of home into a room. Telling her not to be sad would be useless. So he called. She answered after two rings.

“Hello?”

Her voice was soft, still a little rough from the concert, though much better.

“Good morning, Cela.”

She smiled.

“It’s three in the morning there.”

“I’m aware.”

“Why are you awake?”

“I wanted to speak to you.”

She curled up on the sofa. “Happy New Year.”

“Happy New Year. How are you?”

“I’m good.”

He heard the half-second before it. “Really?”

She looked at the table. “I’m a little homesick.”

“I thought you might be.”

“They’re celebrating, and I’m here.”

“What are they making?”

“My father is making butter tarts.”
