“For Lunar New Year?”

She laughed. “Apparently.”

“I’m beginning to understand your family.”

“What does that mean?”

“It sounds as if your father makes whatever he likes and calls it a tradition.”

“He does.”

He let the silence sit, then asked, “Would you like me to say hello to them?”

CC went still.

“What?”

She checked her phone.

His voice stayed easy. “Only if you’d like. They’re celebrating, and I thought it might be nice to wish them a happy New Year.”

She didn’t answer at once. She had imagined introducing him to her parents properly one day. She hadn’t imagined him asking first, from six thousand miles away, at three in the morning.

“You want to meet them?”

“I’d like to.”

“Now?”

“If they’re available. If not, another time.”

She smiled.

“My mum will be happy.”

“And your father?”

She considered.

“He’ll probably ask me why I didn’t tell him earlier.”

Declan smiled.

“Then perhaps we should give him time to finish his butter tarts.”

She laughed.

“That’s probably wise.”

Twenty minutes later, CC propped her phone against the fruit bowl and started a three-way call. In Markham it was nearly ten at night. Her mother appeared first.

“Hello, Cela!”

“Hi, Mum.”

Her mother saw the second face on the screen at once.

“Mum, this is Declan.”

Declan sat up straighter at his desk. “Good evening, Mrs. Chanya. It’s lovely to meet you.”

Her mother smiled warmly.

“Hello, Declan. Happy New Year.”

“Happy Lunar New Year. Xīnnián kuàilè.” He took a small breath.

There was a pause. CC’s mother blinked, then smiled even more broadly.

“Oh, that’s lovely!”

“I hope I said it correctly.”

“You did,” her mother said.

CC pressed her lips together. He had said it the way a man says something he has practised in the mirror for two days.

Declan glanced at her. “Something wrong?”

She shook her head.

“Nothing.”

Her mother looked between them. “Cela, you didn’t tell me he speaks Chinese.”

“He doesn’t,” CC said.

“I’ve learned a greeting,” Declan said.

“That’s not the same thing,” CC said.

Her mother laughed.

“It’s very thoughtful. You didn’t have to learn anything.”

“I wanted to.”

That seemed to please her more than the greeting had. “That’s very sweet.”

She glanced over her shoulder. “Your father is here. He’s finishing something.”

“What?”

“Butter tarts.”

CC sighed.

“Mum.”

“What? He’s nearly done.”

A voice came from somewhere behind her.

“Tell her they’re not for her.”

CC laughed.

“I can hear you!”

Her mother turned towards the kitchen.

“Your daughter is on the phone!”

“I know!”

A moment later her father appeared, in a dark sweater with a tea towel over one shoulder. He looked at CC first, then at Declan.

“Hello.”

“Hi, Dad.”

“Good evening, Mr. Chanya. It’s a pleasure to meet you. Happy New Year.”

Her father considered him. “Hello, Declan.”

Then he glanced towards the kitchen. “Wait a minute.”

And he disappeared.

Her mother laughed. “He’s taking the tray out.”

“Dad!”

CC gave Declan an apologetic look.

“I’m not going anywhere,” he said.

Her mother settled beside the phone. “So, Declan, is it cold in Munich?”

“Very cold at the moment.”

“Are you working tomorrow?”

“A little. But I had some time tonight.”

Her mother nodded, then said, quite naturally, “Do you like butter tarts?”

“I’ve never tried one.”

“Oh, you must. They’re very good.”

CC studied the screen.

“Mum, don’t start.”

Her mother ignored her. “We’ll have to make some for you. You should come to Canada one day.”

Declan’s voice softened. “I’d like that very much.”

Her father came back, put the tray somewhere out of view, wiped his hands and sat down.

“Sorry. I wanted to finish before talking.”

“Of course. I hope they came out well.”

“They did.”

CC looked at her father.

“You haven’t even tried them yet.”

“I know what I’m doing.”

Declan caught himself smiling. Her father leaned closer to the screen.

“You’re Declan. How long have you known my daughter?” He studied him a moment longer.

CC sat up. “Dad.”

“We met in November,” Declan said calmly.

“And you’ve been seeing each other since?”

“We have.”

Her father nodded slowly. “That’s not very long.”

“No, it isn’t,” Declan agreed.

He didn’t try to make it sound more established than it was, and CC loved him a little more for it.

“And you’re serious?”

Declan met his eyes. “Yes. I care about her very much. I know what she means to your family, and I don’t take that lightly.”

CC looked down at the table.

Her father nodded. “Good.”

It wasn’t a blessing. It wasn’t a refusal either.

Then he glanced at the tray. “Would you like to see the butter tarts?”

“What? He hasn’t tried them.”

“I’d be delighted,” Declan said.

Her father held one up to the camera. “It’s sweet. Very sweet.”

“I’ll keep that in mind.”

Her father turned to CC. “Don’t let him work too much.”

Declan raised an eyebrow. “I believe that responsibility may be shared.”

Her father considered that, and then, unexpectedly, smiled. “Fair enough.”

The call went on far longer than Declan had expected.

He learned that CC’s father had strong opinions about pastry, that her mother remembered everyone’s birthdays, and that the family always cooked too much. He learned that CC had been a quiet child until she trusted someone, and that she had insisted on carrying her own little bag everywhere, even when it was heavier than she could manage. CC protested.

“Mum.”

“What? It’s true.”

Her father added, “She wouldn’t let anyone help.”

Declan looked at CC.

“Some things haven’t changed.”

She gave him a look. Her mother laughed.

“She’s still like that.”

Declan smiled.

“I’ve noticed.”

Then her mother asked about his family. He told them about Richard and Eleanor, who lived on the lake outside Munich, and when she asked whether they knew about CC, he said yes. “They know I’m serious about her.”

Her mother smiled.

“That’s good.”

Her father nodded.

“Then one day we should meet.”

Declan’s expression warmed.

“I would be very pleased.”

CC lifted her eyes to his.

Her father added, “Perhaps when we come to Thailand.”

Declan glanced towards her. “Whenever you’re comfortable,” Declan said.

Her mother nodded.

“We’ll see what we can arrange.”

It ended with more New Year wishes. Her father lifted a hand. “Take care, Declan.”

“You too, sir.”

Her mother waved.

“Goodnight, Cela.”

The screen went dark, and Declan sat in his study a moment longer.

It was nearly five in the morning. He should have been asleep. He was smiling. A few minutes later, he called her back.

She tucked her feet beneath her on the sofa. “Did you go back to sleep?”

“Not yet.”

“Why?”

“I was thinking.”

“About what?”

“Your father.”

She laughed.

“What about him?”

“I believe I passed the butter tart inspection.”

She smiled.

“You did.”

“Was there an inspection?”

“Of course.”

“I wasn’t informed.”

“You were being evaluated.”

He laughed.

Then his voice softened. “Your parents are lovely.”

CC looked down at her hands. “I’m glad you met them.”

“So am I.”

She hesitated. Then she said, “I was a little nervous.”

“I know.”

“I didn’t know if it was too soon.”

Declan’s voice was gentle.

“I didn’t want you to feel you had to introduce me before you were ready. I asked because I thought it might make today feel a little less far from home.”

She looked at the mandarins on the table. It had.

“Thank you,” she said.

“You’re welcome.”

She smiled.

“My mum likes you.”

“I’m pleased.”

“My dad too, I think.”

“I hope so.”

“He didn’t tell me.”

He laughed. “Perhaps he prefers to keep me uncertain.”

“He does that.”

“I noticed.”

She laughed. Then she said, “He’ll probably ask me questions later.”

“I’ll be happy to answer any he has.”

She checked the screen.

“Really?”

“Of course.”

Her voice went soft. “I’m glad you’re my boyfriend.”

Hearing it on a day she was missing home went somewhere in him that no deal ever had.

“So am I, sweetheart.”

At five, the doorbell rang while she was making tea.

A courier held out a flat parcel. “Miss Chanya?”

“Yes.”

Inside the parcel was a red envelope. Not one from a shop downstairs: thick, textured paper, deep red, with a thin gold pattern along the edges and her name on the front in handwriting she knew. She opened it. Inside was a folded card.

Xīnnián kuàilè, Cela.

Your birthday is on a Saturday this year. If you would like to spend it in Markham, two seats are held: out on Thursday the twenty-first, back on the Sunday. One for you, and one for me, if you’ll have me there.

Nothing is fixed. Say no, and it all disappears.

With love,
Declan

CC sat down on the sofa, slowly, still holding the card.

She hadn’t asked for this. She had never even said she wanted to be home for her birthday. But he had heard the homesickness in her voice that morning, and he had answered it with something that wasn’t jewellery or flowers or another beautiful object. He was offering her a way home. She called him before she had decided to. She called him. He answered almost immediately.

She looked at the card. “Declan. What’s this?”

A pause, and then a smile she could hear. “Did it arrive?”

“You’re taking me home?”

“I’ve held two seats. Whether anyone sits in them is yours to decide.”

She swallowed. “How long have you had this?”

“Since January. I meant to give it to you nearer the time.”

“Then why today?”

“Because you were homesick this morning. I thought your birthday shouldn’t be another day spent wishing they were closer.”

CC bent her head. Her eyes had begun to sting.

“Declan…”

“Is it too much?”

She shook her head, even though he couldn’t see her.

“No.”

“Then?”

She laughed, unsteadily. “I’m going to cry.”

“That’s all right.”

“You didn’t have to do this.”

“I know.”

“They’ll be so happy.”

“I hope so.”

She wiped beneath one eye.

“I want to call my mum.”

“Then call her.”

“It’s five in the morning there.”

“You told me your father starts at four.”

She laughed.

“You’re very impatient.”

“Only when there’s something I’m looking forward to.”

Her mother answered on the second ring, already dressed, because nobody in that house slept past five.

“Cela? What’s wrong?”

Her mother peered at the screen. “Are you crying?”

CC held the card up to the camera, and watched her mother read it.

“Declan,” CC said.

Her mother looked from the card to her daughter. “Oh, Cela.”

Her father appeared behind her, still in his bakery apron. “What happened?”

“Look.”

He read it. Then he looked at CC. “He’s bringing you home?”

“For my birthday. If I want.”

Her father read the card again and nodded slowly. “That’s thoughtful.”

“I didn’t know he was going to do this,” CC said.

Her mother studied her. “He listens to you.”

CC’s smile softened. “He does.”

Her father leaned in. “Tell him we said thank you. And tell him to bring an apron.”

In Munich, Declan was going through a contract at the kitchen table, nowhere near asleep, when the next message came.

Cela: My parents said thank you.

He smiled.

Declan: You’re welcome.

A moment later:

Cela: My dad says to bring an apron.

Declan: Should I be concerned?

Cela: Yes.

Declan: Then I’ll pack two.

She sent him a photograph of the red envelope on her table beside the mandarins, with the card open. Then:

Cela: I think this is my favourite New Year gift.

Declan: Then I’m very glad I sent it.

She replied:

Cela: I miss you.

He checked the message. Then he typed.

Declan: I miss you too, Cela.

That night CC put the red envelope beside her bed. Her mother had already texted twice about the spare room. She picked up her phone.

CC: Goodnight, Declan.

Declan: Goodnight, sweetheart.

CC: I wish you were here.

Declan: So do I.

A moment later, another message appeared.

Declan: Next New Year, perhaps we can be in the same place.

CC: With my parents?

Declan: If they’ll have me.

She laughed into her pillow.

CC: Dad wants to know if you eat raisins.

Declan: Is there a wrong answer?

She fell asleep with the phone on her chest and the envelope where she could see it.

chapters.title: The Second Verse
chapters.desc: He can’t send flowers on Valentine’s Day, so he sends a piano tuner and the whole score of the song she only half played him. She sends back the whole song. At her midnight, he says it first.
chapters.epigraph: “I’d still like to renegotiate.”
chapters.content:
Valentine’s Day, Declan had discovered, was an inconvenient day to be in love with someone famous.

Bangkok was full of red roses. Restaurants advertised set dinners, shopping centres built arches of flowers, and every feed was full of couples photographing their celebrations. He had looked at several arrangements for her, and decided against all of them. A large bouquet delivered to her building on the fourteenth of February would invite exactly the attention they had been avoiding. The concierge would notice. Someone would photograph the van. She would spend the day wondering who had seen what.

So he arranged something quieter. At half past one, CC got a message from her building’s concierge: a piano technician would arrive shortly for a scheduled service. The appointment had been confirmed with her management, and the technician would call up before coming in.

She read it twice, looked at her piano, and then at her phone.

CC: Did you arrange something?

In Munich, Declan was finishing breakfast.

Declan: Good morning to you too, sweetheart.

CC: Good morning. Did you?

Declan: I may have.

CC: Declan.

Declan: Your piano hasn’t been serviced in a while, has it?

She glanced at the piano by the window. He was right. She had been meaning to book it since the recording sessions, which had made her hear every place the tuning had drifted.

CC: I was going to do that.

Declan: I know.

CC: So you did it for me?

Declan: I arranged for someone qualified to do it. The rest is entirely your piano’s responsibility.

She smiled.

CC: You know that’s not an answer.

Declan: I hope your piano is pleased.

She laughed and put the phone down. A few minutes later, the technician arrived.

He was professional, discreet, and entirely uninterested in why a woman with an internationally recognised career had someone else booking maintenance for her piano. CC liked him at once.

While he worked, she made tea and sat on the sofa with her book. He tuned the piano, checked the mechanism and made a few small adjustments. It was a perfectly ordinary appointment until he packed up his tools.

“There’s one more thing. This came with the booking. I was asked to give it to you myself,” he said, and handed her a flat package he had kept carefully to one side.

It was wrapped in ivory paper and tied with a narrow dark ribbon, with a small envelope tucked under the bow. She knew the handwriting before she opened it.

For the song you played only halfway.
I’d still like to renegotiate.
D.

She untied the ribbon. Inside was a bound score of THE FIRST LIGHT, in a dark-blue cover with her name pressed small into one corner: piano and voice, every verse, every bar.

In December, in her apartment, the evening before his flight, she had played him the first verse and the chorus, taken her hands off the keys and told him that was all he got. He hadn’t asked for more.

Now here was the rest of it, on thick paper, bound to lie open on a music stand: made to be used, not displayed.

On the first page, under the title, he had written:

For Cela,
who gave me the beginning.

She turned the pages slowly. He must have asked AVEN’s music team for the full arrangement, and asked politely, and asked someone to keep quiet about it. He had remembered the title, the night, and exactly where she had stopped.

She took a photograph of the book with the piano behind it.

CC: You remembered.

His reply came a few minutes later.

Declan: I remember quite a lot about that evening.

She looked at the open score.

CC: You know I only played the first verse.

Declan: I remember.

CC: I didn’t finish it.

Declan: I noticed.

She smiled.

CC: You’re teasing me.

Declan: A little.

Declan: And the piano? Does it sound better?

CC: It does.

Declan: Then the appointment was a success.

She looked at the score on the stand and decided she was going to give him something back. Not something delivered. Something he couldn’t buy.

When the technician had gone, she sat at the piano and opened the score at the first page.

She remembered December: the soft light, the flowers on the table, Declan on her sofa with all of his attention on her, and the exact moment she had stopped.

She picked up her phone.

CC: What are you doing tonight?

Declan: Two meetings this afternoon and a call tonight. Why?

CC: Nothing.

Declan: That is rarely nothing.

CC: You’ll see.

Declan: Should I be concerned?

CC: No.

Declan: Then I shall look forward to it.

She put the phone away and began to play.

The first verse came easily. Her fingers knew it before she did.

The second verse was quieter, a slightly different progression that opened slowly and then settled into something more private. She stopped once to fix a note, and again to change the tempo. She didn’t want it perfect the way a studio take had to be. She wanted it honest.

When she reached the end, she sat still until the last chord had gone, and then she started again with her phone recording, and played the whole song and sang it, from the first note to the last chord, without stopping halfway.

She listened back once. There was a breath before the second verse, and a small hesitation near the end. She thought about another take, and didn’t. It sounded like her, and she wanted him to hear her, not a performance. She attached the file, and wrote:

You gave me the whole score.
So here’s the whole song.

Then she pressed send before she could change her mind.

In Munich it was twenty to eleven, and Declan was in his office between a call with the Singapore team and a briefing on an acquisition. His next meeting was in eighteen minutes.

He opened her message, read the two lines, and put down his pen.

He reached for his headphones. “Alexander. Give me ten minutes, please.”

Alexander glanced at the clock and closed the door behind him.

The first notes put him back in December: her apartment, the flowers on the table, the way she had tucked her hair behind her ear before she sat down at the piano.

Then the second verse began, and it was a part of the song he had never heard. It grew fuller and came back to its quiet. He didn’t move. She had recorded this in her own apartment for one person to hear, and the person was him.

When it ended, he played it again. The second time he heard the small things: the breath before the second verse, the way her tempo wandered, how gently she let the ending go. Then he picked up his phone.

Declan: Cela.

She replied almost immediately.

CC: Yes?

Declan: I listened to the whole thing.

CC: I hoped you would.

Declan: Twice.

CC: Already?

Declan: I may listen again.

CC: You don’t have to.

Declan: I’m aware.

Declan: Thank you for giving me the rest.

Her answer took a minute.

CC: I wanted you to have it.

He read it several times. The meeting could wait two more minutes.

At a minute to midnight, CC was on the sofa in her pyjamas, hair loose, with a cup of tea beside her and the dark-blue score open on the piano under the lamp. It would be six in the evening in Munich. He had said he wanted to wish her a happy Valentine’s Day properly. Her phone rang on the minute. His face appeared, and she was already smiling.

“Hello.”

“Hello, sweetheart.”

He was still in his office, jacket off, tie loosened, and the window behind him going dark.

“Happy Valentine’s Day,” he said.

She smiled.

“Happy Valentine’s Day.”

“How was your day?”

“Lovely.”

“Did the piano behave?”

She laughed.

“Very well. It’s never sounded better. Thank you for arranging it.”

“You’re welcome.”

“And the music.”

His face softened.

“Did you like it?”

“I loved it.”

“I’m glad.”

She looked down, smiling.

“How did you find the whole score?”

“I asked nicely.”

She gave him a look that said she would find out.

He took her in. “You’re beautiful.”

“You say that often.”

“Because it’s true.”

She laughed, and he looked pleased with himself. For a while they talked about ordinary things: her day, his meetings, a small disagreement she had had with a stylist about a fitting. Neither of them was in any hurry to hang up.

“You’re still at the office?”

“Yes. I’ll leave shortly.”

“You should go home.”

“I will.”

“Tonight?”

“Within the hour.”

She nodded, satisfied. She rested her chin on her hand.

“Thank you for today.”

He tilted his head.

“For the piano?”

“For everything.”

He was quiet.

“You always find ways to make me feel looked after, even when we can’t be together.”

His eyes softened. “Because I want to.”

“I like being spoiled by you.”

His mouth curved.

“I’ve gathered.”

After a moment she said, “I wish you were here.”

“So do I.”

There was something he had wanted to say for a while. He had considered the right moment, whether to wait until they were in the same room, perhaps a quiet dinner in Bangkok or Munich.

But he was looking at her now: his girlfriend, who had sent him a whole song because he had given her its score. Waiting for the perfect setting seemed unnecessary.

“Cela.”

She looked up. “Hm?”

He held her gaze. “I love you.”

He said it, without an introduction, and without a smile to soften it.

CC went still. Her eyes widened. He didn’t take the words back or rush to fill the silence. He had meant them, and he wanted her to have room to hear them.

Then she looked at him with an expression he had never seen on her, surprised and a little overwhelmed and unmistakably happy, and answered in Mandarin.

“Wǒ yě ài nǐ.”

Her voice was soft. I love you too.

He knew the words. He had heard her speak Mandarin often, when she was tired or comfortable. Hearing those three words, to him, was something else entirely.

She looked down, then up again, and said it in English. “I love you too, Declan.”

His smile came slowly, as if he had been trying not to smile too much and had finally given up.

“Again,” he said.

She blinked.

“What?”

“Not because I didn’t hear you.”

She laughed, cheeks turning pink.

“That’s unfair.”

“Completely. I just liked hearing it.”

She smiled and leaned a little closer to the screen.

“I love you.”

He exhaled a quiet laugh.

“That’s better.”

“Better?”

“Much.”

She shook her head, smiling. “I really do,” she said.

His face settled into something she wanted to keep.

“I know, sweetheart. And I love you.”

There was no music, no room full of flowers, no dinner. Only a video call between Bangkok and Munich. She thought she might remember this particular midnight.

When the call ended, Alexander knocked once and put his head round the door. “Your car is ready, Mr. Lincoln.”

Declan was still at his desk with the phone in his hand.

“Thank you.”

He was the same composed man who had spent the day on contracts, shirt still buttoned, desk still in order. But Alexander had worked for him long enough to tell a good business day from a good day, and this was the second kind.

“Everything all right, sir?”

Declan looked up. “Very.”

“Shall I have dinner sent to the apartment?”

“Yes, please. And Alexander? The recording Miss Chanya sent this morning. Make sure it’s kept somewhere it can’t be lost.”

Alexander didn’t ask what was on it. “Of course.”

Declan put on his jacket. He had always considered Valentine’s Day a commercial occasion, harmless and not his. This year, it had brought him a piano recording from Bangkok, a song she had once played only halfway, and three words he had finally said out loud.

CC was in bed when her phone lit up.

Declan: I’ve listened to it again.

She smiled into her pillow.

CC: The song?

Declan: Yes.

CC: You really like it?

Declan: I do.

CC: Which part?

His reply took a little longer.

Declan: The second verse.

She smiled.

CC: Why?

Declan: Because I hadn’t heard it before.

Declan: Although I like the ending most.

CC: Because it’s the end?

Declan: Because you played the whole thing.

She hugged her pillow closer.

CC: Goodnight, Declan.

Declan: Goodnight, Cela.

Declan: I love you.

She typed her answer in Mandarin first, and then in English, because she knew he liked both.

CC: Wǒ yě ài nǐ.

CC: I love you.

In the back of the car, somewhere between the office and Lehel, Declan read them and smiled.

chapters.title: The Extra Day
chapters.desc: A show in Paris, eleven garment bags, and a detour to the lake, where Eleanor is waiting and Richard is checking the wire on a crooked glass star. Leap day, he says, doesn’t count.
chapters.epigraph: “I think we’ve been given an extra day.”
chapters.content:
CC hadn’t expected to spend the end of February in Paris.

The invitation had come through AVEN ENT several weeks earlier: Maison Élaris, a Paris house known for understated tailoring and architectural silhouettes, wanted her as a guest at its autumn/winter show. The brand was growing in Asia, her image suited the collection, and after several rounds about scheduling, the company said yes.

She landed on Tuesday afternoon with P’Nicha and two of the company’s team. The show was on Wednesday evening, and the team would fly home on Thursday morning.

Declan had known about the invitation almost as soon as she did, and he had known that Munich was an hour’s flight from Paris. He waited until she mentioned that the day after the show was free before he asked.

Declan: How much time do you have before you need to return to Bangkok?

CC: I have a little room. Why?

Declan: I was wondering whether you might consider a detour.

CC: Where?

Declan: Munich.

She read it twice and called him.

“Hello, sweetheart.”

“Are you asking me to visit you?”

“I’m hoping to.”

She smiled.

“When?”

“On Thursday. You fly in that morning, and I’ll have you on a plane home on Friday. I’ll arrange everything, but only if you’re comfortable with it.”

She leaned back in the hotel chair. “You’re making it sound like a business proposal.”

“I thought you might appreciate a clear itinerary.”

“I haven’t even said yes.”

“I know.”

There was a smile in his voice. “But you’re considering it.”

Outside the window, Paris lay grey and elegant under a pale winter sky.

“I’d like to,” she said.

“Good.”

“Very much.”

She could hear him smile.

“Then I’ll look forward to seeing you.”

“Declan? Will I meet your parents?”

“If you’d like to. They’d be very happy. I’ll speak to my mother.”

“Don’t let her prepare too much.”

“I’ll tell her.”

She could tell from his voice that he wouldn’t.

The Maison Élaris show was held in a restored nineteenth-century building whose hall had been turned into a long lit runway.

CC wore tailored ivory with a sculptural neckline, understated jewellery and her hair in a low knot. She watched attentively, spoke with the creative director afterwards, was photographed with several guests and gave a short interview to a fashion magazine. It went well. Nicha was pleased.

“You looked lovely,” she said in the car.

“Thank you.”

“And you didn’t look nervous.”

“I wasn’t.”

Nicha gave her a sideways glance.

“Not even when the photographer asked you to turn around four times?”

CC laughed.

“He wanted a different angle.”

“He wanted you to look at him as if he were the most interesting person in the room.”

“I did my best.”

Back at the hotel, eleven garment bags were hanging in her suite. CC unzipped the first one and found the ivory coat from the third look, the one she had leaned over to Nicha about. The second held the dress from the finale. She stopped counting at the sixth and called him.

“Did you buy the collection?”

“Only the pieces you looked at twice.”

“It was a fashion show, Declan. I looked at everything twice.”

“That explains the number. The house was very helpful.” He sounded entirely unrepentant.

“It’s too much.”

“Keep the coat, at least. Paris is cold.”

She looked at the coat, and at the five bags she hadn’t opened yet, and felt the smile win. “Okay. The coat.”

“And the rest?”

“I’m thinking about it.”

Nicha, in the doorway, said only, “I’m going to need a bigger suitcase,” and went to find one.

Later, there was a message from him.

Declan: I hope the show went well.

CC: It did. The collection was beautiful.

Declan: And you?

CC: I’m tired.

Declan: I suspected as much.

CC: But happy.

Declan: Even better.

A second message arrived.

Declan: You’re on the nine o’clock to Munich tomorrow. Alexander has sent Nicha the details. The team flies home as planned, and no one else needs to know where you went.

She smiled.

CC: You think of everything.

Declan: Good. Then I’ll see you tomorrow.

She paused, then typed:

CC: I’m excited.

His reply came almost immediately.

Declan: So am I, Cela.

She put the phone down, still smiling. For once, the next stop on her schedule wasn’t work. It was someone waiting for her.

The plane came down through pale cloud, and Munich appeared below her, quieter than Paris, the Isar winding through it in the winter light.

A driver was waiting. Declan wasn’t; he had an early meeting he couldn’t move, and he would meet her at the lake.

Still, as the car pulled away, she checked her phone.

CC: I’ve landed.

Declan: Welcome to Munich, sweetheart.

CC: It’s very cold.

Declan: There’s a coat in the car.

She looked at the front passenger seat. A folded cashmere coat was waiting on it.

CC: Of course there is.

Declan: I know you.

She slipped it on. It was soft, warm, and exactly her size.

The city gave way to quieter roads and trees, and then the lake appeared through the branches, grey-blue under the winter sky.

The house on the western shore was elegant without being imposing: pale stone, dark timber, broad windows and a sloping roof, with the lake beyond the garden.

CC had barely stepped out of the car when the front door opened and Eleanor Lincoln came down the steps.

“CC!”

CC smiled. “Eleanor.”

“You remembered. I hope the journey wasn’t too tiring.” Eleanor took both her hands, delighted, and hugged her.

“It was fine. Thank you for having me.”

“My dear, we’re delighted you’re here.”

Richard appeared in the doorway, taller than she had expected, with a composed face that softened when he smiled.

“CC.”

“Mr. Lincoln.”

“Richard, please.”

He offered his hand, then reconsidered and gave her a brief, warm embrace instead.

Eleanor glanced at the car. “Declan arranged the coat, I suppose.”

CC smiled.

“He did.”

Richard gave a small, knowing nod. “Then I imagine there was little opportunity for discomfort.”

CC laughed. She was beginning to see where Declan had got his quiet humour.

He was in the sitting room, out of his suit and into a dark knit sweater, sleeves pushed up. He looked up the moment he heard her, and for a second neither of them moved.

“Cela.”

She smiled.

“Hello.”

He crossed the room and took her into his arms, gently, and held her longer than a greeting needed.

“Welcome,” he said into her hair.

“Thank you.”

“How was the flight?”

“Good.”

“Are you tired?”

“A little.”

“Then we’ll take it slowly.”

He brushed her hair back and kissed her hair. Eleanor, by the window with Richard, became interested in the view.

Richard was less successful. He looked at his son with faint amusement.

“Father.”

Richard lifted his eyebrows.

“Good.”

CC laughed. They spent the next hour over tea. Eleanor asked about the show, the collection and CC’s schedule, interested without prying, and CC slowly relaxed.

Richard asked about her parents. “They’re in Markham?”

“Yes. I’m going home for my birthday. In March.”

“They must be pleased.”

Eleanor smiled.

“I hope we might have the opportunity to meet them one day.”

CC smiled at her.

“I think they’d like that.”

Declan, beside her, laid his hand lightly over hers. Nobody remarked on it. It was only a reminder that she wasn’t doing this alone.

After lunch, Eleanor asked whether CC would like to see something. “Something of mine.”

CC followed her upstairs, past a hallway of framed photographs. In one, Richard and Eleanor stood beside a younger Declan who looked serious for a boy barely out of his teens.

“Is that Declan?”

Eleanor smiled.

“Yes. He was seventeen.”

“He looks very serious.”

“He was.”

“Was?”

Eleanor laughed.

“He’s still rather serious. He simply has better manners about it now.”

CC smiled. In a small sitting room, Eleanor opened a glass cabinet of old Christmas ornaments and took out a small glass star.

It was delicate and slightly uneven, made by hand a long time ago. CC knew it at once.

“The star.”

Eleanor looked pleased.

“Declan told you about it?”

“At Christmas. He sent me a photograph of the tree.”

“His grandmother gave it to me when I married Richard. Every year Richard puts it on top of the tree, and every year I tell him it’s crooked.” Eleanor held it in her palm.

CC looked closely at it.

“It’s beautiful.”

“It has survived several moves, a few enthusiastic Christmas mornings, and one unfortunate incident involving Declan and a ladder.”

CC turned. “What happened?”

“At fourteen, he insisted he could put the star on himself. He was not good at judging distances.”

CC covered her mouth, laughing.

“Really?”

“He nearly knocked over half the tree.”

“I didn’t,” came a voice from the doorway.

Declan stood there with one hand in his pocket. Eleanor didn’t blink.

“You nearly did.”

“Nearly is not the same as did.”

Richard appeared behind him.

“Your mother spent the next twenty minutes rearranging the ornaments.”

Declan gave his father a look. “Thank you for your contribution.”

CC was laughing now.

Eleanor turned the star in her hand. “Would you like to hold it?”

CC took it carefully. It was lighter than she expected. One point was a little shorter than the others.

“Is it always a little crooked?”

Eleanor smiled.

“Always. Declan’s grandmother used to say that was its charm. Richard has tried to straighten it more than once.” She touched a tiny flaw near the centre.

“I have never tried to straighten it,” Richard said.

Eleanor gave him a look.

“You have.”

“I was checking the wire.”

“Several times?”

Richard only smiled, and CC laughed. She held the star a moment longer and looked up at Declan. He wasn’t watching the ornament. He was watching her.

She understood why he had told her about it. It was a piece of his family, kept and loved long enough to become part of their history.

“Thank you for showing me,” she said.

Eleanor’s face softened.

“Of course, darling. It goes back on the tree in December.” She put the star back in the cabinet.

“I hope I get to see it.”

Eleanor glanced at her son.

“So do I.”

Declan met his mother’s eyes and said nothing, but his smile was answer enough. The afternoon was theirs.

Apart from that one early meeting, he had kept the day free, and he drove them into the city himself.

Their first stop was Lehel, because it was where he lived: elegant old residential streets, small shops and cafés, close enough to the centre without feeling like the middle of it.

“I like this area,” CC said.

“I thought you might.”

“Which one is yours?”

He pointed to a building on the corner, and took her up.

The apartment had a great many books, few things, and a long view of the river. She stood in his kitchen and looked around.

“Where’s your coffee machine?”

“I don’t own one.”

She stared at him. “That explains a lot.”

“Someone brings coffee to the office. At home, I make tea,” he said, with dignity.

Afterwards they walked, and stopped at a café, where he ordered for himself and then turned to her.

“What would you like?”

She studied the menu. “Something warm.”

“Tea?”

She nodded. When it came, she wrapped both hands around the cup and looked out at the street. She looked at him over her cup.

“Is this where you come when you want to get away from work?”

“Sometimes. I don’t always manage to get away from work.”

“That sounds like a problem.”

“It can be.”

“Then you should come here more often.”

He considered her suggestion.

“Perhaps I should.”

From there they walked to the Viktualienmarkt, busy despite the cold: fruit, flowers, bread, cheeses, jars of everything. CC moved slowly from stall to stall, and Declan followed without complaint.

At a honey stall she picked up a small jar and read the label.

“What is this?”

“Honey.”

“I know it’s honey.”

He smiled.

“You asked.”

She gave him a look.

“What’s different about it?”

“Different flowers, different valleys. They all taste different.”

She looked along the jars, then up at him.

“Which one do you like?”

He pointed to a dark one.

She picked it up. “Then I’ll remember this one.”

He watched her put it in the basket. “Are you buying it for me?”

She looked innocent. “Maybe. You’re always buying things for me. It’s my turn.”

He looked at the jar, then at her, as if he had been handed something valuable.

“I’ll treasure it.”

“It’s only honey.”

“I’ve been told the person who chooses the honey matters.”

She laughed.

“Who told you that?”

“I’ve just decided.”

She shook her head. They left the market with fruit, bread, the honey, and a pastry CC insisted they share later. Declan carried everything, and she let him.

The Lincoln Group headquarters stood in a modern building in the city, its glass front reflecting the last of the afternoon light. CC had seen photographs. They hadn’t prepared her for the scale of it: stone floors, dark wood, a large sculpture by the entrance. Declan greeted the woman at reception by name.

“Good evening, Mr. Lincoln.”

“Good evening, Frau Brandt.”

CC noticed how the air changed when he walked in. People greeted him, and a few stopped with a question; he answered each one quickly, remembered names and details, and never made anyone feel hurried, even when he clearly had somewhere to be. She had seen him in suits and on calls. This was where those parts of him came together. People relied on him, and he carried it.

He took her up to his office once most of the floor had gone home. It was large but plain: a broad desk, a sitting area, bookshelves, and a wall of windows over the city. CC went to the window.

She turned round. “It’s very you.”

He smiled.

“What does that mean?”

“Neat. Quiet. A little intimidating.”

“Intimidating?”

“Only a little.”

He came towards her.

“I’ll try not to frighten you.”

She laughed. Then she noticed a framed photograph on his desk: the Christmas dinner at the lake, Declan between Eleanor and Richard, in the charcoal suit and the plum tie she had sent him.

She picked it up. “You keep this here.”

“Of course.”

“You like it that much?”

“I told you I did.”

She studied it. “You look very handsome.”

He raised an eyebrow. “Only in that photograph?”

“You’re fishing for compliments.”

“Is it working?”

“A little.”

He took the frame from her and set it back, then opened a drawer and took out a small box.

“I have something for you.”

“Again?”

“Not quite a gift.”

Inside was a small leather notebook, dark green, with her initials pressed discreetly into the cover.

She touched it. “What is it?”

“For your music.”

She looked up. “You already gave me the score.”

“I know. This is for whatever comes next.”

She opened it. The pages were blank and heavy enough for ink, and a ribbon marked the first page, where he had written:

For the beginnings, the unfinished parts, and everything you haven’t written yet.

She looked at him. “Declan.”

“I thought you might like somewhere to keep ideas.”

Her face softened. “I do. Thank you.”

She held the notebook against her chest.

“You’re welcome.”

She looked around the office again.

“Can I ask you something?”

“Anything.”

“Do you ever feel lonely here?”

He thought about it. “Sometimes.”

She hadn’t expected that. He went on, “It’s busy all day. There are always people. But after everyone leaves, it’s very quiet.”

She glanced at the windows. “And you stay late?”

“More often than I should.”

She turned back to him. “Then you should leave earlier.”

He smiled. “You sound like my mother.”

“Maybe she’s right.”

“That is a dangerous alliance.”

He came around the desk and held out his hand. “Come. I’ll show you the rest.”

He walked her through the empty meeting rooms and the executive floor, and showed her the view from the end of the corridor. Nobody interrupted them. She was seeing his working life without its noise, and she liked it, not because it was grand, but because it was his, and he was letting her see it.

They drove back to the lake after dinner, the city lights thinning behind them. CC was tired in the good way that comes after a day of walking and looking, and her hand stayed in his on the gearstick.

The house was warm and lit. Eleanor and Richard had already gone up, and Declan took CC’s coat.

“Would you like tea?”

“Maybe later.”

“Are you tired?”

“A little.”

He ran his thumb over the back of her hand. “Then let’s sit for a while.”

On the sofa in the sitting room, she leaned against his shoulder, and for a few minutes they said nothing.

Then she glanced at the clock. “It’s the twenty-ninth of February.”

“It is.”

“A leap day.”

“Yes.”

“It’s a little strange.”

“Why?”

“Because it only happens every four years.”

He looked down at her.

“That’s true.”

“Do you think it’s a special day?”

He thought about it, and the corner of his mouth lifted.

“I think we’ve been given an extra day.”

“An extra day?”

“One that doesn’t usually exist.”

She laughed.

“That’s not how calendars work.”

“I know.”

“But I think we should treat it that way.”

She smiled.

“How?”

“By not wasting it.”

She leaned closer.

“Did we waste it?”

“Not at all. We walked round my neighbourhood. You found out I don’t own a coffee machine. You bought me honey, and I showed you where I spend most of my life.” He kissed her cheek.

“And I met your parents.”

“Yes.”

“And saw the star.”

“Yes.”

She smiled.

“Then I think it was a very good extra day.”

He looked at her for a while.

“I wanted you to see Munich.”

She lifted her head slightly.

“Why?”

“You’ve seen me in Bangkok, and in the mountains, and on a phone at strange hours. This is where I live. Where I grew up. Where my family is. I wanted you to know this part of me too.”

Her face softened.

“I liked it. The café, and the market, and your office. Especially after everyone had gone.”

“Why?”

“It was quiet. It felt like seeing something not many people get to see.”

He took her hand and brought it to his lips.

“I’m glad you came.”

She smiled.

“Me too.”

He kissed her the way he hadn’t been able to all day: slowly at first, and then not slowly at all, one hand sliding into her hair, until the house and the lake and the leap day went somewhere far away and there was only the warmth of his mouth and her fingers curled in his sweater. When he drew back, neither of them moved. She could feel his heart under her palm, as fast as hers.

“Declan?”

“Hm?”

“Next time, I want to see the tree. With the star on it.”

“December, then.”

“I’ll hold you to that.”

“I’d be disappointed if you didn’t.”

Outside, the lake was dark under the February sky. She fell asleep against his shoulder a little later, and he didn’t wake her.

chapters.title: Exposure
chapters.desc: A photograph from the Munich terminal, a headline, and a contract with a no-dating clause. He wants to fix it. She lets him carry some of it, and asks him to let her walk in herself.
chapters.epigraph: “Then let me carry some of it.”
chapters.content:
The photograph had been taken on Friday morning at the private terminal in Munich, from the public side of the glass, and it wasn’t clear.

CC was in a long camel coat, a cream scarf and dark sunglasses, her hair tucked behind her ears, one hand on the strap of her bag while she listened to the man beside her.

He was easier to recognise. Even without a clear view of his face, his height and his profile were enough for anyone who read the business pages: Declan Lincoln.

It appeared shortly after midnight on Sunday, Bangkok time, on an account that posted celebrity sightings.

CC spotted at a private terminal in Munich?

Someone reposted it within the hour.

Wait. Isn’t that Declan Lincoln?

By morning, the speculation had a headline: CC’S EUROPEAN BUSINESSMAN?

Some people decided he was a brand representative. Others linked him to the Maison Élaris show in Paris. A few remembered the black car at her concert in February. Someone found a photograph of Declan at the Lincoln Foundation gala in Geneva, and someone else found the fan photograph of CC wearing a diamond bracelet in November.

None of it proved anything. All of it together made a story.

By the time CC woke up, the first message on her phone was from P’Nicha.

Nicha: Call me when you’re awake. Not urgent, but we need to discuss something.

She opened the link and studied the photograph. She wasn’t ashamed of being seen with Declan. But neither of them had known the camera was there, and now strangers were discussing her private life as if it were a puzzle they had a right to solve. She called Nicha.

“Good morning,” her manager answered.

“Have you seen it?”

“Unfortunately.”

“How bad is it?”

“Not terrible yet. It’s circulating, but it’s still mostly speculation.”

CC looked at the photograph again.

“Do we know who took it?”

“Not yet. The terminal has security cameras, but I don’t want to start making requests without knowing what we’re dealing with.”

CC nodded, though Nicha couldn’t see her. “All right.”

“Listen to me. Don’t reply to anything. Don’t post anything unusual. And please don’t let the comments dictate your mood today.”

“I’m fine.”

“I know. I’m telling you before someone else decides what you should be feeling.”

CC smiled a little. “Thank you.”

Then Nicha’s voice changed. “There’s something else. The CEO’s office called this morning. They want to see me tomorrow.”

“About the photograph?”

“Probably.”

“Let me know what happens.”

“I will.”

After the call, she opened her conversation with Declan.

Cela: Have you seen the photograph?

His reply came quickly.

Declan: Yes.

Cela: It’s everywhere.

Declan: I’ve seen the coverage. Are you all right?

Cela: I’m okay. Nicha is handling it.

A moment passed.

Declan: I’ll speak to Alexander. We can find the photographer and have the right people deal with whoever published it.

She knew he could do it, probably by lunchtime. That was exactly what made her pause.

CC: Let’s wait until Nicha speaks to the company.

Declan: Of course.

She put the phone down. For now, that was enough.

The meeting request had come with no explanation beyond a discussion regarding CC’s current contractual position and public image. Nicha knew what that meant. When she walked in at ten on Tuesday, the CEO of AVEN ENT was already at the head of the table, with two senior executives and the company’s lawyer.

“Please sit, Nicha. You’ve seen this?” He laid a printout of the photograph on the table.

“Yes.”

“Is the man Declan Lincoln?”

“Yes.”

“How long has this been going on?”

Nicha kept her face neutral.

“CC’s personal relationships are not something I discuss without her permission.”

The CEO studied her.

“I understand your position. But you are her manager. You’re responsible for protecting the company and the artist.”

“I’m aware.”

He leaned back and opened a folder.

“CC’s current agreement is due for renewal in April. As you know, the contract includes a clause regarding romantic relationships and public conduct.”

Nicha knew the clause. It had been in the agreement CC signed at nineteen, when she was new and the company was offering everything she wanted. It barred the artist from any romantic relationship that could harm the company’s commercial interests or public image without prior disclosure and approval. It was worded broadly. Broadly enough to be used as leverage.

“We cannot have an artist entering into an undisclosed relationship with a high-profile businessman while we are negotiating brand partnerships and preparing for the next phase of her career.”

Nicha stayed calm. “Has CC’s work been affected?”

“That’s not the only concern.”

“Has she missed an appointment? Failed to fulfil a brand obligation? Caused any commercial loss?”

The CEO’s mouth tightened. “You’re being defensive.”

“I’m asking what specific issue we’re addressing.”

He closed the folder.

“We need to understand whether this relationship is serious, whether it will continue, and whether she intends to make it public.”

Nicha looked at him. “Those are questions you should ask CC directly.”

He paused. “Her renewal is in April. I would prefer this resolved before then.”

The implication was clear. The company had invested in CC: contracts, endorsements, staff, a carefully managed image. But CC had built her place through years of discipline and talent. She had never missed an obligation or asked for anything unreasonable. And now, because someone had photographed her beside a man at an airport, the company was discussing whether she deserved a renewal.

Nicha folded her hands. “I’ll speak with CC.”

As she stood, the CEO added, “She needs to understand that being an idol comes with certain sacrifices.”

Nicha paused at the door. “She understands that better than most people.”

CC was waiting in Nicha’s office when she came back, and looked up at once. “How was it?”

Nicha put her bag on the chair. “Not ideal.”

CC sat up. “What did they say?”

Nicha took a moment. “They brought up your contract.”

“Because of the photograph?”

“Yes. They’re concerned about the relationship, the public image, and the renewal in April.”

CC looked down. “Did they say they wouldn’t renew?”

“Not directly.”

“But they implied it.”

Nicha didn’t deny it. “They reminded me about the no-dating clause.”

CC was silent. She had signed it young, when it had seemed like something she could live with. She had never expected it to matter.

“Did they ask me to end the relationship?”

“They asked whether it was serious and whether it would continue.”

CC looked at her.

“What did you tell them?”

“That they should ask you.”

CC smiled a little. “Thank you.”

Nicha sat down across from her. “I need you to understand this could get complicated. They may use the renewal to push for changes.”

“I understand.”

“And I don’t want you to make a decision simply because you feel pressured to protect your career.”

CC nodded. “I won’t.”

Nicha studied her. “Are you sure?”

CC thought about it. She wasn’t angry, not yet. Mostly she was disappointed that something as ordinary as travelling with her boyfriend had become a matter for a boardroom.

“I don’t want to lie about my life. But I also don’t want to make everything public just because people are curious,” she said.

“That’s reasonable.”

“I want to keep my work and my relationship separate.”

Nicha nodded, and reached across the table to touch CC’s hand. “Then we’ll work from there. You’re not handling this alone.”

“I know.”

In Munich on Wednesday afternoon, Declan read the report twice while Alexander waited.

Alexander said, “It was taken from the public side of the terminal. We haven’t identified the photographer, but the image was sold to at least one entertainment account.”

“And the coverage?”

“Several outlets have repeated the speculation. None has confirmed the nature of your relationship.”

Declan glanced at the screen.

“Have we contacted the publications?”

“Not yet.”

“Draft a notice asking them not to publish private travel details or present speculation as fact. Legal reviews it before anything is sent.”

“Certainly.”

He closed the report. “And her company?”

“AVEN’s management has been in touch with Nicha. There appears to be a contractual issue.”

Declan went still.

“What kind?”

“Possibly a clause about romantic relationships. Our legal team hasn’t seen the agreement.”

Declan looked up. “Find out what can be done.”

Alexander hesitated. “Shall I contact their legal department?”

He leaned back. “Not yet. First, find out whether there’s any legitimate basis for challenging the clause. If it’s being used to threaten her renewal, I want to know the options.”

“Understood.”

When Alexander had gone, Declan checked his phone. She had told him about the meeting last night, though not every detail. He had listened, and he had been thinking about it ever since. He could call the CEO. He could have his lawyers take the agreement apart and make it plain that interfering with her personal life would be met seriously. He could probably make the company think again.

The question he hadn’t answered was whether that would help her, or only replace one kind of pressure with another.

Declan: Can we talk?

Her reply came a few minutes later.

CC: Of course. Now?

Declan: I can make time.

He called. It was nearly eleven in Bangkok, and CC was on her sofa when his face appeared.

“You’re still at your desk.”

“It’s five o’clock here.”

“That’s not an answer.”

He almost smiled. “It’s the only one I have.”

“How are you?”

“All right.”

He chose his words. “I’ve asked Alexander to look into the contractual position. I’d like our legal team to review the clause. If the company is using it to threaten your renewal, we may be able to challenge it. I could also speak to the CEO privately and make it clear that this isn’t something they should use against you.”

She listened. He wasn’t being aggressive. He was offering what he understood best: information, lawyers, influence, a quiet word with the person in charge. And he was offering all of it to her.

She didn’t answer at once, and he stopped. “Cela?”

“I’m scared. That’s all. It’s the only thing I ever built by myself, and now a boardroom gets to talk about who I love,” she said.

His voice gentled. “Then let me carry some of it.”

“You already are. Have your lawyers read it. Tell me everything they find. I want to know where I stand before I walk in there.” She pulled her knees up.

“Done. And the CEO?”

“Don’t call him. Not because I don’t want your help. Because if they back down for you, they’ll never take me seriously again. I want them to back down for me.” She saw his jaw set and went on before he could argue.

He was quiet. Then the corner of his mouth lifted, slowly. “That’s a much better plan than mine.”

“You’re not upset?”

“I’m proud of you. It’s very inconvenient. The agreement will be on your table tomorrow night, with notes. When you walk in, you’ll know more about that clause than the man who wrote it.” He leaned closer to the camera.

She laughed, and it came out wet. “Is that how you do it?”

“That’s exactly how I do it.”

“Then stay on the phone while I read it.”

“As long as you like.”

When the screen went dark, he sent Alexander two lines: Hold the notice. Find the best entertainment lawyer in Bangkok to read that contract tonight.

On Thursday afternoon, CC and Nicha met the entertainment lawyer Declan’s people had found overnight: independent, with no connection to AVEN or to Lincoln Group, and so good that Nicha had checked her credentials twice.

The clause was broad. It gave the company wide discretion to decide whether a relationship might affect its interests, and it required her to report anything that might cause reputational concern. Whether it could be enforced depended on the whole agreement and on the law, the lawyer said, but it could certainly be renegotiated.

CC asked questions: what the company could reasonably demand, what happened if she refused to disclose private details, whether the clause could change at renewal. She didn’t ask whether she should end her relationship. That wasn’t on the table.

Afterwards, Nicha walked her to the car. “You’re taking this well.”

CC smiled a little. “I’m trying.”

“You don’t have to decide everything today.”

She looked at the folder in her hands. “I want the clause changed.”

Nicha nodded. “That’s reasonable.”

“I want to be responsible for my work. I want to meet my commitments. But I don’t want the company to decide whether I’m allowed to have a relationship.”

Nicha smiled. “Then that’s what we’ll negotiate.”

“Will you help me?”

“Of course.”

“Even if they make it difficult?”

Nicha gave her a look. “If they make it difficult, yes.”

CC laughed. For the first time since the photograph, the situation felt like something she could walk towards, not something happening to her.

Declan was eating lunch at his desk when she called that evening.

“Hello, sweetheart.”

“I saw a lawyer today.”

He put down his fork.

“How did it go?”

“Good. I understand the contract better now. We’re going to negotiate the clause at renewal.”

“What do you want changed?”

“Reasonable expectations about my work. Nothing about who I’m allowed to love.”

“That sounds sensible.”

She smiled.

“I thought so too.”

He paused. “And our lawyer’s notes?”

“Send him the night before. I want both of them on my side. You’re doing well.” She smiled.

He raised an eyebrow. The corner of his mouth lifted.

“I’m making a considerable effort.”

She laughed, and he watched her, and his face softened.

“I don’t think less of you for any of this. And I don’t think your career should be something you have to give up to be with me.”

She grew serious. “Thank you.”

“I’d never want you to look back and feel that being with me cost you something you’d worked so hard to build.”

“I don’t want that either.”

“Then it won’t happen without your say.”

She smiled. “That’s better.”

By Friday, the photograph was losing momentum. There were newer stories and newer pictures for the internet to argue about. CC hadn’t posted anything or denied anything. She had gone to a recording session, a brand fitting and a shoot for a short promotional video, and been exactly as polite and professional as before. What had changed wasn’t how she felt about Declan. It was how clearly she knew her own lines.

That night she sat at her piano with the dark-blue score on the stand and the green notebook beside it, and picked up her phone.

Cela: Are you still at work?

His reply was immediate.

Declan: Leaving soon. Are you finished for the day?

Cela: Finally.

Declan: Then call me.

She did. His face came up on the screen, and she smiled.

“Hello.”

“Hello, Cela.”

She turned the phone towards the piano.

“I was looking at your score.”

“Have you played it today?”

“A little.”

“Did it sound good?”

“Very. I was thinking about this week. I know you wanted to fix it.”

“I did.”

“And that it was hard for you to let me do the talking.”

He didn’t deny it. “It was.”

Her voice was gentle. “Thank you for doing it anyway.”

“I don’t want you to have to ask me twice.”

She shook her head. “You don’t have to be perfect.”

“I’m aware.”

“You can want to help me.”

“I do.”

“You can even be a little overprotective sometimes.”

The corner of his mouth lifted. “How generous of you.”

She laughed. “I mean it. I like being looked after by you. I’m just not used to it yet.”

After a pause he said, “I’ve spent a long time believing that if I could solve a problem, I should.”

“And now?”

“Now I’m learning that sometimes the person I love doesn’t need me to solve it. She needs me to trust her.”

CC’s face warmed. “That’s right.”

He smiled. “And I do.”

She looked down, then back up. “I love you.”

His face changed at once. “I love you too, sweetheart. How was your day?”

“Long.”

“Did anyone feed you between the fitting and the shoot?”

“Twice.”

“Did you rest?”

“A little.”

“Did you—”

She laughed.

“Declan.”

He stopped. “Yes?”

“You’re allowed to spoil me.”

His eyes warmed. “Am I?”

“Yes.”

“Good.”

She leaned closer to the screen. “All of it. I’m learning to like it.”

He smiled, slowly, the way he did when she surprised him. “Then I have a great deal of catching up to do.”

She tilted the phone towards the open score. “Would you like to hear something?”

“Always.”

She propped the phone on the stand and set her fingers on the keys. This time she didn’t play the whole song, only a few bars of the second verse, the part he had never heard until Valentine’s Day.

When she finished, she studied the screen. “Was that all right?”

“It was beautiful.”

“Goodnight, Declan. Don’t work too late.”

“I’m leaving now.”

“You said that an hour ago.”

“This time I’m standing up.”

She laughed and ended the call.

Declan sat with the dark screen. He still wanted to call the CEO. He still wanted his lawyers on every line of that contract, and nobody anywhere able to use her love for him as leverage. Those instincts hadn’t gone anywhere. But loving her didn’t mean making every hard thing disappear before she had decided how to face it. Sometimes it meant standing beside her while she did, which was harder than a phone call, and mattered more.

In Bangkok, CC closed the piano and took in the photograph on her phone one last time. She wasn’t embarrassed by it, and she wasn’t ashamed of him. She just wasn’t ready to let strangers decide what they were. She put the phone away and went to bed.

chapters.title: Terms
chapters.desc: She negotiates her own renewal and wins. He is waiting at the back of the car park with an iced latte, and later with a box that holds the rest of the bracelet’s family.
chapters.epigraph: “The bracelet looked lonely.”
chapters.content:
On Monday night, the contract had been on CC’s dining table for nearly an hour: two copies, several pages of proposed amendments, a folder of notes from her lawyer, and a yellow sticky note on the front with three things written on it. Personal life. Schedule. Creative decisions.

Those were what she meant to discuss tomorrow. She didn’t intend to make unreasonable demands. She wanted to keep working without feeling that every part of her life belonged to the company.

She was reading the proposed wording again on the sofa when her phone buzzed.

Declan: Have you finished reviewing everything?

CC: Almost.

Declan: Are you comfortable with the proposed amendments?

CC: Mostly. I have a few things I want to clarify tomorrow.

Declan: Good.

A moment later:

Declan: A lawyer from our outside counsel will be at your apartment at eight. He’s read the draft and will go through the wording with you. He won’t take part in the negotiation, and he won’t contact AVEN.

CC smiled. It was exactly what she had asked for: one more pair of eyes on the wording, and nothing else. Her own lawyer and Nicha would be in the room. Declan wouldn’t.

CC: Thank you for arranging it.

Declan: You’re welcome.

CC: And thank you for not storming the meeting.

His reply took a little longer.

Declan: I was tempted.

She laughed.

CC: And no flowers tomorrow, whatever happens. People at AVEN still talk about December.

Declan: Understood.

Then another message arrived.

Declan: You’ll do well tomorrow, Cela.

She read that twice.

CC: I hope so.

Declan: You know what you want. That’s usually a good place to start.

She smiled.

CC: Goodnight.

Declan: Goodnight, sweetheart. Get some sleep.

She put the phone down and looked at the contract again. Tomorrow she would speak for herself, and she meant to be heard.

The lawyer arrived at eight exactly, courteous and efficient, and they spent nearly an hour on the revised contract in her living room.

He said, “The existing language on disclosure is broad. It gives the company a great deal of discretion. I’d narrow it to circumstances that directly affect your contractual obligations or demonstrable commercial commitments.”

CC nodded. “That’s what I want.”

“Then your amendment is reasonable. It doesn’t stop the company protecting legitimate business interests. It stops the clause being used as a general restriction on your private life.”

He turned a page. “The scheduling provision matters too. At the moment they can assign you almost anything at any time. Your wording asks for consultation and reasonable notice for non-emergency changes.”

“Can they still change my schedule if there’s an urgent situation?”

“Yes. The wording allows for genuine emergencies, but it prevents routine last-minute changes from becoming standard practice.”

She considered it. “Good.”

He reached the last section. “Creative approval is harder. You may not get control over every group or commercial project, but you can ask for defined consultation and approval rights on your own releases.”

CC looked at the page. “That’s what I want. I don’t need to control everything. I want my input to mean something.”

He nodded. “Then keep that distinction clear.”

When he left, she had a short list of questions and a much better grip on the wording. She sent him a polite thank-you and called Nicha.

“Ready?” Nicha asked.

CC looked at herself in the mirror: a pale blue blouse, tailored black trousers, simple earrings, her hair neatly back.

“I think so.”

“Good. I’ll meet you downstairs.”

At half past ten, the meeting room at AVEN seemed brighter than she remembered, or perhaps she was noticing more. The CEO sat at the head of the table, with the head of talent management beside him, the company’s lawyer and one more executive. Nicha sat on CC’s right. The CEO began with the formalities.

“Thank you for coming, CC. We appreciate your continued contribution to AURELIA. Your work over the past year has been very strong, and we’re pleased with the direction of your individual projects.”

“Thank you,” CC replied.

“We’d like to discuss the renewal and make sure both sides are aligned.”

She nodded. “Of course.”

The first part was straightforward: group activities, solo releases, promotional obligations, the company’s plans for the year. CC listened, asked questions and made a few suggestions about how her solo recording should be scheduled.

Then the CEO turned to the amendments. “We noticed some changes to the personal conduct section.”

“Yes,” CC said.

“Would you explain your concerns?”

She looked at the document.

“The current wording gives the company very broad authority over my personal relationships. I understand that the company needs to protect its commercial interests and public image, and that I have responsibilities as an artist under contract. But I don’t think that should mean the company has the right to approve whether I can have a private relationship.”

The CEO folded his hands. “The clause exists to protect the artist and the company from reputational damage.”

“I understand.”

“Then you understand why it exists.”

“Yes. But the wording should be more specific. I’d like it to apply where personal conduct directly affects my contractual responsibilities, creates a real conflict of interest, or breaches a specific confidentiality or commercial obligation. I don’t think a consensual private relationship should automatically be a contractual issue, especially when it doesn’t affect my work.” She turned a page.

The CEO studied her. “And if the relationship becomes public and causes controversy?”

“Then we can discuss how to handle the public response. I’ll cooperate with reasonable communication planning. But that shouldn’t give the company authority over the relationship itself.”

There was a short silence. Nicha didn’t move. CC didn’t look at her for reassurance; she didn’t need to.

The CEO turned to the lawyer. “Is that workable?”

“Potentially. We would need to retain the company’s right to address genuine conflicts of interest and contractual breaches.”

“Of course,” CC said.

The discussion went on for another fifteen minutes. Some language was narrowed, some clarified, and in the end the company agreed to remove the broad no-dating restriction and replace it with a narrower provision on conflicts of interest, confidentiality, professional obligations, and conduct that materially affected her performance under the contract.

CC read the new wording carefully and turned to the next page. “The scheduling provision.”

The head of talent management leaned forward. “We already make reasonable efforts to accommodate you.”

“I appreciate that. But there are still frequent changes with very little notice.”

“That’s part of the industry.”

“I understand that. I’m not asking for a fixed schedule. But I’d like a consultation period for non-emergency changes, especially when they affect recording sessions or projects I’ve already approved,” she said calmly.

The head of talent management offered forty-eight hours. “That’s standard.”

“Could we make it seventy-two hours where reasonably possible, with exceptions for genuine emergencies or unavoidable production changes?”

The head of talent management glanced at the CEO, and after a short discussion they agreed: reasonable notice, with seventy-two hours as the target for non-emergency changes, and consultation before any major change to a confirmed commitment. Nobody was controlling her schedule. If anything, it was more than she had ever been guaranteed.

The creative section was the hardest. She wanted defined consultation rights on her solo music: material, recording arrangements, parts of the creative direction. The company wouldn’t give her final approval over every production decision, and she hadn’t expected it to. So she asked for something practical instead: mandatory consultation, a written response to her feedback, and approval over how her name and image were used outside the agreed scope.

At one point the CEO looked at her. “You’ve prepared thoroughly.”

CC smiled politely.

“I wanted to understand what I was agreeing to.”

He nodded. “That’s fair.”

Twenty minutes later, the company lawyer closed his folder.

“We can incorporate these amendments into the renewal draft.”

CC looked at the document. She hadn’t got everything she wanted. She had got the things that mattered: a private life, a real say in her schedule, and her creative contribution written into the contract.

The CEO held out his hand. “We look forward to continuing our work together.”

CC shook it. “Thank you. So do I.”

Nicha waited until the door had closed behind them before she smiled. “Well done.”

CC let out a breath. “Was I all right?”

Nicha stared at her.

“CC.”

“What?”

“You negotiated your own contract.”

CC laughed, and the tension finally left her shoulders.

“I know. I’m glad I did it myself.”

Nicha put an arm around her. “So am I.”

The other three members of BLUE HOUR were having lunch in the practice room when CC came in. Nicha had told them only that she was in a contract meeting.

One of them looked up. “You’re back! How did it go?”

“Good.”

The three of them exchanged glances, and one put down her chopsticks.

“Good as in actually good, or good as in you’re trying to make us stop asking?”

CC laughed.

“Actually good.”

“Then sit down and tell us.”

She sat down. Nicha stayed by the door, giving them privacy, and CC put the folder on the table.

“I negotiated some changes to my renewal. Mostly about my personal life, my schedule, and creative decisions.”

There was a short silence. Then one of them asked, “Does this mean you can date?”

It was so direct that CC almost laughed.

“More or less.”

The other two leaned in at once.

“Is it about the man in the photograph?”

CC hadn’t meant to make an announcement. She didn’t want to lie, either.

“Yes.”

All three stared at her, and one of them put both hands over her mouth.

“CC!”

She laughed. “Please don’t shout.”

“You’re dating him?”

CC nodded. “Yes.”

“Seriously?”

“Yes.”

“Since when?”

CC considered it. “Officially, January.”

They exchanged another look, and then the questions began.

“Is he nice?”

“Very.”

“Does he treat you well?”

She smiled. “Yes.”

“Is he really as handsome as the photographs?”

CC laughed. “That’s a very strange question.”

“Answer it.”

She tried to look serious. “Yes.”

They burst out laughing, and one leaned closer.

“Is he the reason you went to Munich?”

“Partly.”

“Partly?”

“I also went to Paris for work.”

“CC!”

She laughed. They were teasing her, but she could see they were glad for her.

The quietest of them reached across the table and touched her arm. “Are you happy?”

CC nodded. “Very.”

The girl smiled. “Then I’m happy for you.”

Nobody was hurt that she had kept it from them. They were pleased she had someone. Then one of them grinned. “So when do we meet him?”

“Meet him?”

“Of course. We need to inspect him.”

The others nodded enthusiastically.

CC laughed. “I don’t think that’s necessary.”

“It is absolutely necessary.”

“At least once.”

“Preferably when he brings food.”

CC shook her head. “I’ll tell him.”

“You know, you’ve been smiling at your phone a lot lately.”

“Especially after midnight,” another added.

CC’s cheeks warmed. “That’s the time difference.”

“Of course.”

They laughed, and so did she. Until now, it had been something between her and Declan, with Nicha in on it. Now three more people knew: people who shared her rehearsals and routines and the ordinary hours of her life. The circle had widened, and it felt surprisingly natural.

The rest of the day went on a recording session and production notes, and it was nearly dark by the time she left. She was tired, in a good way. Nicha walked her out through the staff car park at the back, the way she always did now. Her phone buzzed on the way.

Declan: Finished?

CC: Yes.

Declan: How did it go?

She didn’t answer, because a dark car with tinted windows was parked at the far end of the car park, and its passenger window was coming down. Declan was at the wheel.

CC stopped walking. Then she smiled, and Nicha, beside her, became interested in her own phone. CC opened the passenger door.

“You’re supposed to be in Munich.”

“I landed at two. Hello, sweetheart.” He looked at her.

She got in. The car was cool and quiet, and in the cup holder beside her seat was an iced latte.

She picked it up. “You remembered.”

“You’ve ordered the same thing since November.”

She took a sip. It was exactly right: not too sweet, not too bitter, with enough ice to keep it cold without watering it down.

“How long have you been waiting?”

“Not very long.”

She narrowed her eyes.

“Declan.”

He smiled.

“A little while.”

She shook her head and looked around the car. “No flowers?”

“You told me no flowers.”

She smiled. “Good.”

He glanced at her. “Would you have preferred them?”

“No. I wanted you to come without making it obvious.”

“I thought an unmarked car and coffee were more suitable.”

She laughed. “Much more suitable.”

He waited until she had set the cup down. “How did it go?”

“Good.”

She turned to him, her face lighting up. “I got the personal-life clause changed,” she said.

His face warmed. “Well done.”

“And the schedule. Reasonable notice for non-emergency changes, seventy-two hours as the target. And more consultation rights for my solo projects.”

“You negotiated all of that yourself?”

“Yes.”

The corner of his mouth lifted. “I had no doubt you could.”

“You’re not disappointed you didn’t get to help?”

He thought about it. “I helped by staying out of the room.”

She smiled. “Exactly.”

He brushed his thumb along her cheek. “Look at you.”

Her face softened. “Thank you.”

“Did you celebrate?”

“Not yet.”

“Then we’ll have dinner. Somewhere quiet.”

He nodded at the cup in her hand. “Is the coffee correct?”

She took another sip. “Perfect.”

“Then my contribution to today’s negotiations has been a success.”

She laughed. “Your contribution was coffee?”

“Half-sweet iced latte. A very important distinction.”

She shook her head, and after a moment she reached across the console and took his hand. He looked down at their joined hands.

“Thank you for waiting. And for letting me do it myself.”

His fingers closed around hers. “You were magnificent. I only wish I’d seen it.”

She smiled.

“I know.”

He lifted her hand and kissed her knuckles. “Now tell me everything. I want to hear how you made them agree.”

So she did: the CEO’s questions, the argument over seventy-two hours, the creative wording, Nicha’s face afterwards. Then she told him about the girls.

“They know now?”

CC laughed. “They want to meet you. Apparently they need to inspect you.”

He smiled. “That’s reasonable.”

She stared at him. “You’re agreeing?”

“I’d expect nothing less from people who care about you.”

Her smile softened. “They were happy.”

“I’m glad.”

She leaned back with her coffee as he pulled out of the car park. For the first time in days, she felt entirely at ease. The photograph hadn’t gone away, and nothing had been made public. But she had negotiated the terms of her own career and told the people closest to her at work, and she had done both without giving up anything she wanted to keep.

He dropped her at the side entrance of a restaurant whose staff knew how to be discreet, parked round the corner, and walked into the private room five minutes after her, under a name that wasn’t his.

She ate well. He made sure of it without turning dinner into an inspection.

At one point she looked across the table. “Can I tell you something? I liked today.”

He put down his glass. “Which part?”

“All of it. I liked speaking for myself. I liked telling the girls. And I liked seeing you outside.”

His face warmed. “Even without flowers?”

“Without flowers too.”

He laughed. She reached for her glass.

“Sometimes I think you enjoy giving me things more than I enjoy receiving them.”

“That’s possible.”

She smiled. “But I like the little things too.”

“Noted.”

“And waiting for me.”

“I can do that.”

She gave him a soft smile.

He found her hand on the table. “You’re allowed to have a life that belongs to you, Cela.”

“And you’re allowed to be part of it.”

His face softened. “That’s all I want.”

She squeezed his hand. “Good.”

Over dessert, he slid a long, flat case across the table. She knew the name on the lid. Inside, on dark velvet, lay a necklace, a pair of earrings and a ring, all in the same pale diamonds as the bracelet he had given her in November.

“Declan. This is a collection.” She didn’t touch it.

“It’s a set. They come in sets. The bracelet looked lonely.” He seemed genuinely puzzled by the objection.

“Who buys the whole set?”

“Apparently, I do.”

“It’s too much.”

“You negotiated your own contract today. You don’t get to negotiate this,” he said.

She laughed before she could stop herself. Then she looked at the necklace, and at him, and the smile came anyway. “Okay.”

He came round the table and fastened it at the back of her neck himself, his fingers slow and warm against her skin. She tipped her head back to say thank you, and he kissed her before she could, upside down, in a private room in Bangkok, until she was laughing against his mouth.

They stayed until the restaurant was nearly empty. Tomorrow there would be schedules and rehearsals and all the usual demands. Tonight she had finished something important, and he drove her home with the last of the iced latte rattling in the cup holder.

chapters.title: Four in the Morning
chapters.desc: Four in the morning in a Markham bakery, an apron, and a man being told he holds a rolling pin wrong. Her twenty-fifth birthday, a framed recipe card, and a shop next door he has to give back.
chapters.epigraph: “I intend to love her well.”
chapters.content:
At four in the morning on the Friday before her birthday, Declan Lincoln stood in a bakery in Markham, Ontario, in an apron with flour down the front, being told he was holding a rolling pin incorrectly.

“Not like that.”

Declan looked down at the rolling pin. Mr. Chanya stood beside him with his arms folded.

“How should I hold it?”

“Like this.”

He took the rolling pin, showed him the movement once, and handed it back.

Declan tried again. The dough came out thin on one side and noticeably thicker on the other.

Mr. Chanya stared at it. Declan stared at it. Neither of them spoke.

Then Mr. Chanya sighed. “We’ll try again.”

From behind the counter, CC’s mother laughed. “Don’t be too hard on him. He’s been here twenty minutes.”

“Twenty minutes is enough to learn how to roll dough.”

“Apparently not,” Declan said.
