Her mother laughed harder. He wasn’t embarrassed. He was beginning to understand that the man who had raised CC had a specific standard for butter tarts, and it wasn’t going to be lowered because Declan happened to run Lincoln Group.

They had landed in Toronto the evening before. CC was still asleep at her parents’ house, and didn’t know that he had slipped out a little after three to meet her father at the bakery.

He had arranged it weeks ago, through her mother. He had no illusions about becoming good at it. But CC had told him once that her father made butter tarts every year, and that the smell of them meant home, and her birthday was tomorrow.

“All right. Again,” Mr. Chanya said, pointing at the dough.

Declan rolled up his sleeves. “Yes, sir.”

The bakery was small and warm and already busy: a few lights in the display cases, the ovens heating, the air full of butter and sugar and bread. Mr. Chanya had run it for decades. It wasn’t grand, but the neighbourhood loved it, and the shelves held recipes he had been refining for most of his life.

Declan had seen photographs of CC here as a child. He hadn’t understood how much of her idea of home lived in this one small room until he stood in it.

“Now, filling. Butter. Brown sugar. Eggs. A little vanilla. And raisins,” Mr. Chanya said, putting a bowl in front of him.

“I was told there’s a wrong answer about raisins.”

“There is. How much do you think?”

Declan looked at the bowl. “How much does the recipe say?”

“Enough.”

“That’s not a measurement.”

“It’s a recipe.”

Mr. Chanya gave him a look and began explaining the proportions. Declan listened with the concentration he usually kept for financial reports, and measured carefully. Too carefully, perhaps.

Mr. Chanya watched him crack an egg. “Not like that.”

Declan stopped. “Is there a problem?”

“You’ve got shell in it.”

He looked into the bowl. There was, indeed, a small piece of eggshell. He fished it out.

Mr. Chanya handed him another egg. “Again.”

CC’s mother was making coffee on the other side of the counter. “You’re being very patient,” she told her husband.

“I’m teaching him.”

“You’re interrogating him.”

“I’m not.”

Declan looked between them. “I think I’m learning both.”

She smiled at him. “You’re a good sport, Declan.”

“I’m beginning to understand why CC likes these so much.”

Mr. Chanya glanced at him. “Because they’re good.”

“That too.”

The older man gave a short laugh. It was the first one Declan had heard from him that morning.

CC woke to an empty space beside her and a cool sheet, and she didn’t know where she was. Then she remembered: Markham, her old room, Declan. It was barely light. There was a message on her phone.

Declan: Good morning, Cela. Sleep a little longer.

She smiled. Then another message arrived.

Declan: Your mother says breakfast will be ready soon.

CC frowned and typed.

CC: Where are you?

No reply. She called him, and he answered on the second ring.

“Good morning, sweetheart.”

His voice was quiet, and behind it something metal clattered, and then her father said, clearly, “Not that tray.”

CC sat up. “Declan?”

A pause. “Yes?”

“Where are you?”

In the background, her mother said, “She’s awake?” and laughed.

Declan sighed. “At the bakery.”

She blinked. “What?”

“Your father is teaching me how to make butter tarts.”

She stared at the phone, and then she started laughing.

“You’re what?”

“Learning.”

“At six in the morning?”

“Technically, I started at four.”

She covered her mouth. “Declan!”

“I thought you might appreciate the effort.”

She was still laughing. “You’re making butter tarts?”

“I’m attempting to.”

“How bad is it?”

He paused. “Your father has been very patient.”

That told her everything.

“Can I come?”

“No.”

“Why?”

“Because you’re supposed to be sleeping.”

“I’m awake now.”

“Then you can come over for breakfast when we’re finished.”

She narrowed her eyes. “You’re hiding something.”

“I’m not hiding anything.”

“Declan.”

He smiled; she could hear it.

“Go wash your face, sweetheart.”

Her father, in the background: “Tell her not to come until the kitchen is clean.”

CC burst out laughing. “All right. I’ll see you soon.”

“See you soon.”

She ended the call and sat smiling at the phone for a while before she got up.

When she walked into the bakery, the first thing she saw was Declan, and the second was the apron.

He was beside her father with a tray of butter tarts, sleeves rolled up, a streak of flour along his jaw. He looked up, and his face softened. “Good morning.”

CC looked at him, then at the apron, then at the tray, and pressed her lips together.

“Don’t.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“I haven’t said anything.”

“You look…”

She stopped herself. Her father glanced over. “What?”

“Nothing.”

She came closer, trying hard not to laugh, and Declan put the tray down.

Her eyes went to his jaw. “There’s flour.”

He reached up, but she caught his wrist. “Wait.” She brushed it away with her thumb.

Her father watched this, then turned back to the oven. “Don’t distract him. He still has work to do.”

CC laughed. “Sorry, Dad.”

Declan gave her a quiet look. “Your father has very high standards.”

“I know.”

“Very high.”

She leaned closer. “Did you make these?”

He looked at the tray. “Some of them.”

“Which ones?”

He indicated a small group in one corner. They weren’t identical. One had an uneven crust, one had bubbled over the edge, and one looked suspiciously darker than the rest.

She picked the least damaged one and raised her eyebrows at him.

“Of course.”

She took a bite while he watched, and chewed thoughtfully. “It’s good.”

His face eased. “Really?”

“Yes.”

Her father, who had been listening, said, “That’s because I fixed the filling.”

CC laughed. “Then it’s half yours.”

“More than half.”

Declan accepted this without protest. “That’s fair.”

CC took another bite and looked at the tray again. “I think you did well.”

He smiled. “Thank you.”

She leaned in and added, “Even if they’re a little ugly.”

She laughed, and he wiped his hands on a clean towel. “Happy birthday for tomorrow.”

“Thank you.”

Her father looked between them. “She hasn’t opened her present yet.”

CC turned. “What present?”

Her mother came out of the back room with a small box. “Your father and I have something for you.”

CC smiled. “Already?”

“You’re only twenty-five once.”

The house was warm and familiar. CC had grown up in it before she left for Bangkok, and much of it hadn’t changed: the framed family photographs, the old bookshelf, the ceramic bowl by the door where her father kept the spare keys.

Declan noticed everything, the photographs first: CC with missing teeth, CC with two small ponytails, school concerts and holidays and birthdays. In one she stood beside her father in front of the bakery in an apron far too big for her, holding a tray almost as wide as she was.

He smiled. “How old were you here?”

CC looked over. “Maybe seven.”

“Helping your father?”

“Trying to.”

Her mother laughed from the kitchen. “She always insisted on helping. She was more interested in tasting the filling.”

CC protested. “That’s not true.”

Her father, passing through with a cup of tea, said, “It is.”

She looked at Declan. “Everyone is against me today.”

He smiled. “I wouldn’t dream of joining them.”

She gave him a suspicious look. He was clearly enjoying himself.

They sat in the living room with tea and a plate of pastries, and her father sat across from Declan and asked about Munich, his work and his family. The questions were measured. Not unfriendly. They were the questions of a father who wanted to understand the man in his home.

He didn’t embellish it or list his achievements. He just answered. CC watched him from beside her mother. He wasn’t trying to impress her father, and he wasn’t being stiff. He was himself. Her father leaned back.

“And what do you intend to do with my daughter?”

CC turned sharply. “Dad.”

Her mother laughed a little. “Let him answer.”

Declan looked at CC, and then back at her father.

“I intend to love her well.”

The room went quiet. He went on, calmly.

“I know she has a life and a career that she has worked very hard to build. I don’t want to take her away from any of that. I want to be someone she can rely on, someone she can be comfortable with, and someone who makes her life better.”

Her father studied him. CC looked down at her tea, her cheeks warm, and her mother reached over and touched her knee.

Her father nodded once. “Good. That’s what I wanted to hear. Have another tart.” Then his face softened.

CC laughed. “That’s it?”

Her father looked at her. “What else do you want me to say?”

She smiled. “Nothing.”

He pushed the plate towards Declan. “Eat.”

Declan took one. “Thank you.”

CC leaned towards him. “That’s a good sign.”

“I gathered.”

CC’s mother waited for the right moment and found it after lunch, when CC was upstairs changing and Declan had just helped her husband carry a box of supplies into the kitchen. Eleanor had sent CC a message that morning, wishing her a happy birthday for tomorrow and sending her regards to the family, and CC’s mother had been pleased. But there was something she wanted to show him herself.

When he came back into the living room, she was holding a small frame.

“Declan, would you come here a moment?”

“Of course.”

She set the frame on the table. It was an old newspaper clipping, yellowed at the edges: a girl of ten or eleven behind a bakery counter, holding a tray of butter tarts and looking proud of herself, with her father beside her, one hand on her shoulder.

Declan leaned closer. “Is this CC?”

Her mother smiled. “Yes.”

She pointed to the headline.

Local Baker Shares Family Recipe With Daughter.

“My husband was asked to share a recipe for a community feature. The reporter came to the bakery, and she insisted on being in the photograph.”

Declan looked at the picture. “She looks very happy.”

She sat down.

“Before you came into her life, her father was the one who spoiled her most. He still does, of course. But when she was little, she could get almost anything from him.” She smiled at his expression.

He glanced at the photograph again. “Anything?”

“Within reason. She’d ask for something, and he’d pretend to consider it very seriously, and then he’d give in.” She laughed.

Declan smiled. “That sounds familiar.”

She looked at him. “She told you about her first love?”

“She did.”

“And you know who it was?”

He smiled. “Her father.”

She laughed. “Good. I wondered whether she had. She used to say she’d marry someone just like him.” She tapped the clipping gently.

Declan studied the photograph again, and smiled. “I can understand why.”

She studied him. “She was very loved, Declan.”

“I know.”

“I hope you understand that.”

He met her eyes. “I do.”

She nodded. “Then we’re happy you’re here.”

He understood what she meant. “Thank you,” he said.

At midnight, CC was sitting on the edge of her old bed in white pyjamas when he came up from talking to her father about the bakery’s early orders.

She looked up. “You’re late.”

“I apologise.”

She smiled.

“You’re forgiven.”

He sat beside her. “Happy birthday, Cela.”

He pressed a kiss into her hair, then her cheek, and when she turned towards him, her mouth. It was slow and unhurried, and her parents’ house was quiet around them.

She rested her forehead against his. “Thank you.”

“Twenty-five.”

She smiled.

“Yes.”

He looked at her. “How does it feel?”

“Good.”

“Any birthday wishes?”

She thought about it. “To spend the day with my family.”

He smiled. “Then we’re already making progress.”

She laughed. “And you? Do you have a wish for me?”

He thought about it. “Several.”

“Tell me one.”

He tucked her hair behind her ear.

“That you remain happy with the life you’re building.”

Her face softened. “That’s a very good one.”

“Then I’ll keep the others to myself.”

She leaned against him, and for a while they sat.

She laughed. “Did you make good butter tarts?”

He paused. “Your father was kind enough to call them promising.”

She stared at him. “That’s not the same as good.”

“No.”

She burst out laughing, and he looked pleased with himself despite the failure.

She reached for his hand. “Thank you for coming home with me.”

He squeezed her fingers. “Thank you for bringing me.”

Birthday breakfast was a family affair. Her father had made pastries, eggs and warm bread; her mother had put flowers on the table and hidden a small cake in the fridge for later. CC sat between her parents, with Declan opposite in a pale blue shirt, looking more polished than he had at the bakery.

Her father set a plate of butter tarts in the middle. “These are the good ones.”

CC looked at Declan. “Not yours?”

“Some of mine are there.”

He pointed them out. She examined them, then looked at her father. “Did you fix them?”

“Of course.”

Declan smiled. “He’s being modest. I had a great deal of help.”

Her father gave a short laugh, and CC took a bite.

“Very good.”

Her father nodded. “Naturally.”

She turned to Declan. “Yours are still promising.”

“I’ll take that.”

Her mother laughed, and the talk moved on: CC’s projects, whether her parents might come to Bangkok later in the year. Her father asked Declan about his next trip.

“Probably New York in April. Then Munich again,” Declan said.

“Busy.”

“Usually.”

“And Cela?”

“Her schedule’s still being finalised,” Declan said.

CC looked at him. “I might have a few days free in May.”

He smiled. “Then we’ll find somewhere quiet.”

Her father looked at the two of them. “Make sure she rests.”

“I will.”

CC laughed. “Dad, I can take care of myself.”

Her father gave her a familiar look. “I know. Doesn’t mean I can’t remind him.”

Her presents from her parents were already open in the living room: a book, a small piece of jewellery, and a letter from her mother. Declan hadn’t given her anything yet. She had noticed. She wasn’t waiting for it. But she knew him well enough to suspect there was something.

When they were alone, he took a flat package from the side table. “This is yours.”

It was wrapped in pale cream paper with a narrow ribbon. She untied it. Inside was a small wooden frame, and when she looked down, she went still.

It was a recipe card in her father’s handwriting: the butter tart recipe, the ingredients in blue ink, measurements and instructions and small notes in the margins, and at the bottom, in a different pen:

For Cela. She always gets the first one.

She touched the glass. “Declan…”

“I asked your father if he would write it out.”

She looked up. “He did this?”

“He did.”

She looked back at the frame. The card was mounted against warm ivory, carefully, behind glass. Nothing about it was extravagant. It was a piece of paper her father had written on, framed with care.

She swallowed. “Why?”

He sat beside her. Her eyes were beginning to shine, and he took her hand.

“Because I thought you might like to keep it. His recipe, and his handwriting. You can buy butter tarts anywhere. This is the one you grew up with.”

She looked down, and the note at the bottom blurred.

“Thank you.”

He brushed his thumb over her knuckles. “You’re welcome, sweetheart.”

She hugged him hard, and he held her without saying anything.

She said into his shoulder, “This is my favourite.”

“I’m glad.”

She drew back, still holding the frame, and looked towards the kitchen. “Did Dad know?”

“He helped me choose the card.”

Her face softened further. “You asked him?”

“I thought it should come from him.”

She looked at the recipe again, then leaned over and kissed his cheek. He turned his head and kissed her properly.

When he drew back, he was smiling. “Happy birthday, Cela.”

On Sunday morning, the house was quiet. Declan had gone to the bakery with her father again, to carry boxes and stack trays for the morning orders this time, not to make anything, and CC sat at the kitchen table with her mother and a shoebox of old photographs.

Her mother put the photograph down. “Declan seems like a good man.”

CC looked up. “He is.”

“He listens to you.”

“Yes.”

“And he doesn’t seem to mind being told what to do.”

CC laughed. “Not always.”

Her mother smiled. “That’s good. You need someone who can listen, not someone who just wants to be right.”

CC looked towards the window, where the morning light lay across the garden. “He’s very good to me.”

Her mother touched her hand. “Then we’re happy. Your father likes him too.” She squeezed CC’s fingers.

CC raised an eyebrow. “Really?”

Her mother laughed.

“Of course. He wouldn’t have spent four hours teaching him to make butter tarts if he didn’t.”

CC burst into laughter.

At the bakery, Declan was finishing the last of the morning orders when CC’s father called him over. “A word.”

“Yes?”

He handed him a small paper bag. “Take these.”

Declan looked inside: a few butter tarts. “Thank you.”

“Those are yours.”

He looked up. “Mine?”

“You’ve earned them.”

Declan smiled. “That’s generous.”

Her father gave him a look. “Don’t get pleased with yourself. They’re still not as good as mine.”

“I wouldn’t dispute that.”

Her father laughed, and then grew quieter. “You did well this weekend.”

Declan looked at him. “Thank you.”

“She’s happy. That’s what matters.” The older man paused.

Declan nodded. “I know.”

“And you can give back the shop next door.”

Declan didn’t pretend not to understand. “It was empty. You said you needed room for a second oven.”

“I said it once. In passing.”

“I was listening.”

“Give it back.”

“Yes, sir.”

Her father went back to his trays. A minute later, without turning round, he said, “Keep the lease a month. I’ll think about it.”

Her father looked towards the window. “She works hard. Sometimes too hard. She doesn’t always tell us when she’s tired.”

“I’ve noticed.”

“She likes to take care of herself. Doesn’t like people making decisions for her.”

Declan almost smiled. “She’s made that very clear.”

Her father laughed. “Good. Don’t try to change that.” Then he looked at Declan.

“I wouldn’t.”

Her father nodded. “Then we’ll get along.”

Declan held his gaze. “I hope so.”

The older man clapped his shoulder. “Come on. Let’s get home before your girlfriend thinks I’ve kidnapped you.”

Declan smiled. “She might suspect it.”

“She knows me.”

“That she does.”

That evening their bags were packed, and CC stood by the front door with the framed recipe card in her arms.

Her mother hugged her first. “Call when you land.”

“I will.”

“Sleep on the plane.”

“I will.”

Her father hugged her next, pressed his mouth to her hair and told her to take care of herself.

CC smiled. “I will, Dad.”

Then he turned to Declan. “Look after her.”

Declan nodded. “I will.”

Her father studied him. “And come back.”

Declan smiled. “I’d like that.”

“Good.”

The older man held out his hand, and when Declan took it, pulled him into a brief embrace instead. There was no speech. Declan understood anyway.

CC watched them, and her mother stepped beside her and whispered, “He’s part of the family now.”

CC smiled. “I know.”

At the door, Declan turned back. “Thank you for having me.”

Her father waved a hand. “Next time, we’ll work on your dough.”

Declan smiled. “I’ll practise.”

Her father nodded his approval. “That’s the right attitude.”

On the plane, CC sat beside him with the recipe card wrapped in a scarf in her carry-on and her head on his shoulder, her fingers loosely laced with his.

After a while she said, “Declan?”

“Hm?”

“Did you enjoy coming home with me?”

He looked down at her.

“Very much.”

She lifted her head. “You’re lying.”

He smiled. “Your father is a very good teacher.”

“That’s not what I asked.”

He laughed. “All right. I enjoyed it. I was less talented than I’d hoped.”

She smiled. “You were terrible.”

“Your father was kind enough not to say so.”

“He told me.”

Declan sighed. “Of course he did.”

She laughed and settled against him again. After a moment she said, “I’m glad you met them.”

“So am I.”

“They liked you.”

“I liked them. And I understand you a little better now.” He ran his thumb over her hand.

She looked at him. “How?”

He glanced at the window, where the airport lights were falling away. “I know where some of the things I love about you came from. The way you look after people. The way you remember small things. The way you can be quietly stubborn when something matters.”

She smiled. “Are you saying I’m stubborn?”

“I’m saying your father taught you well.”

She laughed and rested her head on him again.

He kissed her hair. “Happy birthday, Cela.”

She was asleep before they reached cruising height.

chapters.title: Water Festival
chapters.desc: Caps, sunglasses, water guns and a floral shirt she chooses for him. Eleven seconds of video later, three million strangers are asking who the man is.
chapters.epigraph: “Next year, I’ll choose your shirt again.”
chapters.content:
Declan Lincoln had never been to Songkran, and nothing in his life had prepared him for that Saturday morning in Bangkok.

“You’re thinking too much.”

CC stood in front of him, adjusting the brim of his baseball cap.

He was wearing a plain white T-shirt, dark shorts, and sunglasses. She had chosen the clothes herself, insisting that anything too recognisable would defeat the purpose of their outing. His cap was navy. Hers was pale yellow. She stepped back to inspect him.

“Good.”

“Is that all?”

“What else?”

“I was expecting a more detailed assessment.”

She considered him.

“Very handsome.”

He smiled.

“Better.”

She laughed and handed him a water gun. It was bright blue, slightly oversized, and looked ridiculous in his hands. He examined it.

“Is this the equipment?”

“Yes.”

“Does it have instructions?”

She stared at him.

“Declan.”

“What?”

“Just pull the trigger.”

He looked at the water gun again.

“Understood.”

She shook her head, smiling. They had chosen a quieter side street away from the main festival crowds. Nicha knew where they were, as did the driver, who would remain nearby but out of sight. Their security arrangements were discreet, and CC had made sure they wouldn’t be completely isolated.

She wanted Songkran without turning it into an event: no photographs, no entourage, no private venue. Just two people in caps and sunglasses, carrying water guns.

“Ready?” she asked.

Declan turned to her.

“After you.”

She raised her water gun.

“Don’t regret saying that.”

Then she sprayed him. He blinked as cold water hit his shoulder. CC laughed.

“Welcome to Songkran.”

He looked down at his wet shirt. Then back at her.

“I see.”

His expression was perfectly composed. Which made her laugh even harder. He raised his water gun. She immediately stepped behind a nearby stall.

“Declan!”

He smiled.

“You started it.”

That morning, it took approximately fifteen minutes for Declan to lose any remaining concern about getting wet.

It took another five for CC to discover that he was unexpectedly competitive. He wasn’t reckless. He was strategic.

He waited until she was distracted, approached from the side, and sprayed her shoulder with a remarkably accurate shot. She gasped.

“That was unfair!”

“How?”

“You waited!”

“That’s generally how one surprises someone.”

She narrowed her eyes. He smiled. Then she sprayed him directly across the chest. He looked down.

“That was unnecessary.”

She laughed.

“Now we’re even.”

A group of teenagers passing by cheered at the exchange. One of them raised a water gun towards Declan, and he turned just in time to receive a fresh stream of water across his back. CC covered her mouth. He slowly turned around. The teenagers were already laughing and running away. She considered him.

“Are you all right?”

“Perfectly.”

“Really?”

He glanced at her.

“Although I believe I’ve been targeted.”

She laughed.

“That’s the festival.”

He looked around. People were everywhere. Families stood outside their homes with buckets of water. Children chased one another along the pavement. Music played from a nearby shop, and strangers greeted each other with cheerful splashes.

There was no distinction between the people who had arrived in expensive cars and those who lived on the street. Everyone was wet. Everyone was laughing.

Declan watched a little boy attempt to spray his father, only to have the water gun taken away and used against him. He smiled. CC noticed.

“Having fun?”

He held her gaze.

“Yes.”

She grinned.

“Good answer.”

He reached over and adjusted the brim of her cap, which had become crooked.

“Your sunglasses are slipping.”

She held still while he straightened them. Then she looked up at him.

“You look different.”

“Different?”

“Yes.”

“How?”

She tilted her head.

“Less like a chairman.”

He smiled.

“An improvement?”

“Much.”

He leaned a little closer.

“Then perhaps I should dress like this more often.”

She laughed.

“Maybe not to your board meetings.”

“I’ll consider it.”

They continued down the street, stopping at a stall selling drinks. CC bought two iced teas, then insisted on paying. Declan reached for his wallet. She moved the drinks out of his reach.

“No.”

He studied her.

“No?”

“My turn.”

He smiled.

“All right.”

She handed him his drink. He accepted it without argument. She looked pleased.

He found that he liked seeing her pleased over something so small.

That afternoon, in Bangkok, the shirt was entirely her fault.

They had stopped at a clothing stall after Declan’s white T-shirt had become so thoroughly soaked that it was practically transparent.

CC was looking through a rack of inexpensive festival shirts. Then she found it.

A bright, loud shirt covered in large tropical flowers in shades of pink, orange, green, and yellow. She held it up. Declan looked at it.

“No.”

She smiled.

“Yes.”

“Absolutely not.”

“It’s perfect.”

“It is not.”

She held it against his chest. He looked down at the shirt, then at her.

“You’re enjoying this.”

“A little.”

The vendor smiled, clearly entertained.

“Very good colour,” she said.

CC nodded seriously.

“Exactly.”

Declan looked at the vendor.

“You’re not helping.”

The woman laughed. CC turned back to him.

“Please?”

He looked at her face. She was smiling in that particular way he had learned to recognise: not demanding, not expecting him to give in, enjoying the prospect of making him wear something he would never choose himself. He sighed.

“All right.”

Her smile widened.

“Really?”

“Yes.”

She paid before he could reach for his wallet. He watched her hand over the money. Then she turned towards him, looking satisfied.

“Come on. You can change over there.”

A few minutes later, he emerged wearing the shirt. CC stared. Declan adjusted the collar.

“Well?”

She pressed her lips together. He raised an eyebrow.

“Don’t laugh.”

She failed immediately. She laughed harder.

“I’m sorry.”

“You’re not.”

“No, I’m not.”

He shook his head, but there was a smile at the corner of his mouth. She stepped closer and straightened the collar.

“There.”

He looked down at her.

“Good.”

She looked at him again. The shirt was absurd. It was also charming on him.

She reached up and brushed a little water from his cheek.

“You’re handsome.”

He smiled. He kissed her temple.

“Then I’ll wear it for you.”

She smiled. And because she was feeling pleased with herself, she bought him a matching pair of brightly coloured sunglasses. He accepted those too. That afternoon, the photograph was taken by accident.

Or at least, that was what the person who posted it would later say.

A young woman had been filming her friends during the festival. In the background, a couple had stepped into the frame.

The woman was wearing a pale yellow cap and sunglasses. Her face was partly obscured, but there was something familiar about the way she laughed.

The man beside her wore a loud floral shirt and dark sunglasses. He was holding a water gun. The woman had just sprayed him.

He looked down at his shirt, then turned towards her with an expression of exaggerated disbelief. She doubled over laughing.

He reached for her hand, and she pulled him away before another group could soak them. The video lasted eleven seconds. It was posted with a simple caption.

Songkran is better when you have someone to be ridiculous with.

At first, the comments were ordinary. People joked about the floral shirt. Someone asked where the stall was. Another person commented that the couple looked happy. Then someone noticed the woman.

Wait. Is that CC?

Another comment appeared.

The laugh sounds exactly like her.

Someone slowed the video down. Someone else zoomed in.

A few hours later, the clip began circulating beyond the original account. The caption changed.

Is this CC and her foreign boyfriend?

And then, in capitals: IS THAT CC?

That afternoon, they were sitting at a small restaurant when Nicha called. CC was halfway through her meal. She glanced at the screen.

“P’Nicha.”

Declan looked up.

“Would you like to answer?”

She nodded and picked up.

“Hello?”

Nicha didn’t bother with a greeting.

“Where are you?”

CC looked at Declan.

“Having lunch.”

“Are you still near the old market?”

CC paused.

“Yes. Why?”

“Have you been filming anything?”

“No.”

“Has anyone approached you?”

“No. Why?”

A short silence.

Then Nicha said, “I’m sending you something.”

CC’s phone vibrated. She opened the link. The video began playing. She watched herself spray Declan. Watched him turn. Watched herself laugh. Then she watched it again. Her face changed. Declan noticed.

“What is it?”

She turned the screen towards him. He watched the eleven-second clip. Then looked at her.

“That’s us.”

She stared.

“Yes.”

“Your shirt was rather noticeable.”

She let out a small, disbelieving laugh.

“Declan.”

“I’m sorry.”

She looked at the comments. There were already thousands. Nicha was still on the phone.

“CC, I need to know whether it’s you.”

CC glanced at Declan. Then she answered honestly.

“Yes.”

Nicha exhaled.

“All right. Don’t post anything. Don’t reply to comments. I’ll speak with the company and see how far it’s spread.”

“Okay.”

“And please don’t go anywhere else crowded today.”

“We’re finishing lunch.”

“Good. I’ll call you again.”

The call ended. CC put her phone down. She didn’t speak. Declan watched her.

“Are you all right?”

She nodded slowly.

“I think so.”

He reached for her hand.

“Do you want to leave?”

She checked the screen again. The video had been watched more than a million times. She swallowed.

“Yes. I think we should.”

He nodded. He didn’t suggest calling his communications team. He didn’t offer to have the account taken down. He didn’t tell her he could make the problem disappear.

He paid the bill, and they left through the quieter entrance. That afternoon, the apartment was quiet.

CC had showered and changed into comfortable clothes. Her cap and sunglasses sat on the dining table, still damp. Declan had changed too.

The floral shirt was hanging over the back of a chair. She looked at it. Then laughed. He glanced over.

“What’s amusing?”

“Your shirt.”

He followed her gaze.

“I was beginning to think it might become a permanent part of my wardrobe.”

She smiled.

“Would you keep it?”

“If you wanted me to.”

She shook her head. Then her phone vibrated again. A message from Nicha.

Nicha: The clip is still spreading. The company is monitoring it. No confirmation from us for now. Please don’t worry about answering anyone.

CC read it twice. Then she put the phone down. Declan was standing near the window.

“Has Nicha spoken to you?”

“Yes.”

“What does she think?”

“She’s monitoring it. The company hasn’t said anything.”

He nodded.

“All right.”

CC sat on the sofa.

She said, “I didn’t think anyone would recognise me.”

“Your face was mostly covered.”

“My laugh wasn’t.”

He smiled.

“No.”

She glanced up at him.

“Did you know?”

“Know what?”

“That people might recognise us?”

He considered the question.

“I knew there was a possibility. I thought the caps and sunglasses would make it less likely.”

She looked down.

“I wanted to have one day where we didn’t have to think about it.”

He came to sit beside her.

“I know.”

She rested her hands in her lap.

“I don’t regret going.”

“Neither do I.”

“But now everyone is asking.”

He reached for her hand.

“Then we can decide what to do about it.”

She looked up. There was no urgency in his expression. No impatience. Just attention. She appreciated that.

Then she said, “I think we need to talk.”

He nodded.

“All right.”

That evening, for a few moments, neither of them spoke. CC was looking at their joined hands. Declan waited.

Finally, she said, “We’ve been careful for a long time.”

“Yes.”

“We’ve kept things private. We’ve avoided being seen together. We haven’t told the public anything.”

“That’s right.”

“And I still want privacy.”

He nodded.

“I understand.”

“But I don’t know if I want to keep hiding.”

His thumb moved gently over the back of her hand.

“What would you like instead?”

She looked at him.

“I don’t want to make an announcement because of an eleven-second video.”

A faint smile touched his mouth.

“That would be an unusual way to announce a relationship.”

She laughed. Then her face became thoughtful again.

“I also don’t want to deny you if someone asks.”

He watched her.

“Would you be comfortable acknowledging that we’re together?”

She thought about it.

“I think so. If someone asks directly, I don’t want to pretend you’re just a friend.”

“All right.”

“But I don’t want to give interviews about us. I don’t want people asking about our private life, or making everything I do about having a boyfriend.”

“Then we don’t give them that.”

She watched him.

“Can we do that?”

“We can establish boundaries. We can decide what we’re comfortable sharing and what stays ours.”

She considered his words.

“What if the company asks?”

“Then you and Nicha can decide how to respond professionally. I won’t contact them unless you ask me to.”

She smiled a little.

“Thank you.”

His eyes went to her face.

“There’s something I want you to consider, though.”

She waited.

“If we acknowledge the relationship, there may be more attention on me. My name, my company, my family. I can manage that, but I don’t want you to feel responsible for it.”

CC shook her head.

“I know who you are.”

“That doesn’t mean the attention will be pleasant.”

“I know that too.”

He studied her face.

“Are you sure?”

She smiled.

“I don’t want to hide the person I love just because people might be curious.”

His face changed. Not dramatically. But something in his eyes softened.

“All right.”

She moved closer.

“And I don’t want you to think this means I want everyone to know everything.”

“I wouldn’t.”

“Our relationship is still ours.”

“Always.”

She let her head drop onto his shoulder. She murmured, “Your shirt is going to become famous.”

He laughed.

“I suppose I should have chosen a better one.”

She lifted her head.

“No.”

“No?”

“It was perfect.”

He looked at her.

“Then I suppose we have a rather unusual souvenir from our first Songkran.”

She smiled.

“We do.”

He kissed her hair. Then he said, “For the record, I enjoyed it.”

She looked up.

“Even the video?”

“Not particularly.”

She laughed.

“But the day?”

He smiled.

“Very much.”

He kissed her then, still smelling of festival water and sunscreen, slowly enough that she forgot the video and the comments and the three million strangers, and remembered only the way he had laughed in the street with water dripping off his chin. When he finally drew back, she rested her forehead against his.

“Next year, I’ll choose your shirt again.”

He smiled.

“I suspected as much.”

By morning, the video had passed three million views. The comments had become more confident. Some people were convinced it was CC. Others thought it was someone who resembled her.

A few had identified Declan’s watch, though not enough to establish his identity with certainty.

The floral shirt was now the most discussed part of the clip.

CC sat at the dining table, scrolling through the comments while Declan made coffee.

His coffee was better than it had been in February. She looked up.

“People like your shirt.”

He glanced over.

“Do they?”

“Yes. Someone said the man has excellent taste in clothes.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“That’s generous.”

“Another person said his girlfriend chose it.”

He brought her cup over.

“An observant person.”

She smiled. Then she showed him another comment.

I don’t know who they are, but I hope they had a wonderful Songkran. They look so happy.

Declan read it. Then he looked at her.

“We did.”

She smiled.

“Yes.”

Her phone rang. Nicha. CC answered.

“Good morning.”

“Good morning. How are you?”

“Fine.”

“Good. The company wants to discuss the video with you tomorrow. Nothing urgent, but we should agree on a response before the next wave of speculation.”

CC nodded.

“Okay.”

“One more thing. Are you comfortable with us acknowledging the relationship if the question comes up?”

CC looked towards Declan. He was sitting opposite her drinking his coffee. She thought about yesterday’s conversation. Then she answered.

“Yes. But I don’t want a statement unless we really need one.”

“Understood. We’ll keep it simple. No denial, no elaborate explanation.”

“Thank you.”

After the call, she put her phone down. Declan considered her.

“Everything all right?”

“Yes.”

She took a sip of coffee.

“We’ll talk to the company tomorrow.”

He nodded. Then she looked at him with a smile.

“Do you think you should keep the shirt?”

He considered it.

“Perhaps.”

“Really?”

“Yes. It seems to have made a favourable impression.”

She laughed.

“Then you have to wear it again next year.”

He smiled.

“Only if you come with me.”

She reached across the table.

“Of course.”

He took her hand. Outside, Bangkok was still throwing water at itself. Inside, they finished their coffee, and he didn’t let go of her hand.

chapters.title: Small Hours
chapters.desc: He is in New York, eleven hours behind, and the calls keep getting shorter. Nobody is wrong. She types “It’s fine,” and he can tell that it isn’t.
chapters.epigraph: “I miss telling you little things.”
chapters.content:
AVEN’s decision, when it came on Monday morning, was less dramatic than CC had expected. No denial. No statement.

If asked directly, the company would neither confirm nor deny her private relationship. They wouldn’t issue a public clarification, and they wouldn’t encourage speculation with carefully worded hints. The matter would be treated as personal unless it began to interfere with her professional commitments. Nicha had explained it over coffee.

“Basically, we don’t feed it.”

CC nodded.

“And if someone asks?”

“We redirect to your work. If they ask you directly, you can decide how much you want to say. There’s no need to make an announcement.”

“All right.”

Nicha watched her.

“Are you disappointed?”

CC looked up.

“No. I think it’s better this way.”

“Good. Because your solo schedule is about to become very busy.”

CC smiled. Her first solo album was scheduled for June.

The announcement hadn’t yet been made, but the internal preparation had begun. There would be recording sessions, a music video, styling meetings, promotional planning, and a series of discussions about the direction of her first individual release. It was exciting. It was also a little frightening.

“June,” she repeated.

“June, you have enough time, but not as much as you think,” Nicha confirmed.

CC laughed.

“I know.”

Her phone lit up.

Declan: Good morning, sweetheart. How was the meeting?

She smiled and typed.

CC: Good. No statement, no denial. They’re leaving it alone.

Declan: That sounds sensible.

CC: And my album is set for June.

His reply came quickly.

Declan: I know how much you’ve been looking forward to this. I’m very happy for you.

She read it twice.

CC: I’m excited.

Declan: You should be.

Then:

Declan: I wish I could take you to lunch to celebrate.

She glanced at Nicha, who was already looking at her with a knowing expression.

CC: You can celebrate from New York.

Declan: A rather poor substitute.

She smiled.

CC: I know.

She put the phone down and returned to her coffee. It was still morning in Bangkok.

In New York, Declan’s day was only just beginning.

On Tuesday morning, in New York, Declan’s office was already occupied.

Alexander stood beside the conference table, reviewing the day’s schedule. Two executives were waiting for a meeting that had been moved forward, and a call with the European division had been scheduled for later that morning. Declan read through a document. His phone vibrated. A message from CC.

Cela: I heard the first mix today. I think the second verse needs something different.

He glanced at the screen. Then at the document. He typed a reply.

Declan: What do you think it needs?

Before he could send it, Alexander approached.

“The New York team is ready.”

Declan read the message again. Then he sent it.

“Thank you.”

He entered the conference room. The meeting lasted longer than expected.

By the time he returned to his office, there were three missed calls and another message from Bangkok.

Cela: Maybe less piano. I don’t know yet.

He smiled. He began typing.

Declan: I think you should trust your—

Alexander knocked.

“Your father is on the line.”

Declan glanced at the time.

“Put him through.”

He answered the call. The message remained unfinished. Late on Wednesday, in Bangkok, CC was sitting at the piano.

The apartment was quiet, except for the soft sound of the air conditioner and the occasional traffic outside.

She had spent most of the day in the studio.

The first verse was nearly finished, but the second still felt incomplete. She had tried different melodies, changed the phrasing, and recorded several versions. Nothing felt quite right. Her phone was beside the piano. She checked it. A message from Declan, sent three hours earlier.

Declan: Sorry, sweetheart. Meetings ran over. I think less piano might give the vocal more room. But you should follow what feels right to you.

She smiled. It was a good suggestion. She knew he had listened to the earlier version carefully. He had always been attentive to her music, even when he didn’t understand the technical details. She typed.

CC: I think so too. I’ll try tomorrow.

Then she checked the time. It was nearly midnight in Bangkok. In New York, it was lunchtime. She called him. He answered after several rings.

“Hello, Cela.”

His voice sounded slightly tired. She smiled.

“Hi.”

“Have you finished for the day?”

“Almost. Are you busy?”

There was a pause.

“A little. I have another meeting in fifteen minutes.”

“Oh.”

He heard the small change in her voice.

“How was the studio?”

“Good.”

“What did you work on?”

“The second verse.”

“Did you find what you were looking for?”

“Not yet.”

He smiled.

“You usually do.”

She leaned back against the piano.

“I hope so.”

There was a brief silence. He glanced towards the office door.

“I should get ready for the next meeting.”

“Of course.”

“I’ll call you later, if you’re awake.”

She smiled.

“Don’t worry. You have work.”

“I’ll try to call tomorrow.”

“Okay.”

“Goodnight, sweetheart.”

“Goodnight, thi rak.”

The call ended. CC checked her phone. Then she returned to the piano. She played the second verse again.

On Friday morning, in New York, Declan was reading a report when his phone rang. CC. He answered immediately.

“Hello.”

“Hi.”

Her voice was soft. He leaned back.

“Are you home?”

“Just got in.”

“Long day?”

“Quite long.”

He smiled.

“Tell me about it.”

She did. She told him about the recording session, the producer who had suggested a different arrangement, and the small disagreement over the final line of the chorus. He listened. He asked questions.

For several minutes, it felt like their usual conversations. Then Alexander appeared at the open door.

“Mr. Lincoln, the Zurich call is ready.”

Declan glanced at the clock. He had forgotten it was scheduled. He closed his eyes.

“Give me five minutes.”

Alexander nodded and stepped away. Declan turned back to the phone.

“I’m sorry, Cela. I have a call.”

“It’s okay.”

“I don’t want to rush you.”

“You aren’t.”

He looked at the papers on his desk.

“Can we speak tomorrow?”

She hesitated.

“Yes.”

“All right. I’ll call.”

“Goodnight.”

“Sleep well, Cela.”

He ended the call. Then he sat before opening the report again. He had heard the small hesitation. He hadn’t known what to do with it.

In the early hours of Sunday, in Bangkok, the green notebook was open on CC’s piano.

It had travelled from Bangkok to Munich and back again. Its dark green cover was slightly worn at the corners, and the inscription inside was still visible. She had been using it more often lately.

There were fragments of lyrics, melody notes, crossed-out lines, and small observations she had written down between appointments. Tonight, she had written something new. It wasn’t finished.

She wasn’t even sure whether it belonged on the June album. But she liked the melody. She recorded it on her phone.

The voice memo was just under a minute long.

Her voice was quiet, almost conversational at first, before the melody lifted. She listened once. Then again. She considered sending it to Declan.

He was in New York. It was still early afternoon there, but she knew his Saturdays were often taken up by work he couldn’t fit into the week. She hesitated. Then she sent it.

CC: I wrote something in the green notebook. It’s unfinished, but I wanted you to hear it.

She placed the phone beside the notebook. She felt a little shy.

Then she closed the book and went to bed.

On Saturday afternoon, in New York, Declan was in a meeting when the voice memo arrived. His phone vibrated once on the table. He glanced at the screen. Cela — Voice message

He looked at it for a second longer than necessary.

Then he turned his attention back to the presentation. The meeting continued.

A discussion about the European expansion followed. Then a call with Munich, and a private conversation with Richard about a pending board decision.

By the time he returned to his office, the voice memo had been sitting unread for nearly four hours. He saw it immediately.

He picked up his phone and opened the message. Her voice came through the speakers. He listened.

The melody was gentle, a little wistful. There was something unfinished about it, but not in a way that made it feel incomplete. It sounded like a thought she hadn’t quite decided to share with the world. He listened again. Then Alexander knocked.

“Your car is ready.”

Declan checked the time. He had a dinner engagement. He played the final few seconds once more. Then he opened the message field.

He wanted to tell her that the melody was beautiful, that he liked the way she had softened the last line, that he could hear the shape of something important in it. But he was already late. His thumb hovered over the keyboard. He typed one word.

Declan: Beautiful.

He sent it. Then he put the phone away.

On Sunday morning, in Bangkok, CC was having breakfast when she saw his reply.

Beautiful.

She read it. Then she looked at the voice memo.

She had sent it the night before, hoping he would hear it when he had time. She knew he was busy. She knew New York was demanding.

She knew he had meetings, responsibilities, and people waiting for him. Still, she had imagined something else.

Perhaps a question. Perhaps a comment about a particular line. Perhaps hearing his voice. She typed:

Cela: Thank you.

Then she put her phone down. A few minutes later, another message arrived.

Declan: I wish I could have listened properly when you sent it.

She smiled.

Cela: It’s okay.

He read the message. Something about it made him pause.

He knew her well enough to understand that she wasn’t angry. She was also not quite all right. He typed.

Declan: I would like to hear it again when we speak.

Cela: Sure.

He stared at the word. Then he returned to the document in front of him.

On Wednesday morning, in New York, the calls had become shorter.

Not because either of them had decided to speak less. It happened gradually.

A ten-minute call instead of thirty. A message answered several hours later.

A video call postponed because one of them was too tired.

Declan had started keeping his phone beside him during meetings, hoping to catch her messages between discussions. CC had started sending fewer. Not deliberately.

She caught herself wondering whether he would have time to answer. That night, her time, she called him. He answered at his desk.

“Hello, sweetheart.”

“Hi.”

Jacket off, tie loosened, a sandwich he hadn’t touched beside the keyboard.

“How are you?”

“Good. You?”

“Busy.”

She smiled.

“I guessed.”

He laughed.

“How was your day?”

“Fine. We had another meeting about the music video.”

“How did it go?”

“Good. I think we’ve settled on the visual direction.”

“That’s excellent.”

She told him a little about it. He listened, asking a few questions. Then his phone vibrated on the desk. He glanced at it. She noticed.

“Do you need to answer?”

“No. It’s Alexander.”

“Are you sure?”

He turned the phone off.

“Yes.”

She smiled. They continued talking. But there was a strange awareness between them now. She knew he was tired.

He knew she had been waiting when they could talk without interruption. Neither wanted to make the other feel guilty.

After a while, Declan asked, “Did they let you keep the yellow dress from the test shoot?”

She laughed. “No.”

“A tragedy.”

He smiled.

“I should let you sleep.”

She glanced at the screen.

“All right.”

He hesitated.

Then said, “I miss you.”

Her face softened.

“I miss you too.”

They ended the call. Declan sat. Then he picked up his phone. Alexander had sent three messages. He answered them.

Just after midnight on Friday, in Bangkok, CC was sitting on her bed, scrolling through the conversation. There were no arguments. No harsh words. No unanswered questions that had been deliberately ignored. Just a series of small exchanges.

A message from him wishing her luck before a recording session.

A photograph she had sent of a bowl of mango sticky rice.

His reply, three hours later, saying it looked good. A short call. A postponed call. A message from her about the second verse. His response the next morning. She looked at the voice memo again. Then she opened the message field.

CC: I know you’re busy. I don’t want you to feel like you have to answer everything immediately.

She paused. Deleted it. Typed again.

CC: I miss talking to you.

She looked at the words. Then deleted those too.

She didn’t want to make him feel guilty. She didn’t want to sound as if she was keeping track. She knew he loved her. She knew he was trying. So she typed something simpler.

CC: It’s fine. Don’t worry about it.

She sent it. Then she put her phone down.

On Thursday afternoon, in New York, Declan was halfway through a meeting when he read her message.

It’s fine. Don’t worry about it.

He looked at it for several seconds. Then he read it again.

He knew the difference between CC saying something was fine and CC trying to make it fine for him.

He had heard the same carefulness in her voice over the past week.

The way she said she understood when he had to leave. The way she stopped telling him things she might once have sent without thinking.

The way their calls ended before either of them had really finished speaking. He set his phone down. The meeting continued.

He contributed to the discussion, answered questions, and reviewed the figures in front of him.

But his attention returned to the message more than once.

When the meeting ended, Alexander followed him into his office.

“Your next appointment is at three.”

Declan nodded.

“Move it to three-thirty.”

“Of course.”

“And clear my evening.”

Alexander looked at him.

“All of it?”

“Yes.”

Alexander nodded, making a note. Declan picked up his phone. He opened CC’s conversation. He typed:

Declan: Cela, can we speak tonight?

He sent it. Then he waited. In the early hours of Friday, in Bangkok, CC was brushing her hair when the message arrived. She studied the screen.

Declan: Cela, can we speak tonight?

She checked the time. It was already past midnight in Bangkok.

She knew it was still only early afternoon in New York. She replied.

CC: Of course. Are you free?

His answer came quickly.

Declan: I am now.

She looked at herself in the mirror. Then she picked up her phone and called him. He answered immediately.

“Hello, Cela.”

She smiled a little.

“Hi.”

He was quiet. Then he said, “I’ve been thinking about you.”

She sat down on the bed.

“I’ve been thinking about you too.”

“I know I’ve been difficult to reach lately.”

She didn’t answer immediately. He continued.

“I don’t want to make excuses. My schedule has been demanding, but I know that’s not the same as making time.”

CC looked down at her hands.

“I know you’re busy.”

“I am. But you shouldn’t have to make yourself smaller to fit around it.”

Her face changed. She was quiet. He waited.

Finally, she said, “I don’t want to be another thing you have to manage.”

“You’re not.”

“I know. But sometimes I feel like I’m waiting for a space in your day.”

He closed his eyes. The words were quiet. They weren’t an accusation. That made them harder to hear.

“I’m sorry,” he said.

She shook her head, even though he couldn’t see her.

“I don’t want you to be sorry. I know you have work.”

“Both things can be true.”

She looked towards the window.

“I miss you.”

“I miss you too.”

“I miss telling you little things.”

He was silent. Then he said, “Tell me.”

She gave a small laugh.

“Now?”

“Yes.”

She thought. Then she told him about a stray cat that had started appearing near the studio entrance. She told him about the producer who kept forgetting to bring his notebook. She told him that Nicha had bought a ridiculous amount of snacks for the team.

He listened. He didn’t interrupt. He asked about the cat. He laughed at the story about the snacks.

For a while, the distance felt less like something between them. But it was late.

And he had a meeting at half past three. And she had an early recording session.

Eventually, Declan said, “I should let you sleep.”

She nodded.

“Yes.”

He hesitated.

“I’ll make time tomorrow.”

She smiled.

“All right.”

“Goodnight, sweetheart.”

“Night, thi rak. Don’t work too late.”

After the call ended, CC placed her phone on the bedside table. She felt a little better. Not completely. But enough.

In the early hours of Sunday, in New York, Declan was awake.

The apartment was dark except for the small lamp beside the bed.

He had returned from dinner several hours earlier, but sleep hadn’t come easily. His phone lay on the bedside table. He picked it up. The voice memo was still in the conversation. Cela — Voice message. He opened it. Her voice filled the quiet room. The melody began.

He listened to the first verse, then the second. He noticed the small breath she took before the final line. He noticed the way her voice softened at the end, almost as if she had changed her mind about finishing the phrase. He played it again. Then once more.

He had listened to it when she first sent it, of course. But not properly.

Not with the time he should have given it.

Not with the attention she had offered when she shared something unfinished.

He placed the phone against the pillow beside him and listened again. The song was still unfinished.

He could hear where she might change the melody, where she might leave a little more space, where the words might become something different. He wished he could sit beside her at the piano. He wished he could hear her explain why she had chosen that particular line.

He wished he had asked her more questions when she first sent it. At the end, the recording stopped. The room became quiet again. Declan checked the screen. He could have sent her a message. He could have told her he was listening.

But it was already three in the morning in New York, and it was two in the afternoon in Bangkok. She would probably be working, and he didn’t want to interrupt her day with another promise he might struggle to keep. So he didn’t send anything. He pressed play again. And listened.

This time, he didn’t think about the meetings waiting for him in the morning.

He didn’t think about the calls he had missed.

He only listened to the voice of the woman he loved, singing something she hadn’t finished writing yet. At the end, he let the silence remain. Then he played it again.

chapters.title: Bought and Paid
chapters.desc: A tabloid says he bought her contract. Most of it is false. The part that is true, he never told her.
chapters.epigraph: “I only needed to hear it from you.”
chapters.content:
The headline appeared on Monday evening, before CC had finished dinner.

She saw it because Nicha sent her a screenshot with no explanation. She didn’t understand what she was looking at. Then she read the words.

CC’S BILLIONAIRE BOUGHT HER CONTRACT

Below it was a photograph from Songkran. The man in the floral shirt had been cropped out, but another image appeared beside it: Declan Lincoln leaving a private terminal in Munich, wearing the watch that had been visible in the festival video. The article was worse than the headline.

It described Lincoln Group as a multinational conglomerate with extensive interests in Southeast Asia. It identified Declan as its chairman and principal shareholder. It mentioned the Songkran clip, the speculation surrounding CC’s relationship, and her contract renewal with AVEN. Then it presented a sequence of dates.

March 11: Lincoln Group Southeast Asia signed a sponsorship agreement with AVEN.

March 12: CC attended her contract renewal meeting.

The article suggested that the sponsorship had been used to secure favourable terms for CC’s renewal, and that her improved contract conditions—including greater control over her personal life and schedule—had been purchased through her boyfriend’s influence. It didn’t say the arrangement was proven. It didn’t need to. The headline had already done its work. CC read the article twice. Then she called Nicha.

“Have you seen it?”

“Yes.”

“Is the sponsorship real?”

There was a pause.

“I’m checking.”

CC looked at the dates again. March eleventh. The day before her renewal meeting. Her fingers tightened around the phone.

“P’Nicha.”

“I’m here.”

“Please find out.”

“I will. Don’t respond to anything yet.”

“Okay.”

“CC, listen to me. We don’t know the whole story.”

CC looked at the headline. She knew exactly what she needed to know. She needed to ask Declan. And she needed him to answer honestly.

That morning, in New York, Declan was in his office when Alexander brought in the morning press summary.

“The Songkran video has resurfaced. A tabloid has identified you. They’re connecting the relationship speculation to the AVEN sponsorship,” Alexander said.

Declan looked up.

“What sponsorship?”

Alexander paused.

“The Southeast Asia agreement. Lincoln Group’s regional office signed with AVEN on March eleventh.”

Declan’s expression changed. Not with surprise. With recognition. He remembered. Of course he remembered.

Seven weeks earlier, on the Monday morning before her renewal, Alexander had placed a folder on his desk in Munich.

“One signature remains. Lincoln Group Southeast Asia’s sponsorship agreement with AVEN. The regional team has completed their review.”

Declan had been reading a separate report. He glanced at the first page.

“What’s the scope?”

“Corporate sponsorship across selected entertainment and cultural initiatives. The agreement includes brand placements and access to certain promotional opportunities. No individual artist obligations beyond the standard agency arrangements.”

“Commercially sound?”

“Yes. The regional team recommends approval.”

Declan turned a page. AVEN was an established entertainment company. The sponsorship made sense for Lincoln Group’s Southeast Asian brand strategy. It would provide visibility in a market where the group was expanding its consumer and hospitality partnerships.

He hadn’t requested the agreement. He hadn’t negotiated CC’s contract. He hadn’t discussed her renewal with AVEN. But he knew the agency was involved.

He knew the sponsorship would be signed the day before her renewal meeting. He had seen the dates. And he had signed anyway.

“Any conflicts?” he asked.

“None identified by legal.”

Declan signed the agreement and returned the folder.

“Proceed.”

Alexander took it. Neither of them mentioned CC. Now, in New York, Declan looked at the article again. Alexander remained standing.

“Did you tell CC?” he asked.

“No.”

“Did anyone at AVEN know you approved it?”

“The agreement was signed through the regional office. The agency’s commercial team would know the corporate sponsor. I can’t confirm who was aware of your personal connection.”

Declan closed the article.

“Get me the full agreement and the internal approval record.”

“Of course.”

“And Alexander?”

“Yes?”

“Don’t contact AVEN.”

Alexander nodded. Declan looked down at his phone. There was a message from CC.

Cela: Can you call me when you’re free?

He called immediately. Later that night, in Bangkok, CC answered on the first ring.

“Hello.”

“Hi, Cela.”

She didn’t return the greeting.

“Did you know Lincoln Group Southeast Asia signed a sponsorship agreement with AVEN on March eleventh?”

There was no point pretending he hadn’t heard about the article.

“Yes.”

The silence on the other end was immediate. CC looked at the phone.

“Yes?”

“I approved it.”

She closed her eyes.

“Why?”

“Lincoln Group was expanding its regional sponsorship portfolio. AVEN was a commercial partner the regional team had proposed. The agreement was reviewed by legal and approved through the usual process.”

“That isn’t what I asked.”

Declan stood up from his desk.

“I know.”

“Did you know I was renewing my contract the next day?”

“Yes.”

“Did you know the agreement was with my agency?”

“Yes.”

“Did you think to tell me?”

He was quiet. The answer was already there. CC’s voice remained controlled, but it had become still.

“Was it because of me?”

“No. The sponsorship was not designed to buy your contract or secure your renewal.”

“Then why didn’t you tell me?”

“I should have.”

It wasn’t an answer, and they both knew it.

He looked towards the windows. New York was bright beyond the glass, the city moving as if nothing in his office had changed.

“I knew the sponsorship would look complicated because of our relationship. I believed the commercial agreement was legitimate and separate from your contract. I didn’t want to create an unnecessary concern when you were already dealing with the renewal.”

She let out a small breath.

“You decided that for me.”

“Yes.”

“You knew I was worried about exactly this.”

“I remember.”

“You remember? I told you I was scared they’d think I only kept my place because of you. I let your lawyers in because I trusted you. I asked you not to call the CEO so that it would be mine.” Her voice cracked.

“Yes, Cela.”

“And then you signed an agreement with my agency the day before I went into that room to negotiate for myself.”

Declan closed his eyes.

“Yes.”

The word seemed to settle between them. CC stood from the sofa and walked towards the window.

“Did you know they would give me the personal-life clause?”

“No. I wasn’t involved in your negotiations.”

“Did you know I was asking for more control over my schedule?”

“No.”

“Did you know they agreed?”

“No.”

“Then you don’t know what that meeting was worth to me.”

“I know you worked for it.”

“Do you?” she asked.

He didn’t answer immediately. She continued.

“I went into that meeting by myself. I prepared every point. I negotiated the terms. I sat there and made them understand that my private life wasn’t theirs to control. I thought I had done it.”

“You did.”

“But now there’s a sponsorship from your company sitting right next to the date of my renewal. And the headline says you bought my contract.”

“The headline is false.”

“But you approved it.”

“Yes.”

“And you didn’t tell me.”

“No.”

She was silent. Declan wanted to explain the commercial rationale. He wanted to tell her the agreement had been proposed independently, that the legal review had found no conflict, that he hadn’t instructed anyone to give her special treatment. Every one of those facts might be true. None of them answered the question that mattered.

“You told me once not to let strangers decide what I should think about you. Do you remember? In November, after the photographs,” CC said.

He felt the words more sharply than anything else she had said.

“I remember.”

“Tonight strangers told me. And you gave them the story.”

“I know.”

“I would have stood next to you, Declan. Whatever it was. I only needed to hear it from you.”

“Then why?”

He had no answer that would make the decision acceptable.

“I thought I could keep the two things separate. I thought the agreement was commercially justified, and I convinced myself that not telling you was different from interfering with your renewal,” he said finally.

“But you knew it could affect how people saw me.”

“Yes.”

“And you let me walk into that meeting without knowing.”

He looked down at his hand.

“Yes.”

CC’s voice grew smaller.

“How am I supposed to trust the good things, Declan, when you kept something like that from me?”

He couldn’t answer. For the first time since she had known him, she wasn’t asking him to solve something.

She was asking him to understand that he had let her walk into the most important room of her career without the one thing she had asked of him: the truth.

“I am sorry,” he said.

She was quiet. Then:

“Please don’t come.”

Declan straightened.

“Cela—”

“Not yet. I can’t look at you and think at the same time, and I need to think. And don’t make the article disappear. If it vanishes now, everyone will know who made it vanish.” Her voice shook.

“I won’t.”

“And please don’t say anything publicly.”

“All right.”

She swallowed.

“I need you not to make this worse by trying to protect me from something you helped create.”

He took the words without defending himself.

“Understood.”

“Goodnight, Declan.”

“Goodnight, sweetheart.”

But the call had already ended. On Tuesday morning, the company meeting was held in a conference room at AVEN.

CC sat beside Nicha, with the independent lawyer they had retained for the renewal negotiations seated across from them. Two senior executives and the head of communications were present. The atmosphere was professional. Almost painfully so.

The CEO began by saying that the company was aware of the article and was reviewing the situation. CC listened without interrupting.

He said, “We want to be clear. The sponsorship agreement was entered into by AVEN as a corporate partnership. It was not part of your individual contract negotiations.”

“Was the company aware that Mr. Lincoln was my partner when it was signed?”

The CEO paused.

“That information was not formally disclosed to us.”

“Did anyone know?”

“We’re reviewing the internal communication.”

CC nodded. She had expected that answer. Her lawyer asked for a copy of the sponsorship agreement and any related communications between AVEN and Lincoln Group Southeast Asia. The CEO agreed to provide the documents, subject to the usual confidentiality review. Then the communications director spoke.

“We need to consider how the public might interpret the timing. Even if there was no direct exchange, the appearance of a connection could affect the credibility of the renewal.”

CC looked at her.

“My renewal was negotiated before I knew about the sponsorship.”

“Yes.”

“I negotiated the personal-life clause myself. I negotiated my schedule provisions. I asked for those terms because they were important to me.”

“We understand.”

“Do you?”

The room went quiet. CC kept her voice level.

“I don’t want the company to imply that I received those terms because of a relationship. I don’t want my work or my negotiations described as a favour from someone else.”

The CEO folded his hands.

“No one is suggesting that internally.”

“But the article is suggesting it publicly. And if the company doesn’t distinguish the sponsorship from my contract, the implication will remain.”

Nicha glanced at her. CC continued.

“I want the documents reviewed. I want confirmation that my contract was negotiated independently. And I want the company to protect the terms we agreed on rather than treating them as something that needs to be reconsidered because of this article.”

Her lawyer added that the sponsorship agreement and CC’s individual contract were separate legal instruments, and that the company should avoid making statements that blurred the two. The CEO nodded.

“We’ll review the records and come back to you.”

“Thank you.”

The meeting ended without a public statement. Outside, Nicha walked beside her.

“You handled that well.”

CC nodded. But her face didn’t change. Nicha waited until they reached the lift.

“Have you spoken to him again?”

CC looked at the closing doors.

“No.”

“Do you want to?”

She shook her head.

“Not yet.”

Nicha didn’t press. On Wednesday morning, in New York, Declan hadn’t slept properly.

The documents Alexander had requested were on his desk.

The sponsorship was legitimate. The regional team had proposed it independently. The agreement had been negotiated by commercial executives and reviewed by legal. There was no clause involving CC, her individual contract, her renewal, or any preferential treatment. It was a real corporate partnership. That was the problem.

He had approved it knowing AVEN was her agency, knowing her renewal was the following day, and knowing it was the one thing she had told him she was afraid of. He hadn’t bought her contract.

But he had created the circumstances in which the world could reasonably ask whether he had. And he had hidden the decision from her. Alexander stood beside his desk.

“The regional team can provide a formal timeline. The sponsorship proposal originated in February, before the renewal meeting was scheduled.”

Declan looked at the file.

“Was the agreement delayed?”

“No. It proceeded according to the normal approval process.”

“Did anyone discuss CC’s renewal?”

“Not in the commercial correspondence we’ve reviewed.”

Declan nodded.

“Send the full record to her lawyer through an independent channel. Not through AVEN.”

Alexander hesitated.

“Would you like me to ask whether she is willing to receive it?”

“No. Send it to the lawyer she retained. They can decide what to do with it.”

“Understood.”

“And no contact with the agency. No attempt to influence their response.”

Alexander nodded. Declan looked at the phone on his desk. There had been no message from CC. He opened their conversation.

Her last message was from the previous week, a photograph of the studio’s little stray cat.

He had replied that it looked like it owned the building. She had sent a laughing emoji. It seemed impossibly distant now. He put the phone down.

“Alexander.”

“Yes?”

“Cancel my Bangkok travel arrangements.”

Alexander looked at him.

“All of them?”

“Yes.”

“Understood.”

Declan returned to the documents. There were things he could do.

He could call the CEO. He could arrange a formal statement from Lincoln Group. He could have the sponsorship reviewed by an external firm and publish the findings. He could make it difficult for anyone to claim that CC’s contract had been purchased.

But she had asked him not to say anything. So he wouldn’t.

It was the first time he had understood that respecting her decision might mean doing nothing while someone else misunderstood him. He wasn’t sure he was good at it. He would have to learn.

The first day of May passed without a message from Declan. The second passed the same way. CC had expected him to write.

Not because she wanted him to ignore what she had asked, but because part of her still wanted him to say something that might make the facts easier to bear. He hadn’t.

Perhaps he was respecting her request. Perhaps he was angry. Perhaps he had decided that silence was safer. She didn’t know.

She was in the studio when P’Nicha brought her a cup of tea.

“Your lawyer has received the documents.”

CC looked up.

“From Lincoln Group?”

“Yes. Through an independent channel. The agreement was proposed by their regional commercial team in February. There’s no reference to your contract or renewal.”

CC nodded.

“All right.”

“Your lawyer says the documents support the distinction between the two agreements.”

“Good.”

Nicha sat beside her.

“CC.”

She looked over.

“You don’t have to decide what to do about him today.”

CC looked down at the cup.

“I know.”

“Do you want to talk about it?”

She shook her head. Nicha didn’t insist.

After a while, CC said, “I keep thinking about the meeting.”

“The renewal?”

She nodded.

“I remember being nervous. I remember thinking I might not get everything I wanted. And then I did.”

She looked at the pages of lyrics on the desk.

“I was so proud of myself.”

Nicha’s expression softened.

“You should still be.”

CC gave a small, uncertain smile.

“I know the work was mine.”

“Then don’t let a headline take that away.”

CC looked at her. Nicha continued.

“His decision was his. The company’s decision was theirs. Your negotiation was yours. Those things can all be true at the same time.”

CC looked down again. She wanted to believe that. She did believe it, intellectually.

But the thought of people looking at her contract and seeing a wealthy man behind it made something inside her ache.

And the fact that he had known how much it would hurt made it worse.

On Friday morning, in New York, he booked the ticket before eight. New York to Bangkok. A direct flight, departing that evening.

Declan hadn’t told Alexander to arrange it. He had booked it himself, from his phone before the office was fully awake.

He had spent the night considering what he might say. Not an explanation. He had already given her the facts. Not a defence.

He had no defence for withholding something he knew she should have been told. He wanted to see her.

He wanted to sit with her, listen, and let her say everything she hadn’t said on the phone. But she had asked him not to come. He looked at the ticket confirmation. Then he called Alexander.

“I’ll be out this afternoon.”

“Of course. Shall I move the remaining meetings?”

“Yes.”

Alexander paused.

“Are you travelling?”

Declan looked at the confirmation.

“I haven’t decided.”

Alexander understood enough not to ask further.

“All right.”

Declan spent the morning in meetings. He was attentive, precise, and composed. He reviewed a proposal, approved a budget, and gave instructions on a restructuring plan.

No one would have known that he had slept for less than three hours. At noon, he opened CC’s conversation. He typed:

Declan: I won’t come unless you ask me to. I understand why you need space. I am sorry I made a decision that affected your life without giving you the chance to know about it. I won’t ask you to make me feel better about it.

He read the message twice. Then sent it. There was no reply. He didn’t send another. That evening, JFK was busy.

Declan stood near the departure gate with his coat over one arm and his passport in his hand. His luggage had been checked in. His boarding pass was on his phone.

The flight to Bangkok was scheduled to board in twenty minutes. He had told himself that he would go.

Not to demand a conversation, not to ask her to forgive him, not to make an appearance that would force her to deal with him before she was ready. He would go because he missed her.

Because he wanted to be close enough to listen if she wanted to speak.

Because every instinct he had was telling him to cross the distance and stand in front of the person he loved. But she had asked him not to come. He took out his phone. Their conversation remained unchanged. His message from that afternoon sat beneath hers. No reply.

He opened the voice memo she had sent him in April. Her voice began.

He listened to the first few seconds, then stopped it. Not here.

Not when he was about to make another decision that would affect her without asking. He looked towards the gate. Passengers were beginning to queue.

A family moved past him with two small children. A man in a business suit spoke into his phone. Someone was laughing near the windows. The ordinary movement of people going somewhere. Declan looked at the boarding pass again. He could still board.

He could still arrive in Bangkok the following morning and wait somewhere she wouldn’t have to see him unless she chose to.

But that was precisely the kind of reasoning that had brought him here. He could make it sound considerate.

He could tell himself that he wasn’t demanding anything. But she had said not to come.

And he had to let her words mean what they meant. He stepped away from the queue. He stood still.

Then he opened the airline application and cancelled the check-in. He called Alexander.

“Good evening, sir.”

“I’m not boarding.”

There was a brief silence.

“Understood. Shall I arrange a car?”

“Yes.”

“Of course.”

Declan ended the call. He looked at the gate one last time. Then he turned away.

On Saturday morning, in Bangkok, CC woke before her alarm. The room was still dark.

She reached for her phone, not entirely sure why. There was a message from Declan. It had arrived several hours earlier.

Declan: I won’t come unless you ask me to. I understand why you need space. I am sorry I made a decision that affected your life without giving you the chance to know about it. I won’t ask you to make me feel better about it.

She read it once. Then again. She put the phone away. For a while, she lay still. She knew he had probably wanted to come.

She knew he might still be trying to find a way to make things right.

And she knew that part of her wanted him to. That was what made it so difficult.

She wasn’t questioning whether he loved her. She was questioning whether she could trust him with the parts of her life that mattered most. She remembered the renewal meeting.

The papers in front of her. The questions she had prepared.

The way she had looked at the CEO and asked for the right to make decisions about her own private life.

She remembered coming home that evening and telling Declan she had won. She remembered how happy he had sounded.

And now she wondered whether he had been sitting on information that could have changed the way she understood that victory. Her phone remained silent. She didn’t answer.

On Friday evening, in New York, Declan returned to his apartment. The flight had departed without him. His suitcase was still packed.

He placed his phone on the table and removed his watch. He looked at it.

The same watch that had been visible in the Songkran video.

The same watch that had helped a tabloid identify him. He set it down beside his keys.

Then he opened the green notebook’s photograph CC had sent him weeks earlier.

He had saved it because he liked seeing the inscription. He remembered giving it to her in Munich. He remembered her running her fingers over the cover. He remembered thinking that he wanted to be part of all the things she hadn’t written yet.

He had wanted to be someone she could trust with her unfinished thoughts.

Instead, he had made a decision about her life and kept it from her. His phone remained silent. He opened their conversation once more. There was no new message. He didn’t send one.

He sat alone in the quiet apartment, with the cancelled flight confirmation still open on his screen.
