Not boarding wasn’t restraint that deserved credit. It was only the first time he had done what she asked without finding a way around it, and it was nowhere near enough. He turned off the screen.

chapters.title: Her Words
chapters.desc: No gift this time, only a letter. Her father’s question, her own words with the dates in them, and two words on his phone: Bring tea.
chapters.epigraph: “He brought me tea.”
chapters.content:
In New York that Saturday morning, Declan didn’t call.

He had written three messages over the previous day, then deleted each one before sending. They had all begun with an apology. They had all ended with something that asked her to respond.

He was beginning to understand that even an apology could become another request.

So he sat at his desk and wrote a letter.

Not on Lincoln Group stationery, not on a formal sheet bearing his name and title. Just a plain sheet of paper, written by hand.

He started once, crossed out a paragraph, and began again.

He didn’t explain the commercial rationale. He didn’t list the safeguards in the sponsorship agreement. He didn’t tell her that he had never intended to influence her renewal. She already knew the facts.

What she needed to know was that he understood what he had done. When he finished, he read it once.

Then he put it in an envelope and addressed it to her apartment in Bangkok. There was no gift. No flowers. No expensive gesture intended to soften the words. Only the letter.

Cela,

I have been trying to explain what happened without making it sound smaller than it was. I don’t think there is a way.

The sponsorship was real business. The regional team proposed it, our lawyers reviewed it, and it bought nothing in your renewal. But I knew it was with AVEN. I knew your meeting was the next morning. I knew it was the one thing you had told me you were afraid of. And I signed it without a word to you.

I told myself it was separate. The truth is that telling you would have been uncomfortable, and I chose my comfort over your right to know. In November I asked you not to let strangers decide what you should think of me. Then I handed them the story, and let you read it from them.

I’m not writing to ask you to forgive me, or to answer, or to tell me we’ll be all right. You don’t owe me any of that. I won’t come unless you ask, and I won’t say anything in public unless you want me to.

I love you. That doesn’t make it less wrong, and it doesn’t give me the right to decide what happens next.

I hope one day you’ll tell me the unfinished things again.

Declan

He placed the letter inside the envelope. Then he called Alexander.

“Could you arrange for this to be delivered privately?”

“Of course.”

“No flowers. Nothing else.”

Alexander nodded.

“Understood.”

Declan handed him the envelope. For once, there was nothing more to arrange.

On Sunday afternoon, Richard Lincoln called while Declan was reviewing a document. His father rarely called without a reason.

“Good afternoon.”

“How are things?”

“Fine.”

Richard paused.

“Your mother says you’ve been working rather late.”

“There’s been a lot to review.”

“That isn’t what I asked.”

Declan leaned back. He knew his father well enough not to attempt a polite evasion.

“CC and I are having difficulties.”

“Because of the article?”

“Because of something I did.”

Richard was quiet. Declan explained the sponsorship. He didn’t soften the facts or leave out the part about knowing the date of CC’s renewal. When he finished, Richard asked one question.

“Did you tell her before you signed?”

“No.”

“Did she ask you not to interfere with her career?”

“Yes.”

“And you signed anyway.”

“Yes.”

Richard let the silence sit.

Then he asked, “Did you fix it?”

Declan looked down at the document.

“No, sir. It isn’t mine to fix.”

There was another pause.

“Good.”

Declan looked up slightly. His father continued.

“You’ve always been good at finding solutions. Sometimes too good. You see a problem and immediately think about what you can do to make it disappear.”

“I know.”

“That can be useful in business. It isn’t always useful with people.”

Declan said nothing.

“Your mother and I have been married a long time. I have made decisions I thought were best for her. Sometimes I was right. Sometimes I was simply making decisions she should have been allowed to make herself,” Richard said.

Declan listened.

“Don’t confuse protecting her with keeping things from her.”

“I won’t.”

Richard’s voice softened.

“Do you love her?”

“Very much.”

“Then let her have the space to decide what she wants.”

Declan looked towards the window.

“I will.”

“All right.”

His father ended the call without offering further advice. Declan remained at his desk for a while. Then he returned to the document.

On Monday morning, in Bangkok, the letter arrived at CC’s apartment shortly before lunch.

She recognised the handwriting immediately. She left it on the dining table. She had been preparing to go to the studio. Her bag was packed, her phone was charging, and the day’s schedule was already waiting in the group chat. She looked at the envelope again. Then she sat down. The letter wasn’t long. She read it once, slowly. Then she read it again. She stopped at one line.

I chose my comfort over your right to know.

That was the part she hadn’t been able to say to him. The sponsorship didn’t matter. What hurt was that he had known, and had decided she didn’t need to. She folded the letter carefully. Her eyes stung. She didn’t cry.

Not because she wasn’t hurt, but because she was tired of trying to make sense of everything at once. Her phone rang. Nicha.

“Are you ready?”

CC glanced at the clock.

“Almost.”

“Everything all right?”

She looked at the envelope.

“Declan sent me a letter.”

Nicha paused.

“Do you want to talk about it?”

“Not yet.”

“All right. I’ll be downstairs in ten minutes.”

“Thank you.”

CC ended the call. She placed the letter in the drawer beside her piano, then picked up her bag. She wasn’t ready to answer him.

But she no longer felt that he was trying to persuade her to stop being hurt. For now, that mattered.

On Tuesday afternoon, CC and Nicha sat together in a small meeting room at AVEN.

The article hadn’t disappeared, but the initial wave of speculation had begun to settle into a more specific question: whether the sponsorship had influenced CC’s renewal. The company had completed its internal review.

The records supported the distinction between the two agreements. The sponsorship had been proposed by Lincoln Group Southeast Asia’s commercial team in February. It had been approved by Declan on March 11. CC’s contract renewal had taken place on March 12, and her negotiations had been conducted separately. The company was prepared to provide a brief clarification if necessary. But CC wanted to say something herself.

“I don’t want them speaking for me,” she said.

Nicha nodded.

“Then we write your own post. Clear, factual, and not defensive.”

CC looked at the draft on the laptop. The first version was too formal. The second sounded as if she were apologising.

The third was better, but she didn’t like the phrase I would like to clarify.

“It makes it sound like I’ve done something wrong,” she said.

“Then take it out.”

They worked through it together. Nicha suggested keeping the dates. CC agreed. Her lawyer reviewed the wording to ensure it didn’t disclose confidential commercial terms or make claims beyond what the documents established.

They removed a sentence about the company’s intentions. CC couldn’t speak for AVEN’s internal decisions, and she didn’t want to. She wanted to speak about her own. Finally, she read the post aloud.

“That’s it,” Nicha said.

CC looked at her.

“Do you think it’s enough?”

“It’s enough to say what happened. You don’t have to answer every stranger on the internet.”

CC nodded. She took a breath. Then she pressed publish.

A few things about the recent reports on my contract.

On 11 March, Lincoln Group Southeast Asia signed a corporate sponsorship agreement with AVEN. It was an agreement between the two companies.

On 12 March, I attended my contract renewal meeting. I negotiated my own contract, including the terms about my personal life and my schedule.

These were separate. The sponsorship wasn’t payment for my renewal, and it wasn’t part of my negotiation.

I worked hard for those terms and I’m proud of them. Please don’t give my work to someone else’s money.

Thank you for listening, and for staying with my music.

Nicha read it one last time.

“Are you comfortable?”

CC nodded.

“Yes.”

“Then leave it there. Don’t spend the afternoon reading every comment.”

CC smiled.

“I’ll try.”

Nicha closed the laptop.

“You did well.”

CC looked at the published post on her phone.

For the first time in several days, she felt that she had said something without having to defend herself beyond the facts. It was her voice. Her words. Her choice.

On Wednesday evening, the response was mixed, as she had expected.

Some people accepted the clarification. Others continued speculating about the relationship. A few questioned why she hadn’t disclosed the sponsorship earlier, while others pointed out that she had no obligation to disclose a corporate agreement she hadn’t known about. The company shared her post without adding commentary.

Nicha sent her a message telling her to stop reading. CC obeyed for almost an hour. Then she opened her conversation with Declan. His last message was still the same. He hadn’t sent anything after the letter.

She looked at the empty message field. She could ask him how he was. She could tell him that she had read the letter. She could say she was still hurt.

But she didn’t want another long conversation about what had happened. She wanted something simpler. Something ordinary.

Something that belonged to the two of them before the article, before the sponsorship, before every conversation had become an exercise in deciding what could safely be said. She typed.

Cela: Bring tea.

She stared at the message. Then sent it. In New York, it was the morning of the same day.

Declan was in his office when the notification appeared. He picked up his phone. Read the message. Then read it again. For several seconds, he didn’t move.

Alexander, who had just entered with a folder, noticed.

“Everything all right?”

Declan looked up.

“Yes.”

His voice was quieter than usual. Alexander glanced at the phone. Declan didn’t explain. He typed a reply.

Declan: Of course. What kind?

The answer came a minute later.

Cela: The one you brought me in Geneva.

He smiled.

Declan: I remember.

Cela: Don’t forget.

Declan: I won’t.

He put the phone down. Alexander placed the folder on his desk.

“Would you like me to arrange your Bangkok schedule?”

Declan looked at him.

“Not yet.”

Alexander nodded.

“Understood.”

Declan returned to his work, but the morning felt different.

She hadn’t told him everything was forgiven. She hadn’t said they were all right. She had asked him to bring tea.

For now, he would take care not to make that mean more than it did.

On Thursday evening, in New York, Declan called her after work. She answered while walking through her apartment.

“Hello.”

“Hi, Cela.”

She smiled.

“Hi.”

“I received your instruction.”

She laughed.

“Instruction?”

“Bring tea.”

“Yes.”

“What time?”

She paused.

“Are you coming?”

“If you want me to.”

A small silence.

Then she said, “There’s a Lincoln Group Southeast Asia gala on Saturday.”

“I know.”

“AVEN is attending. I’ll be there.”

He understood. She was giving him an opportunity, not making a demand.

“Would you like me to attend with you?”

“Yes.”

He sat back.

“All right.”

“I don’t want a dramatic entrance.”

“I wouldn’t arrange one.”

“And I don’t want the company to make it look like a business appearance.”

“Understood.”

She was quiet. Then she said, “I think I’m ready to be seen with you.”

Declan looked down.

“Are you sure?”

“Yes.”

“Then I’ll come.”

She smiled.

“Good.”

He wanted to say more. He wanted to tell her how much that small sentence meant to him.

But he didn’t want to turn her decision into something she had to take care of emotionally.

So he said, “I’ll bring the tea.”

She laughed.

“Thank you.”

On Saturday evening, in Bangkok, the gala was held at a hotel ballroom overlooking the river.

It was a formal evening celebrating Lincoln Group Southeast Asia’s regional partnerships, with representatives from business, entertainment, hospitality, and the arts. CC arrived with Nicha and the AVEN team.

She wore a simple, elegant dress in a muted champagne shade. Her hair was styled loosely, and her jewellery was understated. She looked composed. But she kept glancing towards the entrance. Nicha noticed.

“He’s coming?”

“Yes.”

“Good.”

CC looked at her. Nicha smiled.

“You look lovely, by the way.”

“Thank you.”

They greeted several guests and exchanged the usual introductions. Then CC saw him. Declan had arrived.

He was wearing a black suit with a white shirt and the muted plum tie she had given him for Christmas. She watched him.

He was speaking with a senior regional executive, listening with the same quiet attention she remembered from their early dinners. He looked entirely at ease in the room. Then he saw her. His face softened. He excused himself and walked towards her.

“Good evening.”

She smiled.

“Good evening.”

He glanced at her.

“You look beautiful.”

“Thank you.”

She glanced at his tie.

“You’re wearing it.”

He followed her gaze.

“I thought it was appropriate.”

She smiled.

“It is.”

He held out his hand: not dramatically, just an invitation.

CC looked at it, then placed her hand in his. His fingers closed gently around hers.

For the first time, they entered a formal public event together without pretending they had arrived separately. Nicha watched them from a short distance. She didn’t say anything. But she smiled. That evening, the evening proceeded without incident.

Declan introduced CC to several executives, but he didn’t make her the centre of attention. When people spoke to her about her work, he let her answer for herself. When someone asked about her upcoming solo release, he listened with quiet interest.

At one point, a senior executive complimented the company’s partnership with AVEN. CC smiled politely. Declan didn’t interrupt or add anything. He stood beside her. It was a small distinction. But she noticed.

Later, they moved towards the quieter side of the ballroom, where the windows overlooked the river.

“Are you tired?” he asked.

“A little.”

“Would you like to leave soon?”

She shook her head.

“Not yet.”

He nodded. They stood together, watching the lights reflected on the water. Then she looked at him.

“You wore the tie.”

“I did.”

“Because I gave it to you?”

“Because I like it.”

She smiled.

“Good answer.”

He looked over.

“How are you feeling?”

She considered it.

“Better.”

He nodded.

“Good.”

She looked down at their hands.

“I read your letter.”

“I hoped you would.”

“I believe you didn’t intend to buy my contract.”

He didn’t speak.

“But I still wish you’d told me.”

“I know.”

She looked up.

“I don’t want to have to wonder what you decide not to tell me because you think it will make things easier.”

His face became serious.

“You shouldn’t have to.”

“Then don’t do it again.”

“I won’t.”

She studied his face. There was no grand promise, no attempt to persuade her that everything would be different immediately. Just his answer. She nodded.

Then she moved closer and rested her hand on his arm. It wasn’t a declaration that everything was repaired. It was a beginning.

That evening, they were making their way back towards the main ballroom when a reporter approached.

“Miss CC?”

She turned.

“Good evening.”

The reporter smiled politely, accompanied by a photographer who kept a respectful distance.

“May I ask you a question?”

“Of course.”

The reporter glanced at Declan.

“There’s been considerable interest in your relationship recently. Is this the first time you’ve attended an event together?”

CC looked at Declan. He didn’t answer for her. He didn’t step forward to introduce himself. He waited.

“Yes. It’s our first time attending an event together like this,” she said.

“May I ask how you met?”

Declan turned slightly towards her. He remembered Geneva. The winter gala, the cold evening, the cashmere shawl he had offered her. He remembered thinking she was beautiful, and how she had smiled at him with such unexpected warmth. He was about to answer. But CC spoke first.

“He brought me tea.”

The reporter blinked. Then smiled.

“Tea?”

CC nodded, her expression perfectly serious.

“Yes.”

Declan looked at her. A faint smile appeared at the corner of his mouth. The reporter laughed.

“That’s a lovely answer. Was it really tea?”

“Not the first thing. But it’s one of the things I remember,” CC admitted.

Declan looked down at her. She turned towards him.

“Isn’t that right?”

He smiled.

“Yes. I have brought her tea on several occasions.”

“Then I suppose it’s a tradition.”

“Apparently.”

The reporter asked whether they had anything to say about the recent speculation. CC answered calmly.

“We’re happy to be here together tonight. We prefer to keep our private life private, but we appreciate everyone’s interest and kindness.”

The reporter nodded.

“Thank you. And congratulations on your upcoming solo release.”

“Thank you.”

The exchange ended there. No elaborate confirmation. No carefully prepared announcement.

No attempt to turn the evening into a spectacle. Just the two of them, standing together.

When the reporter walked away, Declan leaned slightly towards her.

“Tea?”

She smiled.

“Would you have preferred something else?”

“No.”

“Good.”

He watched her.

“That’s how you chose to introduce our relationship?”

She tilted her head.

“It’s true.”

“It is.”

“And it’s a good story.”

He smiled.

“I’ll have to make sure I keep bringing you tea, then.”

She laughed.

“Please do.”

Later that night, the car was waiting outside. CC sat beside Declan in the back seat, her heels resting neatly on the floor mat. The evening had been long, but she didn’t feel tired. She met his eyes.

“Did you enjoy tonight?”

“Very much.”

He smiled. She laughed.

“I didn’t know what else to say.”

“You could have told them about Geneva.”

She glanced at him.

“That’s a little more romantic.”

“I thought you liked romantic.”

“I do.”

He reached for her hand.

“Then why tea?”

She looked down at their joined fingers.

“Because it was something ordinary.”

He waited. She continued.

“Everyone knows your company, your title, your money. They can read all of that in an article. But I wanted to tell them something that was mine.”

His face softened.

“Something that belonged to us.”

She nodded. He lifted her hand and kissed her knuckles.

“Then I’m glad you said it.”

She leaned against his shoulder. For a while, they watched Bangkok pass beyond the windows.

Then she said, “I liked tonight.”

“So did I.”

“I liked not having to pretend you were someone else.”

He brushed his thumb over her hand.

“I didn’t like making you feel you had to.”

She was quiet. Then she said, “We’re not going to be careless about everything now.”

“I know.”

“And I still don’t want people knowing all our business.”

“Neither do I.”

She looked up.

“But I don’t want to hide you.”

He turned towards her.

“Thank you.”

She smiled.

“Don’t make me regret it.”

“I won’t.”

He said it. Not as a grand promise intended to end the conversation.

As something he would have to remember in the decisions that came afterwards.

When they reached her apartment, Declan walked her to the door.

She turned to face him, and he asked before she could. “May I come in?”

“Yes.”

He followed her inside. The apartment was quiet. CC slipped off her shoes and placed her handbag on the console table. Declan removed his jacket and hung it neatly beside hers. She went into the kitchen.

“Tea?”

He tilted his head. She smiled.

“Your turn to be spoiled.”

He laughed.

“That sounds very good.”

She prepared two cups, using the tea she liked. He stood beside the counter, watching her move around her kitchen with familiar ease.

When she handed him his cup, he accepted it.

“Thank you.”

“You’re welcome.”

They sat together on the sofa. For a while, they drank in comfortable silence. Then CC put her cup down.

“Declan?”

“Hm?”

“I’m not completely over it.”

“I know.”

“I might still think about it sometimes.”

“You can.”

She turned to him.

“I don’t want you to think that because I invited you tonight, everything is automatically fine.”

“I don’t.”

She studied his expression.

“Good.”

He reached for her hand.

“I don’t expect you to forget it. I don’t expect one letter or one evening to undo what I did.”

“But I want to do better. Not by telling you I will. By making sure you have the information and the choice you should have had from the beginning,” he said.

She looked at their hands.

“That’s all I wanted.”

“I understand that now.”

She moved closer and leaned into his shoulder. He kissed her hair. Neither of them said anything for a while.

Eventually, he said, “May I stay?”

She smiled against his collar. “I was hoping you’d ask.”

He put his cup down, and then he kissed her for the first time in two weeks: carefully at first, as if she might change her mind, and then with everything he hadn’t been allowed to say, until her fingers were in his hair and the tea was going cold and neither of them cared.

She settled against him, her cheek resting near his collar.

The evening hadn’t erased the difficult days between them.

But she had chosen to let him come closer.

And he understood that the choice was hers to make again tomorrow.

In the early hours, before going to bed, CC noticed his tie draped over the back of the chair. She picked it up.

The muted plum colour looked almost dark in the low light.

“Declan?”

He turned from the bedroom doorway.

“Yes?”

She held up the tie.

“I like seeing you wear this.”

He smiled.

“I know.”

“How?”

“You always look at it.”

She gave him a small, embarrassed smile.

“Maybe.”

He walked over and took the tie from her.

Then he folded it carefully and placed it beside his jacket.

“Would you like me to wear it again?”

She nodded.

“Next time.”

“Then I will.”

She reached for his hand. He took it. And together they went to bed.

In the morning there would be questions. Tonight there was only the tie folded beside his jacket, and her hand in his.

chapters.title: Somewhere Quiet
chapters.desc: Four nights on Koh Kood, the first trip where nobody hides, a conversation about where they might live, and a villa he hears her like.
chapters.epigraph: “I took it the way I take things you say.”
chapters.content:
On Wednesday morning, in Bangkok, CC had mentioned the days off in Markham almost two months ago.

It had been during breakfast at her parents’ house, when her father was packing butter tarts into a box for Declan to take on the plane.

She had been talking about her schedule, about the upcoming solo release and the months of rehearsals, recordings, and promotional work ahead.

“I think I might have a few days free in May,” she’d said. “If everything goes according to plan.”

Her mother had asked whether she would use them to sleep. Her father had suggested she visit home again.

CC had laughed and said she might just disappear somewhere quiet. Declan had remembered.

Now, standing in her apartment with a small suitcase beside the door, she looked at him with mild suspicion.

“You remembered that?”

“I did.”

“I only mentioned it once.”

“That doesn’t mean I wasn’t listening.”

She glanced at the itinerary on her phone. Koh Kood. Four nights.

A private villa by the sea, arranged through a discreet resort. Direct transfer from Bangkok, followed by a short boat journey. No complicated schedule, no formal events, no obligation to attend anything. She looked up.

“Is it very quiet?”

“That was the requirement.”

“Are there restaurants?”

“Several.”

“Good.”

“Are there things to do?”

“If you want to do them.”

She smiled.

“That’s a very good answer.”

Declan took her suitcase. She reached for it at the same time.

“I can carry that.”

“I know.”

“Then why are you taking it?”

“Because I would like to.”

She let go, smiling to herself. He met her eyes.

“Anything else?”

“My sunglasses.”

“They’re in your handbag.”

“My book.”

“Side pocket.”

She checked. He was right. CC looked at him, amused.

“You’re very prepared.”

“I have been given instructions.”

She laughed and followed him out. For once, there was no need to leave separately, no carefully timed arrival, no concern about a photograph taken at the wrong moment. They were going away together. And they weren’t hiding it.

That afternoon, in Koh Kood, the island was quieter than CC expected.

The boat approached the pier through clear water, the coastline appearing gradually beyond the sunlight. There were no towering buildings, no crowded roads, no constant noise.

Just green hills, pale sand, and the occasional long-tail boat passing in the distance.

CC stood beside Declan as they approached the jetty.

“It’s beautiful.”

He turned to her.

“Is it what you imagined?”

“Better.”

The resort staff greeted them by name. Their luggage was taken ahead, and a small electric cart brought them along a shaded path towards their villa. CC looked around as they passed the gardens.

The place was private without feeling isolated. Wooden walkways, tropical plants, open-air spaces, and the sea visible between the trees. Their villa stood slightly apart from the others.

Inside, the room opened towards a private terrace and a small pool. Beyond it, the beach stretched along the coast, almost empty in the afternoon. CC walked straight towards the terrace.

“Oh.”

Declan set down his phone.

“Good?”

She turned around.

“Very good.”

He watched her walk towards the edge of the terrace, looking at the water.

She was wearing a simple white linen dress, her hair loosely tied back. The sunlight fell across her face, and she looked more relaxed than she had in weeks.

He came up behind her, leaving enough space for her to turn if she wanted.

“Do you like it?”

She nodded.

“I think I could stay here.”

“That’s encouraging. We have four nights.”

She laughed.

“Don’t tempt me.”

He rested his hands lightly at her waist.

“Would you like to go down to the beach?”

“After I look at everything.”

“Take your time.”

She turned and looked at him.

“You know, I haven’t checked my schedule since we left Bangkok.”

“An excellent beginning.”

“I might be becoming a very irresponsible person.”

“I’ll try not to encourage you.”

He bent his head and kissed her, slow and warm and tasting of sea air, until the waves and the terrace and the four nights ahead blurred into one long golden moment.

When she drew back, he brushed a strand of hair away from her cheek.

“Welcome to Koh Kood, Cela.”

She smiled.

“Thank you for bringing me.”

On Thursday morning, CC woke to the sound of the sea.

For a few seconds, she didn’t remember where she was.

Then she saw the open curtains, the sunlight on the floor, and Declan’s empty side of the bed. She sat up.

He was on the terrace with two cups of tea.

She found him there a few minutes later, wearing a white shirt with the sleeves rolled up.

“Good morning.”

He looked over.

“Good morning, sweetheart.”

She walked towards him and took the cup he offered.

“Tea.”

“I remembered the instruction.”

She smiled. They had breakfast outside. Fresh fruit, eggs, toast, and coffee for Declan. CC had mango and yoghurt, then stole a piece of his toast. He watched her do it.

“You have your own.”

“Yours tastes better.”

“It’s the same toast.”

“Not necessarily.”

He smiled and let her take another piece. They spent the morning swimming and walking along the beach.

There were a few other guests, but the stretch of sand near their villa was mostly empty. Nobody approached CC for photographs. Nobody whispered her stage name. Nobody seemed interested in the couple walking barefoot near the water.

At one point, she stopped to look at a small shell. Declan waited.

She picked it up, turned it over, then placed it back where she had found it.

“Not taking it?”

“No. It looks nicer here.”

He looked at her.

“That’s unusually restrained.”

She gave him a look.

“I can be restrained.”

“I’ve noticed.”

She laughed and splashed a little water towards him. He looked down at his wet trousers.

“Was that necessary?”

“Yes.”

He stepped closer.

“Are you sure?”

She backed away, smiling.

“Declan.”

He caught her hand before she could retreat, and she laughed as he drew her towards him.

They ended up standing in the shallow water, her hands against his chest, his arm around her waist. She looked towards the beach. Then she looked back at him.

“I like this.”

“What?”

“Being here with you. Without having to think about where we’re standing or who’s looking.”

He brushed his thumb over her waist.

“So do I.”

She rested her forehead against his chest. The island moved slowly around them. And neither of them tried to hurry it.

On Friday afternoon, they went out on a small boat in the afternoon.

The resort had arranged a private trip along the coast, with a stop for swimming and a quiet lunch at a beachside restaurant.

CC sat beside Declan, wearing a wide-brimmed hat and sunglasses. Her feet were tucked beneath her, and she had been looking at the water for most of the journey.

“Are you cold?” he asked.

“No.”

“Thirsty?”

She shook her head.

“Do you need anything?”

She turned towards him.

“Just you to stop asking me if I need things.”

He smiled.

“All right.”

She considered that.

“Actually, I would like some of your water.”

He handed it over.

“Naturally.”

She drank, then returned the bottle.

“Thank you.”

He leaned back.

“Anything else?”

She smiled.

“No.”

A little later, they stopped near a quiet stretch of beach.

CC swam while Declan stayed close, occasionally joining her. They ate lunch under a shaded roof, sharing grilled fish, vegetables, rice, and fresh fruit. The afternoon passed without much conversation.

The silence was the easy sort that came when neither person felt responsible for entertaining the other.

On the way back, CC sat beside him with her head resting on his shoulder.

“Can I ask you something?”

“Anything.”

“Where do you think you’ll live in five years?”

Declan turned his head slightly. It was an ordinary question, but not an insignificant one. He considered it.

“I don’t know.”

She lifted her head.

“You don’t?”

“No.”

She smiled.

“That’s unexpected.”

“Would you prefer a carefully prepared answer?”

“No.”

He looked out at the water.

“Munich will probably remain an important base for me. New York will remain important too. The company has offices in several places, and I can’t pretend that my work will become less international.”

She nodded.

“What about Bangkok?”

“I can spend time here.”

“But would you live here?”

“I could.”

She looked down at her hands.

“I don’t know where I’ll be either.”

“Your work is here, for now.”

“Yes. But I might want to work elsewhere sometimes. Record in London, spend time in Canada, maybe take opportunities in other countries.”

“I would want you to.”

She held his gaze. She smiled, but her expression soon became thoughtful.

“I don’t think I could live in Munich all the time.”

He nodded.

“I wouldn’t ask you to.”

“And I don’t know if I could live in Bangkok forever either.”

“Then perhaps we shouldn’t decide forever while we’re sitting on a boat.”

She laughed.

“That’s very practical.”

“I have my moments.”

She leaned back against him.

“I just wondered whether you had ever thought about it.”

“I have.”

She turned her face towards him.

“What did you think?”

He considered his answer carefully.

“I thought that I would like a home where you felt comfortable. I haven’t decided what city that would be.”

Her face softened.

“A home?”

“Yes.”

“Not an apartment?”

He smiled.

“An apartment can be a home.”

She looked towards the horizon.

“I like that.”

He kissed her temple.

“But you don’t have to choose a place now. Or give up something you love because I have a life already established.”

She was quiet. Then she said, “I don’t want you to give up everything either.”

“I wouldn’t.”

She tilted her head.

“Then we don’t know.”

“No. We don’t,” he said.

She smiled.

“That’s okay.”

He looked down at her.

“It is.”

The boat continued towards the resort. Neither of them tried to turn the conversation into a decision.

It was enough that they had begun to imagine the question together.

On Saturday morning, CC spent most of the morning reading.

She had brought two books and had managed to finish neither.

Declan was beside her on the terrace, reviewing a few documents on his tablet. He had told her he needed an hour, and she had told him she didn’t mind. After forty minutes, she put her book down.

“Declan?”

“Hm?”

“Are you working?”

He glanced at the screen.

“Technically.”

She smiled.

“That’s not a very reassuring answer.”

He put the tablet aside.

“Go ahead.”

She looked at him.

“Do you ever get tired of travelling?”

“Sometimes.”

“Do you get tired of hotels?”

“Yes.”

“Do you get tired of always having somewhere to be?”

He thought about it.

“Occasionally.”

She nodded as if she had confirmed something.

“Then perhaps you need to disappear somewhere quiet too.”

He held her gaze.

“Is that what we’re doing?”

“Yes.”

He reached over and took her hand.

“Then I think it’s working.”

She smiled and returned to her book. A few minutes later, she moved her chair closer to his. He studied her. He didn’t move away.

That afternoon, they walked through a small village and stopped at a local restaurant. CC bought a little woven bag from a shop and insisted on paying for it herself. Declan didn’t offer to take it from her. He held the door.

On their way back, they stopped for ice cream. CC chose coconut. Declan chose coffee. She tried his, then made a small face.

“Too bitter.”

“You chose it.”

“I chose mine.”

He laughed. She held out her spoon.

“Try this.”

He did.

“Better.”

“Of course.”

She looked pleased with herself. On Sunday morning, their last morning arrived too quickly.

CC sat on the terrace with her feet tucked beneath her, watching the light move across the water. Declan brought her tea. She accepted it with both hands.

“Thank you.”

He sat beside her.

“Did you sleep well?”

“Very well.”

“Would you come back?”

She turned towards him.

“Yes.”

“Then we will.”

Something in the way he said it made her look at him properly. “Declan. What did you do?”

“The resort was offering a long lease on this villa.”

“You leased the villa.”

“I bought the lease. Ninety-nine years seemed simplest. You said you could stay here.” He sipped his tea.

“I said it the way people say things on holiday!”

“I know. I took it the way I take things you say.”

She opened her mouth, closed it, and looked at the sea she apparently now had, and started laughing so hard she had to put her cup down. “You can’t just buy a villa.”

“I can, apparently. Too much?” He waited.

She should have said yes. She looked at the terrace, and the little pool, and the man who had heard I could stay here and made it true by breakfast, and the smile won, the way it always did. “Okay.”

She looked at the sea again.

“I don’t want to go back to my schedule.”

“I suspected as much.”

She smiled.

“Can we stay one more day?”

“I can arrange it.”

She shook her head immediately.

“No. I was joking.”

He looked at her.

“I know.”

She smiled.

“You’re too easy to tempt.”

“Only when the suggestion is reasonable.”

She laughed and tucked herself against his shoulder. After a while, she spoke again.

“About what we talked about yesterday.”

He looked down at her.

“The place to live?”

She nodded.

“I don’t want to make it a serious conversation every time. I don’t want us to start planning our whole lives just because we had a nice holiday.”

“Neither do I.”

“But I liked talking about it.”

“So did I.”

She lifted her head.

“Maybe one day we’ll know.”

“Maybe.”

“And maybe we’ll have more than one home.”

He smiled.

“That sounds possible.”

She considered it.

“Somewhere in Munich. Somewhere in Bangkok. Maybe somewhere else.”

“You’re planning quite an extensive property portfolio.”

She laughed.

“Not your kind.”

“Fortunately, I know someone with better taste.”

She studied his face.

“Who?”

He kissed her cheek.

“You.”

She smiled and settled against him again. They stayed there until their tea was finished.

By the time they returned to Bangkok, the city was already settling into its evening rhythm. The car took them to CC’s apartment first.

Declan carried her suitcase inside while she checked her messages. There were several from Nicha, a few from the group chat, and one from her mother asking whether she had enjoyed the trip. CC replied with a photograph of the sea. Then she put her phone down. Declan was standing near the door.

“You’re leaving?”

“I have a call with Munich in an hour.”

She nodded. He walked towards her.

“Thank you for coming with me.”

She smiled.

“Thank you for taking me.”

He brushed his hand over her cheek.

“Did you have a good time?”

“Very good.”

“Good.”

She wrapped her arms around him. He held her close, kissing her hair. She looked up.

“Next time, somewhere else?”

“Where would you like?”

She thought for a second.

“Somewhere with mountains.”

“Switzerland again?”

“Maybe.”

“Or somewhere new.”

She smiled.

“Somewhere quiet.”

He kissed her.

“Then we’ll find somewhere quiet.”

She leaned against him for another moment before letting him go. At the door, he turned back.

“Goodnight, Cela.”

“It’s not night yet.”

“Then I’ll say it again later.”

She smiled.

“Goodnight, Declan.”

He left. CC closed the door and stood there.

The apartment was exactly as she had left it.

Her books were on the table. Her piano stood by the window. The little things that made it hers remained in place. She picked up her phone.

Cela: I miss the sea already.

His reply came a few minutes later.

Declan: So do I.

Cela: And the tea.

Declan: I can arrange that.

Cela: Not the resort tea. Yours.

He smiled at his phone in the back of the car.

Declan: I’ll bring it tomorrow.

Cela: Goodnight ❤️

Declan: Goodnight, sweetheart.

He put the phone away. She went to bed smiling, with the shell she hadn’t taken in her head and the villa she apparently owned in her phone.

chapters.title: The Inspection
chapters.desc: BLUE HOUR and Pim finally inspect him. He brings butter tarts he made himself, and asks them better questions than they ask him.
chapters.epigraph: “What do you hope for her?”
chapters.content:
Declan had been informed that the inspection would take place on Saturday at three.

He had also been informed that it wasn’t optional.

The message had come from CC two evenings earlier.

Cela: BLUE HOUR wants to meet you.

Declan: I was hoping they’d forgotten.

Cela: They never forget.

Declan: I see.

Cela: Pim is coming too.

Declan: Should I be concerned?

Cela: A little.

Declan: Understood. What time?

Cela: Saturday. Three.

Declan: I’ll be there.

Cela: Bring something.

Declan: What would you like?

Cela: Something nice.

He had replied with a simple Of course, which had apparently been insufficient.

Cela: And don’t buy something.

That had made him pause.

Declan: You have something specific in mind?

Cela: You know.

He did. And so, at 3:15 on Saturday afternoon, Declan stood outside CC’s apartment holding a large bakery box. He rang the bell. CC opened the door.

She was wearing a soft blue blouse and cream trousers, her hair tied loosely behind her head. She looked at the box first. Then at him.

“Did you make them?”

“I did.”

Her eyebrows rose.

“All of them?”

“Yes.”

She looked at the box again.

“Declan.”

“I understand the expression.”

She stepped aside to let him in, trying not to smile too obviously.

“How many attempts?”

“That is confidential information.”

She laughed. He dipped his head and kissed her cheek.

“Hello, sweetheart.”

“Hello.”

He handed her the box. She opened it just enough to look inside.

The butter tarts were arranged in neat paper cups. Their tops were golden, though a few had slightly uneven edges. One was noticeably darker than the others. CC looked at them. Then she looked at him.

“They’re actually quite pretty.”

“Thank you.”

“Did you make the pastry?”

“Yes.”

“And the filling?”

“Yes.”

She picked up the darkest one.

“This one looks a little…”

“Overenthusiastic?”

She laughed.

“Burnt.”

“Only slightly.”

She put it back.

“Dad would have something to say.”

“He did.”

CC looked up.

“You spoke to Dad?”

“I sent him a photograph.”

Her eyes widened.

“You did what?”

“He provided some constructive feedback.”

“What did he say?”

Declan took off his jacket.

“He said I had improved the filling but was still being too ambitious with the oven.”

CC laughed until she had to put the box down.

“That’s exactly what he would say.”

“I have taken his advice seriously.”

She looked at him with unmistakable affection. She held out her hand. He stepped closer.

He kissed her before she could say anything else, one hand at her waist, slow enough that the box tilted dangerously in her hands and she didn’t notice.

“Thank you for making them.”

“You’re welcome.”

Then a voice came from the living room.

“Are those the butter tarts?”

CC closed her eyes.

“They’re here.”

His eyes went to her face.

“All of them?”

She smiled.

“All of them.”

That afternoon, the living room had been rearranged. There were drinks on the coffee table, a plate of fruit, and several small dishes of snacks. Someone had brought flowers. Someone else had brought enough food to suggest that the meeting might last until dinner.

The three other members of BLUE HOUR were seated together on the sofa.

Pim sat in an armchair, looking pleased with herself. They all turned when Declan entered. CC made the introductions.

“Everyone, this is Declan.”

There was a brief exchange of greetings. Declan greeted each of them, shaking hands politely. He remembered their faces from the group photographs CC had shown him and the stories she had told him over the past months.

“Thank you for having me,” he said.

One of the members smiled.

“We’ve been waiting.”

“I was told.”

Pim leaned forward.

“Did you know we were going to inspect you?”

“I was warned.”

“Good. We like people who arrive prepared.”

Declan glanced at the box in CC’s hands.

“I brought a peace offering.”

“What’s inside?” another member asked.

“Butter tarts.”

Pim looked at CC.

“Your father?”

“Not this time. Declan made them,” CC said.

There was a moment of silence. Then all four looked at him.

“You made these?” one asked.

“Yes.”

“Yourself?”

“With some guidance from CC’s father.”

Pim stood up.

“Well, now we have to try them.”

CC placed the box on the table. Declan watched as the group gathered around it.

There was a brief discussion about which one looked best, followed by an argument over whether the darkest tart should be given to the person brave enough to try it.

CC picked up one of the better-looking ones and broke it in half. She tasted it. Declan watched her expression. She chewed thoughtfully. Then nodded.

“Good.”

He smiled.

“Good?”

“Very good.”

Pim took one. She bit into it, considered the filling, then looked at Declan.

“Promising.”

CC laughed.

“That’s what my father said.”

“Promising? That’s a dangerous compliment. It means there’s still room for improvement,” Pim repeated.

“I’ve been made aware.”

The group laughed. Declan accepted a tart for himself and took a seat beside CC.

For the first few minutes, the conversation remained easy.

They asked about Munich, his work, how often he travelled, and whether he was enjoying Bangkok.

Declan answered without making the conversation about his position or company. He asked about their recent schedules, the group’s activities, and how they were preparing for the next few months. He listened more than he spoke. And, gradually, the atmosphere shifted. The inspection had officially begun.

That afternoon, “So,” Pim said, putting her cup down.

Declan considered her.

“Yes?”

“How serious are you about CC?”

CC immediately turned towards her.

“Pim.”

“What? We agreed to ask,” Pim said innocently.

One of the members nodded.

“We did.”

Declan didn’t appear offended.

“Very serious.”

Pim waited.

“That’s a good start,” she said. “But what does that mean to you?”

Declan considered the question.

“It means I don’t regard her as someone who fits into my life only when it’s convenient. I want to understand the life she already has, and make room for myself in it without expecting her to give anything up unnecessarily.”

The room became a little quieter. He continued.

“It also means I take her decisions seriously, even when I might have made a different one myself. Especially then.”

CC looked down at her cup. Pim studied him for another moment.

“All right.”

CC glanced at her.

“That’s it?”

“For now.”

Another member leaned forward.

“What happens when she’s upset with you?”

Declan looked towards CC, then back at the speaker.

“I listen.”

“Even when she’s not telling you what’s wrong?”

“Then I try not to assume I already know.”

CC’s mouth curved.

“That’s a very diplomatic answer.”

“It’s also true.”

“Do you always wait for her to tell you?”

“No. I ask. But I don’t insist that she explain herself before she’s ready.”

The member nodded slowly.

“Good.”

The third member had been quiet, watching him over the rim of her glass.

“Do you understand how much her work matters to her?”

“Yes.”

“Because sometimes people say they support her career, but what they really mean is that they support it as long as it doesn’t interfere with their own plans.”

Declan’s expression became thoughtful.

“I wouldn’t want her to have to choose between her work and being with me simply because I found the distance inconvenient.”

Her eyes went to his. He continued.

“Her career is not a temporary arrangement that she will eventually grow out of. It’s part of who she is. I admire her for it.”

The member seemed satisfied, though she didn’t say so immediately. Then Pim spoke again.

“And what if she becomes more successful than you?”

CC stared at her.

“Pim!”

“What? It’s a valid question.”

Declan smiled.

“I would be delighted.”

“Really?”

“Yes.”

“Not intimidated?”

“No.”

“Not jealous?”

He considered it.

“I might be jealous of the people who get to spend more time with her.”

CC laughed.

“But I wouldn’t want her to become less successful to make me feel more comfortable.”

Pim leaned back.

“All right. That’s a good answer.”

CC shook her head, smiling.

“You’re all being very serious.”

“We’re taking this seriously,” one member replied.

“We’re taking you seriously,” another corrected.

CC’s smile softened. She looked around the room.

“I know.”

That afternoon, after a short break for more tea, Declan did something unexpected.

He put his cup down and turned towards the group.

“May I ask you all something?”

Pim raised an eyebrow.

“You’re interviewing us now?”

“Only if you don’t mind.”

She smiled.

“Go ahead.”

Declan looked first at the member seated closest to CC.

“What’s something about her that you think people misunderstand?”

The member seemed surprised. She glanced at CC before answering.

“People think she’s quiet because she’s shy. Sometimes she is, but mostly she’s just thinking. She doesn’t always need to fill the silence.”

Declan nodded.

“I’ve noticed.”

“And people sometimes mistake her being agreeable for not having an opinion. She has plenty. She just doesn’t always feel the need to argue.”

CC looked at her.

“That’s not entirely true.”

The member laughed.

“It is when you’re tired.”

Declan smiled.

“Thank you. I’ll remember that.”

He turned to the second member.

“What do you think she needs most when work becomes overwhelming?”

The question made her pause.

“Honestly?”

“Please.”

“She needs people who don’t make her feel guilty for resting.”

CC looked down. The member continued.

“She’s responsible. Sometimes too responsible. She’ll finish something even when she’s exhausted because she doesn’t want to inconvenience anyone.”

Declan listened carefully.

“Does she tell you when she’s tired?”

“Sometimes. But not always.”

He nodded.

“I’ll keep that in mind.”

The third member smiled a little.

“You’re taking notes?”

“Mentally.”

“That’s very CEO of you.”

He laughed. Then he turned towards Pim.

“And you?”

Pim seemed to have been waiting for her turn.

“What do you want to know?”

“What do you worry about when it comes to CC?”

The room became quiet again. Pim looked at CC. Then at Declan.

“I worry that she makes herself smaller when she thinks someone else needs more space.”

CC’s expression changed. Pim continued, more gently.

“She’s good at being considerate. She’ll adjust her schedule, her mood, her expectations. She doesn’t complain much. Sometimes I think she assumes that if something is difficult, she should just manage it herself.”

Declan didn’t interrupt.

Pim said, “I don’t want her to feel like she has to do that with you. I want her to be able to ask for things. To be difficult sometimes. To say she misses you. To be upset without worrying that she’s asking too much.”

Declan looked at CC. She was looking at her hands. He turned back to Pim.

“Thank you for telling me.”

Pim studied him.

“That’s all?”

“For now.”

She smiled.

“Good.”

He looked around at all four of them.

“I have one more question.”

Pim groaned playfully.

“How many questions do you have?”

“One.”

“All right.”

Declan’s expression softened.

“What do you hope for her?”

Nobody answered immediately. It was a different question from the others.

Not what they wanted him to do, not what they worried about, not what they thought he should know. Just what they hoped for CC. One of the members spoke first.

“I hope she keeps enjoying music.”

Another added, “I hope she gets to do the projects she wants, not just the ones people think will work.”

The third smiled.

“I hope she has a life outside work. A really happy one.”

Pim looked at CC.

“I hope she gets spoiled without having to earn it.”

CC let out a small laugh, but her eyes were bright. Then he turned back to them.

“I hope those things for her too.”

Pim nodded.

“All right.”

She reached for another butter tart.

“I think we can continue.”

CC stared at her.

“Continue what?”

“The inspection.”

“Didn’t you just finish?”

“We haven’t discussed the butter tarts properly.”

Declan smiled.

“I would welcome the feedback.”

Pim took another bite.

“Still promising.”

That evening, the conversation eventually became less formal. Someone asked Declan whether he had always been so composed. CC immediately said yes, although she had evidence that he could be quite competitive when playing games. Declan looked at her.

“That was one occasion.”

“It was several.”

“Two.”

“Three.”

Pim leaned forward.

“What games?”

CC smiled.

“I’ll tell you later.”

Declan gave her a look. She only smiled more brightly.

They talked about food, travel, music, and the group’s upcoming schedules. Declan asked about their individual interests rather than treating BLUE HOUR as a single unit.

He learned who liked travelling, who preferred staying home, who was interested in fashion, and who was currently obsessed with learning a new language.

When one of them mentioned that they had been trying to improve their cooking, Declan asked what she liked making.

“Nothing very impressive.”

“That’s all right. I have a limited standard.”

CC laughed.

“He’s terrible at coffee.”

“I’ve improved.”

“Have you?”

“I have been told so.”

“By whom?”

He glanced at her. She smiled innocently. The others laughed.

At some point, Pim moved to sit beside CC and whispered something that made her cover her face. Declan looked over.

“Should I be concerned?”

“Yes,” CC said.

Pim smiled.

“Only a little.”

The box of butter tarts had become noticeably emptier.

One of the members picked up the darkest tart.

“I think this one deserves a second opinion.”

She took a bite. Then nodded.

“Actually, it’s not bad.”

Declan smiled.

“Thank you.”

“Still a little too dark.”

“I’ll inform the oven.”

CC laughed. Pim pointed at him.

“Next time, less ambitious.”

“Understood.”

“Your future father-in-law has given you a lot of responsibility.”

CC nearly choked on her tea.

“Pim!”

Declan, however, looked perfectly composed.

“I take his instructions seriously.”

The room erupted in laughter. CC turned towards him, her cheeks pink. He leaned slightly closer.

“Was that inappropriate?”

She gave him a look.

“You’re enjoying this.”

“Quite a lot.”

She tried not to smile. She failed. When the others finally began gathering their things, the atmosphere had changed completely. The initial curiosity had softened into something warmer.

Pim stood near the door, putting her bag over her shoulder.

“Thank you for the butter tarts.”

Declan smiled.

“You’re welcome.”

“Tell your future father-in-law I approve of the filling.”

“I’ll pass that along.”

“And tell him the pastry needs work.”

“I suspect he already knows.”

Pim laughed. Then she looked at CC.

“We’ll talk later.”

CC nodded.

“I know.”

One of the members hugged her before leaving. The others followed, offering their goodbyes to Declan.

“Nice meeting you.”

“Likewise.”

“Come again.”

“I’d be happy to.”

Pim was the last to leave. She looked at Declan.

“Take care of her.”

His face softened.

“I intend to.”

Pim nodded. “And let her take care of you sometimes,” said Pim.

Declan smiled.

“I’ll try.”

“Good.”

She turned to CC.

“Bye.”

“Bye, Pim.”

The door closed. The apartment was quiet. Then CC turned towards Declan.

He was looking at the empty butter tart box.

“Well?”

She walked closer.

“Well, what?”

“Have I passed?”

She pretended to consider it.

“Promising.”

He laughed.

“That seems to be the standard.”

She wrapped her arms around his waist.

“They liked you.”

“Did they?”

“Yes.”

“All of them?”

“Mostly.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“Mostly?”

“Pim will probably need another meeting.”

“I expected as much.”

CC smiled against his chest.

“They were happy to meet you.”

“I’m glad.”

She looked up.

“You asked them good questions.”

“I wanted to know them.”

“Why?”

“Because they’re important to you.”

Her face softened.

“They’ve been with me for a long time.”

“I know.”

“They know me in ways you don’t yet.”

Declan nodded.

“I would expect that.”

She studied him.

“Does that bother you?”

“No.”

He brushed his hand over her hair.

“I don’t need to know every version of you before I can love you. I’d rather keep learning.”

She lifted her eyes to his. He kissed her then, properly, slow and sure, until the empty box and the inspection and Pim’s whispered verdict went quiet. When he drew back, he rested his forehead against hers.

“Did I do all right?”

She nodded.

“Very well.”

“Then I suppose the inspection was successful.”

“Mostly.”

He laughed. She reached up and straightened his collar.

“Thank you for coming.”

“Thank you for inviting me.”

“And thank you for making the butter tarts.”

“You’re welcome.”

She looked towards the empty box.

“Although I think you should practise more.”

“I agree.”

“Perhaps next time you can make them for everyone again.”

He smiled.

“Next time?”

She nodded.

“They’ll want another inspection.”

“Then I’ll prepare accordingly.”

CC laughed and hugged him again. He held her close, looking down at the woman who had introduced him to the people who had shared so much of her life before he arrived. He had come expecting to be examined.

He hadn’t expected to leave knowing more about her.

And that, he thought, had been the better part of the afternoon.

That evening, As they began clearing the table, CC picked up the last butter tart.

She broke it in half and offered him a piece. He accepted. She tasted hers, then looked at him.

“Still promising.”

Declan smiled.

“I’ll take it.”

She leaned over and kissed his cheek.

“Good. Because I like them.”

He looked at her.

“Then I’ll make them again.”

And this time, she didn’t tease him. She smiled.

chapters.title: Her Own Song
chapters.desc: Her first album, a front-row seat in plain sight, a second verse about two quiet cups, and a key to a studio with a blank sign on the door.
chapters.epigraph: “You bought me a studio because I complained once.”
chapters.content:
The green notebook had been on the dressing table all Friday afternoon.

CC had brought it with her to the venue, although she had already memorised every line of the song.

Its dark green leather cover had become slightly worn at the corners. Several pages were filled with handwritten lyrics, crossed-out sentences, little musical notes, and fragments she had written at inconvenient hours. Declan had given it to her in Munich.

She had written quite a lot in it since then.

And tonight, one of those unfinished beginnings would open her first album.

“You’re staring at it again.”

CC looked up. Nicha was standing behind her, holding a garment bag.

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

CC smiled and closed the notebook. Nicha placed the garment bag on the sofa.

“Everything is ready. The soundcheck went well. Your musicians are here, the lighting team has the final cues, and the company has confirmed the running order.”

CC nodded.

“Thank you.”

“How are you feeling?”

She considered the question.

“Nervous.”

“Good.”

CC looked at her.

“Good?”

“It means you care.”

Nicha sat beside her.

“You’ve worked on this for months. You don’t need to be perfect tonight. Just sing the song.”

CC looked at the notebook again.

“I want it to sound like the recording.”

“It will.”

“And I don’t want to forget the second verse.”

Nicha smiled.

“You’ve been singing that verse for three weeks.”

“I know.”

“Then perhaps you should worry about something else.”

CC laughed. Her phone vibrated.

Declan: I’ve arrived.

She smiled before opening the message.

CC: Already?

Declan: I was told the front row was available.

CC: It is.

Declan: Then I thought I should make use of it.

She studied the screen for another moment.

CC: Are you nervous?

His reply came quickly.

Declan: A little.

Her eyebrows rose.

CC: You?

Declan: I have a considerable interest in the person performing tonight.

She smiled.

CC: That’s a very serious responsibility.

Declan: I intend to fulfil it.

She put the phone down. Nicha glanced at her.

“Declan?”

CC nodded.

“He’s here.”

“Good.”

Nicha stood.

“Then let’s get you ready.”

That evening, the venue was smaller than the arenas where BLUE HOUR usually performed.

It had been designed for the solo showcase: an intimate stage, carefully arranged lighting, a live band, and an audience that included fans, industry guests, collaborators, friends, and family.

The showcase was called Until Morning, after the album. It wasn’t an album launch. It was an introduction.

The audience began filling the hall shortly after seven. There were cameras near the back, but the atmosphere felt more like a concert than a press event.

Declan arrived with Alexander shortly before the doors closed.

He wore a charcoal suit and a white shirt, without a tie. He had considered wearing the plum one CC had given him, but decided against it tonight. He wanted her to be the focus, not another reminder of their relationship. There was no private viewing suite. No concealed entrance.

No attempt to sit somewhere the audience couldn’t see him. His seat was in the front row.

Alexander accompanied him to the row and checked the reserved seating.

“Everything is in order, sir.”

“Thank you.”

“Would you like me to remain nearby?”

“No. Enjoy the performance.”

Alexander nodded and moved towards the side seating. Declan sat down.

A few people nearby recognised him. There were discreet glances, some whispers, and one person who seemed to be debating whether to take a photograph. He didn’t react. He was there to watch CC. A moment later, the lights dimmed. The audience quietened. And the stage went dark.

That evening, the opening film showed a sunlit corridor. A quiet room. An empty piano.

The camera moved slowly through familiar spaces, catching little details: a cup left on a table, sunlight across a wooden floor, a curtain moving in an open window. Then CC’s voice came through the speakers.

“Yǒuxiē guāng, bú shì wèile zhàoliàng shìjiè.”

Some light wasn’t meant to illuminate the world.

A pause.

“Zhǐ shì wèile ràng yí gè rén, zhīdào zìjǐ bìng bù gūdān.”

Only to let one person know they aren’t alone.

The screen faded. A single spotlight appeared at the centre of the stage. CC walked into it.

She wore an ivory dress with delicate, flowing sleeves. Her hair fell naturally over her shoulders, and her makeup was soft, almost understated. The audience applauded. She smiled and bowed.

“Good evening.”

The applause grew louder.

“Thank you for coming tonight.”

She looked around the room. There were familiar faces, fans holding light sticks, members of her team, and her friends from BLUE HOUR. Then, in the front row, she saw Declan. He was looking directly at her. No private suite. No distance. Just him, sitting where she could see him. Their eyes met. He smiled. Her own smile softened.

For a brief moment, she felt the nervousness leave her shoulders. She turned towards the microphone.

“This song is called Until Morning.”

The piano began. That evening, the first verse was quiet.

Her voice carried over the piano without needing to compete with it.

The song wasn’t about a dramatic heartbreak or a single moment of loss. It was about the small, difficult spaces between one day and the next.

About feeling tired without knowing how to explain it. About having words that never quite reached the person they were meant for.

About learning that not every uncertainty needed to be resolved before morning. Declan listened without moving. He knew some of the lyrics.

He had heard early recordings, unfinished melodies, and voice notes sent at inconvenient hours. He had heard her sing fragments while making tea in her apartment and hum little phrases while looking through the pages of the green notebook. But this was different.

The arrangement was fuller now. The melody had found its shape. Her voice moved through it with a confidence he hadn’t heard in the earliest recordings. Then came the second verse. And Declan realised she had changed something. The melody softened. The piano became lighter, almost playful. CC sang:

You came with tea when the evening ran too long, Two quiet cups, a little warmth to lean upon. You never asked me to explain the things I couldn’t say, You stayed until the shadows slipped away.

Declan’s expression changed. He knew. The audience heard a tender verse about someone bringing comfort during a difficult time. But he heard something else.

He remembered the first tea he had brought her.

The cups in her apartment. The messages asking whether she had eaten.

The time she had told him not to buy anything, only to bring tea.

He remembered the evening she had asked him to come back into her life with two words.

Bring tea.

And now those words, or something close to them, had found their way into a song. She continued.

Somewhere between the silence and the morning light, I learned that being held could feel like being alright.

She was singing to the room, but for one brief moment, her eyes found his again. A small smile touched her lips. He didn’t look away.

When the final note faded, the audience remained quiet for a second. Then the applause began. CC smiled, visibly relieved. She bowed.

“Thank you.”

The applause continued. She looked towards the musicians and thanked them before turning back to the audience.

“I wrote this song over several months. Some parts were written when I was very tired. Some parts were written when I was happy. And some parts took a little longer than I expected.”

The audience laughed gently. She smiled.

“I think I wanted to write something that felt like my own life. Not necessarily the biggest moments. Just the little things that make ordinary days feel important.”

She glanced towards the front row. Declan was still watching her.

“I hope you can find something of your own in it.”

She bowed again. The lights changed, and the next segment began.

But Declan remained seated, listening to the applause around him. He was proud of her.

Not because the performance was beautiful, or because the song would likely become successful.

He was proud because she had made something that sounded like her.

And she had let him become part of it without allowing him to become the whole story.

That evening, after the showcase, the guests moved into the reception area.

CC was still backstage, changing out of her performance dress and greeting members of the production team. Declan waited near the designated reception area.

He had already spoken with several executives and congratulated the music director. He had no intention of interrupting CC’s work. Then she appeared.

She had changed into a simple pale blue dress, her hair still styled from the performance. She spotted him immediately. Her face brightened.

“Hi.”

He smiled.

“Hello, sweetheart.”

She walked towards him.

“Did you enjoy it?”

He looked over.

“Very much.”

“Really?”

“Very much.”

She smiled.

“What did you think of the song?”

“I liked it.”

She tilted her head.

“Only liked?”

He laughed.

“I thought it was beautiful.”

Her face softened.

“Thank you.”

He looked at her.

“Especially the second verse.”

She tried to look innocent.

“What about it?”

He smiled.

“Would you like me to pretend I don’t know?”

Her cheeks warmed.

“Declan.”

He leaned slightly closer.

“You wrote about the tea.”

She looked away, smiling.

“Perhaps.”

“Two quiet cups?”

She laughed.

“You heard that?”

“I was in the front row.”

“Of course you were.”

He brushed a loose strand of hair away from her cheek.

“I recognised it.”

She considered him.

“Was it too obvious?”

“No.”

“Really?”

“To anyone else, it was a lovely verse about a quiet evening. To me, it was very familiar.”

She smiled.

“Good.”

He looked at her with a warmth that made her lower her eyes.

“Thank you for putting me in your song.”

She shook her head slightly.

“It’s not only about you.”

“I know.”

“It’s about other things too.”

“I know, Cela.”

She looked up.

“But that part is.”

He smiled.

“Then I am especially grateful.”

She laughed and slipped her hand into his. Later that night, the other members of BLUE HOUR found them near the reception area. One of them hugged CC first.

“You were wonderful!”

“Thank you.”

“That second verse!”

CC immediately looked at her.

“What about it?”

The member grinned.

“Nothing.”

Pim appeared behind them.

“Nothing at all.”

CC narrowed her eyes.

“You all heard it?”

“Of course we heard it. We were sitting right there,” Pim said.

Declan smiled. Pim looked at him.

“Did you recognise it?”

“Yes.”

Pim nodded, looking satisfied.

“Good.”

CC sighed.

“You’re all impossible.”

One of the members laughed.

“You’re the one who wrote it.”

Pim turned to Declan.

“Now you understand why we inspect people.”

Declan smiled.

“I believe I have a better understanding.”

“Good. Because now you’re officially part of the song.”

CC covered her face.

“Pim!”

Everyone laughed. Declan leaned slightly towards CC.

“I don’t mind.”

She glanced up at him.

“You’re enjoying this too much.”

“Perhaps.”

Pim pointed at him.

“See? He’s learning.”

Later that night, the reception gradually became quieter. CC had finished greeting the guests and was finally able to sit with Declan in a small private lounge away from the main room.

She removed her earrings and placed them carefully on the table. Declan handed her a glass of water.

“Thank you.”

“Are you tired?”

“A little.”

“Did anyone feed you?”

“Nicha. Twice.”

“Good.”

She drank some water. Then she looked at him.

“What was your favourite part?”

“The second verse.”

She smiled.

“Aside from that.”

He considered it.

“The opening. When you walked onto the stage.”

“Why?”

“Because you looked happy.”

She was quiet. Then she said, “I was.”

He nodded.

“I could tell.”

She leaned back against the sofa.

“I was nervous before the first note. Then I saw you.”

He turned towards her.

“And?”

“I felt better.”

His face softened.

“Good.”

She looked at him.

“I liked that you were in the front row.”

“I wanted to be.”

“You didn’t mind everyone seeing you?”

“No.”

She smiled. She looked down at her hands.

“I think I liked knowing I didn’t have to look for you somewhere hidden.”

Declan reached for her hand.

“You don’t.”

She looked up.

“I know.”

He lifted her hand and kissed it.

“I was proud of you tonight.”

She smiled.

“Thank you.”

“Not because you performed well. Though you did.”

She laughed.

“Then why?”

“Because you made something that was yours. You let people hear it, and you didn’t make it smaller to make it easier for them to understand.”

Her eyes softened.

“I think I wanted to do that.”

“You did.”

She let her head drop onto his shoulder. For a while, they sat.

Then she said, “I have more songs in the notebook.”

He smiled.

“I would expect nothing less.”

“Some are unfinished.”

“Those are my favourite.”

She lifted her head.

“Why?”

“Because I get to hear them before anyone else.”

She smiled.

“Sometimes.”

“Sometimes?”

“Only when you’re behaving.”

He laughed. “I’ll try. Since we’re on the subject of songs.” Then he took an envelope from his jacket.

Inside were a key, a floor plan and a deed with her name on it: a small recording studio in Ari, two rooms and a vocal booth, ten minutes from her apartment.

She read it twice. “Declan.”

“You said in April that booking studio time was the worst part of writing.”

“I said it was annoying.”

“I don’t like you being annoyed. Tonight’s engineer is happy to run it. The sign on the door is yours. I had them leave it blank.” He looked entirely sincere.

“You bought me a studio because I complained once.”

“Twice.”

She had a speech ready for exactly this kind of thing. She looked at the key in her palm, and at him, and forgot every word of it. “Okay.”

“Okay?”

“Okay. But I’m putting the sign up myself.”

“I hoped you would.”

Just after midnight on Saturday, they returned to CC’s apartment after midnight. She carried the green notebook inside herself. Declan noticed.

“Is that the one?”

She nodded.

“The original.”

He took off his jacket and placed it over the chair.

“May I see?”

She handed it to him. He opened it carefully.

The first few pages contained rough notes and fragments. Some lines were crossed out; others had small annotations in the margins.

He turned to a page with UNTIL MORNING written at the top. Below it were the earliest lyrics. The first verse was almost unchanged. The second verse was different.

There were several lines crossed out, replaced by the ones she had sung tonight. He read them. Then he looked at her.

“You changed this part.”

She nodded.

“I wasn’t sure about it at first.”

“Why?”

“It felt too personal.”

He looked down at the page again.

“And now?”

“Now I think it belongs there.”

He closed the notebook.

“Then I’m glad you kept it.”

She took it back and placed it on the table.

“Thank you for the notebook.”

He smiled.

“You’re welcome.”

“And for coming tonight.”

“I wouldn’t have missed it.”

She walked towards him and wrapped her arms around his waist. He held her close.

“You’re going to have a very busy few weeks,” he said.

“I know.”

“Interviews, performances, promotions.”

She sighed.

“Don’t remind me.”

He laughed and pressed a kiss into her hair.

“Then let’s not discuss them tonight.”

She looked up.

“Can we just sit?”

“Of course.”

They settled on the sofa. CC leaned against him, and Declan rested his arm around her shoulders. After a few minutes, she spoke.

“Declan?”

“Hm?”

“Do you know what I was thinking when I wrote the second verse?”

“What?”

She smiled.

“I remembered the first time you brought me tea. You didn’t know what I was thinking, and you didn’t try to make me explain it.”

He listened.

“I think I liked that you didn’t need me to be interesting all the time. I could just sit there and drink tea.”

He brushed his thumb over her shoulder.

“You never have to be interesting for me.”

She smiled.

“That’s good. Sometimes I’m very boring.”

“I’ll take my chances.”

She laughed. Then she settled against him again. She settled against him again, the key still in her hand, and he didn’t move until she was asleep.

chapters.title: His Turn
chapters.desc: His birthday, planned by her from the first croissant to the last candle. He finds it very hard to be spoiled, and then he lets her.
chapters.epigraph: “So let me.”
chapters.content:
On Friday evening, in Munich, Declan had received a message from CC three hours earlier.

Cela: What time are you free tomorrow?

He had replied while leaving a meeting.

Declan: My afternoon is clear. Why?

Cela: Nothing. Just asking.

He had reread the message.

Declan: Should I be concerned?

Cela: No.

Declan: That wasn’t particularly reassuring.

Cela: Goodnight, Declan.

He smiled at his phone. Now, standing in his Munich apartment, he received another message.

Cela: Also, don’t make plans for tomorrow morning.

He typed a reply.

Declan: I wasn’t aware I had plans.

Cela: You do now.

He put his phone down, amused. It wasn’t unusual for CC to be secretive when she was planning something. She had a habit of asking apparently innocent questions before revealing that she had already made arrangements.

He suspected she was preparing something for his birthday.

He hadn’t told her what he wanted because he didn’t want anything.

His birthday had never been an occasion he considered especially important. There would usually be a call from his parents, dinner at the family residence, perhaps a few messages from colleagues and friends. The company would acknowledge it discreetly. His mother would insist on a cake. That was enough.

He was accustomed to arranging things for other people. Being the recipient of arrangements was less familiar. He picked up his phone again.

Declan: May I at least know what I should wear?

The reply came almost immediately.

Cela: Something comfortable.

He raised an eyebrow.

Declan: That’s unusually vague.

Cela: You’ll survive.

He smiled.

Declan: I expect to.

A moment later, another message arrived.

Cela: Happy almost birthday, sweetheart.

He read it twice. Then he put the phone down, his expression softer than before.

On Saturday morning, Declan woke to the sound of his doorbell.

He checked the time before getting out of bed. It was a little after eight.

He had expected CC to call, but not quite this early.

When he opened the door, she was standing outside with a small paper bag in one hand and a bouquet of flowers in the other.

White lisianthus, pale yellow roses, and a few delicate branches of greenery.

She was wearing a cream cardigan over a simple dress, her hair loosely tied back.

“Good morning.”

He looked at her, then at the flowers.

“Good morning.”

“Happy birthday.”

She smiled and held the bouquet out. He accepted it.

“Thank you.”

She glanced at his face.

“You’re supposed to look happier.”

He laughed.

“I’m trying to understand how you got here before nine.”

“I took a flight.”

“I gathered that.”

“And I came here.”

“I gathered that too.”

She gave him a small, pleased smile. He stepped aside.

“Come in, sweetheart.”

She walked inside, setting the paper bag on the kitchen counter.

“Did you sleep well?”

“Very well.”

“Good. I brought breakfast.”

He looked at the bag.

“You didn’t need to.”

“I know.”

She took out two small boxes. One contained pastries from a bakery she had found the previous afternoon. The other held a selection of fruit.

“I didn’t know what you usually eat for breakfast on your birthday,” she explained, “so I brought a few things.”

He looked at the boxes. Then at her.

“You arranged all this?”

“Most of it.”

“Cela.”

She turned.

“What?”

He was smiling, but there was something slightly uncertain in his expression.

She approached him and gently adjusted the collar of his shirt.

“Today is your birthday.”

“I know.”

“So let me.”

He looked down at her. It was a simple request.

He could have argued that she had travelled, that she didn’t need to spend her morning arranging breakfast, that he would have been perfectly happy with a phone call. Instead, he nodded.

“All right.”

Her smile grew.

“Good.”

She reached up and kissed his cheek.

“Now go wash your face. Breakfast is waiting.”

He watched her walk towards the kitchen. He remained where he was.

Then he went to do as he had been told.

That morning, breakfast was served at the small dining table beside the window.

CC had arranged everything herself, including the flowers in a vase she had found in his kitchen.

Declan sat opposite her, watching as she poured coffee.

“Careful,” she said.

He glanced at the cup.

“Why?”

“Because I made it.”

He smiled.

“Should I be concerned?”

“Very.”

She handed him the cup. He took a sip. It was good. He watched her.

“Excellent.”

She looked pleased.

“I practised.”

“On whom?”

“Myself.”

“A brave decision.”

She laughed. They ate slowly, talking about her flight, her work, and the weather. CC had arrived in Munich the previous evening and had stayed at the hotel she had booked for herself.

Declan had offered to have a car collect her, but she had declined. She wanted to manage the arrangements herself.

He had respected that, though he had asked her to message him when she arrived.

Now, as she cut a pastry in half, he noticed a small envelope beside her plate.

“What is that?”

She followed his gaze.

“Oh.”

She picked it up and slid it towards him.

“Your first present.”

He opened it. Inside was a photograph. It showed the two of them in the Swiss countryside, standing beside a wooden fence. CC was laughing at something outside the frame, while Declan was looking at her rather than the camera. He remembered the photograph.

It had been taken during their first holiday together, when she had been trying to persuade him that a particular goat liked her more than the others. He turned it over. On the back, she had written:

For all the places we’ve been, and all the ordinary days still waiting for us.

He tilted his head.

“You kept this?”

“I liked it.”

“So did I.”

She smiled.

“I thought you might like having it somewhere you can see it.”

He looked at the photograph again. Then he stood, walked around the table, and kissed her temple.

“Thank you, Cela.”

She smiled against his shirt.

“You’re welcome.”

He returned to his seat and placed the photograph carefully beside him. Not in a drawer.

Not among the other things he had been given. Somewhere he could see it.

That morning, the first part of the day was deliberately ordinary.

CC had planned a walk through the English Garden.

She had checked the weather, chosen a route, and even looked up a small café where they could stop for lunch.

Declan discovered this when she took a folded piece of paper from her handbag. He looked at it.

“Is that an itinerary?”

She looked down.

“Maybe.”

He smiled.

“Of course it is.”

“It’s not very detailed.”

He unfolded it. There were three handwritten notes.

Walk.

Lunch.

Something else.

He looked up.

“What is something else?”

“You’ll find out.”

“Should I be worried?”

“No.”

He folded the paper and returned it to her.

“Then I shall remain patient.”

They walked beneath the trees, occasionally stopping to look at the river or watch people cycling past. CC held his hand.
