Sometimes she talked about something she had seen in Bangkok. Sometimes she was quiet, looking around with the relaxed curiosity he had come to recognise.

At one point, she stopped beside a small flower stall.

She examined a bunch of pale yellow flowers before turning to him.

“Do you like these?”

He looked at them.

“They’re lovely.”

She bought them. Declan watched as she handed them to the vendor.

“More flowers?”

“Yes.”

“You’ve already brought me some.”

“Those are for your home.”

“And these?”

She smiled.

“For you.”

He laughed. She looked pleased with herself.

“You don’t have to understand.”

“I see.”

He took the flowers from her when they left. He carried them himself.

That afternoon, lunch was at a small restaurant CC had found near the garden.

It wasn’t one of the places Declan usually visited.

The menu was uncomplicated, the room bright, and the tables close enough together that they could hear a family celebrating at the next table.

CC had chosen it because she thought he would like the food.

She had also made a reservation under her own name. Declan noticed.

“You made the reservation?”

“Yes.”

“Not Alexander?”

“No.”

He smiled.

“Then I must congratulate you on your excellent administrative work.”

She laughed.

“I can make reservations.”

“I never doubted your abilities.”

She looked at him over her glass.

“You say that as if you’re surprised.”

“Not at all.”

He reached for his water.

“I’m simply enjoying being the person who doesn’t have to arrange anything.”

She smiled.

“Are you?”

He considered the question.

“More than I expected.”

She looked satisfied. They ordered lunch. When the waiter came to ask about dessert, CC turned to Declan.

“Do you want cake?”

He looked at her.

“Is there a reason you’re asking?”

“It’s your birthday.”

“Then I suppose cake is appropriate.”

She ordered one for him. A small chocolate cake with a candle. When it arrived, she lit the candle herself. Declan looked at it, then at her.

“You’re taking this very seriously.”

“Of course.”

She rested her chin on her hand.

“Make a wish.”

He looked at the candle. He wasn’t accustomed to making wishes.

Most of the things he wanted, he had learned to pursue through decisions, work, and persistence. Wishes weren’t a language he used often. But CC was watching him. So he closed his eyes. Then he blew out the candle. She clapped.

“What did you wish for?”

“If I tell you, it won’t come true.”

She narrowed her eyes.

“That’s convenient.”

He smiled.

“Very.”

She cut the cake and placed the first slice on his plate. He took a bite.

“Good?”

“Very good.”

She watched him with an expression of quiet satisfaction.

He reached across the table and touched her hand.

“You’re enjoying this.”

“I am.”

“Why?”

She thought about it.

“Because you always make everything feel special for me.”

He was quiet.

“And I wanted you to have a day where you didn’t have to think about anything.”

He met her eyes. Then he turned her hand over and kissed her knuckles.

“You’re doing very well.”

She smiled. That afternoon, the surprise was waiting at his apartment.

When they returned, CC asked him to close his eyes. He stopped in the entrance.

“Should I be concerned?”

“No.”

“That’s becoming a recurring answer.”

She laughed.

“Please.”

He closed his eyes. She took his hand and guided him towards the living room.

“Careful.”

“I’m walking.”

“You’re walking too quickly.”

He slowed down. She positioned him in front of the sofa.

“All right.”

He opened his eyes. The room was filled with warm afternoon light.

On the coffee table was a small arrangement of flowers, a bottle of wine, and a carefully wrapped box. Beside it was a second, smaller box.

And on the sofa was a soft grey cashmere throw. Declan looked around. CC stood beside him, smiling.

“I thought we could spend the evening here.”

He looked at the table.

“All of this?”

She nodded.

“I arranged dinner. It will be delivered later.”

He turned towards her.

“You arranged dinner here?”

“Yes.”

“From where?”

She told him. It was a restaurant he liked, but rarely ordered from because he was usually too busy to wait for delivery. He looked at the boxes.

“And those?”

“Open them.”

He picked up the smaller one first. Inside was a leather cardholder in dark brown, understated and beautifully made. He ran his thumb over the surface.

“It’s lovely.”

“I noticed yours was getting old.”

He turned to her. She smiled.

“You’ve been using the same one for years.”

He laughed. He examined the stitching.

“Thank you.”

Then he opened the larger box. Inside was a framed piece of handwritten music. He recognised it immediately.

It was the melody of the first song she had played for him on the night of their first kiss. The notes were written in her handwriting.

At the bottom, beneath the final bar, she had added a small sentence.

For the person who stayed to hear the rest.

He didn’t speak immediately. CC watched his face.

“I thought you might like it.”

He looked at the music. Then at her.

“Did you write this out yourself?”

“Yes.”

“When?”

“A few weeks ago.”

He ran his fingers lightly over the edge of the frame.

It wasn’t expensive in the way most things he owned were expensive. It wasn’t rare or difficult to acquire. But it was entirely hers. He looked at her.

“This is one of the loveliest things anyone has given me.”

Her face softened. She smiled. He set the frame carefully on the table and drew her into his arms.

“Thank you, sweetheart.”

She hugged him back.

“Happy birthday.”

He held her a little longer than usual. That evening, dinner was delivered shortly after seven.

CC had changed into a soft blue dress, and Declan wore a dark knit shirt with the sleeves pushed up.

They ate at the dining table, with the flowers she had bought earlier arranged nearby. There was no large gathering. No formal dinner. No speeches. Just the two of them.

At one point, Declan looked at her across the table.

“May I ask you something?”

She nodded.

“Of course.”

“How long have you been planning this?”

She smiled.

“Since May.”

“May?”

“After the gala.”

He looked amused.

“You’ve been keeping this from me for two months?”

“Yes.”

“Impressive.”

“I had to make sure you didn’t find out.”

“Was that difficult?”

She considered it.

“A little.”

He laughed. She reached for his water.

“I asked Alexander about your schedule.”

His eyebrows lifted.

“You did?”

“Only the dates. I didn’t ask him anything private.”

He looked at her with quiet amusement.

“And what did Alexander say?”

“He said you were likely to have a clear weekend if you didn’t arrange something yourself.”

Declan smiled.

“That sounds like him.”

“I also asked Eleanor about your birthday.”

He looked up.

“My mother?”

“Yes.”

“What did she tell you?”

“That you used to have birthday breakfasts at home, and that you liked chocolate cake when you were younger.”

He shook his head slightly.

“She remembers everything.”

“She was very happy when I asked.”

“I imagine.”

CC smiled.

“She also said I should make sure you don’t work.”

Declan laughed.

“That sounds exactly like her.”

She watched him.

“Did you want to work today?”

He paused.

“Not particularly.”

“Good.”

She reached across the table and touched his hand.

“Then don’t.”

He held her gaze. There was something in the simplicity of the request that stayed with him.

He was used to having his time accounted for. Even when he wasn’t working, he was often thinking about the next meeting, the next decision, the next responsibility. He had become so accustomed to being the person who made things happen that he rarely considered what it might feel like to let someone else take care of the day. He squeezed her hand.

“All right.”

Later that night, the evening ended on the sofa.

The framed music was now on the shelf beside the photograph from Switzerland.

CC had curled up beside him beneath the cashmere throw.

Declan held a glass of water while she leaned against his shoulder.

“Did you have a good birthday?” she asked.

He looked down at her.

“Yes.”

“Just yes?”

He smiled.

“An excellent birthday.”

She nodded, satisfied.

“Good.”

He set his glass down.

“Thank you for today.”

She looked up.

“You don’t have to thank me.”

“I know.”

He brushed his fingers over her hair.

“But I want to.”

She smiled. He looked at her.

“I find it rather difficult.”

“What?”

“Being spoiled.”

She lifted her head.

“Why?”

He thought about it.

“I suppose I’m accustomed to being responsible for things. If something needs arranging, I arrange it. If someone needs something, I make sure it’s taken care of.”

She listened.

“And when someone does something for me, I sometimes find myself thinking about what I should do in return.”

CC was quiet. Then she reached up and touched his cheek.

“You don’t have to do anything in return.”

He studied her.

“I know.”

“Today wasn’t a favour.”

“I know.”

“It was your birthday.”

He smiled.

“You’re very determined.”

“Yes.”

She settled against him again.

“Besides, I like taking care of you.”

His arm tightened gently around her.

“I like that you do.”

She looked up, almost surprised.

“Really?”

“Very much.”

He kissed her hair.

“I think I could get used to it.”

She smiled.

“Good. Because I’m not finished.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“You’re not?”

“No.”

“What else have you planned?”

She shook her head.

“That’s a secret.”

He laughed.

“Another one?”

“Yes.”

He looked at her, his expression warm.

“Then I suppose I’ll have to wait.”

She nodded.

“You can.”

He kissed her, slowly, the throw sliding off her shoulders and his hand warm at the back of her neck, until she made a small sound against his mouth and forgot entirely that she had been in charge all day. When he drew back, she was smiling.

“Happy birthday, Declan.”

He touched his forehead to hers.

“Thank you, Cela.”

For once, he didn’t think about the next morning, the work waiting for him, or the things that needed his attention. He let the evening continue. The flowers were on the table. Her handwriting was framed beside the photograph.

And CC was warm against his side, pleased with the day she had made for him.

chapters.title: Two Keys
chapters.desc: A piano he can’t play in a room she hadn’t seen, a key on a silver ring, and a pale blue charm she has been carrying since May.
chapters.epigraph: “Take it anyway.”
chapters.content:
By Saturday morning in Munich, CC was beginning to suspect that Declan had planned something.

Not because he had said anything suspicious. In fact, he had been unusually ordinary that morning. He had made coffee. Badly.

She had watched him take the first sip, pause, and decide not to comment on it.

“Is it terrible?” she asked.

“It’s drinkable.”

It wasn’t an answer, and they both knew it.

“It’s an answer.”

She laughed and reached for his cup. He moved it out of her reach.

“Don’t.”

“I want to try.”

“I don’t recommend it.”

“Then why are you drinking it?”

His eyes went to her face.

“Because I made it.”

She laughed again, and he smiled before returning to his newspaper.

They were spending the weekend in Munich. CC had arrived on Thursday evening, and Declan had collected her from the airport himself. She was staying with him at his apartment in Lehel, as she had on previous visits. The morning had been slow.

Breakfast, coffee, a little conversation, and no particular urgency to leave the apartment. Until Declan folded his newspaper.

“Would you like to see something?”

She looked up.

“What?”

“Come with me.”

He stood and offered her his hand. She took it.

He led her down the corridor, past his study, towards a room she had seen before but never really explored.

It was a smaller room at the far end of the apartment, with tall windows overlooking the quiet street. CC stepped inside. And stopped. There was a piano.

A beautiful upright piano in a warm, natural wood finish, positioned near the window. Its lines were simple and elegant, with a small bench in front of it. She looked at it. Then at Declan.

“Is this new?”

“Relatively.”

She approached it slowly.

“Since when?”

“Since last month.”

She turned towards him.

“Last month?”

He nodded.

“Yes.”

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

“I wanted you to see it first.”

She looked back at the piano. It was already tuned. A small vase with fresh flowers sat on the nearby table, and a few sheets of music were arranged neatly on the stand. She touched the edge of the instrument.

“It’s lovely.”

“I thought you might like it.”

She met his eyes.

“Declan…”

He smiled.

“Would you like to try it?”

She sat on the bench and lifted the fallboard. Her fingers found the keys.

She played a few notes, then a short phrase from a melody she had been working on. The sound was warm and clear. She smiled.

“It’s beautiful.”

“I’m glad.”

She played another few notes. Then she stopped and looked at him.

“You bought a piano?”

“I did.”

“For this apartment?”

“Yes.”

She narrowed her eyes slightly.

“Because of me?”

He didn’t pretend otherwise.

“Partly.”

She looked at the keys again. He leaned against the doorframe.

“You mentioned once that you sometimes missed having a piano nearby when you travelled. I thought it might be nice to have one here.”

CC was quiet.

She remembered the conversation: a passing comment, one evening in February, that Munich was lovely but quiet without a piano.

She hadn’t expected him to remember.

“You didn’t have to.”

“I know.”

She looked at him.

“Do you even play?”

“Not particularly well.”

She smiled.

“Then who is going to use it?”

He considered her.

“I was hoping you might.”

She laughed.

“That’s a very expensive way to encourage me to practise.”

“I can think of worse ways.”

She shook her head, smiling. Then she turned back to the piano. For a few minutes, she played. Declan stayed where he was, listening.

He liked seeing her at a piano. There was something about the way she became absorbed in the music, the way her shoulders relaxed and her face changed when she found the right notes. When she finished, she looked over her shoulder.

“Thank you.”

“You’re welcome.”

He held out his hand.

“There’s something else.”

She looked at him suspiciously.

“More?”

“One thing.”

She stood and followed him back into the living room.

That morning, Declan went to the small console table near the entrance.

He opened a drawer and took out a key. It was attached to a simple silver keyring. CC looked at it. Then at him. He held it out.

“Here.”

She didn’t take it immediately.

“What is it?”

“A key.”

“I can see that.”

He smiled.

“To the apartment.”

She looked at the key again. She didn’t say anything. Declan waited.

He said, “I thought you might like to have one. So you don’t need to arrange your arrival around me being here. If I’m working, travelling, or delayed, you can come in whenever you like.”

She looked up.

“Declan.”

He spoke gently.

“There’s no expectation attached to it. You don’t have to use it. I simply thought it might make things easier.”

She looked at the key in his hand. It was such a small object. But it represented something much larger.

Not a hotel room, not a carefully arranged visit.

Not a weekend that began when he collected her from the airport and ended when he took her back. A place she could enter without asking.

A place where her presence was expected, even if he wasn’t there yet. She took a small breath.

“You’re giving me a key to your home?”

“Yes.”

She turned to him.

“That’s quite a big thing.”

“I know.”

“You make it sound very simple.”

He smiled.

“It is simple, in one sense.”

She waited.

“I want you to have a place here. Not as a guest who needs to be invited every time. As someone who belongs here whenever she wants to be.”

Her face softened.

Then she looked down at the key again. “It’s too much.”

“It’s a key.”

“You know what I mean.”

“I do. Take it anyway.” He didn’t lower his hand.

She looked at it: the small silver ring, the door it opened, all the ordinary arrivals it promised. Then the smile came, the one he waited for every time, and she held out her hand. “Okay.”

He placed the key in her palm. She closed her fingers around it.

“Thank you.”

He watched her. Then he reached for her hand and kissed her knuckles.

“You’re welcome, sweetheart.”

She looked at the key again. Then she slipped it into the small pocket of her handbag. Declan smiled.

“Is that where it lives now?”

She nodded.

“Yes.”

“Good.”

She looked up at him.

“But I’m still going to call you when I arrive.”

He laughed.

“Of course you are.”

“Even if you aren’t home.”

“Especially then.”

She smiled. Then she stepped closer and wrapped her arms around him. He held her. There was no grand declaration.

No promise about where they would live, or how often she would visit, or what the key meant for the future. It was a key. And she had chosen to accept it. That afternoon, they had lunch at home. CC returned to the piano afterwards.

She played for nearly an hour, moving between familiar pieces and fragments of her own compositions.

Declan worked at the dining table with his laptop, occasionally looking up when she found a melody she liked.

At one point, she played the first few bars of the song from THE FIRST LIGHT. He looked up.

“That one?”

She nodded without turning.

“I wanted to hear how it sounds here.”

He closed his laptop.

“Would you like me to listen?”

She held his gaze.

“You’re already listening.”

“Then I shall continue.”

She smiled and began again. When she finished, he applauded. She turned on the bench.

“You’re very polite.”

“I am your most loyal audience.”

“Your only audience, perhaps.”

“That is a competitive position.”

She laughed. He stood and came over to her.

“May I?”

She moved slightly to make room. He sat beside her on the bench.

The two of them were a little too close for the instrument, and she smiled when his shoulder brushed hers.

“Are you going to play?”

“I was considering it.”

“Should I be worried?”

“Probably.”

He pressed a few keys. The notes were hesitant and uneven. CC tilted her head.

“That’s what you know?”

“More or less.”

She laughed.

“You’re terrible.”

“I warned you.”

She reached over and adjusted his fingers.

“Here.”

He looked down at their hands. She guided him through a simple chord.

“Now this.”

He tried again. The sound was better. He looked at her.

“Impressive.”

“You’re welcome.”

He turned his head slightly.

“Thank you for teaching me.”

She smiled.

“You’re welcome.”

He leaned over and kissed her cheek. Then he stood, leaving the bench to her.

“Your piano now.”

She studied his face.

“Our piano.”

His face softened. “Yes.”

He bent and kissed her where she sat, one hand flat on the piano lid beside her head, and when her elbow pressed three low keys at once, neither of them stopped. That evening, they stayed in. Dinner was simple, and the apartment was quiet.

CC sat on the sofa with her legs tucked beneath her, reading while Declan answered a few messages. At some point, she put her book down.

“Declan?”

He looked up.

“Yes?”

“Can I ask you something?”

“Always.”

“Where would you keep a key to my apartment?”

He looked up. “In my wallet, I imagine. Why?”

She looked thoughtful. Then she stood.

“Wait here.”

He watched her walk towards her handbag. She took out a small keyring and returned.

It was a simple key, attached to a pale blue charm. She placed it in his palm. He looked at it. Then at her.

“What’s this?”

“My apartment key.”

He turned it over.

“You’re giving me your key?”

She nodded.

“Yes.”

He was quiet. Then he looked at her.

“Are you sure?”

She smiled.

“Yes.”

“You’re not doing this because I gave you mine?”

“No.”

She sat beside him.

“I’ve been thinking about it for a while.”

He listened.

“I want you to be able to come in without waiting for me, too. If I’m working late or you’re arriving before me. I don’t want you to have to stand outside and call.”

He smiled.

“That would be inconvenient.”

“Very.”

She leaned back against the sofa.

“And I want you to have a place in my home, too.”

His face softened. Her eyes went to his.

“Not because I expect you to come all the time. Just because I want you to know you can.”

He closed his fingers around the key.

“Thank you.”

She smiled.

“You’re welcome.”

He looked down at the little blue charm.

“Did you choose this?”

“Yes.”

“When?”

“A few months ago.”

He looked at her again.

“You’ve been planning this?”

She nodded.

“Since I started thinking about your birthday.”

He laughed.

“Apparently, we’re both better at keeping secrets than I thought.”

She smiled.

“Maybe.”

He slipped the key into his wallet. Then he put it back into his pocket. CC watched him.

“You’re keeping it there?”

“Yes.”

“Not in a drawer?”

“No.”

She smiled.

“Good.”

He reached for her hand.

“Then I suppose we have two keys now.”

She lifted her eyes to his.

“Two keys.”

“Two homes we can enter without asking.”

Her smile became softer.

“Yes.”

He lifted her hand and kissed it.

“I like that.”

She leaned against him.

“So do I.”

For a while, neither spoke. Then CC looked up.

“Although…”

He glanced down.

“Although?”

“You still have to tell me when you’re coming to Bangkok.”

He laughed.

“I thought I had a key.”

“You do.”

“Then why?”

“Because I might not be home.”

“That’s a reasonable objection.”

“And I might want to clean.”

He smiled.

“Your apartment is always lovely.”

“Declan.”

“All right.”

She laughed and leaned into his shoulder. He kissed her hair. The next morning, CC woke before him.

She found him asleep on his side, one arm resting across the empty space between them. She watched him. Then she carefully slipped out of bed. She made coffee. It was better than his.

She placed two cups on the kitchen counter and returned to the bedroom.

“Declan.”

He opened his eyes.

“Good morning.”

“Good morning.”

She sat at the foot of the bed.

“Your coffee is ready.”

He glanced at her.

“Did you make it?”

“Yes.”

“Then I have high expectations.”

She smiled.

“You should.”

He reached for her hand and pulled it gently towards him, kissing her palm.

“Thank you.”

He asked, “When are you leaving?”

“Tomorrow afternoon.”

He nodded.

“Then we have today.”

“Yes.”

She looked towards the bedroom door.

“I want to play the piano again.”

“Then you should.”

“And maybe we can go out for lunch.”

“Wherever you like.”

She smiled.

“Good.”

He sat up and drew her into a brief embrace.

The key was in her handbag, waiting for the next time she came. His was in his wallet.

Neither of them had made a promise about how often they would use them. They didn’t need to. On Monday evening, in Bangkok, CC was home.

Her suitcase stood beside the bedroom door, still unopened. The apartment was quiet, familiar, and warm.

She placed her handbag on the console table and took out her key. She looked at it.

Then she opened the small drawer where she kept spare keys and other little things. She didn’t put it there.

Instead, she placed it in the small ceramic dish beside the entrance. A place she could see. A place she would remember. Her phone rang. Declan. She answered.

“Hello.”

“Home?”

“Just arrived.”

“How was the flight?”

“Good. A little tired.”

“Did you sleep on the plane?”

“Some.”

“Liar.”

She laughed. He was in Munich, probably back at his desk, with the workday still waiting for him.

“Declan?”

“Yes?”

“Your key is by my door.”

He smiled.

“I know.”

“And mine is in your wallet.”

“Yes.”

She leaned against the kitchen counter.

“That’s nice.”

He was quiet. Then he said, “I thought so too.”

She smiled.

“I’ll see you soon.”

“I’ll come back soon.”

“Goodnight, thi rak.”

“Goodnight, Cela.”

After the call, she looked at the little key in the ceramic dish.

It was an ordinary key. She left it where she could see it.

chapters.title: Two Families
chapters.desc: Thanksgiving in Markham: two mothers, two fathers, a new oven nobody is supposed to mention, and Richard, unexpectedly, better at pastry than his son.
chapters.epigraph: “Your father won’t tell you, so I will.”
chapters.content:
On Sunday afternoon, in Toronto, CC spotted them before Declan did.

“There’s Eleanor.”

Declan followed her gaze towards the arrivals hall. His mother was standing beside Richard, wearing a camel coat and holding a small bouquet of flowers. Richard had one hand on the handle of their luggage and the other resting lightly against his wife’s back. Eleanor saw them. Her face brightened.

“CC!”

CC smiled and stepped forward.

“Eleanor.”

Eleanor embraced her warmly, careful not to crush the flowers between them.

“Oh, it’s so lovely to see you.”

“You too.”

“I’ve been looking forward to this for weeks.”

CC laughed. Richard approached next.

“Hello, CC.”

“Richard. Welcome to Canada.”

He offered her a warm hug.

“Thank you. It’s good to finally be here.”

Declan greeted his father with a handshake that turned into a brief embrace, then kissed his mother’s cheek.

“How was the flight?”

“Long,” Eleanor answered, “but perfectly comfortable.”

Richard looked at him.

“Your mother slept for most of it.”

“That’s not true.”

“You were asleep before we finished dinner.”

Eleanor turned to CC.

“He exaggerates.”

CC smiled.

“I think I’ll believe you.”

Richard gave a small, approving nod.

“Good decision.”

Declan looked between them.

“You’re already taking sides?”

“Your mother and I have been exchanging messages,” CC said.

Eleanor smiled.

“Quite a few, actually.”

Declan looked over.

“Have you?”

“Of course. I wanted to know what time you were arriving, whether you had packed warm clothes, and whether CC had eaten.”

He looked at CC.

“Did you answer?”

“Yes.”

“All of them?”

“Most of them.”

Eleanor gave him a look.

“She answers much more politely than you do.”

Richard picked up the second suitcase.

“That has never been difficult.”

Declan sighed. CC laughed. It was only a few minutes into their reunion, and already she felt the warmth of something she had hoped for. Not a formal meeting. Not two families carefully observing one another.

Just people who had been looking forward to sharing a table.

That evening, in Markham, the drive to Markham was filled with conversation.

Eleanor asked about CC’s latest recording sessions, her group, and whether she had been sleeping enough. Richard asked Declan about a recent business trip, then listened as CC explained how the solo album had developed since its release.

When they arrived, CC’s mother was already waiting at the front door.

She opened it before they had reached the steps.

“You’re here!”

CC smiled.

“Mum.”

Her mother embraced her first, then stepped back to greet Eleanor.

For a brief moment, both women seemed to hesitate.

They had spoken before, of course. They had exchanged greetings over video calls, talked about birthdays and travel, and sent messages through CC and Declan. But meeting in person was different. Then Eleanor reached for her hands.

“Finally.”

CC’s mother laughed.

“Finally.”

They embraced. It was warm and immediate, the kind of greeting that made the distinction between acquaintance and family feel less important.

“I’m so happy you could come,” CC’s mother said.

“We’ve wanted to visit for a long time. And thank you for inviting us into your home,” Eleanor replied.

“Oh, please. You’re very welcome.”

Richard greeted her next. CC’s father appeared from the kitchen, wiping his hands on a tea towel.

“Richard.”

“Good to meet you.”

They shook hands.

“Likewise. I hope you had a comfortable flight.”

“Very comfortable, thank you.”

CC’s father looked at Declan.

“You’re looking after everyone?”

“Trying to.”

“Good. Come inside before your mother freezes.”

Eleanor laughed. Richard took off his coat.

“Already being assigned responsibilities.”

CC’s father smiled.

“You’re in Canada now. We have rules.”

On Monday morning, thanksgiving morning began with the smell of butter. CC woke to voices downstairs.

She stayed beneath the duvet for another minute, listening. Her mother’s voice came from the kitchen. Eleanor answered. Then she heard her father’s familiar laugh. And another voice. Declan. She smiled.

When she came downstairs, she found the kitchen already busy.

Her mother and Eleanor were preparing vegetables at the island. Richard was standing near the counter, examining a tray of pastry dough. Her father was measuring something into a mixing bowl. Declan was wearing an apron. CC stopped in the doorway. He looked up.

“Good morning.”

She glanced at his hands.

“You’re baking again?”

He smiled.

“Apparently.”

Her father looked over.

“He volunteered.”

Richard gave a small laugh.

“I believe he was encouraged.”

Eleanor turned.

“Good morning, darling.”

“Good morning.”

CC kissed her mother’s cheek, then Eleanor’s. Her mother handed her a cup of tea.

“You’re just in time.”

“For what?”

“Your father has decided to make more butter tarts.”

CC looked at the mixing bowl.

“Again?”

Her father nodded.

“Thanksgiving.”

“Of course.”

Her mother leaned closer and lowered her voice. “Your father won’t tell you, so I will. The new oven at the bakery is very good.”

CC turned slowly. “What new oven?”

Across the kitchen, Declan became interested in his pastry.

“It arrived in September. Your father made him send the first one back because it was too big. The second one fits,” her mother said.

“Declan.”

“He mentioned in March that the old one ran hot on the left,” Declan said, without looking up.

Her father didn’t turn round. “It bakes evenly. That’s all I’ll say,” he said gruffly.

“And the shop next door?”

“Storage. For now,” her father said.

It was, CC understood, the highest praise he had ever given anything. Declan leaned slightly towards her.

“I’ve been assigned pastry.”

She considered him.

“How is that going?”

He glanced at the dough.

“Promising.”

Her father made a quiet sound.

“That’s a generous description.”

CC laughed. Richard was examining the mixture with a level of concentration she hadn’t expected.

“May I?”

Her father moved aside.

“Certainly.”

Richard washed his hands, rolled up his sleeves, and began working the dough. CC watched. He was surprisingly comfortable.

His movements were measured, but not hesitant. He handled the pastry gently, bringing it together without overworking it. Declan looked at his father.

“Have you done this before?”

Richard didn’t look up.

“A little.”

“A little?”

“Enough.”

CC’s father watched him. Then he nodded.

“You’re not bad.”

Richard smiled.

“I’ll take that as a compliment.”

“It is.”

Declan looked at the dough in front of him. Then at his father.

“Apparently, I was not given the same ability.”

Richard finally looked up.

“You were given the same instructions.”

CC laughed so much she had to put down her tea.

That morning, the two mothers had settled into conversation as naturally as if they had known each other for years.

CC noticed it while helping her father arrange the tart shells.

Eleanor and her mother were talking about family traditions, childhood photographs, and the different ways they had celebrated holidays.

“Declan was never particularly interested in cooking,” Eleanor was saying.

Richard, still working on the dough, glanced over.

“He was interested in eating.”

“That’s true,” Eleanor agreed.

CC smiled. Her mother laughed.

“CC was always in the kitchen with her father.”

“Even when she was very little. She wanted to help with everything,” her father added.

“Did she make a mess?” Eleanor asked.

Her mother smiled.

“An enormous one.”

CC looked offended.

“I was helping.”

“You were helping yourself to the filling.”

“Quality control.”

Richard laughed. Declan looked at her.

“That sounds familiar.”

She gave him a smile.

“Don’t start.”

Eleanor turned towards CC’s mother.

“She was always very thoughtful, even when she was young. Declan told me about the little gifts she gives him.”

CC glanced up at him. He was concentrating on his pastry. She narrowed her eyes.

“What did you tell her?”

“Nothing compromising.”

“Declan.”

He smiled.

“Only that you’re thoughtful.”

Eleanor continued, clearly enjoying herself.

“He keeps everything.”

CC looked back at him.

“Everything?”

Richard answered before his son could.

“Everything.”

Eleanor nodded.

“Her Christmas tie. The music she recorded. The little notes.”

CC’s cheeks warmed.

“That’s not—”

“He even has the photograph from Switzerland displayed in his apartment,” Eleanor said.

CC looked at Declan. He met her eyes with a perfectly calm expression.

“I like the photograph.”

She smiled despite herself. Her mother looked between them.

“I think that’s lovely.”

Eleanor smiled.

“So do I.”

CC watched the two women. Her mother was speaking with her hands, explaining how CC used to insist on bringing home small things from walks. Eleanor listened with genuine interest, asking questions and laughing at the right moments. It was a strange, lovely feeling.

The two people who had loved them first were finally sharing the same room. That morning, the pastry competition had become unofficial. Declan had finished his first batch. His father examined it. Richard said nothing.

CC’s father picked up one of the pastry shells and looked at it from several angles.

“Not bad.”

Declan smiled.

“Thank you.”

“Edges are a little thick.”

His smile diminished slightly.

“And this one is uneven.”

Declan looked down. Richard, standing beside him, had already rolled out another sheet. His pastry was smooth, consistent, and remarkably thin. CC looked between the two.

“Dad, I think Richard’s is better.”

Her father nodded.

“Yes.”

Declan watched her.

“You’re not supposed to say that.”

She smiled.

“I’m being honest.”

Richard laughed.

“Your girlfriend has excellent judgement.”

Declan glanced at his father.

“You’re enjoying this.”

“A little.”

CC’s father picked up a piece of Richard’s dough.

“How did you learn?”

Richard shrugged.

“My mother baked. I spent time in the kitchen when I was young.”

“Did you make pastry?”

“Occasionally. I was more interested in bread.”

CC’s father nodded with interest.

“That’s useful. Pastry is less forgiving.”

Richard smiled.

“I’ve noticed.”

Declan looked at the two older men.

“Are we going to discuss the pastry as though I’m not here?”

His father patted his shoulder.

“You can listen and learn.”

CC laughed. She stepped closer to Declan and examined his work.

“Yours are getting better.”

He looked at her.

“Are you trying to comfort me?”

“Yes.”

“Thank you.”

She picked up one of the shells.

“This one is quite nice.”

He smiled.

“Keep that one.”

“Why?”

“Because it’s yours.”

She laughed.

“That’s not how baking works.”

“It is today.”

That afternoon, lunch was a relaxed affair. There was no elaborate seating arrangement. The family gathered around the dining table, passing dishes and helping themselves. CC sat between Declan and her mother. Eleanor sat opposite Richard, beside CC’s father.

The conversation moved easily between work, travel, and family.

At one point, Richard asked CC’s father about the bakery.

“Do you still enjoy it?”

Her father considered the question.

“Very much. It has been part of my life for a long time.”

“And you have family working there?”

“Sometimes CC comes to help when she’s home. Though she spends more time eating than working.”

CC looked up.

“That’s not true.”

Her mother laughed.

“Your father has photographic evidence.”

Declan smiled.

“I’ve seen it.”

She turned towards him.

“You too?”

“Your father showed me.”

“Dad.”

Her father looked pleased.

“Good memories.”

Richard smiled.

“I understand. Eleanor has kept boxes of photographs from when Declan was young. There are several I would prefer she didn’t show anyone.”

Eleanor turned towards him.

“There’s one of him in a sailor outfit.”

Declan closed his eyes.

“Mother.”

CC looked up immediately.

“A sailor outfit?”

Richard nodded.

“Very small. Very serious.”

CC smiled.

“I would like to see that.”

Declan tilted his head.

“Perhaps another time.”

Eleanor smiled.

“I’ll find it.”

He turned towards his mother.

“Please don’t.”

CC was laughing now. Her mother reached across the table and touched Eleanor’s hand.

“I have a few photographs of CC with flour all over her face. Perhaps we can exchange them.”

Eleanor looked delighted.

“I would love that.”

Declan glanced at CC. He could already see where this was going. He decided not to intervene.

That afternoon, after lunch, the family returned to the kitchen. The butter tarts were cooling on the counter. Richard’s pastry had come out beautifully.

Declan’s was less uniform, though improved from his first attempt in March. CC’s father tasted one from each batch. He took his time. Eleanor watched.

“Well?”

Her husband considered the two tarts.

“Richard’s pastry is better.”

Richard smiled. Declan shook his head.

“Of course.”

“But yours has improved.”

“Thank you.”

“Filling is good.”

CC took a bite of Declan’s tart. She nodded.

“Very good.”

He met her eyes. She took another bite.

“Although Richard’s pastry is better.”

He laughed.

“You’re enjoying this.”

“Very much.”

Richard cut one of his tarts in half and offered the other piece to his son.

“Try it.”

Declan did. He looked at the pastry. Then at his father.

“That’s very good.”

Richard nodded.

“Thank you.”

CC’s father smiled.

“Next time, I’ll teach you both.”

Richard looked interested.

“I’d like that.”

Declan glanced between them.

“Both?”

His father smiled.

“Of course.”

CC leaned towards him.

“You need the practice.”

He looked at her.

“I have noticed.”

She smiled and brushed a little crumb from his sleeve. That evening, the evening settled into something quieter.

The dishes had been washed. The kitchen was tidy again, except for a few boxes of leftover tarts waiting to be packed.

CC found Eleanor in the living room, looking through an album of childhood photographs.

“May I?”

“Please.”

CC sat beside her. Eleanor turned a page. There was a photograph of CC at about five years old, standing on a small stool beside her father. Her hands were covered in flour, and she was looking at the camera with a serious expression. Eleanor smiled.

“Oh, look at you.”

CC laughed.

“I remember this.”

“Your father told me you insisted on making the first tart.”

“He always let me.”

Eleanor took in the photograph.

“He must have loved having you there.”

CC smiled.

“He did. He still does.”

Eleanor turned another page. There was a photograph of Declan as a young boy, sitting beside Richard at a kitchen table. His hair was untidy, and he was holding a wooden spoon. CC looked at it.

“Is this him?”

Eleanor nodded.

“His father was teaching him to make bread.”

CC studied the photograph again.

“He’s very serious.”

“He was always serious when he wanted to do something properly.”

CC smiled.

“That hasn’t changed.”

Eleanor laughed. Then she looked at CC.

“Thank you for bringing us here.”

CC turned towards her.

“I’m glad you came.”

“I know we’ve spoken before, but I wanted to meet your parents properly. I wanted to understand the home he has been welcomed into.”

CC’s expression softened.

“They like you.”

Eleanor smiled.

“I like them too.”

She hesitated, then added:

“And I think your mother and I will become friends.”

CC laughed.

“I think so too.”

Eleanor closed the album.

“Declan is very happy with you.”

CC looked down at her hands.

“I know.”

“He doesn’t always say everything he feels. He has always been rather like his father in that respect.”

CC smiled.

“I think he says enough.”

Eleanor reached over and touched her hand.

“Good. He deserves someone who understands him, but he also deserves someone who lets him be understood.”

CC looked at her.

“I try.”

“I can see that.”

Later that night, the evening ended with tea. Both families sat together in the living room, the adults talking while CC leaned against Declan on the sofa. Richard and CC’s father were discussing bread.

Eleanor and CC’s mother were discussing a possible visit to Munich next spring.

“Perhaps when the weather is warmer,” Eleanor suggested.

“That would be lovely.”

“We could spend a few days together.”

CC’s mother smiled.

“I’d like that.”

Richard glanced towards them.

“Perhaps we should have another baking day.”

CC’s father nodded.

“Yes. We need to improve Declan’s pastry.”

Declan looked up.

“Must we continue discussing this?”

Richard smiled.

“I thought it was a useful topic.”

CC laughed against his shoulder. Her father looked at him.

“Don’t worry. You’ll improve.”

Declan gave a small nod.

“I appreciate the encouragement.”

Richard leaned back.

“Though I may have to teach you myself.”

“That would be helpful.”

CC turned towards him.

“Are you accepting that your father is better?”

Declan turned to her.

“Apparently.”

She smiled.

“Good.”

He lowered his voice.

“I’ll have you know that I was considerably better than him at several other things today.”

She looked amused.

“Such as?”

“Driving.”

She laughed.

“That’s not baking.”

“I wasn’t aware we were restricting the competition.”

She shook her head. He kissed her temple. Across the room, their mothers were still talking. Their fathers were comparing notes about pastry.

And for the first time, the two families weren’t separated by a screen, a time zone, or a carefully arranged visit. They were together.

On Tuesday morning, CC woke to the sound of someone moving around downstairs. She found Declan in the kitchen, making coffee. She stood in the doorway, watching him.

“Good morning.”

He looked over.

“Good morning.”

“You’re awake early.”

“I couldn’t sleep.”

She approached him.

“Are you all right?”

He nodded.

“Yes.”

He handed her a cup. She took a sip. It was surprisingly good. She looked at him.

“Your coffee is improving.”

He smiled.

“I’ve had an excellent teacher.”

She leaned against the counter.

“Are you thinking about going home?”

“In a few hours.”

She nodded. He held her gaze.

“I enjoyed yesterday.”

“So did I.”

“Your parents are wonderful.”

She smiled.

“Your parents too.”

He reached for her hand.

“I think our mothers have already planned three more visits.”

“At least.”

“And our fathers have apparently arranged a pastry lesson.”

She laughed.

“Yes.”

He studied her.

“I’ll have to practise before then.”

She smiled.

“Definitely.”

He drew her closer.

“Thank you for having us here.”

She rested her cheek against his chest.

“I’m happy you came.”

He pressed his mouth to her hair. Outside, the morning was cool and quiet.

Inside, the kitchen still smelled of butter and sugar.

There were two families now sharing photographs, recipes, and plans for another visit.

On the counter, among the packed leftovers, sat a box of butter tarts. Richard’s pastry was noticeably better, and Declan had already decided to do something about that before next Thanksgiving.

chapters.title: One Year
chapters.desc: One year since Geneva. The same room, booked for two, the same tea, and a question he has been carrying in his jacket all evening.
chapters.epigraph: “It seemed rude to share.”
chapters.content:
The first thing CC noticed in Geneva that Monday evening was the curtains.

They were the same deep ivory curtains she remembered from the previous year, framing the tall windows of the ballroom at the Hôtel des Bergues. Beyond them, Geneva was turning gold beneath the late autumn light.

The gala had been on Saturday. Tonight the ballroom held a single table, white and pale green flowers, and a string quartet still tuning, and when CC asked the manager where everyone else was, he only smiled and said that Mr. Lincoln had booked the room. All of it.

“You booked the ballroom,” she said.

“I wanted the same room.”

“For two people.”

“It seemed rude to share.” He said it with perfect seriousness, and she laughed so that one of the violinists looked up.

The room itself was unmistakable. She stood near the entrance, looking around.

“Do you remember?”

Declan, standing beside her, glanced at her.

“Very clearly.”

She smiled.

“Exactly here?”

“Almost.”

She looked towards the far side of the ballroom.

A year ago she had sung one song at the Lincoln Foundation’s winter gala, in a champagne gown with an open back, and then sat by the window trying not to shiver. Declan had noticed. He had brought her tea, put his cashmere shawl around her shoulders, and asked for her number as if it were the simplest question in the world.

At the time, she had thought he was handsome, confident, and difficult to read.

She hadn’t known that he would become the person she called when she had something to tell someone, the person whose apartment key she carried in her handbag, or the person who knew exactly how she liked her tea. She looked at him now.

“You were standing there.”

He followed her gaze.

“I was.”

“And I was standing here.”

“Yes.”

“You looked very serious.”

“I was trying to make a good impression.”

She laughed.

“You were succeeding.”

He smiled.

“Good to know.”

She slipped her hand into his.

“One year.”

“One year.”

She looked around again.

“It’s strange.”

“What is?”

“How much can happen in one year.”

He lifted her hand and kissed her knuckles.

“Quite a lot.”

She looked up.

“Are you happy we came back?”

“Very.”

He glanced towards the room.

“I wanted to see it with you again.”

She smiled.

“Me too.”

A member of the hotel staff approached to let them know their table was ready. Declan offered his arm.

“Shall we?”

She took it. That evening, the table was in the same quiet corner.

Not the exact arrangement of the gala, but close enough that CC recognised it immediately.

There were two chairs, a small vase of white flowers, and a view of the ballroom that allowed them to watch the guests without being in the middle of the room. On the table sat a small silver teapot. CC looked at it.

“Tea?”

Declan pulled out her chair.

“I thought we should have it.”

She smiled as she sat down. The waiter poured two cups.

CC lifted hers, inhaled the familiar fragrance, and took a sip. Then she looked at Declan.

“Do you remember the first time you brought me tea?”

“I remember.”

“You chose it without asking me.”

“I had made an educated guess.”

“You were lucky.”

He smiled.

“Was I?”

She nodded.

“Very.”

He took a sip from his own cup.

“I believe I’ve become better at choosing since then.”

“Have you?”

“Considerably.”

She smiled.

“Perhaps.”

He watched her over the rim of his cup.

She had changed in a year, though not in ways that would necessarily be obvious to anyone else.

She was more comfortable with him now. She no longer hesitated before reaching for his hand, or worried that a quiet evening together meant she ought to make conversation. She had learned that she could be tired, distracted, playful, stubborn, or silent, and he would still be there.

He had changed too. He had learned to ask rather than assume. To wait rather than arrange. To understand that being able to give someone something didn’t mean he should decide they needed it. He had learned to leave room.

And, perhaps most importantly, he had learned that there were parts of his life he no longer wanted to experience without her. CC put her cup down.

“What are you thinking?”

He smiled.

“That you look lovely.”

She gave him a small look.

“That’s not what you were thinking.”

“No?”

“No. You had a very serious expression.”

He laughed.

“Perhaps I was remembering something.”

“What?”

“The first time I saw you here.”

She smiled.

“You remember what I wore?”

“Yes.”

“What colour?”

“Pale champagne.”

She looked surprised.

“You remember?”

“Of course.”

“What else?”

He considered it.

“You were sitting by that window with a glass of water, pretending you weren’t cold. You’d just sung, and you were the only person in the room who didn’t seem to know how good it was.”

She laughed.

“I was.”

“I thought so.”

“And you came over.”

“I did.”

“Why?”

His eyes went to her face.

“Because I wanted to meet you.”

She smiled.

“That was a good decision.”

“It was.”

That evening, dinner was served slowly. They talked about the year behind them.

Their first lunch in Bangkok. The flowers at her apartment. The first kiss. The Christmas tie. The Swiss farmhouse, the cows, and the goat that had apparently developed a personal interest in CC’s pockets.

She laughed when he reminded her of the goat.

“It stole something from me.”

“It attempted to.”

“It succeeded.”

“It took a tissue.”

“Still.”

He smiled. They spoke about Paris, Munich, Markham, and the birthday she had planned for him.

Declan told her that his mother still talked about the Thanksgiving visit.

“She has already suggested that we invite your parents to Munich next year.”

CC smiled.

“Mum would like that.”

“Richard has also mentioned another baking lesson.”

She laughed.

“Your father?”

“Apparently, he has decided your father is an excellent teacher.”

“He is.”

“I agree.”

She looked at him with amusement.

“Are you still practising?”

“Occasionally.”

“How is the pastry?”

“Improving.”

She smiled.

“Good.”

He watched her. There was something he wanted to tell her, but he wasn’t in a hurry.

He wanted to remember this evening exactly as it was: her laughter, the tea, the familiar room, the small movements of her hands as she spoke. He had spent several months thinking about this.

Not because he was uncertain about what he wanted.

Because he wanted to be certain that he was asking her at a time when she could hear the question without feeling that the answer had already been decided for her. He had spoken with his parents. He had spoken with her parents.

Not to ask permission, but because they mattered to her, and because he respected the place they held in her life.

He had spoken with no one else about the details. The decision was his. The answer would be hers.

Later that night, after dinner, Declan asked whether she wanted another cup of tea. CC looked at him.

“Again?”

He smiled.

“Would you object?”

“No.”

He signalled to the waiter. The ballroom had grown quieter. Some guests had moved towards the reception area, and the musicians were playing something soft in the background. CC wrapped both hands around her cup.

“Do you remember what you said to me the first time we spoke?”

He considered her.

“Several things.”

“You said I looked cold.”

“You were.”

“And then you gave me your shawl.”

“You were shivering.”

She smiled.

“Then you asked for my number.”

“I did.”

“You were very confident.”

He laughed.

“I was trying to be.”

“Did you think I would give it to you?”

“I hoped you would.”

She tilted her head.

“What if I hadn’t?”

“I would have thanked you for the conversation and wished you a pleasant evening.”

She smiled.

“Very polite.”

“I try.”

She reached across the table and touched his hand.

“I’m glad I did.”

He turned his palm upward, letting her fingers settle into his.

“So am I.”

There was a quiet pause. Then Declan looked at her.

“Cela.”

She lifted her eyes.

“Yes?”

“I’ve been thinking about what I wanted to say to you tonight.”

Her face changed slightly. Not alarmed, but attentive. He held her hand.

“One year ago, I met you in this room. I didn’t know much about you then. I knew your name, your work, and that you were cold.”

She smiled.

“I was.”

“I thought you were beautiful. I wanted to know you. And I was fortunate enough that you allowed me to.”

He paused.

“Over the past year, I’ve come to know much more than I could have imagined that evening.”

He glanced at her.

“I know how you take your tea. I know you sometimes speak Mandarin when you’re tired. I know you like to have a piano nearby, and that you can spend an unreasonable amount of time deciding whether a mango is ripe enough.”

She laughed.

“I can.”

“I know you can be very quiet when you’re thinking, and very difficult to persuade when you’ve already made up your mind.”

She smiled.

“And I know that you are thoughtful in ways you don’t always realise. You remember small things. You make room for people. You give affection very naturally, even when you pretend you’re being practical.”

Her eyes softened.

“Declan…”

He squeezed her hand gently.

“I love the life you have. Your music, your work, your family, your friends, the places you want to go, and the things you haven’t decided yet.”

He paused.

“I don’t want to ask you to make your life smaller so that it can fit around mine. I don’t want you to have to choose a city today, or a career path, or a version of yourself you think I would find easier to love.”

She was looking at him steadily now.

“I want to build a life with you. One where we both have room to become whatever we still want to become.”

He drew a breath.

“And I would like to spend the rest of my life choosing you.”

For the first time that evening, CC seemed to understand why he had been so quiet. Her fingers tightened around his. Declan rose from his chair. He didn’t rush.

He reached into the inside pocket of his jacket and took out a small dark-blue box. CC looked at it. Then at him. Her lips parted slightly.

He came around the table and stopped in front of her.

“Cela Chanya.”

She looked up at him, eyes already shining.

“Will you marry me?”

He opened the box.

Inside was a ring: an elegant oval diamond set in a delicate platinum band, with two smaller diamonds resting discreetly at either side. Beautiful, but not ostentatious. A ring that seemed to belong to her rather than announce itself to everyone else.

CC couldn’t speak. Declan waited. He didn’t fill the silence. He had asked her a question. She deserved the time to answer it. She looked at the ring, then at him.

“You’re asking me?”

A soft smile appeared on his face.

“I am.”

“To marry you?”

“Yes.”

She let out a small, unsteady laugh. He watched her carefully.

“Are you all right?”

She nodded, though her eyes were wet.

“Yes.”

She looked at him again. Then she smiled.

“Yes, Declan.”

His face changed. Not dramatically. He didn’t lose his composure or say anything extravagant.

But the relief and happiness in his face were unmistakable.

“Yes?”

She laughed through her tears.

“Yes. I’ll marry you.”

He exhaled, smiling. Then he reached for her hand.

“May I?”

She nodded. He slipped the ring onto her finger. It fitted perfectly. CC looked down at it. Then she looked at him.

“How did you know my size?”

He smiled.

“I had some assistance.”

She narrowed her eyes.

“Who?”

He laughed.

“Your mother.”

CC stared at him.

“Mum?”

“She was very helpful.”

She shook her head, laughing.

“Of course she was.”

He took her hand and kissed the ring, then her knuckles. When he looked up, she was still smiling.

“Come here,” she whispered.

He stood, and she rose to meet him. She wrapped both arms around his neck. He held her close. The room seemed to disappear.

There was no audience that mattered, no music she needed to perform to, no words she needed to find. Only him. She pressed a kiss to his cheek.

“You’re going to be my husband.”

His smile softened.

“If you’ll still have me.”

She pulled back enough to look at him.

“Declan.”

He laughed.

“I know.”

He kissed her, and it was nothing like any kiss before it: slow and certain and a little unsteady, her ring cool against his jaw where her hand had come up to hold him, the quartet still playing for no one, until she had to break away to breathe, laughing, and he kissed her again.

When they separated, he touched his forehead to hers.

“Hello, fiancée.”

She smiled, a little shyly.

“Hello.”

Later that night, they remained at the table for a while. CC kept looking at her hand.

Every few minutes, she would turn it slightly, watching the diamond catch the light. Declan noticed.

“Do you like it?”

She looked up.

“I love it.”

“I’m glad.”

She turned her hand again.

“It’s beautiful.”

He smiled.

“I hoped you would think so.”

She watched him.

“Did you choose it yourself?”

“I did.”

“Without asking anyone?”

“I had the setting made to the design I wanted. Your mother helped me with the size.”

CC laughed.

“She must have been so excited.”

“She was.”

“What about your mother?”

He smiled.

“She was also rather excited.”

CC met his eyes.

“You told Eleanor?”

“Yes.”

“When?”

“A few weeks ago.”

Her eyes widened.

“A few weeks?”

“I wanted to tell our parents before tonight.”

She stared at him.

“Our parents?”

He smiled.

“Your mother and father were very happy.”

She looked down at her ring again, then back at him.

“What did Dad say?”

Declan’s expression softened.

“He said that if I intended to marry his daughter, I should continue to remember that she was a person with her own mind, not something I had been fortunate enough to acquire.”

CC laughed, her eyes filling again.

“That sounds like him.”

“He also told me that if I ever made you unhappy, he knew where to find me.”

She covered her mouth.

“Dad.”

“I assured him he wouldn’t need to.”

She smiled.

“And Mum?”

“She cried.”

CC laughed.

“Of course.”

“Then she asked whether I was certain I wanted to surprise you.”

She looked at him.

“What did you say?”

“That I was certain about asking. But that the answer was yours.”

CC was quiet. She reached across the table and held his hand.

“Thank you.”

He looked over.

“For what?”

“For understanding that.”

He lifted her hand and kissed it.

“Always.”

Later that night, they walked through the hotel corridor slowly. CC’s hand was in his. She kept glancing down at the ring. At one point, Declan stopped.

“What is it?”

She looked up.

“Nothing.”

He smiled.

“You’re looking at it again.”

“I know.”

“Do you want to take it off?”

She immediately shook her head.

“No.”

He laughed.

“All right.”

She turned to him.

“Can I ask you something?”

“Of course.”

“Have you been planning this for a long time?”

He considered it.

“I knew I wanted to marry you before I knew exactly when I would ask.”

She smiled.

“When?”

“Somewhere between watching you make breakfast in your apartment and seeing you at the piano in Munich.”

She laughed.

“Those are very ordinary moments.”

“Exactly.”

He brushed his thumb over her hand.

“I didn’t decide because of one extraordinary evening. I decided because I kept finding myself wanting the ordinary ones with you.”

She looked at him. Then she stepped closer and rested her cheek against his chest.

“I want those too.”

He kissed her hair.

“I know.”

She lifted her head.

“Do you?”

He smiled.

“I hope so.”

She laughed. Then she reached for his hand again.

“Come on, fiancé.”

He looked down at her.

“Where are we going?”

“Back to our room.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“Our room?”

She smiled.

“Yes.”

He laughed and followed her. Just after midnight on Tuesday, CC was sitting on the end of the bed when Declan came out of the bathroom.

She had changed into a soft white robe, and her ring was resting on the bedside table. He looked at it.

“Why did you take it off?”

“I was washing my hands.”

He smiled.

“Practical.”

She picked it up and slipped it back onto her finger. Then she looked at him.

“Declan?”

“Hm?”

“Can I tell you something?”

He sat beside her.

“Always.”

She looked down at her hand.

“Last year, when you asked for my number, I didn’t think I would be here.”

“Neither did I.”

“I thought you were handsome.”

He smiled.

“That is a promising beginning.”

She laughed.

“But I didn’t know you. I didn’t know what you were like when you were tired, or when you were worried, or when you were trying to make coffee.”

He laughed.

“An unfortunate discovery.”

She smiled.

“I didn’t know you would remember things I only mentioned once. Or that you would come to my concerts. Or that you would let me be quiet without asking me to explain.”

He listened.

“I didn’t know I would want to give you a key to my apartment.”

She looked up.

“Or that I would want you to have one.”

He touched her cheek.

“I didn’t know either.”

She smiled.

“Now I know.”

He leaned forward and kissed her cheek.

“Now we know.”

She moved closer, resting her head against his shoulder. She spoke again.

“Can we still take our time?”

He looked down at her.

“Of course.”

“I don’t want everything to change tomorrow.”

“It won’t.”

“And I still want to work. I still want to travel. I still want to make music.”

“I know.”

She held his gaze.

“And you still have your company, your parents, Munich, New York…”

“And you have your life.”

She smiled.

“We’ll figure it out?”

“Together.”

He kissed her gently.

“An engagement isn’t a deadline, Cela. It’s a promise.”

She rested her hand against his chest.

“Then I like that promise.”

He smiled.

“So do I.”

Just after midnight, before turning off the lights, CC reached for her phone. Declan watched her.

“Who are you messaging?”

“Mum.”

He smiled.

“At this hour?”

“She’ll be awake.”

She typed.

CC: Mum.

CC: I said yes.

The reply came almost immediately.

Mum: I KNOW. YOUR FATHER HAS BEEN WAITING FOR YOUR MESSAGE.

CC laughed. Another message arrived.

Mum: Congratulations, sweetheart. We love you both so much.

CC showed Declan. He smiled.

“Tell her thank you.”

She typed again. Then she opened another conversation.

CC: Dad.

CC: I’m engaged.

A moment later:

Dad: I know, sweetheart.

Dad: Your mother has told me about six times.

CC laughed. Then another message appeared.

Dad: Congratulations. I’m happy for you. And tell Declan he still owes me a proper baking lesson.

She turned the phone towards Declan. He read it. Then nodded seriously.

“Tell him I accept.”

She sent the message. A few seconds later, her father replied.

Dad: Good. He needs it.

CC laughed and put her phone down. Declan slipped an arm around her waist.

“Happy?”

She turned towards him.

“Very.”

He kissed her.

“Goodnight, fiancée.”

She smiled.

“Goodnight, fiancé.”

The next morning, tea arrived at their table. The same table. The same quiet corner. The same view of the ballroom.

CC sat opposite Declan, her engagement ring resting beside her teacup as she reached for the handle. He watched her.

“Good?”

She took a sip.

“Very good.”

He smiled.

“Then I chose correctly.”

She tilted her head.

“You did.”

He reached across the table. She placed her hand in his. They said nothing.

One year ago, they had sat in this room as two people who had only just met. He had offered her a shawl. She had accepted his number. They had no idea what would follow.

Now there was a ring on her finger, two keys in two different cities, two families who had welcomed them, and a life that was still unfolding. Declan lifted her hand.

“One year ago, I asked you for your number.”

She smiled.

“And now?”

He kissed her knuckles.

“Now I’ve asked for considerably more.”

She laughed.

“Much more.”

He smiled.

“Was it too much?”

She looked at him, then at the ring.

“No.”

She leaned forward.

“It was exactly what I wanted.”

And over tea, in the same room where everything had begun, they started talking about what came next.

chapters.title: The Life Between
chapters.desc: Two cities, two keys, one ring, and an apartment across the hall that has no reason to exist except a study. The life between, not yet arranged, and theirs.
chapters.epigraph: “Okay to the study, or okay to the wall?”
chapters.content:
On Monday morning, in Bangkok, CC had three phones on the table.

One was displaying her recording schedule. Another had a message from her manager. The third was playing a demo of a song she had been working on since the previous week.

She sat cross-legged on the sofa, her hair clipped loosely away from her face, a pencil tucked behind one ear.

“Again,” she murmured.

The demo restarted. She listened carefully, tapping her finger against the notebook. Then she stopped it.

“No.”

She rewound the recording. A few seconds later, her phone rang. Declan. She answered without looking away from the notebook.

“Good morning.”

“Good morning, sweetheart.”

“You’re awake early.”

“It’s afternoon here.”

“Oh.”

He laughed.

“How is the song?”

She glanced at the screen.

“Not finished.”

“That sounds familiar.”

She smiled.

“I don’t like the bridge.”

“What’s wrong with it?”

“It sounds too much like the chorus.”

“Then perhaps it needs to become something else.”

She looked down at the notebook.

“That’s what I’m trying to do.”

He heard the faint sound of the demo playing again.

“Are you working?”

“A little.”

“Have you had breakfast?”

She paused. Declan waited.

“Cela.”

“I had coffee.”

“That wasn’t the question.”

She smiled.

“I was going to eat.”

“Good. What?”

She looked towards the kitchen.

“Toast.”

“With?”

“Something.”

He laughed.

“An excellent nutritional plan.”

She giggled.

“I’ll make eggs.”

“Better.”

There was a short silence.

Then he said, “I have a meeting in twenty minutes. I wanted to hear your voice before it.”

She softened.

“You’re going to be busy today?”

“Until this evening.”

“All right.”

“I’ll call you later.”

“Don’t worry if you can’t.”

“I’ll make time.”

She smiled.

“Okay.”

“Eat your breakfast.”

“Yes, sir.”

He laughed.

“Goodbye, sweetheart.”

“Bye, Declan.”

The call ended. CC put her phone down, looked at the unfinished lyrics, and played the demo once more. Then she stood and went to make breakfast.

On Thursday evening, in Munich, Declan was reading a report when his phone vibrated. A photograph.

CC was sitting in a recording studio, wearing a large pair of headphones. Her expression was serious, and she had one hand raised as if she were explaining something to the producer.

Cela: They finally got the bridge right.

He enlarged the photograph.

Declan: You look pleased.

Cela: I am.

Declan: May I hear it?

Cela: Tomorrow. I want to listen once more before I send it.

Declan: I’ll wait.

A few seconds later, another message appeared.

Cela: Also, I miss you.

He settled back.

Declan: I miss you too.

Cela: A lot?

He smiled.

Declan: An inconvenient amount.

She sent a laughing emoji. Then:

Cela: When are you coming to Bangkok?

He opened his calendar. There were several meetings, a regional review, and a flight to New York that he couldn’t move without consequences. He considered the dates.

Declan: Thursday evening, if that works with your schedule.

Cela: I have a recording session Friday morning.

Declan: Then I won’t expect you to change it.

Cela: We can have dinner after.

Declan: I’d like that.

She sent a small heart. He returned to his report. The work still needed to be done.

But now, in the space between two paragraphs, he caught himself looking forward to Thursday.

Late on Saturday, in Bangkok, CC was sitting at the dining table with Nicha.

Her solo career had become busier over the previous months. There were new songs, brand meetings, interviews, performances, and discussions about a possible international collaboration.

Her first solo release had opened doors she had wanted to explore for years. She was grateful. She was also tired. Nicha looked at the schedule on her tablet.

“You have two days off next month.”

CC looked up.

“Really?”

“Yes. Unless you accept the radio appearance.”

“When?”

“Saturday and Sunday.”

CC considered it.

“Can we move the radio appearance?”

Nicha looked at her.

“Why?”

“I’d like to keep the weekend.”

Nicha studied her.

“Declan?”

CC smiled.

“Maybe.”

Nicha laughed.

“You don’t have to look guilty.”

“I’m not guilty.”

“You’re smiling.”

CC lowered her eyes. Nicha closed the tablet.

“Keep the weekend, then. I’ll tell them you’re unavailable.”

CC looked up.

“Really?”

“Yes. You have been working hard. Two days won’t ruin your career.”

CC smiled.

“Thank you.”

Nicha leaned back.

“And don’t spend the entire weekend answering emails.”

“I won’t.”

“You’re already planning to.”

CC laughed. Nicha shook her head.

“Go and enjoy your life. You’re allowed to have one.”

CC looked down at the schedule. Then she picked up her phone.

CC: I have two days off next month.

Declan replied several minutes later.

Declan: Should I reserve them?

She smiled.

CC: Yes.

Declan: Consider them reserved.

CC: Surprise me.

Declan: I was hoping you’d say that.

She laughed. A second message arrived.

Declan: What would you like to do?

She thought about it.

CC: Nothing very ambitious.

Declan: My favourite kind of plan.

On Friday evening, in Munich, the apartment in Lehel was quiet when CC arrived. She had used her key.

Her suitcase was beside the entrance, and her handbag was on the console table. The flowers she had bought at the airport were already in a vase. Declan wasn’t home yet. She sent him a message.

CC: I’m here.

Declan: Welcome home, Cela.

She smiled at the words. She took off her shoes, went to the kitchen, and opened the refrigerator.

There was fruit, yoghurt, cheese, and a small container of soup.

She recognised the handwriting on the note attached to it.

For when you arrive. Heat gently.

She smiled. He had arranged food, but he hadn’t filled the apartment with flowers or presents. He had remembered that she would be tired after travelling and left something simple for her to eat. She heated the soup.

Then she carried it to the living room and sat beside the window. A little while later, the door opened. Declan came in, loosening his tie. He stopped when he saw her.

“Hello.”

She looked up.

“Hello.”

He put his briefcase down.

“How was the flight?”

“Good.”

“Did you eat?”

She pointed at the bowl.

“Your soup.”

He smiled.

“Good?”

“Very good.”

He came over and pressed a kiss into her hair.

“Welcome back.”

She stood and wrapped her arms around him. He held her close. For a few moments, neither spoke. Then she looked up.

“You’re late.”

“Twenty minutes.”

“I know.”

He smiled.

“Did you miss me?”

She nodded.

“Yes.”

He brushed his thumb over her cheek.

“I missed you too, thi rak.”

He kissed her in the middle of his own living room with his coat still half on, slowly and thoroughly. When they separated, he looked towards the kitchen.

“Have you finished eating?”

“Almost.”

“Then I’ll change, and we can have the evening to ourselves.”

She smiled.

“Can we play the piano?”

“Of course.”

“And can you make tea?”

He watched her.

“I can.”

She narrowed her eyes.

“Drinkably?”

He laughed.

“I have improved considerably.”

“Let’s see.”

On Sunday morning, they spent the morning without an agenda. CC played the piano. Declan read beside the window.

At some point, she stopped playing and looked over.

“Do you have work?”

He lowered his book.

“Not today.”

She smiled.

“Then can you come here?”

He closed the book and walked over. She moved along the bench to make room. He sat beside her.

“What’s this?”

She played a few notes.

“A new melody.”

He listened. It was unfinished, but it had a gentle quality he liked. When she stopped, she looked at him.

“Do you like it?”

“I do.”

“Does it sound sad?”

“Not exactly.”

“What does it sound like?”

He considered it.

“Like someone who has stopped waiting for the world to become quiet before allowing herself to be happy.”

She studied his face. Then she smiled.

“That’s very specific.”

“Was I wrong?”

She shook her head.

“No.”

He touched her cheek.

“Keep it.”

She looked at the keys again.

“I will.”

He kissed her temple. She leaned against him, and they remained there for a while.

The music room was quiet except for the distant sound of traffic.

The piano stood beside the window, just as it had when he first showed it to her.

She had played it often enough now that a few pages of sheet music had accumulated on the stand.

It no longer looked like an instrument he had bought for a guest. It looked like hers. And perhaps, in a small way, it was.

On Wednesday evening, in Bangkok, CC was standing in front of her wardrobe when Declan arrived.

She had a fitting the following morning and was trying to decide between two dresses.

He placed a small paper bag on the table.

“What’s that?”

“Something for you.”

She looked at him.

“Declan.”

He smiled.

“Would you like to open it?”

She came over. Inside was a soft silk scarf in a muted shade of blue. She lifted it carefully.

“It’s beautiful.”

“I saw it in Munich.”

She ran her fingers over the fabric.

“Thank you.”

He watched her.

“Do you like it?”

“I do.”

She wrapped it loosely around her neck.

“How does it look?”

He smiled.

“Very lovely.”

She looked at herself in the mirror. Then she turned towards him.

“You know, you don’t have to buy me something every time you see something you think I’ll like.”

“I know.”

She smiled.

“I’m serious.”

“So am I.”

He came closer.

“I don’t buy you things because I think you need them. I buy them because sometimes I see something and think of you.”

She looked down at the scarf. He continued, gently:

“And I enjoy giving you things. But if it ever feels like too much, you can tell me.”

She looked up.

“I know.”

He touched the edge of the scarf.

“Good.”

She smiled.

“Then I like this one.”

“Good. Because there’s one more thing, and it isn’t small.” He held up a key she didn’t recognise.

“What’s that?”

“The apartment across the hall.”

She stared at him. “Mrs. Malee’s apartment?”

“Mrs. Malee has moved to her daughter’s in Chiang Mai, with a very generous offer and my best wishes. Your apartment doesn’t have a study. I take calls at your dining table at three in the morning. This seemed kinder to both of us.” He seemed to feel this explained everything.

“You bought the apartment across the hall so you’d have a desk.”

“And a wall I can knock through, if you ever want one.”

She should have been appalled. She was, a little. But mostly she was thinking of him at her table at three in the morning, keeping his voice down so she could sleep, and the smile came the way it always did with him, slowly and then all at once. “Okay.”

“Okay to the study, or okay to the wall?”

“Ask me again in a year.”

He kissed her temple.

“I’m glad.”

She took his hand and led him towards the sofa.

“Come sit. I want to show you something.”

“What?”

“The new choreography.”

He tilted his head.

“Should I be prepared?”

“Yes.”

She played the music. He watched as she demonstrated the movements, occasionally stopping to correct a step. At the end, she looked at him expectantly.

“Well?”

He smiled.

“Very impressive.”

“You’re only saying that because you love me.”

“That is certainly a contributing factor.”

She laughed and sat beside him. He put his arm around her.

“Would you like to show me again?”

Her smile widened.

“Really?”

“Yes.”

She stood immediately. He laughed. There were many ways to spoil her, he had learned. Some came with deeds. Some meant watching the same choreography six times because she was so pleased with it. Late on Friday, the concert had ended late.

CC returned to her apartment with tired feet and a slightly hoarse voice. Declan was waiting.

He had arrived earlier that evening, but she had insisted he attend the show rather than wait backstage. He had watched from the audience.

Now, when she entered, he stood to greet her.

“Hello, sweetheart.”

She smiled tiredly.

“Hi.”

He took her bag.

“How was it?”

“Good.”

“Did you enjoy it?”

She nodded.

“Very much.”

He touched her cheek.

“Then it was a good night.”

She leaned into his hand.

“Did you like it?”

“I loved it.”

She smiled. He led her towards the kitchen, where a warm drink was waiting. She looked at the cup.

“Is that honey?”

“And ginger.”

She laughed.

“You always have ginger.”

“Experience.”

She took a sip. He watched her.

“Better?”

“A little.”

He guided her towards the sofa.

“Sit down.”

She obeyed, stretching her legs. He sat beside her and began gently rubbing her ankle. Her eyes went to his.

“Declan.”

“Hm?”

“You don’t have to.”

“I know.”

She smiled. Then she tucked herself against his shoulder.

“Thank you.”

He kissed her hair.

“You’re welcome.”

After a while, she said, “I have another performance next week.”

“I know.”

“And a recording session.”

“I know.”

“And then the interview.”

He looked down at her.

“Busy.”

“Very.”

“Do you want me to come?”

She thought about it.

“To the performance, yes. The interview, no.”

He smiled.

“Then I’ll come to the performance.”

She looked up.

“You don’t mind?”

“Not at all.”

She smiled.

“Good.”

He continued rubbing her ankle.

“Tell me when you want me there, and when you want to go alone.”

She looked at him.

“I like that.”

He smiled.

“I’ve learned.”

On Tuesday evening, in Geneva, one year had passed since the proposal. They returned to Geneva.

Not for another gala this time, but because CC had a few days between promotional commitments and Declan had arranged his schedule around them. They had dinner at the hotel. The same tea was served. The same quiet table.

CC wore a simple black dress, and Declan had chosen a dark suit with the plum tie she had given him on their first Christmas. She noticed it when he sat down.

“You’re wearing it.”

He glanced at the tie.

“Of course.”

She smiled.

“You still like it?”

“Very much.”

She reached over and straightened it. He watched her.

“Thank you.”

She smiled. Then she looked at her ring. She still wore it every day.

They were engaged, but not married. They hadn’t set a date, and neither felt the need to rush. They had discussed possibilities. A wedding in Europe, perhaps. Something small, perhaps. A celebration with both families, certainly.

But they had also discussed the practical things: her career, his work, the cities they might live in, the places they wanted to travel, and the possibility that their lives would never fit neatly into one address. They had decided to keep talking. To make plans when the plans felt right. Not because they were uncertain about one another.

Because they wanted the life they built to belong to both of them. CC lifted her teacup.

“Do you remember the first time we had tea here?”

Declan smiled.

“Very clearly.”

“You were trying to impress me.”

“I was succeeding.”

She laughed.

“Perhaps.”

He took her hand across the table.

“One year since I asked you to marry me.”

She nodded.

“One year.”

“Are you still happy with your answer?”

She lifted her eyes to his.

“Very.”

He smiled.

“Good.”

She squeezed his hand.

“Are you?”

“More than I can say.”

She smiled and looked out towards the windows. Geneva was turning gold again.

The city looked almost exactly as it had a year ago.

But they weren’t the same two people who had sat at that table then.

They had travelled, worked, argued, learned, celebrated, and made room for each other. They hadn’t solved every question. They hadn’t chosen a wedding date.

They hadn’t decided which city would eventually feel most like home.

And there were still songs CC hadn’t written, meetings Declan hadn’t attended, and mornings they would wake up in different countries.

The next morning, CC woke to find Declan already dressed.

He was standing near the window, speaking on the phone. She watched him.

He looked composed, as he always did when discussing work. His voice was calm, his words precise. Then he noticed her. His face softened.

He finished the call and put the phone down.

“Good morning.”

She smiled sleepily.

“Good morning.”

He came over and sat beside her.

“Did I wake you?”

“No.”

He brushed her hair away from her face.

“How did you sleep?”

“Well.”

“Good.”

She considered him.

“Are you working?”

“One call at ten. Then I have the afternoon free.”

She smiled.

“Can we go somewhere?”

“Anywhere.”

She thought about it.

“Maybe the lake.”

“All right.”

“And tea.”

He smiled.

“Of course.”

He kissed her good morning, unhurried, until she forgot what she had been about to ask. Then she remembered, and looked at him with a little smile.

“Do you know what I want?”

“What?”

“To have a very ordinary day.”

He touched her cheek.

“Then that’s what we’ll have.”

She slipped out of bed and walked towards the window. He watched her, smiling.

On the table beside the bed sat her phone, her notebook, and the small box that held her ring when she took it off at night. There were messages waiting from her manager. A recording session to confirm. A meeting to prepare for. There was work waiting for him, too.

But for the next few hours, they had a lake to walk beside, tea to drink, and nowhere they needed to be. CC turned back towards him.

“Coming?”

He stood.

“Always.”

She held out her hand. He took it. And they walked into the day together.
